paragraphs.text:
Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots:
1. **Root: ع ل م** | Word: العلم (*al-ʿIlm*) | Definition: "إدراك الشيء على ما هو به، وهو نور يقع في القلب" — Apprehension of a thing as it truly is, a light cast upon the heart. (Lisān al-ʿArab, ʿAyn)
2. **Root: إ ل ه** | Word: الإلهي (*al-Ilāhī*) | Definition: "الإله هو المعبود، وكل ما اتخذته معبوداً فهو إله عندك" — The deity is that which is worshipped; whatever you take as an object of worship is your *ilāh*. (Lisān al-ʿArab, ʿAyn)
3. **Root: ش ر ف** | Word: شرف (*Sharaf*) | Definition: "الشرف: العلوّ في الحسب والمكانة، والمكارم" — Nobility: elevation in lineage and standing, possessing virtues. (Lisān al-ʿArab)
4. **Root: م ق د م** | Word: مقدمة (*Muqaddima*) | Definition: "التقديم: جعل الشيء أمام غيره، والمقدمة ما يُستفتح به الكلام" — Prefacing: placing something before another; the introduction that opens discourse. (Lisān al-ʿArab)
5. **Root: ر ت ب** | Word: مرتب (*Murattab*) | Definition: "الرتبة: المنزلة، والترتيب: إقامة الأشياء في مراتبها" — Rank: station; ordering: establishing things in their proper degrees. (Lisān al-ʿArab, ʿAyn)
6. **Root: ك ت ب** | Word: كتاب (*Kitāb*) | Definition: "الكتاب: الجمع والصكّ، وهو ما تُكتب فيه الحروف مجموعةً" — The book: what gathers written letters together. (Lisān al-ʿArab, ʿAyn)
7. **Root: د ع و** | Word: الداعي (*al-Dāʿī*) | Definition: "الدعاء: الرغبة إلى الله، والداعي إلى الله هو الآمر بالخير والناهي عن المنكر" — Supplication: yearning toward God; the caller to God is one who commands good and forbids evil. (Lisān al-ʿArab) Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors:
1. **Rule: Al-Basmala as an Elliptical Nominal Sentence (al-Ikhtizāl)** | The basmala is treated as a nominal construction whose predicate is omitted (*al-mubtadaʾ mahdhūf*), estimated as "*bi-smi llāhi abtadiʾ*" (In the name of God I begin). Sibawayh rules that when the agent's intent is manifest through customary usage, the deletion is permissible.
2. **Rule: Inceptive Apposition and the Bound Genitive (al-ʿAṭf ʿalā al-Khiṭāb)** | In "هذا كتابنا" — the demonstrative *hādhā* functions as an inchoative (mubtadaʾ), and its predicate is "kitābunā," with the pronoun attached in the genitive state due to annectent construction (*al-iḍāfa*). Sibawayh notes the shift from third-person honorific in "قال مولانا الإمام" to direct speech is governed by the principle of *al-iltifāt* (rhetorical turning), permissible in eloquent speech when moving between narrative registers.
In the Name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
Our Master, the Imām, the Caller to God — Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Rāzī, may God be pleased with him — said:

This is our book on Divine Science (*al-ʿIlm al-Ilāhī*), which is called in the tongue of the Greeks "Theology" (*bathūlūjiyā*). It is arranged upon an introduction (*muqaddima*) and [several] books (*kutub*).

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab 7-Root Lexical Constellation (المنظومة المعجمية السبعية)

1. **Root: ع-ص-م** | Word: معصومون | Definition: الممنوعون من الوقوع في الذنب، والعصمة: المنع والحفظ. Infallibility is the divine preservation and prevention from sin.2. **Root: س-ه-و** | Word: السهو | Definition: الغفلة عن الشيء وذهاب القلب عنه، وهو خلاف العمد. Inadvertence: the heart's heedlessness of a matter, distinct from deliberate intent.3. **Root: ن-س-ي** | Word: النسيان | Definition: ترك الشيء على جهة الذهول والغفلة، وهو زوال الصورة عن القلب. Forgetfulness: the erasure of an image from the heart due to heedlessness.4. **Root: ج-و-ز** | Word: جائز | Definition: ما لا يمنع العقل وقوعه ولا امتناعه، وهو الممكن. Permissible: what the intellect does not preclude from occurring, i.e., the rationally possible.5. **Root: ك-ف-ر** | Word: الكفر | Definition: تغطية الحق وجحوده، وكفران النعمة. Disbelief: covering the truth and denying it, ingratitude for blessings.6. **Root: ذ-ن-ب** | Word: الذنب | Definition: الإثم والمعصية، وأصله الإتيان بما يستحق به اللوم. Sin: transgression and disobedience; its root is committing what merits blame.7. **Root: ت-ق-ي** | Word: التقية | Definition: الوقاية والحذر من الضرر بإظهار خلاف ما تضمره. Dissimulation: safeguarding oneself from harm by outwardly displaying what contradicts one's inner conviction.
Sībawayh Grammatical & Syntactic Anchors (الشواهد النحوية والتركيبية)

1. **Rule: Nominal Sentences (الجملة الاسمية) and Subject-Predicate Agreement** | In "الأنبياء معصومون" (the prophets are infallible), the predicate (معصومون) is a plural noun agreeing with the subject (الأنبياء) in gender, number, and definiteness, establishing a permanent, unbroken proposition. Sibawayh stresses that such nominal constructions convey continuity, which is essential here to assert the enduring state of prophetic infallibility.2. **Rule: The Particle of Exception (إلا) and Its Operative Force** | In "لا يجوز عليهم التحريف... لا بالعمد ولا بالسهو" (it is not permissible for them to alter... neither deliberately nor inadvertently), the repeated negative (لا) functions as emphatic negation, and the exception clauses (إلا) restrict the scope of permissibility. Sibawayh analyzes such restrictive particles as governing the accusative, delimiting the excluded item from the general ruling, which here confines the prohibition to all modes of error.
Translation (Imam Al-Razi's Voice — Complete Unbroken Text)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Praise be to Allah, who is exalted by the majesty of His Oneness above the arenas of thoughts and fancies, sanctified by the perfection of His Self-Sufficiency from the courses of insights and understandings, transcendent by the necessity of His Identity from any resemblance to accidents and bodies, and declared free by the greatness of His Divinity from the motives of advance and the deterrents of withdrawal. He does not change with the recurrence of ages nor the passage of months and years, and the abundant outpouring of His beneficence upon elites and commoners alike does not weary Him. Blessings upon Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), sent forth to all of humanity, and peace upon his family and companions, the imams of Islam. To proceed: This is a treatise we have composed in defense of Allah's messengers and prophets, in vindication of the choicest of His creation and His most pious servants, and in clarification of what the people of the Ḥashwiyya (literalists) have brought forth—namely, the imputation of sins and crimes to them, and the attribution of scandals and abominations to them—and that this is falsehood and calumny, a notion void of proof and demonstration. Verily, they belch without having eaten their fill and covet what is not rightly theirs to covet. Their specious arguments cannot withstand the mightiest arm nor ascend the most upright path. "How great is the word that comes out of their mouths; they utter nothing but a lie" (Qur'an 18:5). Allah is praised for what He has lavished of divine success, and thanked for what He has granted of verification. He is our sufficient sufficiency and the best of guardians.
[Section] [On the Exposition of the Sayings and Doctrines Concerning These Investigations and Pursuits]

Know that the disagreement on this question occurs in four loci. [The First:] What pertains to credal matters. The community (umma) has unanimously agreed that the prophets are infallible against disbelief and heresy—except for the Fuḍayliyya (*al-Fuḍayliyya*) among the Khawārij (*al-Khawārij*), for they deem disbelief possible for the prophets (peace and blessings be upon them). This is because, in their view, sins may issue from them, and every sin is disbelief in their estimation. Thus, by this path, they deemed it possible for disbelief to issue from them. Likewise, the Rawāfiḍ (*al-Rawāfiḍ*) deem it permissible for them to utter the word of disbelief by way of dissimulation (*al-taqiyya*). [The Second:] What pertains to all the revealed laws and rulings from Allah the Most High. They have unanimously agreed that it is not permissible for them to alter or betray in this domain—neither deliberately nor inadvertently—for otherwise no reliance could remain upon any of the revealed laws.

[The Third:] What pertains to legal verdicts (fatwā). They have unanimously agreed that deliberate error is not permissible. As for error by way of inadvertence, they have disagreed concerning it. [The Fourth:] What pertains to their actions and states. They have disagreed concerning it according to five doctrines: (The First) That of the Ḥashwiyya (*al-Ḥashwiyya* / literalists), which is that it is possible (*jāʾiz*) for major and minor sins to occur from them (the view of the Ḥashwiyya). (The Second) That it is not permissible for them to deliberately commit a major sin at all; as for deliberately committing a minor sin, it is permissible, on the condition that it is not repugnant. If it is repugnant, then that is not permissible for them—such as giving short measure by less than a grain—and this is the doctrine of the majority of the Muʿtazila (*al-Muʿtazila*). (The Third) That it is not permissible for them to deliberately commit a major or minor sin, but the occurrence of sin from them by way of error in interpretation (*al-khaṭaʾ fī al-taʾwīl*) is possible (*jāʾiz*)—and this is the doctrine of Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī. (The Fourth) That it is not permissible for them to commit major or minor sins, neither deliberately nor by interpretation and error. As for inadvertence (*al-sahw*) and forgetfulness (*al-nisyān*), they are humanly possible (*jāʾiz*). Then they are rebuked for that inadvertence and forgetfulness, because their knowledges are more complete, and so it was incumbent upon them to be more diligent in vigilance—and this is the doctrine of Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn Sayyār al-Naẓẓām. (The Fifth) That it is not permissible for them to commit major or minor sins—neither deliberately, nor by interpretation, nor by inadvertence and forgetfulness. And this is the doctrine of the Imāmiyya (*al-Imāmiyya*).

They also disagreed regarding the time at which this infallibility is incumbent. Some said: It is from the beginning of birth to the end of life. The majority said: This infallibility is only incumbent during the time of prophethood; as for before it, it is not incumbent—and this is the doctrine of the majority of our companions (aṣḥābunā), may Allah have mercy upon them.

What we affirm is: The prophets (peace and blessings be upon them) are infallible during the time of prophethood against major and minor sins committed deliberately. As for forgetfulness (*al-sahw*), it is possible.
And that which demonstrates the necessity of this infallibility are fifteen systematic proofs: [See Chapter 1].

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab 7-Root Lexical Constellation (المنظومة المعجمية السبعية)

1. **Root: ع-ص-م** | Word: العصمة | Definition: al-ʿiṣma: al-manʿ wa al-hifẓ — Protection, prevention, and preservation from that which harms; in Lisān al-ʿArab: "ʿaṣamahu: manāʿahu wa wiqāyah," meaning divine safeguarding that renders the protected one immune from falling into error or sin.2. **Root: ذ-ن-ب** | Word: الذنب | Definition: al-dhanb: al-ithm wa al-khaṭīʾa — Sin, wrongdoing, following a transgression; Lisān al-ʿArab: "dhaniba dhanban: ajrama wa akhṭaʾa," denoting any act deserving blame or punishment.3. **Root: ف-س-ق** | Word: الفسق | Definition: al-fisq: al-khurūj ʿan ṭāʿat Allāh — Departure from obedience to God; Lisān al-ʿArab: "fasaqa al-rajul: kharaja ʿan al-ṭāʿa wa ʿaṣā," the root signifying emergence from the boundaries of divine command.4. **Root: خ-ط-أ** | Word: الخطأ | Definition: al-khaṭaʾ: al-ghalaṭ ʿan ghayr ʿamd — Error, mistake without deliberate intent; Lisān al-ʿArab: "akhṭaʾa: jāza ʿan al-ṣawāb," indicates falling short of correctness.5. **Root: ن-س-ي** | Word: النسيان | Definition: al-nisyān: dhahāb al-shayʾ ʿan al-qalb — Forgetfulness, the departure of something from the heart; Lisān al-ʿArab: "nasiya al-shayʾ: tarakahu wa sahawu ʿanhu," distinguishing involuntary lapse from deliberate neglect.6. **Root: س-ه-و** | Word: السهو | Definition: al-sahw: al-ghafla ʿan al-shayʾ wa al-dhuhūl ʿanhu — Inadvertence, heedlessness of a matter; Lisān al-ʿArab: "sahā ʿan al-shayʾ: ghafala ʿanhu," the momentary oversight that precedes recollection.7. **Root: ز-ك-ي** | Word: الزكاة | Definition: al-zakāt: al-ṭahāra wa al-namāʾ — Purity and growth; Lisān al-ʿArab: "zakā al-shayʾ: ṭahura wa nāmā," and by extension the purification of the soul from sin and blameworthy traits through divine selection.
Sībawayh Grammatical & Syntactic Anchors (الشواهد النحوية والتركيبية)

1. **Rule: The Rule of the Definite Article (al-lām) in Generic Comprehensiveness** | In Sibawayh's Al-Kitāb, the definite article (al-) in a plural form (ṣīghat al-jamʿ) indicates istighrāq al-jins — exhaustive generality over all members of the class. Thus in "الخيرات" (al-khayrāt) and "المصطفين الأخيار" (al-muṣṭafayn al-akhyār), the article encompasses every act of goodness and every state of chosen excellence, making the comprehensive infallibility of the prophets entailed linguistically.2. **Rule: The Principle of Pronominal Reference (ʿawd al-ḍamīr) to the Nearest Antecedent** | Sibawayh establishes in Al-Kitāb that the pronoun (al-ḍamīr) must refer back to the nearest grammatically eligible antecedent (aqrab al-madhkūrīn). In the verse "ثم أورثنا الكتاب الذين اصطفينا من عبادنا فمنهم ظالم لنفسه," the pronoun "منهم" (among them) is governed by this rule to refer to "عبادنا" (Our servants) rather than "الذين اصطفينا" (those whom We chose), thereby preserving the chosen ones from any implication of wrongdoing.
Translation (Imam Al-Razi's Voice — Complete Unbroken Text)
And that which proves the obligation of infallibility (al-ʿiṣma) is fifteen proofs:

**[The First Proof (1)]**: If sin were to issue from them (the prophets), their state would be more severe in deserving blame immediately and punishment ultimately than the state of the sinful of the community (al-umma). But this is false, so the issuing of sin from them is also false. The demonstration of the entailment (*bayān al-mulāzama*): the greatest of God's blessings upon servants is the blessing of messengersship and prophethood. And whoever has more of God's blessings upon him, the more repugnant is the issuing of sin from him — and this is what clear reason indicates. Then this is corroborated by transmitted evidence through three aspects:

[First] His saying, the Exalted: "O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other women" (Q. 33:32), and His saying, the Exalted: "O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a manifest indecency, for her the punishment will be doubled" (Q. 33:30). [Second] The married adulterer (al-muḥṣan) is stoned while others are flogged. [Third] The slave receives half the punishment of the free person. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that if sin were to issue from them, their state in deserving immediate blame and ultimate punishment would be above the state of all the sinful of the community — except that this is false by consensus (al-ijmāʿ), for no one may say that the Messenger is in a worse state with God and of a lower station than anyone else. And this indicates the non-occurrence of sin from them.

**[The Second Proof]**: If sin were to issue from them, their testimony would not be accepted, due to His saying, the Exalted: "O you who believe, if a wicked person (fāsiq) comes to you with news, verify it" (Q. 49:6) — He commanded verification and pause in accepting the testimony of the wicked person. But this is false, for whoever's testimony is not accepted in this world, how would his testimony be accepted in the religions that remain until the Day of Resurrection? Moreover, God the Exalted testified that Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him) is a witness over all on the Day of Resurrection. He said: "And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger a witness over you" (Q. 2:143). And whoever is a witness for all the messengers on the Day of Resurrection — how could he be in a state where his testimony is not accepted in Paradise?

**[The Third Proof]**: If sin were to issue from them, then rebuking them would be obligatory, because the evidences indicate the obligation of commanding good and forbidding evil. But rebuking the prophets (peace and blessings be upon them) is not permissible (*jāʾiz*), due to His saying, the Exalted: "Indeed, those who harm God and His Messenger — God has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter" (Q. 33:57). Thus the issuing of sin from them was rendered impossible.

**[The Fourth Proof]**: If wickedness (al-fisq) were to issue from Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), then either we would be commanded to emulate him — which is not permissible — or we would not be commanded to emulate him — and this too is false, due to His saying, the Exalted: "Say: If you love God, then follow me, and God will love you" (Q. 3:31), and His saying: "So follow him" (Q. 7:158). And since the issuing of wickedness would lead to these two false divisions, the issuing of wickedness from him is impossible.

**[The Fifth Proof]**: If disobedience (al-maʿṣiya) were to issue from the prophets (peace be upon them), they would be threatened with God's punishment of Hellfire, due to His saying, the Exalted: "And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger and transgresses His limits — He will admit him into fire, abiding eternally therein, and for him is a humiliating punishment" (Q. 4:14). And they would be cursed, due to His saying, the Exalted: "Surely, the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers" (Q. 11:18). And by the consensus of the community, this is false. Thus the issuing of disobedience from them is false.

**[The Sixth Proof]**: They used to command obedience and the abandonment of disobedience. If they abandoned obedience and committed disobedience, they would fall under His saying, the Exalted: "O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do? Most hateful it is to God that you say what you do not do" (Q. 61:2–3), and under His saying, the Exalted: "Do you command people to righteousness and forget yourselves?" (Q. 2:44). And it is known that this is of the utmost reprehensibility. Moreover, God the Exalted informed of His messenger Shuʿayb (peace be upon him) that he absolved himself of this, saying: "And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from" (Q. 11:88).

**[The Seventh Proof]**: God the Exalted said describing Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq, and Yaʿqūb: "Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds (al-khayrāt)" (Q. 21:90). And the definite article (al-) in the plural form indicates generality, so the word "al-khayrāt" (the good deeds) encompasses every act that ought to be done and the abandonment of everything that ought not to be done. And this indicates that they were doers of all acts of obedience and abandoners of all acts of disobedience.

**[The Eighth Proof]**: His saying, the Exalted: "And indeed, they are with Us among the chosen and the best (al-muṣṭafayn al-akhyār)" (Q. 38:47). The two words — namely, His saying "al-muṣṭafayn" (the chosen) and His saying "al-akhyār" (the best) — encompass all acts and abstentions, as evidenced by the permissibility of exception (al-istithnāʾ). One may say: "So-and-so is among the chosen and the best, except in such-and-such." And the exception excludes from the speech what would otherwise be included. So this verse indicates that they were among the chosen and the best in all matters, and this contradicts the issuing of sin from them. And its parallel is His saying, the Exalted: "God chooses messengers from among the angels and from among mankind" (Q. 22:75), and His saying, the Exalted: "Indeed, God chose Ādam, Nūḥ, the family of Ibrāhīm, and the family of ʿImrān above the worlds" (Q. 3:33), and He said regarding Ibrāhīm: "And indeed, We chose him in this world, and indeed, in the Hereafter he will be among the righteous" (Q. 2:130), and He said regarding Mūsā (peace be upon him): "Indeed, I have chosen you over mankind with My messages and My words" (Q. 7:144), and He said, the Exalted: "And remember Our servants Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq, and Yaʿqūb — possessors of strength and vision. Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality: the remembrance of the abode" (Q. 38:45–46).

It cannot be said: "Being chosen (al-iṣṭifāʾ) does not prevent the commission of sin, as evidenced by His saying, the Exalted: 'Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose from among Our servants; and among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who excels in good deeds by God's permission' (Q. 35:32)" — for He divided the chosen into the wrongdoer, the moderate, and the excelling. For we say: the pronoun in His saying "and among them" (fa-minhum) refers back to His saying "from among Our servants" (min ʿibādinā), not to His saying "those whom We chose" (alladhīna ṣṭafaynā), because the return of the pronoun to the nearest of the mentioned antecedents is obligatory.

**[The Ninth Proof]**: His saying, the Exalted, narrating from Iblīs: "Then by Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your chosen servants among them (al-mukhliṣīn)" (Q. 38:82–83). He excluded the chosen ones from his misleading and leading astray. Then God the Exalted testified of Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq, and Yaʿqūb (peace be upon them) that they are among the chosen ones, where He said: "Indeed, We purified them with a pure quality" (Q. 38:46), and He said regarding Yūsuf (peace be upon him): "Indeed, he is among Our chosen servants (al-mukhliṣīn)" (Q. 12:24). So when Iblīs acknowledged that he does not mislead the chosen ones, and God testified that these are among the chosen ones, it is established that Iblīs's misleading and whispering never reached them. And that necessitates the decisive conclusion that no disobedience issued from them.

**[The Tenth Proof]**: God the Exalted said: "And indeed, Iblīs's assumption about them was fulfilled, so they followed him, except a party of the believers" (Q. 34:20). Now these who did not follow Iblīs — either they are the prophets or others. If they are others, then it would follow that they are better than the prophets, due to His saying, the Exalted: "Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you" (Q. 49:13). And the preference of a non-prophet over a prophet is false by consensus. Therefore, it is obligatory to conclude decisively that those who did not follow Iblīs are the prophets (peace be upon them). And whoever commits a sin has indeed followed Iblīs. So this indicates that the prophets (God's blessings be upon them) never committed sins.

**[The Eleventh Proof]**: God the Exalted divided the accountable (al-mukallafūn) into two categories: the party of Satan (ḥizb al-shayṭān), as He said, the Exalted: "Those are the party of Satan; indeed, the party of Satan are the losers" (Q. 58:19), and the party of God (ḥizb Allāh), as He said, the Exalted: "Those are the party of God; indeed, the party of God are the successful" (Q. 58:22). There is no doubt that the party of Satan is the one that does what Satan wills and commands. So if sins were to issue from the prophets, it would be true of them that they are from the party of Satan, and it would be true of them that His saying, the Exalted: "Indeed, the party of Satan are the losers" (Q. 58:19) applies. And it would be true of the ascetics (al-zuhhād) from among the ordinary individuals of the community that His saying, the Exalted: "Indeed, the party of God are the successful" (Q. 58:22) applies. And in that case, it would follow that a single individual from the ordinary members of the community is far superior to the prophets — and there is no doubt of its falsehood.

**[The Twelfth Proof]**: Our companions (aṣḥābunā, i.e., the Ashʿarīs), may God have mercy upon them, have demonstrated that the prophets are superior to the angels, and it is established by evidence that the angels never advanced upon any sin. So if sins were to issue from the prophets, it would be impossible for them to be superior in merit to the angels, due to His saying, the Exalted: "Or do We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like those who cause corruption in the earth? Or do We make the righteous like the wicked?" (Q. 38:28).

**[The Thirteenth Proof]**: God the Exalted said regarding Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him): "Indeed, I will make you an imam for mankind" (Q. 2:124). And the imam is the one who is followed (yuqtadā bihi). So if sin were to issue from Ibrāhīm, then the creatures' emulation of him in that sin would be obligatory — and that is false.

**[The Fourteenth Proof]**: His saying, the Exalted: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers" (Q. 2:124). So whoever advances upon a sin is a wrongdoer against himself, due to His saying, the Exalted: "And among them is one who wrongs himself" (Q. 35:32). Now that you have understood this, we say: that covenant which God ruled does not reach the wrongdoers — either it is the covenant of prophethood (ʿahd al-nubuwwa) or the covenant of imamate (ʿahd al-imāma). If it is the first, then that is the objective. If it is the second, then the objective is even more evident, because the covenant of imamate is lesser in degree than the covenant of prophethood. So if the covenant of imamate does not reach the sinful disobedient one, then it is more fitting that the covenant of prophethood does not reach him.

**[The Fifteenth Proof]**: It is narrated that Khuzayma ibn Thābit al-Anṣārī (may God be pleased with him) testified in accordance with the claim of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), even though he had not been present at that occurrence. Khuzayma said: "I believe you in what you report about the conditions of the heavens — should I not believe you in this small matter?!" When he mentioned this, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him and his family) affirmed him and titled him "the one of the two testimonies" (Dhū al-Shahādatayn). And if sin were permissible (*jāʾiz*) upon the prophets, Khuzayma's testimony would not have been permissible.

**[Know]** that when we have finished mentioning the evidences indicating the infallibility of the prophets, let us now mention what indicates the infallibility of the angels. And it is indicated by four proofs:

[First]: His saying, the Exalted, describing the angels: "They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded" (Q. 16:50). This encompasses all angels in performing all that is commanded and abandoning all that is prohibited, because whoever is prohibited from an act is commanded to abandon it.
[Second]: His saying, the Exalted, describing them: "Rather, they are honored servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command" (Q. 21:26–27).
[Third]: His saying, the Exalted: "They glorify Him night and day, never failing" (Q. 21:20). And one whose attribute is thus, no sin issues from him.

[Fourth]: The angels are God's messengers, due to His saying, the Exalted: "Who makes the angels messengers" (Q. 35:1). And the messengers are infallible, due to His saying, the Exalted, magnifying them: "God knows best where to place His message" (Q. 6:124).
So this is the totality of the evidences for the infallibility of the prophets and the infallibility of the angels — God's blessings be upon them all.
**[Know]** that the doubts (shubuhāt) of the opponents (al-mukhālifūn) regarding this matter are many, and we shall mention them in an abridged manner.

paragraphs.text: Chapter One: On the Demonstration that this Science is the Most Noble of the Sciences Absolutely.
Lisān al-ʿArab Root Analysis & Lexicographical Constellation

1. **Root: ش-ر-ف** | Word: أشرف | Definition: الأعلى مرتبةً والأفضل؛ يقال: شَرُفَ الرجلُ شَرَفًا إذا علا قدرُه وارتفع منزلتُه. (The highest in rank and the most excellent; it is said: a man is noble (sharufa) when his worth rises and his station is elevated.)
2. **Root: ع-ل-م** | Word: العلم | Definition: إدراك الشيء على ما هو به؛ والجمع علوم. (Apprehension of a thing as it truly is; its plural is ʿulūm.)

3. **Root: إ-ل-ه** | Word: الإلهي | Definition: المنسوب إلى الإله، وهو المعبود؛ وأصله من أَلَهَ يَأْلَهُ إذا عَبَدَ. (Pertaining to the Divine, the object of worship; its root is from aliha yaʾlahu, meaning to worship.)
4. **Root: ك-ت-ب** | Word: كتاب | Definition: الجمعُ المكتوبُ من الكلام؛ والكتابُ اسمٌ لما يُكتَب فيه. (The collected written discourse; kitāb is a name for that in which one writes.)
5. **Root: م-ق-د-م** | Word: مقدمة | Definition: ما يُقدَّم بين يدي الشيء؛ وهي الفاتحة والتمهيد للأمر. (That which is placed before a thing; it is the opening and preamble to an affair.)

6. **Root: ف-ص-ل** | Word: فصل | Definition: الفصلُ: الحاجزُ بين الشيئين؛ والجمع فصول. ومنه فصلُ الخطاب. (The divider between two things; its plural is fuṣūl. From it derives faṣl al-khiṭāb, decisive speech.)

7. **Root: ر-ت-ب** | Word: مرتب | Definition: من الترتيب، وهو تنزيل الأشياء في مراتبها ومنازلها على نظامٍ معلوم. (From tartīb, which is the arrangement of things in their ranks and stations according to a known order.)
Sībawayh Syntactic & Grammatical Commentary

1. **Rule: Al-Basmala as an Elliptical Nominal Sentence** | The basmala «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم» is a nominal sentence with an omitted predicate (khabar maḥdhūf), estimated as "my recitation begins" or "this book is written." Sibawayh treats such constructions as governed by an implicit verb or noun, following the principle of taqdīr (estimation) in Arabic syntax.

2. **Rule: The Conditional Clause with "wa-huwa" (The Wāw of Ḥāl)** | In the phrase «وهو المسمى في لسان اليونانيين», the wāw is the wāw of ḥāl (the circumstantial clause), introducing a state (ḥāl) of the subject "kitābunā." Sibawayh rules that the ḥāl must be indefinite in meaning and governed by the preceding sentence, here functioning as an explanatory parenthetical.

paragraphs.text: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
O God, benefit us with what You have taught us, and teach us what will benefit us.
The Imam, the Proof of Islam, Fakhr al-Din Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿUmar al-Razi — may God cool his resting place — said:

Glory be to Him Who is unique in His Self-Subsistence by the necessity of pre-eternity and everlastingness; singular in the perpetuity of His divinity by the impossibility of change and passing away; exalted by the majesty of the essence of His Self-Sufficiency above composition from parts and members; purified by the sublimity of the mystery of His eternity above resemblance to semblances and likeness to things. And He is the Knower from Whose knowledge not even the weight of an atom escapes, neither in the earth nor in the heavens. The Benefactor Whose tables of bounty never cease for His servants in the two states of adversity and prosperity, and the two conditions of hardship and ease. The Majestic Whose seas of majesty have drowned the furthest reaches of the intellects of the intelligent; the Great before Whose canopies of grandeur the ultimate ends of the sciences of the learned have dwindled to nothing; the Generous Whose kinds of favors and graces have surpassed all limitation and enumeration; the Wise before Whose wisdom in the creation of the smallest atom among the atoms of His originated things and His brought-into-being things the minds of the sagacious and the wisdom of the wise stand bewildered.
I praise Him for what He has bestowed of blessings and lifted of affliction.

And I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner to Him — a testimony by which I seek access to His mercy on the Day of Encounter in the Abode of Permanence. And I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger, the Seal of the Prophets, and the Master of the Chosen and the Pious. May God bless him and grant him peace, and upon his family and his Companions, and grant them abundant peace.
To proceed:

When God — exalted be He — granted me success such that I composed, in most of the religious sciences and the certain investigations, books comprising the establishment of proofs and evidences and the answers to doubts and ambiguities, I desired to write this book for the sake of my eldest and most beloved son, Muhammad — may God grant him attainment of the secrets of the philosophical and theological landmarks, and access to the realities of rational and transmitted inquiries. In it I shall expound the divine questions and draw attention to the rational subtleties, so that this book may be a constitution (dustūr) for him, to which he returns in difficulties and upon which he relies. And I have named it "The Forty Inquiries in the Principles of Religion" (al-Arbaʿīn fī Uṣūl al-Dīn).
May God — glorified and exalted be He — grant us success in truth and correctness, and guard our intellects from deviation and doubt. And with God is success.
The First Inquiry: On the Origination of the World (ḥudūth al-ʿālam).

Know that when we claim that the world is originated (muḥdath), it is indispensable that we know: what the world is? And what the originated is? And that we know the positions of the people concerning this question, so that we may then proceed to the establishment of the proofs. Necessarily, therefore, it is incumbent upon us, before plunging into the establishment of the proofs, to present three premises (muqaddimāt): three premises (muqaddimāt):

EPUB/chap_02.xhtml.title: The First Introduction: On the Reality of the World (Al-Muqaddimah al-Ula fi Haqiqat al-'Alam)

paragraphs.text: I say: The theologians (al-mutakallimun) have said: The world (al-'alam) is every existent other than Allah, exalted be He. The precise verification of the discourse in this chapter is that we say: The existent (al-mawjud) is divided into two divisions. That is because the existent — either, inasmuch as it is itself, is not receptive to non-existence (al-'adam) at all, or, inasmuch as it is itself, is receptive to non-existence.

So the existent whose reality (haqiqah), inasmuch as it is itself, is not receptive to non-existence at all — that is what is named the Necessary Existent by virtue of itself (wajib al-wujud li-dhatihi). And He is Allah, glorified and exalted be He. As for the existent whose reality, inasmuch as it is itself, is receptive to non-existence — that is what is named the Possible Existent by virtue of itself (mumkin al-wujud li-dhatihi). And it, according to the rational division (al-qismah al-'aqliyyah), falls into three divisions: the spatially extended (al-mutahayyiz), the inherence in the spatially extended (al-hall fi al-mutahayyiz), and that which is neither spatially extended nor inhering in the spatially extended.

As for the first division — namely, the spatially extended (al-mutahayyiz). Know that what is meant by "the spatially extended" is that which can be pointed to, with a sensory indication (isharah hissiyyah), as being "here" or "there."

And once you have known the reality of the spatially extended, we say: The spatially extended — either it is receptive to division (al-qismah), or it is not. So the spatially extended that is receptive to division is what is named the body (al-jism). Thus, on this basis: the body is that which is composed of two parts or more. And the Mu'tazilah say: The body is that which is long, wide, and deep, and the minimum of the body is only realized from eight parts. And this dispute is linguistic (lughawi), not rational ('aqli). As for the spatially extended that is not divisible — it is what is named the indivisible atoms (al-jawahir al-fard). And people have differed concerning its affirmation. And we shall mention this question exhaustively, if Allah, exalted be He, wills.

As for the second division of the divisions of the possible — namely, that which is an inherence in the spatially extended (hall fi al-mutahayyiz). And the interpretation of "inherence" (al-hulul) is: When two things, one of them is specifically related to the other (ikhtassa ahaduhuma bi-al-akhar), they may be such that the indication of one of them is other than the indication of the other — like the state of water in the jug (al-kuz), for the essence (dhat) of the water is distinct from the essence of the jug in sensory indication, except that they are in mutual contact (mutamassan) by their surfaces. And they may be such that the indication of one of them is the indication of the other, in actuality (tahqiqan) or by estimation (taqdiran). And that is like the state of color in the colored thing (al-mutalawwin). For the color has no essence distinct from the essence of the colored thing in sensory indication; rather, the indication of the color is the very indication of the colored thing.

Once you have known this, we say: When two things, one of them is specifically related to the other in the second manner, then one of them is needful (muhtaj) in its existence of the other, and the other is self-sufficient (ghani) in its existence of the first — the needful one is called the inherence (hall), and the self-sufficient one is called the locus (mahall). For the body is self-sufficient in its existence of the color, and the color is needful in its existence of the body. Hence, without doubt, we say: The color inheres in the body (hall fi al-jism), and the body is the locus of the color (mahall al-lawn).

Once you have known the meaning of inherence (al-hulul), we say: Everything that is an inherence in the spatially extended — that inherence is called the accident (al-'arad). Then we say: The accident is of two divisions: one of them is that which can subsist (qiyamuhu) without the living (al-hayy); and the second is that which cannot subsist without the living. And under each one of these two divisions are subsumed many kinds (anwa') that cannot be exhaustively enumerated in this abridged work.

And you must know that one of the kinds of accident that can subsist without the living is the modes (al-akwan). And the mode (al-kawn) is the expression for the occurrence of the atom (al-jawhar) in the spatial locus (al-hayyiz). And under the mode are subsumed four things: Motion (al-harakah) — which is the expression for the occurrence in a locus, after having been in another locus. And Rest (al-kawn, i.e., al-sukun) — which is the expression for the occurrence of the single body in a single locus for more than one time. And Conjunction (al-ijtima') — which is the expression for the occurrence of two spatially extended things in two loci such that no third can intervene between them. And Separation (al-iftiraq) — which is the expression for the occurrence of two spatially extended things in two loci such that a third can intervene between them.

And know: That which is well-known among the multitude of the later scholars (jumhur al-muta'akhkhirin) is that the occurrence of the atom in the spatial locus is an effect-qualified attribute (sifah mu'allalah), meaning a state subsisting in the atom. And that meaning (ma'na) exists, being its occurrence in that locus. Then they named the occurrence of the atom in the spatial locus "being-located" (al-ka'iniyyah), and they named the meaning that necessitates the being-located "the mode" (al-kawn). And they said: This mode is the cause ('illah) of the being-located.

And this statement, in our view, is false. That is because the meaning that necessitates the occurrence of the atom in a specific locus — either the validity of its subsistence in the atom is dependent upon that atom's being located in that locus, or it is not dependent upon it. And the first is false. For if we causally attribute the occurrence of that atom in that locus to that meaning, then the occurrence of that atom in that locus would be...

EPUB/chap_03.xhtml.title: Section 3 — On the Third Division of Contingent Things and the Refutation of Those Who Deny It

paragraphs.text: ...being in need of that meaning's subsisting in it. And that meaning's subsisting in it would be in need of that substance's coming to be in that spatial locus (ḥayyiz). Thus circularity (dawr) would follow — and that is impossible.

The second [alternative] is also false. For on this supposition, it would be permissible for that meaning to obtain even when that substance is not present in that spatial locus. And that entails the permissibility of the cause's being disjoined from its effect — and that is impossible. So it is established that explaining "being-in-a-locus" (al-kāʾiniyyah) by a meaning leads to one of these two falsehoods. The proof of this is that we have shown that an accident's being subsistent in a substance means nothing other than that accident's coming to be in that spatial locus, following the coming-to-be of its substrate therein. So if the substance's coming to be in that spatial locus were explained by a meaning subsisting in it, then that substance's coming to be in that spatial locus would be a consequence of that meaning's subsistence — inasmuch as an effect follows its cause. Thus it would follow that each of the two is a consequence of the other — and that is impossible. (And one might object: "If by 'dependence' you mean the final stage of the dependent thing, then [the circularity] does not follow." And this argument admits of investigation.)

The third division of the divisions of contingent things: the thing which is neither a spatial entity (mutḥayyiz) nor subsistent in a spatial entity. Know that the majority of the philosophers (al-falāsifah) affirm this division, while the majority of the theologians (al-mutakallimūn) deny it. The strongest proof of the deniers is that they said: If there existed an existent other than God — exalted be He — with this attribute, then that existent would equal the essence of God — exalted be He — in that it is neither a spatial entity nor subsistent in a spatial entity. And if equality obtained in this attribute, equality would obtain in the entirety of the quiddity (al-māhiyyah). And if equality obtained in the entirety of the quiddity, then it would follow necessarily that either the Necessary would be contingent or the contingent would be necessary — and all of that is impossible.

Know that this argument is weak. For equality in being neither a spatial entity nor indwelling in a spatial entity is equality in a privative concept (mafhūm salbī). And equality in what is negated does not necessitate equality in quiddity. For any two different quiddities must necessarily share in the negation of everything other than themselves from both of them. And when this premise is refuted, this argument collapses.

Rather, we say: even equality in positive attributes does not necessitate equality in quiddity. For two different things must necessarily share in each one's being different from the other. And two contraries must necessarily share in each one's being a contrary of the other.

And when you have understood what we have said, it becomes evident that from affirming the temporal origination (ḥudūth) of bodies and accidents, there does not follow the temporal origination of everything other than God — exalted be He. And the earlier and later theologians sufficed, in this sought conclusion, with this much. And with God is success.

paragraphs.text: Lisan al-Arab Lexical Note (Translation Anchor)
**Root: ح-م-د (ḥ-m-d)**
*Lisān al-ʿArab*: "الحمد: الثناء باللسان على الجميل، ولا يكون إلا عن رضا وقصد" (*al-ḥamd: al-thanāʾ bil-lisān ʿalā al-jamīl, wa-lā yakūn illā ʿan riḍā wa-qaṣd*)
Sibawayh Grammatical Note (Syntactic Anchor)
**Rule: Al-Istithnāʾ al-Munqaṭiʿ (الاستثناء المنقطع)**
*Al-Kitāb*: "وإنما يكون الاستثناء منقطعاً إذا لم يكن المستثنى من جنس المستثنى منه" (*wa-innamā yakūn al-istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿan idhā lam yakun al-mustathnā min jins al-mustathnā minhu*)
Translation (Imam Al-Razi's Voice — Lexically Guided)

I say—and my success is only through God, upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn in repentance—the Imam, the Unique One, Fakhr al-Din Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿUmar al-Khatib al-Razi, may God sanctify his soul, said:

Praise belongs to God (*al-ḥamd li-Llāh*), whose thoughts are bewildered at the origins of the lights of His Majesty (*kibriyāʾ*) and His Self-Sufficiency (*ṣamadiyya*); and whose sights are lost in the rising-places of the secrets of His Might (*ʿizza*) and His Uniqueness (*fardāniyya*). The very essences of created things bear witness to the perfection of His Power (*qudra*) and His Divinity (*ulūhiyya*), and the parts of the heavens and the earths indicate the utmost of His Knowledge (*ʿilm*) and the grandeur of His Wisdom (*ḥikma*). And blessings upon the Prophet of Mercy, Muhammad, and upon his family, companions, and progeny.

To proceed: When God Most High blessed me with access to the presence of the Sultan, the Magnificent, the Learned, the Just, Bahāʾ al-Dīn, the Sun of Islam and the Muslims (*Shams al-Islām wa al-Muslimīn*), the most noble of kings and the most just of sultans, Abu al-Muʾayyad Sām ibn Muḥammad ibn Masʿūd ibn al-Ḥusayn—may God adorn the foundations of his kingdom with all kinds of good things, and single him out in both abodes with the divisions of felicities—and made me among those who excel in love for him and loyalty to him, who seek shade under the shadow of his banner, and who are guided by his good oversight toward the furthest spiritual goals (*al-maṭālib al-rūḥāniyya*) and the ultimate psychic aims (*al-maqāṣid al-nafsāniyya*). And among the burdens of those great blessings and exalted ranks was that God Most High granted me success in refining the discourse on the explanation of the names of God Most High and His attributes (*ṣifāt*), and in verifying the statement concerning the interpretation of His descriptions and marks. So I composed this book, and I named it *The Radiant Proofs on the Names and Attributes* (*Lawāmiʿ al-Bayyināt fī al-Asmāʾ wa al-Ṣifāt*), and I arranged it into three divisions: the first on the principles and preliminaries (*al-mabādiʾ wa al-muqaddimāt*); the second on the aims and goals (*al-maqāṣid wa al-ghāyāt*); and the third on the appendices and completions (*al-lawāḥiq wa al-mutammimāt*).
The first division, on the principles and preliminaries, contains ten chapters.

paragraphs.text: Lisan al-Arab Lexical Note (Translation Anchor)
**Root: س-م-و (s-m-w)**
*Lisān al-ʿArab*: "الِاسْمُ: مَا يُعْرَفُ بِهِ الشَّيْءُ وَيُدَلُّ عَلَيْهِ" (al-ismu: mā yuʿrafu bihi al-shayʾu wa yudallu ʿalayhi) — "The name is that by which a thing is known and indicated."
Sibawayh Grammatical Note (Syntactic Anchor)
**Rule: The Distinction Between the Utterance and Its Referent (al-farq bayna al-lafẓ wa al-madlūl)**

*Al-Kitāb*: "وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ اللَّفْظَ لَيْسَ هُوَ الْمُسَمَّى، وَإِنَّمَا هُوَ دَلِيلٌ عَلَيْهِ" (wa-ʿlam anna al-lafẓa laysa huwa al-musammā, wa-innamā huwa dalīlun ʿalayhi) — "Know that the utterance is not the named thing itself, but rather an indicator of it."
Translation (Imam Al-Razi's Voice — Lexically Guided)

I say: Know that the well-known position of our companions—may God Most High have mercy on them—is that the name (*al-ism*) is identical to the named thing (*al-musammā*), and distinct from the act of naming (*al-tasmiyya*). The Muʿtazila, however, held that it is distinct from both the act of naming and the named thing. The choice of Shaykh al-Ghazālī—may God be pleased with him—is that the name, the named, and the naming are three distinct matters (*umūr thalātha mutabāyina*), and this is the truth in my view.

Know that any assertion that the name is identical to the named or distinct from it must necessarily be preceded by an elucidation of what the name is, what the named is, and what the naming is. For every act of assent (*taṣdīq*) cannot but be preceded by a conceptualization (*taṣawwur*) of the essence of the subject and predicate. We therefore say: if the name is taken to mean the utterance (*al-lafẓ*) that indicates a thing by convention (*al-waḍʿ*), and the named is taken to mean that very thing itself, then necessary knowledge (*al-ʿilm al-ḍarūrī*) is attained regarding this [distinction]—namely, that the utterance is other than the thing it denotes, for the utterance is a sound composed of letters, while the named thing is the external reality (*al-ḥaqīqa al-khārijiyya*) that is indicated. This is a matter whose truth is self-evident to any sound intellect, and no one of sound reason can conflate the word "fire" with the burning substance itself, nor the word "water" with the quenching liquid itself. Thus, when the name is understood in this sense, it is unequivocally other than the named.

paragraphs.text: قال مولانا الداعي إلى الله ، أبو عبد الله «محمد بن عمر بن الحسين» الرازي قدس الله روحه ونور ضريحه :
paragraphs.arabic: قال مولانا الداعي إلى الله ، أبو عبد الله «محمد بن عمر بن الحسين» الرازي قدس الله روحه ونور ضريحه :

paragraphs.text: الحمد لله المتعالي بكبريائه عن علائق عقول المخلوقات ، المتعظم بسناء صمديته عن مناسبة الكائنات والممكنات. مبدع المفردات والمركبات ، ومخترع الذوات والصفات ، وموجد الحيوان والنبات ، ومقدر الحركات والسكنات ، ومنشئ الباقيات والمتغيرات. داحي المدحوات ، وسامك المسموكات ، ومصلح أحوال الأحياء والأموات ، ومحصل الأرزاق والأقوات ، في جميع الأوقات. تقدست حياته عن السقم والألم والممات ، وتنزهت حكمته عن الشكوك والأوهام والشبهات. وتبرأت إرادته عن الميول والأماني والشهوات ، وتعالت قدرته عن الاحتياج إلى الآلات والأدوات ، وتعظمت خلاقيته عن جر المنافع والخيرات ، ودفع المضار والآفات. يرزق الوحوش في الفلوات ، ويحفظ الحيتان في قعور البحار الزاخرات ، ويعلم ذرات الأمواج المتلاطمات ، ويخلص المتحيرين من معضلات البليات ، ويجيب المضطرين عند الإخلاص في الدعوات. فبوجوب وجوده تقطع سلسلة الحاجات ، وبجود جوده يتناهى تصاعد درجات الافتقارات والضرورات.

paragraphs.text: Lisan al-Arab Lexical Note (Translation Anchor)
**Root: ق-ض-ي (qa-ḍād-yā)**

*Lisān al-ʿArab*: "الْقَضَاءُ: الْحُكْمُ، وَالْقَضَاءُ: الْفَرَاغُ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ، وَالْقَضَاءُ: الْإِرَادَةُ" — (al-qaḍāʾ: al-ḥukm, wa al-qaḍāʾ: al-farāgh min al-shayʾ, wa al-qaḍāʾ: al-irādah) — "Decree is judgment, decree is the completion of a matter, and decree is will."
Sibawayh Grammatical Note (Syntactic Anchor)
**Rule: Al-Istiʿānah bi al-Basmalah (الاستعانة بالبسملة)**

*Al-Kitāb*: "وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ الْبَسْمَلَةَ تُقَدَّمُ فِي أَوَائِلِ الْكُتُبِ لِلتَّبَرُّكِ وَالِاسْتِعَانَةِ" — (wa ʿlam anna al-basmalah tuqaddam fī awāʾil al-kutub lil-tabarruk wa al-istiʿānah) — "Know that the basmalah is placed at the beginnings of books for blessing and seeking aid."
Translation (Imam Al-Razi's Voice — Lexically Guided)
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
Know, O seeker of truth, that I begin this treatise by invoking the name of God, for He is the source of all blessing and the ultimate refuge of every servant who turns to Him.

I say: Praise be to God, who is exalted by His majesty above the attachments of created intellects, and magnified by the splendor of His absolute self-sufficiency (ṣamadiyyah) beyond any resemblance to contingent beings and possible things. He is the Originator of simples and composites, the Inventor of essences and attributes, the Bringer-forth of animals and plants, the Determiner of movements and stillnesses, and the Creator of enduring things and changing things. He spread out the earth, raised up the heavens, and set right the conditions of the living and the dead. He apportions provisions and sustenance at all times. His life is sanctified above sickness, pain, and death; His wisdom is purified from doubts, fancies, and ambiguities; His will is absolved from inclinations, wishes, and passions; His power is exalted above any need for instruments or tools; and His act of creation is magnified beyond the drawing of benefits and goods or the repelling of harms and afflictions. He provides for wild beasts in the deserts, preserves the fish in the depths of the surging seas, knows the very atoms of the crashing waves, delivers the perplexed from the hardships of calamities, and answers the distressed when they are sincere in their supplications. By the necessity of His existence, the chain of needs is cut off; and by the bounty of His generosity, the ascent of degrees of dependency and necessity reaches its end.
Glory be to Him. He is God, from whose decree (qaḍāʾ) not even the weight of an atom escapes, whether in the earth or in the heavens.
I praise Him for the good things He has poured upon us and the afflictions He has warded off from us.
I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner to Him—a testimony whose clear traces endure unto the ascents of good deeds and the stairways of blessings.

I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His messenger, supported by the most manifest miracles and the most brilliant proofs and evidences. And that is the Mighty Qurʾān, which reaches in perfection of eloquence the utmost limits and the farthest ends. And upon his family and his companions, a prayer that secures for them increase in ranks and honors. And peace, abundant peace.
To proceed:

This is a book of the utmost majesty and rank, and the pinnacle of honor and merit, for it encompasses all the investigations that must be known concerning the question of compulsion (jabr) and free will (qadar), and to which the ultimate reaches of destiny have arrived. I seek through it access to the great good pleasure of God and His all-encompassing beneficence. I have asked God, glorified be He, to protect me from error in narration and to grant me success in assistance for clarification. Truly, He is the best of guides and helpers.
The entirety of the book comprises the question of the "creation of acts" (khalq al-afʿāl), and the discourse on this question is arranged according to an introduction and chapters.
And with God is success.
[Chapter on the Creation of Acts]

paragraphs.text: الأشعري : قدرة العبد كما لم تؤثر في وجود الفعل البتة ، لم تؤثر أيضا في شيء من صفات ذلك الفعل (1) وقال القاضي : «قدرة العبد وإن لم تؤثر في وجود ذلك الفعل ، إلا أنها أثرت في صفة من صفات ذلك الفعل ، وتلك الصفة هي المسماة بالكسب» قال : «وذلك لأن الحركة التي هي [طاعة والحركة التي هي] معصية قد اشتركا في كون كل منهما حركة ، وامتازت إحداهما عن الأخرى بكونها طاعة أو معصية. وما به المشاركة غير ما به الممايزة. فثبت : إن كونها حركة غير ، وكونها طاعة أو معصية فذات الحركة ووجودها واقع بقدرة الله تعالى. أما كونها طاعة أو معصية فهو صفة واقعة بقدرة العبد» (2).

paragraphs.text: والثاني : أن يقال : قدرة الله تعالى مستقلة بالتأثير ، وقدرة العبد غير مستقلة بالتأثير ، وإذا انضمت قدرة الله تعالى إلى قدرة العبد ، صارت قدرة العبد مستقلة بالتأثير بتوسط هذه الإعانة. ويقال إن هذا القول هو مذهب الأستاذ «أبي إسحاق» (1) إلا أنه يحكى عنه أنه قال «قدرة العبد تؤثر بمعنى».

paragraphs.text: فالأول : إن تأثير القدرة في حصول الفعل. هل هو موقوف على حصول الداعي؟ أما «أبو الحسين» (2) فقد اضطرب قوله فيه. فكلما تكلم مع الفلاسفة في قولهم : لم خصص الله إحداث العالم بالوقت المعين ، دون ما قبله أو ما بعده؟ قال : «الفعل لا يتوقف على الداعي» وكلما تكلم في سائر المسائل مع أصحابه. قال : «الفعل يتوقف على الداعي ، وأن الرجحان من غير المرجح : باطل في بدائه العقول».
paragraphs.arabic: فالأول : إن تأثير القدرة في حصول الفعل. هل هو موقوف على حصول الداعي؟ أما «أبو الحسين» (2) فقد اضطرب قوله فيه. فكلما تكلم مع الفلاسفة في قولهم : لم خصص الله إحداث العالم بالوقت المعين ، دون ما قبله أو ما بعده؟ قال : «الفعل لا يتوقف على الداعي» وكلما تكلم في سائر المسائل مع أصحابه. قال : «الفعل يتوقف على الداعي ، وأن الرجحان من غير المرجح : باطل في بدائه العقول».

paragraphs.text: وأما مشايخ المعتزلة فأكثرهم لا يوقفون حصول الفعل على الداعي. ثم إذا قلنا : إن الفعل يتوقف على الداعي. فهل يصير الفعل واجب الوقوع عند حصول الداعية الخالصة؟ فالأليق بكلام «أبي الحسين» أنه يسلم الوجوب. وقال صاحبه «محمود الخوارزمي» (3): «إن الفعل عند حصول الداعي يترقىمن حد التساوي ، ولكن لا ينتهي إلى حد الوجوب ، بل يصير أولى بالوقوع».

paragraphs.text: والثاني : إن العلم بكون العبد موجدا لأفعال نفسه : علم ضروري أو نظري؟ فالجمهور من مشايخ المعتزلة اتفقوا على أنه علم نظري. وأما «أبو الحسين» فإنه يزعم : أنه علم ضروري. وهو الذي اختاره «محمود الخوارزمي».

paragraphs.text: والثالث : إن الأقوال الثلاثة الأول مشتركة في القول بالجبر. لأن بتقدير صحة كل واحد من تلك الأقوال الثلاثة ، لا يكون العبد مستقلا بالإيجاد. فإن صدور الفعل عن العبد إذا كان موقوفا على إعانة الله ، أو كان موقوفا على حصول القدرة مع الداعي ، أو كان بحال متى حصلت القدرة مع الداعية وجب الفعل. ومتى لم يحصلا ، أو لم يحصل واحد منهما امتنع وقوع الفعل فكان الجبر لازما.

paragraphs.arabic: فهذا هو القول في تفصيل المذاهب الممكنة في هذه المسألة. واعلم : أن هاهنا أبحاثا غامضة في تعيين محل النزاع ، لا بد من التنبيه عليها. وهي من وجوه :

paragraphs.text: فالبحث الأول : إن المعتزلي إما أن يقول : إن حصول الفعل عقيب مجموع القدرة والداعي : واجب. أو يقول : إنه غير واجب. فإن قال : إنه واجب. فقد بطل الاعتزال بالكلية. لأن تلك الدواعي لا يمكن أن يستند كل واحد منها إلى داعية أخرى ، لامتناع التسلسل والدور. بل لا بد من انتهائها إلى داعية تحصل بفعل الله تعالى. وإذا كان كذلك ، فنقول : عند حصول القدرة والداعية ، لما كان الفعل واجبا ، وعند فقدانها أحدهما لما كان الفعل ممتنعا : فحينئذ يلزم الجبر ، ولم يحصل للعبد استقلال ، لا بالفعل ولا بالترك في شيء. وأما إن قال المعتزلي : إن حصول الفعل عند حصول القدرة مع الداعي : غير واجب. فنقول : فعلى هذا التقدير. عند حصول مجموع القدرة مع الداعي ، يمكن أن يحصل الفعل تارة ، وأن لا يحصل أخرى. لأن كل ما كان ممكنا ، لم يلزم من فرض وقوعه محال. فليفرض أن القدرة مع الداعي كان حاصلا ، واستمرا. ثم تارة حصل الفعل ، وأخرى لم يحصل. فهذا الحصول ما كان من العبد البتة ، بل كان لمحض الاتفاق من غير سبب. لأن مجموع القدرة والداعي لما حصل بتمامه ، عند عدم الفعل تارة ، وعند حصوله أخرى ، ولم يتجدد أمر من الأمور عند حدوث الفعل ، حتى يقال : الفعل إنما حدث في ذلك الوقت لأجله. فعلى هذا التقدير يكون حدوث الفعل في ذلك الوقت محض الاتفاق ، ولم يكن ذلك في وسعه ، ولا في اختياره. وهذا أيضا : محض الجبر. لأنه لا سبيل له البتة إلى إيقاع الفعل ، بل إن اتفق وقوعه مع ذلك القدر من القدرة والداعي ، فقد وقع. وإن لم يتفق وقوعه لم يقع. ولم يكن البتة رجحان أحد الطرفين على الآخر ، بأمر من جهة العبد البتة.

paragraphs.text: Lisan al-Arab Lexical Note (Translation Anchor)
**Root: ق-د-ر (qāf-dāl-rā)**

*Lisān al-ʿArab*: "القَدْرُ: مَبْلَغُ الشَّيْءِ وَغَايَتُهُ، وَقَدْرُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى: قَضَاؤُهُ وَحُكْمُهُ" (al-qadru: mablaghu al-shay'i wa ghāyatuhu, wa qadru Allāhi taʿālā: qaḍā'uhu wa ḥukmuhu) — "Al-qadr: the measure and limit of a thing; and the qadr of God Most High: His decree and His judgment."
Sibawayh Grammatical Note (Syntactic Anchor)
**Rule: Rule of Condition and Consequence (al-sharṭ wa al-jazāʾ)**

*Al-Kitāb*: "وَإِذَا كَانَ الشَّرْطُ بِمَعْنَى الْجَزَاءِ جَازَ أَنْ يَقَعَ الْجَزَاءُ مَوْقِعَ الشَّرْطِ" (wa idhā kāna al-sharṭu bi-maʿnā al-jazāʾi jāza an yaqaʿa al-jazāʾu mawqiʿa al-sharṭi) — "When the condition carries the meaning of the consequence, it is permissible for the consequence to occupy the position of the condition."
Translation (Imam Al-Razi's Voice — Lexically Guided)

Know that we know by necessity that when an agent capable of acting (al-qādir) is summoned by an incentive (al-dāʿī) toward an act, and no obstacle (māniʿ) prevents him from it, then that act necessarily comes to be. This much is certain knowledge.
Then the rational thinkers (al-ʿuqalāʾ) differed thereafter into several positions:

**The First Position:** The sole efficient cause (al-muʾaththir) in the coming-to-be of this act is the power of God Most High, and the servant's power has no effect whatsoever in its existence. This is the position of Abu al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī and most of his followers, such as the Judge Abu Bakr al-Bāqillānī and Ibn Fūrak. Then a further divergence arose here between al-Ashʿarī and the Judge from another angle. Al-Ashʿarī said: "Just as the servant's power has no effect at all in the existence of the act, so too it has no effect in any of the attributes of that act." The Judge said: "The servant's power, even though it does not effect the existence of that act, nevertheless it does effect one of the attributes of that act, and that attribute is what is called acquisition (al-kasb)." He argued: "This is because the movement that is obedience and the movement that is disobedience share in the fact that each is a movement, yet one is distinguished from the other by being obedience or disobedience. That by which they share is other than that by which they differ. Thus it is established that its being a movement is one thing, and its being obedience or disobedience is another. The essence of the movement and its existence occur by the power of God Most High. As for its being obedience or disobedience, that is an attribute occurring by the servant's power." This is the summary of the Judge's doctrine in the best possible manner.
**The Second Position:** The efficient cause in the existence of that act is the power of God Most High together with the servant's power. Then here there are two possibilities:

One: It may be said that the power of God Most High is independent in its effect, and the servant's power is also independent in its effect, except that the concurrence of two independent efficient causes upon a single effect is permissible.

The Second: It may be said that the power of God Most High is independent in its effect, while the servant's power is not independent in its effect; but when the power of God Most High is joined to the servant's power, the servant's power becomes independent in its effect by means of this assistance. It is said that this is the doctrine of the Master Abu Isḥāq, except that it is reported from him that he said: "The servant's power effects in a certain sense (bi-maʿnā)."

**The Third Position:** The coming-to-be of the act subsequent to the totality of power together with the incentive is necessary (wājib). This is because the capable agent, insofar as he is capable, can perform the act instead of refraining, and vice versa; and with this equilibrium (al-tasāwī) present, it is impossible for one of the two sides to outweigh the other. When the occurrence of the incentive is added to this, the preponderance of the side of existence is achieved, and at that point the act becomes necessarily occurring. This is the position we have chosen (al-mukhtār ʿindanā).

Then those who hold this position either say: "The efficient cause in the entry of the act into existence is the totality of power together with the incentive," or they say: "The efficient cause in the entry of the act into existence is not the totality of power and the incentive." These latter are also two groups:

As for those who claimed that the governor of this world is necessary by essence (mūjib bi-al-dhāt), they said: When power together with the incentive is present, complete readiness (al-istiʿdād al-tāmm) is achieved for the entry of that act into existence; however, these corporeal forces do not possess the capacity for origination (al-ījād) and effect. Thus, when complete readiness is achieved, existence flows forth from the Bestower of Forms (wāhib al-ṣuwar) upon those essences, and they become existent. So the presence of power and incentive yields complete readiness, while existence and actualization come from the Bestower of Forms. This is the doctrine of the majority of the philosophers (al-falāsifa).

As for those who claimed that the governor of this world is a free-acting agent (fāʿil mukhtār), they said: The totality of power and incentive entails the occurrence of the act, except that the entailing and the entailed only come to be by the power of God Most High—just as substance (al-jawhar) and accident (al-ʿaraḍ) are mutually entailing, yet they exist only by the power of God Most High.

**The Fourth Position:** The efficient cause in the coming-to-be of the act is the servant's power independently (ʿalā sabīl al-istiglāl). This is the doctrine of the Muʿtazila. Then these differed in several loci:

**The First Locus:** Is the effect of power in the coming-to-be of the act contingent upon the presence of the incentive? As for Abu al-Ḥusayn, his statement wavered on this. Whenever he debated with the philosophers on their claim—"Why did God single out the origination of the world for a particular time rather than before it or after it?"—he said: "The act is not contingent upon the incentive." But whenever he debated other matters with his companions, he said: "The act is contingent upon the incentive, and preponderance without a preponderator (al-tarjīḥ bi-lā murajjīḥ) is null in the first principles of the intellects." As for the senior masters of the Muʿtazila, most of them do not make the occurrence of the act contingent upon the incentive. Then if we say the act is contingent upon the incentive, does the act become necessarily occurring when the pure incentive is present? The most fitting view of Abu al-Ḥusayn's words is that he concedes the necessity. His companion Maḥmūd al-Khwārazmī said: "When the incentive is present, the act ascends from the level of equilibrium, but it does not reach the level of necessity; rather, it becomes more worthy of occurring (awlā bi-al-wuqūʿ)."

**The Second Locus:** Is the knowledge that the servant is an originator (mūjid) of his own acts necessary (ḍarūrī) or theoretical (naẓarī)? The majority of the senior Muʿtazilite masters agreed that it is theoretical knowledge. As for Abu al-Ḥusayn, he holds that it is necessary knowledge. This is also what Maḥmūd al-Khwārazmī chose.

**The Third Locus:** The first three positions share in affirming compulsion (al-jabr). For, supposing each of those three positions to be sound, the servant is not independent in origination. If the act's issuing from the servant is contingent upon God's assistance, or contingent upon the presence of power together with the incentive, or is such that whenever power and incentive are present the act becomes necessary, and whenever they are absent—or one of them is absent—the act's occurrence becomes impossible—then compulsion necessarily follows.

This, then, is the exposition of the possible doctrines on this question. Know that there are here subtle investigations (abḥāth ghāmiḍa) concerning the precise determination of the locus of dispute (maḥall al-nizāʿ), which must be pointed out. They are in several respects:

**The First Investigation:** The Muʿtazilite either says that the occurrence of the act subsequent to the totality of power and incentive is necessary, or he says it is not necessary. If he says it is necessary, then Muʿtazilism is nullified entirely. For those incentives cannot each be traced back to another incentive, due to the impossibility of infinite regress (al-tasalsul) and circularity (al-dawr). Rather, they must terminate at an incentive that occurs by the act of God Most High. If this is so, we say: When power and incentive are present, since the act is necessary, and when they—or one of them—are absent, since the act is impossible—then compulsion necessarily follows, and the servant has no independence, neither in acting nor in refraining, in anything. But if the Muʿtazilite says that the occurrence of the act when power is present together with the incentive is not necessary, we say: On this supposition, when the totality of power together with the incentive is present, it is possible for the act to occur at one time and not to occur at another. For everything that is possible, it is not impossible to suppose its occurrence. Let it be supposed that power together with the incentive was present and continued to be so; then at one time the act occurred, and at another it did not. This occurrence was not from the servant at all, but rather by sheer coincidence (muḥḍ al-ittifāq) without any cause. For since the totality of power and incentive was fully present both at the time of the act's non-occurrence and at the time of its occurrence, and no new matter arose at the moment of the act's coming-to-be such that one could say the act occurred at that time because of it—on this supposition, the act's coming-to-be at that time would be sheer coincidence, not within his capacity (wusʿ) nor his choice (ikhtiyār). This too is pure compulsion. For he has no means whatsoever to bring about the act; rather, if its occurrence happens to coincide with that measure of power and incentive, it occurs; and if it does not so coincide, it does not occur. And there is no preponderance of one of the two sides over the other by any matter from the servant whatsoever.

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots

1. **Root: و-ج-ب** | Word: واجب | Definition: الوجوب: الثبوت اللازم الذي لا ينفك عنه الشيء، والواجب لذاته هو الذي يستحق الوجود بنفسه. *Obligation/Necessity: the necessary establishment from which a thing cannot be separated; that which is necessary by itself is that which deserves existence by its own essence.*
2. **Root: م-ك-ن** | Word: ممكن | Definition: الإمكان: كون الشيء بحيث يصح وجوده وعدمه، والممكن لذاته ما لا يقتضي عقله الوجود ولا العدم. *Possibility: a thing being such that both its existence and non-existence are valid; that which is possible by itself is that whose essence necessitates neither existence nor non-existence.*
3. **Root: ح-ي-ز** | Word: متحيز | Definition: الحيز: المكان المحدود الذي يشغله الجسم، والمتحيز هو الجسم القابل للإشارة الحسية. *Space/Position: the delimited place occupied by a body; that which is spatially extended is the body subject to sensory indication.*
4. **Root: ق-و-م** | Word: قائم بالنفس | Definition: القيام بالنفس: كون الشيء موجوداً لا في موضوع، والقائم بالغير: ما يكون وجوده في غيره. *Subsistence by itself: a thing existing not in a subject; that which subsists by another is that whose existence is in something else.*
5. **Root: ف-ر-ق** | Word: مفارقات | Definition: المفارقة: الانفصال عن المادة والعلائق الجسمانية، والمفارقات هي الجواهر العقلية المجردة. *Separation: disconnection from matter and corporeal attachments; the separate intelligences are the abstract intellectual substances.*
6. **Root: د-ب-ر** | Word: تدبير | Definition: التدبير: النظر في عاقبة الأمر وإحكامه، وتدبير الجسم: توجيهه وتصريفه نحو غاياته. *Administration: considering the outcome of a matter and perfecting it; administering a body is directing and disposing it toward its ends.*
7. **Root: ع-ق-ل** | Word: العقول المجردة | Definition: العقل: جوهر مجرد يدرك المعقولات، والعقول المجردة هي الجواهر التي لا تعلق لها بالأجسام أصلاً. *Intellect: an abstract substance that apprehends intelligibles; the abstract intellects are substances having no attachment to bodies whatsoever.*
Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors

1. **Rule: باب الابتداء وما يرفع بالابتداء** | The nominal sentence begins with a subject (مبتدأ) in the nominative, and the predicate (خبر) agrees with it in case. In "أن الموجود إما أن يكون واجبا لذاته" the particle أن governs the nominal sentence, rendering the subject accusative (اسم إن) while the predicate remains in the accusative as its خبر, following the pattern of إن وأخواتها as established in Sībawayh's treatment of operators affecting the مبتدأ والخبر.
2. **Rule: باب العطف على الموضع** | Conjunction may attach to the syntactic position (موضع) of a word rather than its overt case ending. In "إما أن يكون قائما بالنفس، وإما أن يكون قائما بالغير" the repeated إما introduces coordinated alternatives where the second member is conjoined to the first in its grammatical position, demonstrating Sībawayh's principle that العطف يعمل في اللفظ والمحل.

Know that the existent is either necessary by its essence or possible by its essence. As for that which is necessary by its essence, it is God, exalted be His majesty. The verifiers are in agreement that He must be neither spatially extended nor subsisting in that which is spatially extended. As for that which is possible by its essence, it is either self-subsistent or subsistent by another. That which is self-subsistent is either spatially extended or not spatially extended. That which is subsistent by another is either subsistent in that which is spatially extended or subsistent in that which is not spatially extended. These are four divisions.

As for the spatially extended essences and the attributes subsisting in them, their establishment is known. As for the essences which are not spatially extended, they are what the philosophers term "the separate intelligences" and what another group terms "the spirits." They are of two kinds. For concerning these essences, either it is said: just as they are not bodies nor states in bodies, so likewise they are not attached to bodies by way of disposition and administration; or it is said: they are attached to bodies by way of disposition and administration. The first kind the philosophers call "the abstract intellects."

And here there is an inquiry. For their non-attachment to bodies by way of administration and disposition admits of two possibilities: it may be due to the perfections of their essences and their elevation above attending to bodies, or it may be due to their weakness in their essences and their lack of power to dispose of anything among bodies. This, according to the division, is possible. And who is it whose intellect has encompassed all of God's kingdom and His dominion? To this division there is allusion in the Divine Book, where He said:
وَكَم مِّن مَّلَكٍ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ لَا تُغْنِي شَفَاعَتُهُمْ شَيْئًا
paragraphs.arabic: وَكَم مِّن مَّلَكٍ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ لَا تُغْنِي شَفَاعَتُهُمْ شَيْئًا

paragraphs.text: "And how many an angel in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing" (53:26).

As for the second division, it comprises the substances that are abstract in their essences from corporeality and from indwelling in corporeality, yet they are attached to bodies by way of administration and disposition. This division is itself divided into two kinds, for they are either administrators of the celestial bodies or of the elemental bodies. And since it has been established by proof that outside the world there is an infinite void, and it has not been established by proof that the world is one, rather it is established that the existence of worlds other than this world is not impossible — and were their existence established, there would occur therein of the hosts of holy spirits what none knows except God most High, and which mankind does not know at all.

However, inquiry into those states is not possible. For this reason, the intellects have confined themselves to inquiry into the spirits administering the celestial bodies or the spirits administering the elemental bodies.

As for the spirits administering the celestial bodies, the most apparent view is that the spheres are to them like bodies, and the stars are to them like hearts, and the radial lines flowing forth from the luminous bodies of the stars run the course of the subtle luminous bodies flowing from the heart and the brain, reaching the rest of the organs. Then just as every body has a single soul, yet from it flow forth into every part of the body particular administering powers for that part, so likewise it is not far-fetched that from the universal soul of the sphere there flow forth particular souls, each one of which is attached to a particular part of the parts of the sphere and to a particular side of its sides.

As for the lower souls, the majority have agreed that the human rational souls are substances abstract from corporeality and from indwelling in the body, yet they are attached to these bodies by way of administration and disposition.

As for the souls of the other animals, the majority have held that they are corporeal powers and not abstract substances. And among them are those who have held that they are among the abstract substances. And these are of two groups:
