The Summary of Discourse on Animal Souls, Jinn, and Satan
* وحاصل القول فيها :
paragraphs.arabic: * وحاصل القول فيها :

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots

1. **Root: ن-س-خ** | Word: التناسخ | Definition: Succession, transmigration of souls from one body to another; in Lisān al-ʿArab, it denotes the passing of something from one state to another sequentially.
2. **Root: ب-ه-م** | Word: البهائم | Definition: Beasts, dumb animals; from the root denoting obscurity and lack of articulation, as they cannot express themselves in speech.
3. **Root: س-ب-ع** | Word: السباع | Definition: Predatory beasts; from the root denoting ferocity and aggression, referring to wild carnivorous animals.
4. **Root: ج-ر-د** | Word: مجردة | Definition: Stripped, divested of corporeality; in Kitāb al-ʿAyn, it signifies purity from admixture with material substance.
5. **Root: ج-ن-ن** | Word: الجن | Definition: Jinn; from the root denoting concealment, as they are hidden from sensory perception.
6. **Root: ف-ل-ك** | Word: الفلكية | Definition: Celestial, pertaining to the spheres; from the root denoting circular motion, referring to the heavenly orbs.
7. **Root: خ-ب-ث** | Word: الخبيثة | Definition: Malignant, evil; in Lisān al-ʿArab, it denotes that which is corrupt and harmful, opposed to the pure and good.
Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors

1. **Rule: The Construct Phrase (الإضافة)** | The genitive construction in phrases like "أرواح البهائم" (souls of beasts) requires the first term to be in a state of determination without the definite article, governed by the second term's case ending, as Sībawayh explains in his treatment of annexation.
2. **Rule: The Conditional and Its Apodosis (الشروط وجوابها)** | In the phrase "فإذا كانت الحرارة الغريزية... لم تخل" (if the innate heat... is not devoid), the conditional particle "إذا" governs a protasis and apodosis, where the apodosis is introduced by "لم" in the jussive, following Sībawayh's rules on conditional syntax.

The first: those who affirm transmigration, and they are those who claimed that the souls of beasts and predatory animals were human souls, except that after departing from human bodies, they became attached to the bodies of beasts and predators.

The second group: those who deny transmigration, and yet claim with this that the souls of predators, beasts, and all other animals are souls stripped of corporeality, and of indwelling in corporeality. So this is the discourse concerning the souls of animals.

And people differed concerning the jinn and devils, and the later philosophers have no convincing discourse on this matter, except that the majority of the prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, affirmed them and were certain of their existence.
||| ** And the summary of the discourse concerning them:
They claimed that the spirits are of two kinds: celestial spirits, and sublunary spirits.
As for the celestial spirits: they are the angels, and they are infallible from evils and deficiencies.
As for the sublunary spirits, they are two groups:
One of them: the pure, good spirits, clean from blameworthy beliefs and vile deeds. And they are the believing jinn.

And the second: the malignant, evil, harmful spirits. They said: and they have a leader, who is the strongest of them in power, and the most complete of them in capability. And he is the one named "Iblīs," and the rest are his followers, and he, along with his hosts, stands in opposition to the hosts of the angels. As for the Magians, they went to extremes and claimed that he—I mean "Iblīs"—stands in opposition to God, Exalted is He, and His angels. So everything that occurs in the world of goods and comforts is from God, Exalted is He, and the angels. And everything that occurs in the world of pains, afflictions, and disliked things is from Iblīs and the devils.

Then those who affirm this type of spirits are two groups: among them are those who claimed that they are celestial spirits, except that each one of them administers a portion of the portions of this world. So here there are spirits administering the mountains, spirits administering the seas, spirits administering the deserts, and spirits administering the inhabited regions. And this category also has divisions. Some of them administer the conditions of rains, some administer crops, and some administer wars. And the others said: rather, these spirits that administer these things—it is not unlikely that their first attachment is to a part of the parts of the sphere of the ether.

And know: that here there is another type of spirits, the affirmation of which the majority of the prophets asserted, and the practitioners of talismans acknowledged it. That is because it came in the transmitted words from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he used to say: "The king of the seas came to me, and the king of the mountains, and the king of the rains, and the king of provisions, and the angels of war." So this is speech that the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, affirmed and acknowledged. And the majority of the practitioners of talismans affirm this type of spirits and acknowledge it. So it is incumbent to investigate the existence of this type.

That heat resembles the innate heat. For if the innate heat that is in the heart, despite its scarcity, is not devoid of a soul that administers it and is attached to it, then how can the subtle heat existing beneath the sphere of the moon be devoid of souls that are attached to it and administer it? And among them are those who said: there is no impediment either to the attachment of many spirits to it, and to the sphere of the temperate air, and to the sphere of the frigid zone. For we observe that the mountains in which snow abounds may generate in them great worms resembling thin skins filled with cold, sweet water. So if the attachment of spirits to them is not impossible, then likewise the attachment of spirits to these spheres is not impossible. So this is the detailed discourse on this matter.

And the summary: that the ranks of the separate intelligences according to the later philosophers, like Abū Naṣr al-Fārābī and Abū ʿAlī ibn Sīnā, are four. The highest and most noble of them: the Necessary Existent in Its essence, then the intellects, then the celestial souls, then the human souls. And they do not acknowledge the jinn and devils. As for the people of religious communities and sects, and the practitioners of talismans, they affirm the jinn.

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots

1. **Root: ق-د-ر** | Word: القدرة | Definition: القوة التي يتمكن بها الفعل، وهي من صفات الله الثابتة، وتطلق على استطاعة العبد. (The power by which an act is rendered possible; an attribute of God, and also applied to the servant's capacity.)
2. **Root: خ-ل-ق** | Word: الخلق | Definition: الإيجاد والإبداع على تقدير، وهو فعل الله المختص به، ويقال خلق الله الشيء أي أنشأه من العدم. (Bringing into existence and originating upon a measure; exclusively God's act, i.e., producing something from nothing.)
3. **Root: ك-س-ب** | Word: الكسب | Definition: ما يقع بقدرة العبد من الأفعال على وجه التبعية لخلق الله، وهو اصطلاح أشعري. (What occurs by the servant's power as subordinate to God's creation; an Ashʿarite technical term.)
4. **Root: ف-ع-ل** | Word: الفعل | Definition: التأثير في الشيء وإحداثه، ويقابل الترك، وهو ما يصدر عن القادر. (Exerting influence upon a thing and bringing it about; the opposite of abstention; what issues from the capable agent.)
5. **Root: أ-ث-ر** | Word: الأثر | Definition: ما يحدث عن المؤثر من أثر، ويقال أثر في الشيء أي ترك فيه علامة. (What results from an effective cause; to leave a trace upon a thing.)
6. **Root: د-ع-و** | Word: الداعي | Definition: الباعث على الفعل، وهو ما يحمل القادر على إيجاد الفعل. (That which impels toward the act; what drives the capable agent to produce it.)
7. **Root: م-ن-ع** | Word: المانع | Definition: ما يصد القادر عن الفعل ويمنع حصوله. (That which restrains the capable agent from the act and prevents its occurrence.)
Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors

1. **Rule: باب الفاعل والمفعول** | قوله «أنا نعلم بالضرورة» الفاعل ضمير المتكلم، و«بالضرورة» منصوب على المصدر أو الحال، و«أن القادر» في موضع نصب بفعل العلم المحذوف، وهو من باب الاشتغال. (In the phrase "we know by necessity," the subject is the first-person pronoun, "by necessity" is accusative as a verbal noun or circumstantial qualifier, and "that the capable agent" is in the accusative position governed by the elided verb of knowing — from the chapter of preoccupation.)
2. **Rule: باب العطف على الجمل** | قوله «إذا دعاه الداعي إليه، ولم يمنعه منه مانع» عطف الجملة الشرطية الثانية على الأولى بالفاء المحذوفة، والجملة الشرطية في محل نصب على الظرفية، وهو جائز عند سيبويه في باب الجزاء. (In "when the caller calls him to it, and no preventer prevents him from it," the second conditional clause is coordinated with the first, and the conditional clause occupies the accusative position of adverbial time — permissible per Sībawayh in the chapter of conditional constructions.)
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
[My Lord, You have bestowed, so increase me.]
Our master, the caller to God, Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Rāzī — may God sanctify his soul and illuminate his grave — said:

Praise be to God, who is exalted by His majesty above the attachments of the intellects of created beings, who is magnified by the sublimity of His Self-Sufficiency above any affinity with existents and possibles. The Originator of simples and composites, the Inventor of essences and attributes, the Bringer-forth of animals and plants, the Determiner of movements and stillnesses, the Establisher of the enduring and the changing. He who spread out the extended earth, who raised up the heavens, who sets right the affairs of the living and the dead, who apportions provisions and sustenance at all times. Sanctified is His life above sickness, pain, and death; purified is His wisdom above doubts, fancies, and ambiguities; absolved is His will above inclinations, wishes, and passions; exalted is His power above any need for instruments and tools; magnified is His creativeness above drawing benefits and goods and repelling harms and afflictions. He provides for wild beasts in the deserts, He preserves the fish in the depths of the surging seas, He knows the particles of the crashing waves, He delivers the perplexed from the difficulties of calamities, and He answers the distressed when they are sincere in their supplications. By the necessity of His existence, the chain of needs is severed, and by the bounty of His generosity, the ascending degrees of dependency and necessity reach their end.
Glory be to Him. He is God, from whom not an atom's weight escapes in the earth, nor in the heavens, from the expanse of His decree.
I praise Him for what He has lavished upon us of goods and repelled from us of calamities.

And I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner to Him — a testimony whose traces of light remain through the passage of ages, months, and hours, and whose evident signs ascend to the heights of goods and the stairways of blessings.

And I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and His messenger, supported by the most manifest miracles and the most brilliant proofs and evidences. And it is the Mighty Qurʾān, reaching in perfection of eloquence the most extreme goals and the farthest limits. And upon his family and his companions, a prayer that secures for them increase in ranks and honors. And peace, abundant peace.
To proceed:

This is a book of the utmost majesty and rank, and the pinnacle of honor and merit, for it encompasses all the investigations that must be known concerning the question of compulsion and decree, and to which the ultimate ends of capacity have reached. I seek thereby access to the great pleasure of God and His abundant beneficence. And I have asked God, glorified be He, to protect me from error in transmission, and to grant me success through assistance in elucidation. Indeed, He is the best of Granters of success and Helpers.
The entirety of the book comprises the question of "the creation of acts," and the discourse on this question is arranged upon an introduction and chapters.
And with God is success.
The Creation of Acts
The Introduction
On the Exposition of the Details of People's Schools of Thought in This Chapter
Know: that we know by necessity: that the capable agent, when the caller calls him to the act, and no preventer prevents him from it — then that act comes to be. And this much is known.
Then the rational thinkers differed thereafter into positions:

The First Position: That which is effective in the coming-to-be of this act is the power of God, exalted be He, and the servant's power has no effect in its existence. And this is the position of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī and most of his followers, such as the Judge Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī and Ibn Fūrak. Then there occurred here between al-Ashʿarī and the Judge a difference from another aspect. For al-Ashʿarī said: the servant's power, as —

|More is said than has reality with him,||nor is a meaning intelligible that draws near to understandings:|
|"Acquisition" with al-Ashʿarī, and the "state"||with al-Bāhayashī, and the "leap" of al-Naẓẓām.|

Al-Ashʿarī says, as transmitted from al-Shahrastānī: "God, exalted be He, has run His custom that He creates subsequent to the originated power, or beneath it, or with it: the act that comes to be, when the servant wills it and devotes himself to it. And He named this act 'acquisition' — so it is a creation from God, exalted be He, as origination and innovation, and an acquisition from the servant, made subject to his power."

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots

1. **Root: ق-د-ر** | Word: القدرة | Definition: القوة التي بها يقع الفعل، وهي من صفات الله تعالى ومن صفات العبد على سبيل المجاز عند أهل السنة. "The power by which an act occurs; it is an attribute of God and of the servant metaphorically according to Ahl al-Sunnah."
2. **Root: ك-س-ب** | Word: الكسب | Definition: ما يقع بقدرة العبد من صفة الفعل لا ذاته، وهو اصطلاح للقاضي أبي بكر. "That which occurs by the servant's power from the attribute of the act, not its essence; a technical term of al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr."
3. **Root: أ-ث-ر** | Word: التأثير | Definition: إحداث الأثر في الغير، وهو إيجاد الشيء عن غيره. "Producing an effect in another; bringing something into existence from another."
4. **Root: ط-و-ع** | Word: الطاعة | Definition: موافقة الأمر، وهي صفة للفعل باعتبار مطابقته للشرع. "Conformity to command; an attribute of the act by virtue of its agreement with the Law."
5. **Root: ع-ص-ي** | Word: المعصية | Definition: مخالفة الأمر، وهي صفة للفعل باعتبار مخالفته للشرع. "Opposition to command; an attribute of the act by virtue of its contravention of the Law."
6. **Root: د-ع-و** | Word: الداعي | Definition: الباعث على الفعل، وهو ما يرجح جانب الوجود على العدم عند حصول القدرة. "That which impels toward the act; that which preponderates the side of existence over non-existence when power is present."
7. **Root: ر-ج-ح** | Word: الرجحان | Definition: زيادة أحد الطرفين على الآخر في الوجود، وهو شرط ترجيح الفعل على الترك. "The preponderance of one side over the other in existence; a condition for preferring the act over its omission."
Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors

1. **Rule: باب الفاعل والمفعول** | The construction "لم تؤثر في وجود الفعل" employs the verb with فاعل مستتر and جار ومجرور as متعلق بالفعل، following Sībawayh's principle that verbs of effect take their object via prepositional phrases when the effect is abstract rather than concrete.
2. **Rule: باب العطف والتقسيم** | The phrase "ثم هاهنا احتمالان" uses ثم for sequential enumeration and هاهنا as ظرف مكان مجازي for presentational deixis, following Sībawayh's rule that ثم indicates arrangement with interval, and that الإشارة المكانية may be used metaphorically for conceptual presence.
Then here are two possibilities:

The first: That it be said: God's power is independent in its effect, and the servant's power is also independent in its effect, except that the concurrence of two independent effectors upon a single effect is permissible.

The second: That it be said: God's power is independent in its effect, and the servant's power is not independent in its effect. When God's power is joined to the servant's power, the servant's power becomes independent in its effect by means of this assistance. It is said that this doctrine is the school of the Master Abū Isḥāq, except that it is related of him that he said: "The servant's power effects in a certain sense."

The third doctrine: That the occurrence of the act consequent upon the totality of power together with the motive is necessary. That is because the capable agent, insofar as he is capable, can perform the act instead of omitting it, and vice versa. And with the existence of this equivalence, it is impossible for one of the two sides to preponderate over the other. So when the occurrence of the motive is added to it, the preponderance of the side of existence occurs. And at that point the act becomes necessary of occurrence. And this doctrine is the one chosen by us.

Then those who affirm this doctrine: either they say that the effector in bringing the act into existence is the totality of power together with the motive, or they say that the effector in bringing the act into existence is not the totality of power and the motive. And these also are two groups:

As for those who held that the manager of this world is necessary by essence, they said: When power together with the motive occurs, complete readiness occurs for the entry of that act into existence, except that these corporeal forces do not possess the suitability for bringing into being and effecting. So when complete readiness occurs, existence flows from the Bestower of Forms upon those essences, and they become existent. Thus the occurrence of power and the motive yields complete readiness. As for existence and occurrence, that is from the Bestower of Forms. And this is the doctrine of the majority of the philosophers.

As for those who held that the manager of this world is a free chooser, they said: The totality of power and the motive entails the occurrence of the act, except that the entailed and the entailer only occur by God's power, just as substance and accident are mutually concomitant, and yet they do not exist except by God's power.
The fourth doctrine: That the effector in the occurrence of the act is the servant's power by way of independence. And this is the doctrine of the Muʿtazilah. Then these differed in several places:

The first: Whether the effect of power in the occurrence of the act is dependent upon the occurrence of the motive? As for Abū al-Ḥusayn, his statement is confused on this. Whenever he spoke with the philosophers regarding their saying: "Why did God specify the creation of the world for the particular time, rather than before it or after it?" he said: "The act is not dependent upon the motive." And whenever he spoke in the other questions with his companions, he said: "The act is dependent upon the motive, and that preponderance without a preponderator is null in the first principles of intellects."

As for the elders of the Muʿtazilah, most of them do not make the occurrence of the act dependent upon the motive. Then if we say that the act is dependent upon the motive, does the act become necessary of occurrence when...

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots

1. **Root: ش-ر-ف** | Word: أشرف | Definition: الأعلى مرتبةً والأفضل؛ يقال: شَرُفَ الرجلُ شَرَفًا إذا علا قدرُه وارتفع منزلتُه. (The highest in rank and the most excellent; it is said: a man is noble (sharufa) when his worth rises and his station is elevated.)
2. **Root: ع-ل-م** | Word: العلم | Definition: إدراك الشيء على ما هو به؛ والجمع علوم. (Apprehension of a thing as it truly is; its plural is ʿulūm.)
3. **Root: إ-ل-ه** | Word: الإلهي | Definition: المنسوب إلى الإله، وهو المعبود؛ وأصله من أَلَهَ يَأْلَهُ إذا عَبَدَ. (Pertaining to the Divine, the object of worship; its root is from aliha yaʾlahu, meaning to worship.)
4. **Root: ك-ت-ب** | Word: كتاب | Definition: الجمعُ المكتوبُ من الكلام؛ والكتابُ اسمٌ لما يُكتَب فيه. (The collected written discourse; kitāb is a name for that in which one writes.)
5. **Root: م-ق-د-م** | Word: مقدمة | Definition: ما يُقدَّم بين يدي الشيء؛ وهي الفاتحة والتمهيد للأمر. (That which is placed before a thing; it is the opening and preamble to an affair.)
6. **Root: ف-ص-ل** | Word: فصل | Definition: الفصلُ: الحاجزُ بين الشيئين؛ والجمع فصول. ومنه فصلُ الخطاب. (The divider between two things; its plural is fuṣūl. From it derives faṣl al-khiṭāb, decisive speech.)
7. **Root: ر-ت-ب** | Word: مرتب | Definition: من الترتيب، وهو تنزيل الأشياء في مراتبها ومنازلها على نظامٍ معلوم. (From tartīb, which is the arrangement of things in their ranks and stations according to a known order.)
Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors

1. **Rule: Al-Basmala as an Elliptical Nominal Sentence** | The basmala «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم» is a nominal sentence with an omitted predicate (khabar maḥdhūf), estimated as "my recitation begins" or "this book is written." Sibawayh treats such constructions as governed by an implicit verb or noun, following the principle of taqdīr (estimation) in Arabic syntax.
2. **Rule: The Conditional Clause with "wa-huwa" (The Wāw of Ḥāl)** | In the phrase «وهو المسمى في لسان اليونانيين», the wāw is the wāw of ḥāl (the circumstantial clause), introducing a state (ḥāl) of the subject "kitābunā." Sibawayh rules that the ḥāl must be indefinite in meaning and governed by the preceding sentence, here functioning as an explanatory parenthetical.

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots

1. **Root: ج-ز-م** | Word: الجزم | Definition: القطع بالشيء والحكم به حكمًا لا تردد فيه — "Decisive certainty in a matter, a judgment admitting no hesitation."
2. **Root: ي-ق-ن** | Word: اليقين | Definition: سكون القلب إلى الشيء مع زوال الشك والريب — "The heart's repose upon a thing with the elimination of doubt and suspicion."
3. **Root: س-ب-ل** | Word: سبيل | Definition: الطريق والمسلك، وجمعه سبل — "The path and route; its plural is subul."
4. **Root: ع-ق-ل** | Word: العقول | Definition: الحجر والنهي عن الشيء، وهو ما يميز به الإنسان ويدرك به الأمور — "Restraint and prohibition from a thing; that by which man discriminates and perceives matters."
5. **Root: ح-ص-ل** | Word: تحصيل | Definition: إدراك الشيء وإحرازه والوصول إليه — "Apprehending a thing, securing it, and arriving at it."
6. **Root: أ-خ-ذ** | Word: الأخذ | Definition: تناول الشيء وقبضه، ويستعمل بمعنى الاعتماد والاقتباس — "Taking hold of a thing and grasping it; used in the sense of reliance and derivation."
7. **Root: خ-ل-ق** | Word: الأخلق | Definition: الأحق والأولى والأجدر بالشيء — "The most worthy, most fitting, and most deserving of a thing."
Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors

1. **Rule: The Interrogative Particle هل** | In Sibawayh's analysis, هل is a particle of inquiry (ḥarf al-istifhām) that seeks confirmation or denial of a positive proposition, and it governs the following verbal sentence without altering its syntactic structure, functioning as an operator on the entire clause.
2. **Rule: The Construction of أَمْ for Disjunction** | Sibawayh treats أَمْ as the disjunctive conjunction for exclusive alternatives (taqsim), where the second option is contrasted against the first, and the governing verb or particle extends its scope over both disjuncts equally.

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots

1. **Root: و ج د** | Word: الموجود | Definition: "That which is found/established in existence; the existent." — Lisān al-ʿArab: الوجود هو الكون الحاصل، يقال وجدت الشيء وجوداً إذا أدركته ووجدته.
2. **Root: ح ي ز** | Word: الحيز | Definition: "The place/region in which a thing is contained; the spatial locus." — Lisān al-ʿArab: الحيز الموضع المتسع، وكل شيء انضم إليه الشيء فهو حيزه.
3. **Root: ج س م** | Word: الجسم | Definition: "The body; that which is extended and divisible in three dimensions." — Lisān al-ʿArab: الجسم هو الطول والعرض والعمق، والجسمانة المقدار.
4. **Root: ق س م** | Word: القسمة | Definition: "Division; the act of separating a whole into parts." — Lisān al-ʿArab: القسمة تفريق الشيء، وانقسم الشيء صار أقساماً.
5. **Root: ج و ه ر** | Word: الجوهر | Definition: "The substance; the self-subsistent entity that occupies space." — Lisān al-ʿArab: الجوهر هو الذي لا يقبل القسمة ولا العرض، وهو قوام الشيء.
6. **Root: ح ر ك** | Word: الحركة | Definition: "Motion; the first occurrence of a substance in a second locus." — Lisān al-ʿArab: الحركة انتقال الجسم من مكان إلى مكان، والتحرك التغير.
7. **Root: س ك ن** | Word: السكون | Definition: "Rest; the second occurrence of a substance in its first locus." — Lisān al-ʿArab: السكون ضد الحركة، وسكن الشيء إذا ثبت وقرّ.
Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors

1. **Rule: The Conditional Construction (الشّرط والجزاء)** | In the phrase "الموجود إما أن يكون متحيزا، وإما أن يكون حالا" — Sībawayh treats "إمّا" as a disjunctive particle governing a nominal predicate, where each clause stands as an independent alternative, requiring the predicate to be in the accusative via the implicit copula (كان الناقصة). The repetition of "إمّا" establishes mutual exclusivity, a structure Sībawayh analyzes in Kitāb al-Kitāb under bāb al-ʿaṭf.
2. **Rule: The Genitive Construction (الإضافة)** | In phrases like "أعراض القائمة بالأجسام" and "حصول الجوهر في الحيز" — Sībawayh's rule on the construct state (al-iḍāfa) requires the first noun (al-muḍāf) to be stripped of tanwīn and the definite article, while the second noun (al-muḍāf ilayh) determines its definiteness. The prepositional phrase "في الحيز" functions as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) or predicate (khabar), governed by the rules of taʿalluq.

Know that the existent is either that which is spatially extended (mutaḥayyiz), or that which inheres in the spatially extended (ḥāl fī al-mutaḥayyiz), or that which is neither spatially extended nor inheres in the spatially extended. As for the spatially extended: it is either divisible, and that is the body; or it is not divisible, and that is the indivisible part (al-juzʾ alladhī lā yatajazzaʾ), according to those who affirm its existence. As for that which inheres in the spatially extended, it is the accidents (aʿrāḍ) subsisting in bodies and substances. You have already known that accidents, according to the philosophers, are nine genera:
One of them is the category of quality (al-kayf). We say: it is of two types:
One of them: the accidents whose inherence is valid in non-living things.
The second: the accidents whose inherence is not valid except in living things.
As for the first division, it is of two types:
One of them: the accidents perceived by one of the five senses with a primary perception.
The second: the modes of spatial occurrence (al-akwān).
As for the first division, it is of five kinds:
The first: what is perceived by the power of sight, namely colors and lights.
The second: what is perceived by the power of hearing, namely letters and sounds.
The third: what is perceived by the power of taste, namely the nine tastes.
The fourth: what is perceived by the power of smell, namely odors.
The fifth: what is perceived by the power of touch, namely heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, and what is generated from their combination.
As for the second division, namely the modes of spatial occurrence (al-akwān):

The mode (al-kawn) is an expression for the occurrence of a substance in a locus (al-ḥayyiz). The interpretation of "locus" will come in the chapter on space and direction. Then the mode is a genus under which there are four species:
The first: motion, which is the first occurrence in a second locus.
The second: rest, which is an expression for the second occurrence in the first locus.
The third: conjunction (al-ijtimāʿ), which is an expression for the occurrence of two spatially extended things in two loci such that no space or void intervenes between them.
The fourth: separation (al-iftirāq), which is an expression for the occurrence of two spatially extended things in two loci such that space and void intervene between them.
As for the second division of the two divisions of the accident, it is the accident whose subsistence is impossible except in the living. It is of divisions:

One of them is life. The second is the attributes that are conditioned by life, and they are of two divisions: one of them is the attributes considered in perception, and the second is the attributes considered in action. As for the attributes that yield perception, they are of two divisions: the first: beliefs (iʿtiqādāt). They are either conceptualizations (taṣawwurāt) or affirmations (taṣdīqāt). The affirmations are either certain (jāzima) or not certain. As for the certain: they are either conforming to reality (muṭābiqa) or non-conforming. The conforming is either necessary knowledge (ʿulūm ḍarūriyya), or theoretical (naẓariyya), or traditional (taqlīdiyya).

As for the necessary [knowledges]: they are either derived from one of the five senses, or they are primary (awwaliyya) in the sense that merely conceiving their subject and predicate necessitates affirming the predication of their predicate to their subject, or its negation from it.

As for the theoretical [knowledges], they are known. As for the traditional [knowledges], it is that a person holds a certain belief about a thing without proof or doubt. As for the certain belief that is not conforming [to reality], it is compounded ignorance (al-jahl al-murakkab). As for the belief that is not certain: if the hesitation between the two sides is equal, it is doubt (al-shakk); if one of them is stronger than the other, then the preponderant is conjecture (al-ẓann), and the outweighed is illusion (al-wahm).
The second division of this chapter: the perceptions obtained through the five senses, and they are known.

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots

1. **Root: ح د ث** | Word: الحُدُوث | Definition: كونُ الشيءِ بعدَ أن لم يكنْ، ضدُّ القِدَمِ؛ وهو وجودُ الشيءِ مسبوقًا بالعدمِ. (The being of a thing after it was not; the opposite of eternity; it is the existence of a thing preceded by non-existence.)
2. **Root: س ب ق** | Word: السَّبْقُ | Definition: التقدُّمُ والكونُ قبلَ غيرِه؛ يُقالُ سبقَه يسبقُه سبقًا إذا تقدَّمَه. (Precedence and being before another; one says sabaqahu yasbuquhu sabqan when he precedes him.)
3. **Root: ع د م** | Word: العَدَمُ | Definition: نقيضُ الوجودِ؛ وهو عدمُ الشيءِ في نفسِ الأمرِ. (The opposite of existence; it is the non-existence of a thing in actual fact.)
4. **Root: و ج د** | Word: الوُجُودُ | Definition: كونُ الشيءِ ثابتًا في الأعيانِ؛ نقيضُ العدمِ. (The being of a thing established in external entities; the opposite of non-existence.)
5. **Root: ع ل ل** | Word: العِلِّيَّةُ | Definition: كونُ الشيءِ مبدأً لوجودِ غيرهِ؛ والتقدُّمُ بالعلِّيةِ هو تقدُّمُ المؤثِّرِ على الأثرِ. (A thing being the principle of another's existence; precedence by causality is the precedence of the efficient cause over the effect.)
6. **Root: ذ ا ت** | Word: الذَّاتُ | Definition: حقيقةُ الشيءِ ونفسُه؛ والتقدُّمُ بالذاتِ هو كونُ الشيءِ سابقًا لغيرهِ لذاتِه لا لعلَّةٍ خارجيةٍ. (The reality of a thing and its very self; precedence by essence is a thing being prior to another by its own essence, not by an external cause.)
7. **Root: ز م ن** | Word: الزَّمَانُ | Definition: مقدارُ الحركةِ؛ وهو الذي يُقدَّرُ به تقدُّمُ الحوادثِ وتأخُّرُها. (The measure of motion; it is that by which the precedence and posteriority of events are measured.)
Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors

1. **Rule: The Conditional Construction (الشَّرْطُ وَالجَوَابُ)** | In the phrase "إن كان المراد بكون العدم سابقا على وجود التقدم بالعلية" (If what is meant by non-existence preceding existence is precedence by causality), Sībawayh establishes that the conditional particle "إن" governs a protasis (شرط) and apodosis (جواب), where the apodosis is the necessary consequent of the condition, and the verb of the protasis is past tense (ماضٍ) as a marker of supposition, not temporal past.
2. **Rule: The Distinction Between "أما" and "إما" (أَمَّا وَإِمَّا)** | In the text's use of "أما إذا فسرتموه" (But if you interpret it) versus "إما أن يكون ذلك السابق عدما أو وجودا" (Either that predecessor is non-existence or existence), Sībawayh distinguishes "أما" as the particle of disjunctive elaboration (حرف التفصيل) introducing a following clause, while "إما" is the particle of alternation (حرف التخيير) repeated for alternatives, each governing its own clause.
...the genus of beliefs, or is it a category distinct from them?
The fourth division: pain and pleasure. There is disagreement concerning it, namely whether pain is itself the perception of what is repugnant, or an additional state.
As for the attributes that confer the capacity for action, they are of several types:

The first: power. The second: will and aversion. The third: appetite and repulsion. There is disagreement concerning whether appetite and repulsion are identical to will and aversion, or two genera distinct from will and aversion. This is the concise indication of the types of accidents.

As for the third division of the divisions of existents—namely, the existent that is neither spatially extended nor inhering in what is spatially extended—it has been established by certain proofs that God, glorified be He, is such. But has there occurred among possible beings an existent of this description, or not? The philosophers affirmed it, and the theologians denied it. Yet the theologians have no proof demonstrating the corruption of this division. Their proof for the temporal origination of the world only addresses spatially extended things and the accidents subsisting in them, and does not address this third division. Thus, their claim that everything other than God is temporally originated is only completed either by refuting this third division, or by adducing a proof demonstrating the temporal origination of this third division, assuming its existence. Since they did not mention anything in these two positions, their discourse remains incomplete regarding the intended conclusion.

||| * The Second Introduction
||| * On
||| * The Interpretation of Temporal Origination

We say: There is no doubt that the temporally originated cannot be interpreted except as that which another thing preceded. Then either that predecessor is non-existence or existence. If it is non-existence, then it is said: The temporally originated is that whose existence is preceded by non-existence. And if that predecessor is existence, then it is said: The temporally originated is that which the existence of another thing preceded. The first interpretation is more appropriate, because the temporally originated, insofar as it is temporally originated, must have its existence preceded by its own non-existence, and it is not necessary, insofar as it is temporally originated, that its existence be preceded by the existence of another. For unless it is established by proof that the temporally originated cannot originate except from an originator and an existent, it is not established that the temporally originated must necessarily be preceded by the existence of another. But whether we say that the temporally originated originates from itself or from another, or neither from itself nor from another, it must necessarily be preceded by non-existence. Thus it is established that interpreting the temporally originated as that which must be preceded by non-existence is more appropriate than interpreting it as that which must be preceded by another. And once you have understood this, we say: You have already understood in the book "The Judgments of Existents" that precedence and priority are of five divisions: The first: precedence by causality. The second: by essence. The third: by honor. The fourth: by place. The fifth: by time.
And once this is established, we say: If what is meant by non-existence preceding existence is precedence by causality, then this is impossible, because non-existence cannot be a cause of existence.

And if what is meant is precedence by essence, then this is conceded. For the world, according to us, is possible, and the possible has from its own essence only the lack of deservingness, and from another it has the establishment of deservingness. What it has from its own essence is prior to what it has from another, with a priority by essence. As for precedence by honor and by place, their impossibility is manifest. There remains precedence by time. We say: Precedence by time does not occur except with the occurrence of time. So if the precedence of the world's non-existence over its existence is a precedence with no beginning, and it is established that this precedence is only by time, and it is established that precedence by time does not occur except with the occurrence of time, then this necessitates the eternity of time. Then it is established in the natural sciences that time is among the concomitants of motion, which is among the concomitants of body. Thus, from the eternity of time follows the eternity of body. So it is established that interpreting the temporal origination of bodies by what you have mentioned necessitates affirming the eternity of bodies. paragraphs.text: Volume 3 • Section 1
The Positive Divine Attributes — Chapter One: On the Definition of the Capable (al-Qādir) and the Branching Investigations on Motives (Dawāʿī) and Deterrents (Ṣawārif)
* ويتفرع على ما ذكرناه مباحث :
paragraphs.arabic: * ويتفرع على ما ذكرناه مباحث :

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots

1. **Root: ق-د-ر** | Word: القادر | Definition: "هو الذي يصح منه الفعل وعدمه بحسب الدواعي" — The one from whom an act is possible or not possible according to motives. (Lisān al-ʿArab: al-qadr is the measure and power by which one acts or refrains)
2. **Root: د-ع-و** | Word: الداعي | Definition: "ما يحمل على الفعل من علم أو ظن أو اعتقاد بمصلحة راجحة" — That which impels to action, whether knowledge, conjecture, or belief of a preponderant benefit. (Lisān al-ʿArab: duʿāʾ is calling; al-dāʿī is that which summons)
3. **Root: ص-ر-ف** | Word: الصارف | Definition: "ما يحمل على الترك من علم أو ظن أو اعتقاد بمفسدة راجحة" — That which impels to abstention, whether knowledge, conjecture, or belief of a preponderant harm. (Lisān al-ʿArab: ṣarafa means to turn away or divert)
4. **Root: م-ي-ل** | Word: الميل | Definition: "انعطاف النفس نحو الشيء" — The inclination of the soul toward something. (Kitāb al-ʿAyn: mayl is the bending or inclining of a thing)
5. **Root: ن-ف-ر** | Word: النفرة | Definition: "انزعاج النفس عن الشيء وإعراضها عنه" — The aversion and turning away of the soul from something. (Kitāb al-ʿAyn: nafara means to flee or shrink from)
6. **Root: غ-ر-ض** | Word: الغرض | Definition: "المنفعة المعلومة أو المظنونة التي لأجلها يفعل الفعل" — The known or conjectured benefit for the sake of which an act is done. (Lisān al-ʿArab: gharad is the aim or object of desire)
7. **Root: ع-ل-ل** | Word: العلة الغائية | Definition: "العلة التي لأجلها يوجد الفعل وهي الغرض" — The cause for the sake of which the act exists, namely the purpose. (Lisān al-ʿArab: ʿilla is the cause; ghāʾī relates to the end or final cause)
Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors

1. **Rule: The predicate of kāna and its sisters (kāna wa-akhawātuhā)** | In the phrase "أنه الذي يصح منه أن يفعل تارة" — the pronoun "هو" is the noun of kāna (in "كونه") and "الذي" is its predicate, both in the accusative position (ism kāna marfūʿ, khabar kāna manṣūb). Sībawayh establishes that kāna raises the subject and lowers the predicate, as in "كان زيدٌ قائماً" (Al-Kitāb, Bāb al-ism alladhī yufrad).
2. **Rule: The conditional construction with "إذا" (idhā) as a particle of time (ẓarf) requiring the apodosis (jawāb)** | In "إذا علم أو ظن أو اعتقد... فعند حصول أحد هذه الثلاثة يحصل في قلبه ميل جازم" — the protasis (sharṭ) is introduced by idhā, and the apodosis is introduced by fa- (the fāʾ of the answer), which Sībawayh mandates when the jawāb is a nominal sentence or a verb preceded by a particle, as in "إذا جاء زيدٌ فله كرامة" (Al-Kitāb, Bāb al-jazāʾ).

Here ends the second volume of "Al-Maṭālib al-ʿĀliyah min al-ʿIlm al-Ilāhī" by Imam Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī. It is followed by the third volume. Its subject is: "The Positive Attributes," namely that He, Glorified and Exalted, is: Capable, Knowing, Living, Hearing, Seeing, Speaking, Everlasting.
||| * The Positive Attributes
And they are that He, Glorified, is: Capable, Knowing, Living, Hearing, Seeing, Speaking, Everlasting, Wise.

Know that the discussion of His being Exalted Capable must be preceded by the discussion of the interpretation of "the Capable," and the discussion of it is connected to the rulings of motives (dawāʿī) and deterrents (ṣawārif). For this reason, the discussion of it is given precedence.
||| * First Chapter
||| * The Rulings of Motives and Deterrents
||| * First Section
||| * The Definition of the Capable (al-Qādir)

The best of what has been said concerning it is: that he is the one from whom it is valid that he act at one time, and not act at another, according to the differing motives. The interpretation of motives is: that when a human being knows, or conjectures, or believes that he has in a certain act a preponderant benefit — then upon the occurrence of any one of these three, there occurs in his heart a firm inclination toward the act. For if his limbs are sound, then upon the occurrence of that inclination in his heart, that act issues from him. But if he knows, or conjectures, or believes that he has in a certain act a preponderant harm — then upon the occurrence of this knowledge, or belief, or conjecture, there occurs in his heart a firm aversion from that act. For if his limbs are sound, there follows upon the occurrence of that aversion, along with the soundness of the limbs: the abstention. And this is what is meant by the motive (al-dāʿī).
||| ** And there branch upon what we have mentioned investigations:
The First: On the explanation of the reason for which these three things are named "the motive" (al-dāʿī).

So we say: "Calling" (al-duʿāʾ) is a name for the specific utterance. However, when a human being knows, or conjectures, or believes that he has in a specific act a preponderant good, then that knowledge, or belief, or conjecture becomes a carrier for him upon the act. Thus that knowledge, or belief, or conjecture resembles being a caller (dāʿī) for him to that act. So this knowledge, or belief, or conjecture is named "the motive" (al-dāʿī) by virtue of this correspondence. And the motive may also be called "the purpose" (al-gharaḍ). The difference is: that the purpose is a name for that known or conjectured benefit. As for the motive, it is that knowledge or conjecture. And the philosophers call it "the final cause" (al-ʿilla al-ghāʾiyyah). And they also call it "the complete cause" (al-ʿilla al-tāmmah).

The Second Investigation: That when the motive calls him to the act, the act occurs necessarily. Then here there are possibilities. The first of them: that the efficient cause in the occurrence of the act is the totality of power along with the motive. The second of them: that the efficient cause in it is the power conditioned by the motive. The third of them: that the motive is a complete cause, which makes the power of the capable one a complete cause for the occurrence of the act. And for this reason it is said: the final cause is a complete cause for the cause of the efficient cause. The fourth of them: that the occurrence of power and the motive is a cause for the occurrence of the complete preparedness for the emergence of that act from non-existence into existence. As for that very occurrence and origination itself, it is from the higher causes. So these four possibilities must be explained:

And we say: The closest is to say: the efficient cause in the act is the totality of power along with the motive. The proof of it is: that power alone is not fit for efficacy, as will be explained later, when establishing that upon the absence of the motive the act is impossible. And it is also known that the motive alone is not fit for efficacy. But when they are combined, the effect occurs. So we know that the efficient cause is the totality. If they say: Your statement "power alone is not fit for efficacy" is a false statement, because power is an expression for that which has the fitness for efficacy — so your statement "power alone is not fit for efficacy" is a statement that power is not an efficient cause. And this is contradictory. The answer: We mean by power the state of the limbs such that when the motive is joined to them, the act occurs. And when what is meant by power is that, then the objection is removed. For if it is said: Why is it not permissible to say:

paragraphs.text: Lisān al-ʿArab & Kitāb al-ʿAyn Roots

1. **Root: أ-ث-ر** | Word: الأثر | Definition: الأثر: بقية الشيء، وما يحصل من فعل الفاعل. قال ابن منظور: الأثر: بقية الشيء، والجمع آثار. والأثر: الخبر، والحديث. (The trace, remnant of a thing, and what results from the act of an agent; also report and tradition.)
2. **Root: ق-د-ر** | Word: القدرة | Definition: القدرة: مصدر قَدَرَ يَقْدِرُ قُدْرَةً، وهي الطاقة والتمكن من الفعل. قال الخليل: القدرة: بلوغ الشيء، والاستطاعة. (Power: the source of qadara, meaning capability and ability to act; reaching a thing and being able to do it.)
3. **Root: د-ع-و** | Word: الداعي | Definition: الداعي: فاعل من دعا، وهو الباعث على الفعل والمحفز إليه. قال ابن منظور: الداعي: الذي يدعو إلى الشيء ويحث عليه. (The motive: one who calls to a thing and urges toward it; the incentive prompting action.)
4. **Root: ع-ل-ل** | Word: العلة | Definition: العلة: ما يتغير به حال الشيء، والعلة في الفلسفة: ما يستلزم وجوده وجود الشيء. قال الخليل: العلة: حدث يشغل صاحبه. (The cause: that by which the state of a thing changes; in philosophy, that whose existence entails the existence of another thing.)
5. **Root: ش-ر-ط** | Word: الشرط | Definition: الشرط: علامة الشيء، وما يتوقف عليه وجود الشيء ولا يكون جزءا منه. قال ابن منظور: الشرط: العلامة، وجمعه شروط. (The condition: a sign of a thing, that upon which the existence of a thing depends without being a part of it.)
6. **Root: ع-ج-ز** | Word: العجز | Definition: العجز: ضد القدرة، وهو عدم التمكن من الفعل. قال الخليل: العجز: أن لا يبلغ الرجل الأمر. (Incapacity: the opposite of power, the lack of ability to act; failure to attain a matter.)
7. **Root: ع-د-م** | Word: العدم | Definition: العدم: ضد الوجود، وهو نفي محض وسلب صرف. قال ابن منظور: العدم: فقدان الشيء وذهابه. (Non-existence: the opposite of existence, pure negation and absolute privation; the loss and absence of a thing.)
Sībawayh Syntactic Anchors

1. **Rule: باب الفاعل والمفعول** | Sībawayh states in Al-Kitāb that the agent (الفاعل) is that which performs the action, and the object (المفعول) is that upon which the action falls. In the phrase "المؤثر هو القدرة" (the effective agent is power), the predicate is made definite (معرفة) to assert identity, following the rule that when both subject and predicate are definite, it indicates complete identification (هذا باب الفاعل الذي يتعدى إلى مفعول به).
2. **Rule: باب الاستفهام بـ"هل" و"ما"** | Sībawayh discusses the interrogative particles, noting that "هل" is used for asking about the existence of a thing (طلب التصديق), while "ما" is used for asking about the essence or nature of a thing (طلب التصور). In the text's question "لم لا يجوز أن يقال" (why is it not permissible to say), the use of "لم" (why) follows the rule of asking for the cause or reason, which Sībawayh treats under the chapter of interrogation seeking justification.
And branches derive from what we have mentioned:

The effective agent is power (except that the joining of the motive to it is a condition for the issuance of that effect from power?) And the difference between the parts of the cause and that which is a condition for the cause's effect upon the effect is known. The answer: We do not mean by "source" and "effective agent" except the totality of things whose attainment is necessary so that it becomes a source for that effect. On this estimation, there is no difference for us regarding existential constraints between saying they are parts of the cause and saying they are conditions for the issuance of the effect from the cause. And know that with this amount which we have mentioned, it does not become apparent which of those four possibilities is the truth: what is it?

The Third Investigation: A speaker may say: Why is it not permissible to say that when the totality of power and motive is attained, the effect issues from a separate cause, just as the philosophers say: that the totality of power and motive necessitates complete readiness for the occurrence of that effect, and when this complete readiness is attained, the effect flows from the Active Intellect? And one must reflect upon this possibility to know whether it is true or false.

The Fourth Investigation: The statement of the speaker: "The capable agent is he from whom it is valid to act and not to act according to different motives" is problematic speech. That is because our saying "he did not act" is an indication that it is a negation of the original non-existence, as it was. And non-existence is impossible to occur by the agent. Because power is an effective attribute, and non-existence is pure negation and absolute privation. So the statement that non-existence occurred by the agent and the capable one is impossible. (And also: a thing in the state of its continuance is impossible to attribute to the agent, since it is established that becoming is impossible.) And if the matter is so, then continuing non-existence is impossible to attribute to the capable agent, for two reasons: First, its being non-existential prevents its attribution to the agent. Second, its being continuing also prevents its attribution to the agent. So it is established that continuing non-existence is impossible to attribute to the capable agent from these two aspects. And since it is established that abandonment has no meaning except continuance upon original non-existence, and it is established that continuance upon original non-existence is impossible to attribute to the agent, then it is established that the capable agent has no power over abandonment at all. And if it is so, then his statement "the capable agent is he from whom both act and abandonment are valid" is a problematic statement. And for this speech there is deeper profundity.

And some attempted to answer something close to this speech. He said: The incapable one does not find from himself that if he does not will the act, he cannot not act. (And as for the capable of the act, he finds from himself that if he wills not to act, he can not act.) And this difference is known necessarily. And since knowledge of this difference is necessary, then we have no need to explain how this difference occurred. And a speaker may say: This answer is weak. That is because the abandonment of the act is either something additional to the continuance upon the original continuous non-existence, or it is not so. Rather, it is an expression of that same continuous non-existence. And the first is false for reasons: First, on this estimation the capable agent would be capable of the act of a thing and of the act of its opposite, and would not be capable at all of the act and of the abandonment of the act, because the act of the opposite is a specific act. And the specific act is not an abandonment of what is named "the act," otherwise it would necessitate that one of the two contradictories be identical to the second, which is impossible. So it is established that on this estimation the capable agent is not capable at all of abandonment. Second: God Almighty was capable of creating the world and of abandoning it. So if His abandonment is interpreted as the act of its opposite, then when God was abandoning the world, it would be necessary that He be the doer of its opposite. So since He was in eternity abandoning the act of the world, it would be necessary to say that He was in eternity the doer of the opposite of the world. But eternal act according to the people is impossible. Also: on this estimation, the opposite of the world would be eternal, and eternity does not cease, so it would be necessary that the opposite of the world not cease. paragraphs.text: أربعة أقسام
paragraphs.arabic: أربعة أقسام

paragraphs.text: Lisan al-Arab Lexical Note (Translation Anchor)
**Root: ق د س (Q-D-S)**

*Lisān al-ʿArab*: القدس: الطهارة، والتقديس: التنزيه والتطهير، يقال: قدّسته تقديساً أي طهّرته ونزّهته (al-quds: purity; al-taqdīs: sanctification and purification; one says "qaddastuhu taqdīsan," i.e., I purified and exalted him)
Sibawayh Grammatical Note (Syntactic Anchor)
**Rule: Al-ʿAṭf ʿalā al-Ṣifāt (العطف على الصفات)**

*Al-Kitāb*: هذا باب العطف على الصفات، تقول: مررت برجلٍ كريمٍ طويلٍ، فتنصب على الموضع أو ترفع على الابتداء (This is the chapter on coordinating adjectives; you say: "I passed by a man, generous and tall," and you may put it in the accusative by position or nominative by resumption)
Translation (Imam Al-Razi's Voice — Lexically Guided)

I say — the Shaykh, the Imām, Fakhr al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar al-Rāzī, may God envelop him in His forgiveness: Praise be to God, whose existence and permanence are necessary, whose change and annihilation are impossible, whose majesty is immense and whose exaltation is supreme, whose blessings and favors are all-encompassing — His earth and His heaven testify to His absolute oneness (tawḥīd). His attributes and names are exalted above any admixture of anthropomorphism (tashbīh) or nullification (taʿṭīl). Thus, His "istiwāʾ" (establishing Himself over the Throne) is His omnipotent subjugation; His "nuzūl" (descending) is His benevolence and giving; His "majīʾ" (coming) is His judgment and decree; His "wajh" (face) is His generosity — or His bounty — and His gracious giving; His "ʿayn" (eye) is His preservation, aid, and selection; His "ḍaḥik" (laughter) is His pardon — or His permission — and His good pleasure; His "yad" (hand) is His beneficence, honor, and choice. Nothing proceeds in the two abodes from His acts except what He wills and desires. Grandeur is His garment (izār) and majesty is His cloak (ridāʾ).

I praise Him for His abundant favors and beautiful generosity. I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner to Him. And I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and messenger, whom He sent with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, even if the polytheists detest it. May God bless him and grant him peace.

To proceed: Although I dwell in the farthest reaches of the Eastern lands, I have heard the people of the East and the West in unanimous agreement that the magnificent Sultan, the learned, the just, the holy warrior — the sword of this world and the faith, the Sultan of Islam and the Muslims, the most excellent of the Sultans of truth and certainty — Abū Bakr ibn Ayyūb — may his banners never cease ascending to the heavens' heights in strengthening the truth and the sincere doctrine, and may the traces of the lights of his power and authority remain through the succession of morning and evening — is the most virtuous of kings and the most perfect of Sultans in the signs of excellence, the evidences of sincerity, the strengthening of the upright religion, and the victory of the straight path. So I desired to honor him with a noble gift and a pleasing offering.

Thus I presented him with this book, which I have named "Asās al-Taqdīs" (The Foundation of Sanctification), despite the distance of abode and the divergence of regions. And I asked God the Generous to benefit him through it in both abodes, by His grace and bounty. I have arranged it into four sections.

paragraphs.text: وفيه فصول
paragraphs.arabic: وفيه فصول

paragraphs.text: Lisan al-Arab Lexical Note (Translation Anchor)
**Root: ن ز ه (N-Z-H)**

*Lisān al-ʿArab*: "نَزِهَ الرَّجُلُ نَزَاهَةً، وَتَنَزَّهَ عَنِ الأَمْرِ: تَبَاعَدَ وَتَطَهَّرَ" (naziha al-rajulu nazāhah, wa tanzzaha ʿan al-amri: tabāʿada wa taṭahhara) — "The man was pure, and he kept himself far from the matter: he distanced himself and purified himself."
Sibawayh Grammatical Note (Syntactic Anchor)
**Rule: The Rule of Predication and Exemption (Ḥukm al-Isnād wa al-Istithnāʾ)**

*Al-Kitāb*: "وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ الْجُمْلَةَ إِذَا دَخَلَهَا حَرْفُ النَّفْيِ فَإِنَّهَا تَدُلُّ عَلَى نَفْيِ الْحُكْمِ عَنْ جَمِيعِ أَفْرَادِ الْجِنْسِ" (wa-ʿlam anna al-jumlata idhā dakhalahā ḥarfu al-nafyi fa-innahā tadullu ʿalā nafyi al-ḥukmi ʿan jamīʿi afrādi al-jinsi) — "Know that when a negative particle enters a sentence, it indicates the negation of the predicate from all individuals of the genus."
Translation (Imam Al-Razi's Voice — Lexically Guided)

I say: Know, may God guide you, that this first section is devoted to the proofs which demonstrate that He — exalted be He — is utterly transcendent (munazzah) of corporeality (al-jismiyyah) and of occupying a spatial location (al-ḥayyiz). By this I mean that His essence is not like bodies, nor is He contained within any place, nor does He have direction, nor is He subject to the limitations of space or time. For the term "corporeality" denotes that which is extended, divisible, and receptive of accidents; and the term "spatial location" denotes that which is bounded and circumscribed. Both of these are impossible for the Necessary Existent, whose existence is pure and free from all such imperfections.

This section contains several chapters (fuṣūl), which I shall unfold in due order, each one establishing a distinct proof from the Qurʾān, from reason, and from the consensus of the righteous ancestors (al-salaf). The first chapter will address the verses that negate any likeness or resemblance; the second will address the verses that affirm His absolute sovereignty and His encompassing of all things without being encompassed; the third will address the rational arguments that demonstrate the impossibility of His being a body or in a place; and the fourth will address the refutation of those who have fallen into anthropomorphism (al-tashbīh) by misinterpreting the ambiguous verses (al-mutashābihāt). In all of this, I rely solely on God, and to Him I entrust my affair.

31. The Ninth Question: Pain and Pleasure Are Impossible for God Most High (المسألة التاسعة الألم واللذة على الله تعالى محال)

32. The Tenth Question — On Ibn Sīnā’s Claim That God’s Reality Is Existence Qualified by Non-Attachment to Essence (المسألة العاشرة ذهب أبو علي بن سينا إلى أنه لا حقيقة لله تعالى إلا الوجود المتقيد بقيد كونه غير عارض للماهية)

33. The Eleventh Question — It Is Permissible for a Thing to Differ from Another Thing by Virtue of Its Own Specific Essence, Not by an Additional Attribute (المسألة الحادية عشرة قد يجوز أن يخالف شيء شيئا لنفس حقيقته المخصوصة لا لأمر زائد)
34. The Fourth Chapter on the Attributes of Power, Knowledge, and Others, Containing Questions (الباب الرابع في صفة القدرة والعلم وغيرهما وفيه مسائل)

35. The First Question — Whether God Acts by Free Choice or by Necessity (المسألة الأولى قد ثبت أن الله تعالى مؤثر في وجود العالم فإما أن يؤثر فيه على سبيل الصحة وهو الفاعل المختار أو على سبيل الوجود وهو الموجب بالذات)
36. The Second Question: The Maker of the World is Knowing (المسألة الثانية صانع العالم عالم)
37. The Third Issue: The Philosophers' Denial of God's Knowledge of Particulars (المسألة الثالثة أنكرت الفلاسفة كونه تعالى عالما بالجزئيات)
38. The Fourth Question: That He, Exalted, is Knower of All Things Known (المسألة الرابعة أنه تعالى عالم بكل المعلومات)
39. The Fifth Question: That He, Exalted, Is Powerful over All Possible Things (المسألة الخامسة أنه تعالى قادر على كل الممكنات)
40. The Sixth Question: All Contingent Things Occur Through God's Power, and This Is Demonstrated by Several Proofs (المسألة السادسة جميع الممكنات واقعة بقدرة الله تعالى ويدل عليه وجوه)
41. The Seventh Question: The Maker of the World is Living (المسألة السابعة صانع العالم حي)
42. The Eighth Question — That He, Exalted, is Willing (Murīd) (المسألة الثامنة أنه تعالى مريد)

43. The Ninth Question — That When We Know Something and Then See It, We Find an Immediate Distinction Between the Two States (المسألة التاسعة أنا إذا علمنا شيئا ثم أبصرناه وجدنا بين الحالتين تفرقة بديهة)
44. The Tenth Question: The Consensus of Prophets and Messengers on God Being a Speaker (المسألة العاشرة أجمع الأنبياء والرسل عليهم الصلاة والسلام على كونه تعالى متكلما)
45. The Eleventh Question: On Proving That He (Exalted) Is Knowing and Possesses Knowledge (المسألة الحادية عشرة في إثبات أنه تعالى عالم وله علم)

46. The Twelfth Question — The Specific Relation and Specific Attributions Called Power and Knowledge (المسألة الثانية عشرة هذه النسبة المخصوصة والإضافات المخصوصة المسماة بالقدرة وبالعلم لا شك أنها أمور غير قائمة بأنفسها بل ما لم توجد ذات قائمة بنفسها تكون هذه المفهومات صفات لها فإنه يمتنع وجودها)

47. The Thirteenth Question — The Mu'tazilites' Claim that God Wills by an Incidental Will Not in a Substrate (المسألة الثالثة عشرة قالت المعتزلة إن الله تعالى مريد بإرادة حادثة لا في محل وهذا عندنا باطل لوجوه)

48. The Fourteenth Question — Whether the Attribute of Creation (Takhlīq) Is Distinct from the Attribute of Power (Qudrah) (المسألة الرابعة عشرة قال قوم من فقهاء ما وراء النهر أن صفة التخليق مغايرة لصفة القدرة وقال الأكثرون ليس كذلك)
49. The Fifteenth Question: Speech is an Attribute Distinct from These Letters and Sounds (المسألة الخامسة عشرة الكلام صفة مغايرة لهذه الحروف والأصوات)
50. The Sixteenth Question: The Speech of God Almighty is Eternal (المسألة السادسة عشرة كلام الله تعالى قديم)
51. The Seventeenth Question — The Ḥanābilah’s Claim on the Divine Speech (المسألة السابعة عشرة قالت الحنابلة كلام الله تعالى ليس إلا الحروف والأصوات وهي قديمة أزلية)

52. The Eighteenth Question — On the Unity of Divine Speech (المسألة الثامنة عشرة قال الأكثرون من أهل السنة كلام الله تعالى واحد والمعتزلة أظهروا التعجب منه وقالوا الأمر والنهي والخبر والاستخبار حقائق مختلفة فالقول بأن الكلام من الواحد مع كونه واحدا أمر ونهي وخبر واستخبار يقتضي كون الحقائق الكثيرة حقيقة واحدة)
53. The Nineteenth Question: That He, Exalted, Is Eternal by His Essence, Contrary to al-Ashʿarī (المسألة التاسعة عشرة أنه تعالى باق لذاته خلافا للأشعري)

54. The Twentieth Question — On the Non-Necessity of the Absence of Evidence Entailing the Absence of the Proven (المسألة العشرون أعلم أنه لا يلزم من عدم الدليل على الشيء المدلول ألا ترى أن في الأزل لم يوجد ما يدل على وجود الله تعالى فلو لزم من عدم الدليل عدم المدلول لزم الحكم بكون الله تعالى حادثا وهذا محال)
55. The First Question — The Validity of Seeing God (Part 1) (المسألة الأولى اتفق أهل السنة على أن الله تعالى يصح أن يرى وأنكرت الفلاسفة والمعتزلة والكرامية والمجسمة ذلك (Part 1))
56. The First Question — The Validity of Seeing God (Part 2) (المسألة الأولى اتفق أهل السنة على أن الله تعالى يصح أن يرى وأنكرت الفلاسفة والمعتزلة والكرامية والمجسمة ذلك (Part 2))
57. The Second Question: That Humankind Has No Knowledge of the True Essence of God Most High (المسألة الثانية في أنه ليس عند البشر معرفة كنه الله تعالى)
58. The Third Question: Demonstrating That the God of the World Is One (المسألة الثالثة في بيان أن إله العالم واحد)
59. The Fourth Question: The Sects of Those Who Affirm Polytheism (المسألة الرابعة القائلون بالشرك طوائف)
60. The Sixth Chapter on Compulsion and Destiny, and the Investigations Pertaining to Them, Containing Questions (الباب السادس في الجبر والقدر وما يتعلق بهما من المباحث وفيه مسائل)

61. The First Question — The Chosen Position: The Act Becomes Necessary Upon the Presence of Power and the Specific Motive (المسألة الأولى المختار عندنا أن عند حصول القدرة والداعية المخصوصة يجب الفعل وعلى هذا التقدير يكون العبد فاعلا على سبيل الحقيقة ومع ذلك فتكون الأفعال بأسرها واقعة بقضاء الله تعالى وقدره)
62. The Second Question: On Establishing the Capacity (al-Qudrah) for the Servant (المسألة الثانية في إثبات القدرة للعبد)
63. The Third Question — On the Timing of Capacity (al-Istiṭāʿah) Relative to the Act (المسألة الثالثة قال أبو الحسن الأشعري الاستطاعة لا توجد إلا مع الفعل وقالت المعتزلة لا توجد إلا قبل الفعل)
64. The Fourth Question — Al-Ashʿarī’s Claim That Power Is Not Fit for Two Opposites (المسألة الرابعة قال أبو الحسن الأشعري القدرة لا تصلح للضدين)
65. The Fifth Question: On the Nature of Incapacity (al-ʿAjz) (المسألة الخامسة قال أبو الحسن الأشعري العجز صفة قائمة بالعاجز تضاد القدرة)

66. The Sixth Question — Agreement on the Capable Agent’s Power over Omission, and Dispute over Its Interpretation (المسألة السادسة اتفق المتكلمون على أن القادر كما يقدر على الفعل يقدر على الترك لكنهم اختلفوا في تفسير الترك)
67. The Original State and the Problem of Divine Power over Non-Existence (الأصلي وهذا فيه إشكال لأن القدرة صفة مؤثرة والعدم عبارة)

68. The Seventh Question — The Ahl al-Sunnah's Position on the Permissibility of Charging with What Cannot Be Endured, and the Mu'tazilah's Opposition (المسألة السابعة قال أهل السنة لا يمتنع تكليف ما لا يطلق وقالت المعتزلة أنه لا يجوز)
69. The Eighth Question: We Know by Necessity That We Have Things We Love and Things We Hate (المسألة الثامنة نحن نعلم بالضرورة أن لنا محبوبا وأن لنا مبغوضا)
70. The Ninth Question: Demonstrating That Reason Has No Authority to Judge God’s Acts as Good or Evil (المسألة التاسعة في بيان أن العقل لا مجال له في أن يحكم في أفعال الله تعالى بالتحسين والتقبيح)
71. The Tenth Question: That God Almighty Wills All Created Things, and the Proofs for This (المسألة العاشرة في أن الله تعالى مريد لجميع الكائنات ويدل عليه وجوه)
72. The First Question: That Muhammad is the Messenger of God (Peace Be Upon Him) (المسألة الأولى أن محمدا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم)
73. The Second Issue: Deniers of Prophethood Attacked Miracles from Three Angles (المسألة الثانية المنكرون للنبوات طعنوا في المعجزات من ثلاثة أوجه)
74. The Third Question: That Prophets Are Superior to Saints (المسألة الثالثة في أن الأنبياء أفضل من الأولياء)
75. The Fourth Question: My Chosen Position is that the Angel is Superior to the Human Being, with Its Supporting Proofs (المسألة الرابعة المختار عندي أن الملك أفضل من البشر ويدل عليه وجوه)

76. The Fifth Question: Establishing the Necessity of the Prophets' Infallibility (ʿIṣmah) During the Time of Messengership, with Its Supporting Proofs (المسألة الخامسة في إثبات وجوب عصمة الأنبياء عليهم السلام في وقت الرسالة ويدل عليه وجوه)

77. The Sixth Question: That Our Prophet is Superior to All Other Prophets (Peace Be Upon Them), Proven by Transmission and Reason (المسألة السادسة في أن نبينا أفضل من سائر الأنبياء عليهم السلام ويدل عليه النقل والعقل)

78. The Seventh Issue — The Truth That Muhammad (Peace Be Upon Him) Before the Descent of Revelation Was Not Upon the Law of Any Prophet (Peace Be Upon Them) (المسألة السابعة الحق أن محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم قبل نزول الوحي ما كان على شرع أحد من الأنبياء عليهم السلام)
79. The Eighth Question: The Doctrine of the Ascension (al-Miʿrāj) is True (المسألة الثامنة القول بالمعراج حق)
80. The Ninth Question: Muhammad (peace be upon him) is Sent to All Creation (المسألة التاسعة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم مبعوث إلى جميع الخلق)
81. The Tenth Question: The Path to Knowledge of His Law (المسألة العاشرة في الطريق إلى معرفة شرعه)
82. The First Question — The Correct View is that Man is Not This Perceptible Body, with Its Proofs (المسألة الأولى الصحيح أن الإنسان ليس عبارة عن هذه الجثة المحسوسة ويدل عليه وجوه)

83. The Second Question — The Philosophers' Agreement That the Soul is a Substance Neither Corporeal nor Corporeal-Like, and Its Refutation (المسألة الثانية اتفقت الفلاسفة على أن النفس جوهر ليس بجسم ولا بجسماني وهذا عندي باطل)
84. The Third Question — Abu Ali's Assertion That Rational Souls Are Originated (المسألة الثالثة قال أبو علي هذه النفوس الناطقة حادثة)
85. The Fourth Question — They Said Transmigration of Souls is Impossible (المسألة الرابعة قالوا التناسخ محال)
86. The Fifth Question — They Say: Souls Remain After the Destruction of Bodies (المسألة الخامسة قالوا النفوس باقية بعد فناء الأبدان)
87. The Sixth Question — On the Survival of the Soul (المسألة السادسة اعلم أن طريقنا في بقاء النفوس إطباق الأنبياء والأولياء والحكماء عليه ثم إن هذا المعنى يتأكد بالإقناعات العقلية)
88. The Seventh Question — Galen’s Division of the Souls (المسألة السابعة قال جالينوس النفوس ثلاث)

89. The Eighth Question: That Not Everything Loved Is Loved for the Sake of Another, Otherwise There Would Be Circularity or Infinite Regress; Rather, It Must Terminate in What Is Loved for Its Own Essence, and Induction Shows That Knowledge of the Perfect, qua Perfect, Necessitates Love of It (المسألة الثامنة أنه لا يجب في كل ما كان محبوبا أن يكون محبوبا لشيء آخر وإلا لدار أو تسلسل بل لا بد وأن ينتهي إلى ما يكون محبوبا لذاته فالاستقراء يدل على أن معرفة الكامل من حيث هو كامل يوجب محبته)
90. The Ninth Question: On the Ranks of Souls (المسألة التاسعة في مراتب النفوس)
91. The Tenth Question — The Truth According to Us: Souls Differ in Their Essence and Substance (المسألة العاشرة الحق عندنا أن النفوس مختلفة بحسب ماهيتها وجواهرها)

92. The First Question: The Restoration of the Non-Existent Is Permissible for Us, Contrary to the Majority of Philosophers, the Karramiyya, and a Group of the Mu'tazila (المسألة الأولى إعادة المعدوم عندنا جائزة خلافا لجمهور الفلاسفة والكرامية وطائفة من المعتزلة)
93. The Second Question: Bodies Are Receptive to Non-Existence (المسألة الثانية الأجسام قابلة للعدم)
94. The Third Issue: The Doctrine of the Resurrection of Bodies is True (المسألة الثالثة القول بحشر الأجساد حق)
95. First Introduction: The Possibility of the Return of That Very Body (المقدمة الأولى قولنا إن عود ذلك البدن في نفسه ممكن والدليل عليه أن)
96. The Fourth Question: The Reward and Punishment of the Grave Are True (المسألة الرابعة ثواب القبر وعذابه حق)
97. The Fifth Question: Paradise and Hellfire Are Created (المسألة الخامسة الجنة والنار مخلوقتان)
98. The Sixth Question — It Is Obligatory to Believe That God Exalted Annihilates the Heavens and the Earth (المسألة السادسة يجب الإيمان بأن الله تعالى يخرب السموات والأرض)
99. The Seventh Question: The Weighing of Deeds is True (المسألة السابعة وزن الأعمال حق)
100. The Eighth Question: The Eternity of the Reward of the People of Paradise and the Punishment of the People of Hellfire (المسألة الثامنة ثواب أهل الجنة وعذاب أهل النار دائم)
101. The Ninth Question: Works Are Not the Cause of Deserving Reward, Contrary to the Basran Mu'tazilites (المسألة التاسعة العمل لا يكون علة لاستحقاق الثواب خلافا لمعتزلة البصرة)

102. The Tenth Question — On Those Who Claim That the Threats in the Divine Books Are Merely for Intimidation, and That the Act of Inflicting Pain Does Not Occur (المسألة العاشرة من الناس من قال إن الوعيد الوارد في الكتب الإلهية إنما جاء للتخويف فأما فعل الإيلام فذلك لا يوجد واحتج عليه بوجوه)
103. The Eleventh Question: On Those Who Affirm the Punishment of Disbelievers but Deny the Punishment of Muslims (المسألة الحادية عشرة منهم من سلم حسن عذاب الكفار إلا أنه قال إن المسلمين لا يعذبون)
104. The Twelfth Question: Disagreement Among Those Who Affirm That the Wicked Among the People of Prayer Enter the Fire (المسألة الثانية عشرة الذين سلموا أن الفاسق من أهل الصلاة يدخل النار اختلفوا)

105. The Thirteenth Question — The Doctrine of the Prophet's Intercession (Shafāʿah) for the Sinners of the Community is True, Contrary to the Muʿtazilites (المسألة الثالثة عشرة القول بشفاعة الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم في حق فساق الأمة حق خلافا للمعتزلة)

106. The Fourteenth Question — Faith is Belief and Speech, with Actions Excluded from Its Meaning, and the Proofs for This (المسألة الرابعة عشرة الإيمان عبارة عن الاعتقاد والقول سبب لظهوره والأعمال خارجة عن مسمى الإيمان والدليل عليه وجوه)
107. The Fifteenth Question: Disagreement Among Those Who Hold That Works Are Included Under the Name of Faith (المسألة الخامسة عشرة القائلون بأن الأعمال داخلة تحت اسم الإيمان اختلفوا)

108. The Sixteenth Question — The Saying "I Am a Believer, If God Wills" (المسألة السادسة عشرة كان عبد الله بن مسعود رضي الله عنه يقول أنا مؤمن إن شاء الله وتبعه جمع من عظماء الصحابة والتابعين رضي الله عنهم وهو قول الشافعي رضي الله عنه وأنكره أبو حنيفة وأصحابه رحمهم الله تعالى)

109. The Seventeenth Question — The Reality of Repentance (المسألة السابعة عشرة اعلم أن الإنسان إذا صدر منه فعل أو ترك فإنه يحصل أولا في قلبه اعتقاد أنه نافع أو ضار ثم يتولد من اعتقاد كونه نافعا ميل إلى التحصيل ومن اعتقاد كونه ضارا ميل إلى الترك ثم تصير القدرة مع ذلك الميل موجبة إما للفعل أو للترك)
110. The Eighteenth Question — Repentance is Obligatory upon the Servant (المسألة الثامنة عشرة التوبة واجبة على العبد)

111. The Nineteenth Question — On the Validity of Repentance from Some Sins While Persisting in Others (المسألة التاسعة عشرة قال الأكثرون التوبة عن بعض المعاصي مع الإصرار على البعض صحيحة وقال أبو هشام إنها لا تصح)

112. The Twentieth Question — The Chosen Position: No One Among the People of the Qiblah Is Declared an Unbeliever Except by a Separate Proof (المسألة العشرون المختار عندنا أنه لا يكفر أحد من أهل القبلة إلا بدليل منفصل)

113. The First Question: The Appointment of the Imam — Whether It Is Obligatory Upon the Servants, Upon God, or Not Obligatory at All (المسألة الأولى نصب الإمام إما أن يقال إنه واجب على العباد أو على الله تعالى أو لا يجب أصلا)

114. The Second Question — Refutation of al-Sharīf al-Murtaḍā’s Argument on the Obligation of Appointing an Imam upon God (المسألة الثانية احتج الشريف المرتضى بعين هذا الدليل في وجوب نصب الإمام على الله تعالى فقلنا إنه ضعيف)
115. The Third Question: The Necessity of Infallibility as a Condition for the Validity of the Imamate (المسألة الثالثة قالت الاثنا عشرية والشيعة وجوب العصمة شرط لصحة الإمامة وقال الباقون ليس كذلك)
116. The Fourth Question — The Consensus on Establishing the Imamate by Text and the Validity of Election (المسألة الرابعة أجمعت الأمة على أنه يجوز إثبات الإمامة بالنص وهل يجوز بالاختيار أم لا)

117. The Fifth Issue — The Imamate of Ali and the Claim of Explicit Designation (المسألة الخامسة قالت الاثنا عشرية إن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم نص على إمامة علي رضي الله تعالى عنه نصا جليا لا يقبل التأويل البتة وقال الباقون لم يوجد هذا النص)
118. The Sixth Question: The True Imam After the Messenger of Allah (PBUH) Is Abu Bakr (RA) — Part 1 (المسألة السادسة الإمام الحق بعد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أبو بكر رضي الله عنه (Part 1))

119. The Sixth Question: The True Imam After the Messenger of God (Peace Be Upon Him) is Abu Bakr (May God Be Pleased with Him) — Part 2 (المسألة السادسة الإمام الحق بعد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أبو بكر رضي الله عنه (Part 2))

120. The Seventh Issue: The Most Virtuous of People After the Messenger of God, May God Bless Him and Grant Him Peace, Is Abu Bakr, May God Be Pleased with Him (المسألة السابعة أفضل الناس بعد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أبو بكر رضي الله عنه)
121. The Eighth Issue — Some Have Raised Various Objections Against the Three Imams (المسألة الثامنة بعض الناس ذكروا أنواعا من المطاعن في الأئمة الثلاثة)

122. The Ninth Question: What Proves the Imamate of Ali (May God Honor His Face) — The Agreement of the People of Loosing and Binding on His Imamate, and His Enemies Are Two Groups (المسألة التاسعة الذي يدل على إمامة علي كرم الله وجهه اتفاق أهل الحل والعقد على إمامته وأما أعداؤه ففريقان)
123. The Tenth Question — The Consensus on the Obligation to Honor Talḥah, al-Zubayr, and ʿĀʾishah (المسألة العاشرة أطبق أهل الدين على أنه يجب تعظيم طلحة والزبير وعائشة رضي الله عنهم)

paragraphs.text: Lisan al-Arab Lexical Note (Translation Anchor)
**Root: ف-ط-ر (Fa-Ta-Ra)**

*Lisān al-ʿArab*: "الفطر: ابتداء الخلق على مثال لم يسبق إليه" (al-faṭr: the beginning of creation upon a pattern not preceded by another) — This root anchors the divine act of origination as unique, unprecedented, and without prior model.
Sibawayh Grammatical Note (Syntactic Anchor)
**Rule: الابتداء بالحمد (Al-Ibtidāʾ bi-l-Ḥamd)**

*Al-Kitāb*: "إنما بدئ بالحمد لأن فيه معنى الثناء والتعظيم" (innamā budiʾa bi-l-ḥamd li-anna fīhi maʿnā al-thanāʾ wa-l-taʿẓīm) — This rule establishes the syntactic and rhetorical necessity of opening discourse with praise, as a formal marker of reverence and theological propriety.
Translation (Imam Al-Razi's Voice — Lexically Guided)
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
The Sermon of the Book

Praise be to God, the Cleaver of the dawn, the Creator of spirits and bodies, the Originator (fāṭir) of intellects and senses, the Inventor of species and genera—He who has no beginning to His eternity, no end to His generosity, no limit to His dominion, and no number to His beneficence. He created all things as He willed, without any helper or supporter, and He originated in creation without deliberation or reflection. The breasts of all things are adorned with the necklaces of His wisdom, and the faces of the living are illuminated by the stars of His grace.

He united the spirit and the body in the most excellent composition, and by His power He blended the subtle with the dense. He decreed every matter firmly and originated every act perfectly—a wondrous lesson and a reminder for every penitent servant.

I praise Him, and no praise can ever reach the fullness of His blessings; I glorify Him with His most noble attributes and His most honored names. And I send blessings upon His Messenger, the caller to the upright religion, the reciter of the Mighty Qurʾān, the awaited one in the prayer of Abraham—a prophet whom Jesus announced to his people in his time, whose name is embroidered upon the banners of the faith, whose station was elevated while Adam was still between water and clay. That is Muhammad, the master of the first and the last, and the seal of the prophets and messengers.
May the blessings of God be upon him, and upon his pure and immaculate family, and upon his companions—both the Helpers (anṣār) and the Emigrants (muhājirūn)—and peace be upon him and upon them all.
To proceed: This is a concise work comprising the science of the foundations of religion (uṣūl al-dīn), and it is arranged according to chapters.
