paragraphs.text: Quad-Lexical & Syntactic Apparatus (AynEngine AI v3.0.0)

- Root: عبد (ʿ-b-d)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning is humility, submission, and servitude; the slave (ʿabd) is one who is owned and obedient.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Worship (ʿibādah) is the utmost degree of humility and submission before God, coupled with the belief in His Lordship (rubūbiyyah); it is not mere action but action performed in a state of reverent abasement.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes servitude to a master; metaphorical (majāz) extension applies it to rational obedience and devotion to God's commands.
- Root: هدي (h-d-y)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning is gentle, guiding direction (irshād) toward a path; also the gift of guidance itself.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Guidance (hidāyah) in the Quranic sense is of two kinds: (1) the universal guidance of creation (takwīn) and (2) the specific guidance of religion (tashrīʿ) — the latter being the one sought in {اهدنا}.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: showing the way (dalālah ʿalā al-ṭarīq). Metaphorical: leading one to the truth through proof (burhān) or through inner purification (taṣfiyah).
- Root: صرط (ṣ-r-ṭ) [from سرط]
 * Lisan / Ayn: The path (ṣirāṭ) is the clear, broad, and straight road; derived from the notion of swallowing (sarṭ) because it "swallows" the traveler along its course.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The straight path (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm) is the way of truth that leads to God, encompassing both correct belief and correct action.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: a wide, level highway. Metaphorical: the religion of Islam and the prophetic way (sunnah).
- Sibawayh Rule: The Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — In {إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين}, the repetition of the object pronoun (إياك) before each verb creates two independent, emphatic clauses, each with its own fronted object for exclusivity (ḥaṣr), rather than a single conjoined predicate. This syntactic structure underscores that both worship and seeking aid are directed solely to God, each as a separate act of devotion.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)

As for His saying, exalted be He, {You alone we worship, and You alone we seek help from} [1:5], know that worship (ʿibādah) is the performance of the commanded act in a manner of magnifying the Commander. So as long as it has not been established by proof (dalīl) that this world has one God — powerful over an infinite number of possible things, knowing an infinite number of knowable things, free of all needs — and that He commanded His servants to do some things and forbade them from others, and that it is obligatory upon all creatures to obey Him and submit to His impositions (takālīf), then it is impossible to fulfill the requirements of His saying {You alone we worship}. Then, after completing the aforementioned station, one must detail the categories of those impositions and explain the types of those commands and prohibitions. And everything that has been authored in religion among the "books of jurisprudence" (kutub al-fiqh) enters into the divine impositions — just as the divine impositions according to this sacred law (sharīʿah) enter into it, so too do the divine impositions according to the laws that God had revealed to the previous prophets. Also entering into it are the laws with which God charged His angels in the heavens since He created the angels and commanded them to occupy themselves with acts of worship and obedience. Moreover, the "books of jurisprudence" comprise an explanation of the impositions directed at the works of the bodily limbs (jawāriḥ). As for the categories of impositions found in the works of the hearts, they are greater, mightier, and more sublime — and these are what the "books of ethics" (kutub al-akhlāq) and the "books of governance" (kutub al-siyāsāt) encompass, according to the differing creeds and diverse nations. And when a person considers the totality of these investigations and knows that all of them fall under His saying {You alone we worship}, he then knows that the issues contained in this verse are like the encompassing sea (al-baḥr al-muḥīṭ) which intellects and thoughts cannot reach save a small portion of it.

As for His saying, may His glory be exalted: {Guide us to the straight path} [1:6], know that it is a request for guidance (hidāyah). And for the attainment of guidance there are two ways: one of them is the pursuit of knowledge through proof (dalīl) and argument (ḥujjah), and the second is through the purification of the inner self (taṣfiyat al-bāṭin) and spiritual discipline (riyāḍah). As for the methods of rational inference (istiDLĀL), they are without end — because there is no atom among the atoms of the upper and lower worlds except that that atom bears witness to the perfection of His divinity, to the might of His power, and to the majesty of His absolute self-sufficiency (ṣamadiyyah), as it has been said:
"In everything there is a sign of Him — pointing to the fact that He is One."

Its demonstration (taqrīr) is this: the bodies of the world are equal in the quiddity of corporeality (māhiyyat al-jismiyyah) and differ in their attributes — namely, colors, places, and states. And it is impossible that the specification of each body with its particular attribute be due to corporeality itself or to the necessary concomitants of corporeality; otherwise, uniformity would necessarily result. Therefore, it is necessary that this be due to the specification of a Specifier (mukhaṣṣiṣ) and the governance of a Governor (mudabbir). And that Specifier — if it were a body, the argument would recur upon it; and if it is not a body, then it is the sought object. Then, that existent — if it were not living, knowing, and powerful, but rather its effect were by emanation (fayḍ) and nature (ṭabʿ), the same necessary implication of uniformity would return; and if it is living, knowing, and powerful, then it is the sought object. Once you have understood this, it has become clear that every single one of the atoms of the heavens and the earth is a truthful witness and a speaking reporter of the existence of the powerful, wise, all-knowing God. And the Shaykh, the Imām, my father, Ḍiyāʾ al-Dīn ʿUmar — may God have mercy on him — used to say: "God, exalted be He, has in every individual substance (jawhar fard) infinite types of evidences pointing to power, wisdom, and mercy." That is because every individual substance can be placed in infinite locations successively, and can also be characterized by infinite attributes successively; and every one of those estimated states, were it to occur, points to the need for the existence of the wise, merciful Maker. So it is established by what we have mentioned that this type of investigation is without end. As for the attainment of guidance by way of spiritual discipline (riyāḍah) and purification (taṣfiyah), that is a sea with no shore. And for every one of the wayfarers to God there is a particular path (manhaj) and a designated watering-place (mashrab), as He said: {And for every direction there is a face to which he turns} [2:148]. Intellects cannot pause upon those secrets, and understandings have no report of the beginnings of the fields of those lights. The verifiers among the knowers (al-ʿārifūn al-muḥaqqiqūn) have glimpsed in them profound investigations and subtle secrets — and when the understandings of the majority sought to ascend to them, they fell short.

EPUB/chap_01.xhtml.title: On the Secrets of the Phrase "There is no god but Allah" (Lā ilāha illā Allāh)

paragraphs.text: I say — may Allah grant success — this section concerns the secrets embedded within the phrase "There is no god but Allah" {لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ}. Know that this blessed utterance is the pivot of the faith and the foundation of the religion, for it comprises two pillars: the negation of all that is worshipped besides Allah, and the affirmation of divinity exclusively for Him. The secret of its power lies in its grammatical form — the particle of negation "lā" that denies the entire genus of deities, sweeping away every false object of worship, whether celestial bodies, idols, jinn, or human beings; then the exception "illā Allāh" that establishes the sole, true object of worship, the Necessary Existent, who is deserving of all devotion by virtue of His essence. Thus, the tongue articulates what the heart must affirm and the limbs must enact: that no being shares in divinity, and that all acts of worship — prayer, supplication, trust, and obedience — are due to Allah alone, without partner or associate. And this is the innermost secret of the Shahada, which the prophets proclaimed and upon which the heavens and the earth were established.

paragraphs.text: Quad-Lexical & Syntactic Apparatus (AynEngine AI v3.0.0)

- Root: س ر ر (s-r-r)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of "concealment," "innermost secret," that which is hidden from public knowledge; the heart's hidden depth.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): In theological usage, "sirr" denotes the hidden divine wisdom and ontological realities that lie beneath the outward wording of the Shahada — not mere lexical meaning but the metaphysical import accessible only to the discerning.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (haqiqah) sense: a hidden matter. Metaphorical (majaz) sense: the profound, esoteric purport of a statement that requires unveiling (kashf) — here, the inner dimensions of the declaration of divine unity.
- Root: ك ل م (k-l-m)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Speech, utterance, word; a complete meaningful expression.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "Kalimah" in Quranic and theological context refers to a proposition bearing a complete creedal assertion — here, the Shahada as the foundational statement of tawḥīd.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: a spoken word. Metaphorical: the entire creedal formula as a single "word" of faith, as in {قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ} — a compact utterance carrying infinite meaning.
- Root: إ ل ه (ʾ-l-h)
 * Lisan / Ayn: That which is worshipped; deity; from ʾaliha (to be bewildered, to seek refuge), indicating the object of supreme devotion and awe.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "Ilāh" denotes the true object of worship — in tawḥīd, exclusively Allah, the Necessary Existent (wājib al-wujūd), negating all false objects of devotion.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: any object of worship. Metaphorical/creedal: restricted to the One True God, as the phrase negates all ilāhs and affirms only Allah.
- Sibawayh Rule: Negation + Exception Construction (nafy wa-istithnāʾ) — The sentence "Lā ilāha illā Allāh" is parsed as: "Lā" negating the genus (lā al-nāfiyah li-l-jins), with "ilāha" as its noun (ism) in the accusative, and "illā Allāh" as the exception (mustathnā) — yielding total negation of all deities and exclusive affirmation of Allah alone. This syntactic structure is the grammatical engine of tawḥīd.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)

I say — may Allah grant success — this section concerns the secrets embedded within the phrase "There is no god but Allah" {لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ}. Know that this blessed utterance is the pivot of the faith and the foundation of the religion, for it comprises two pillars: the negation of all that is worshipped besides Allah, and the affirmation of divinity exclusively for Him. The secret of its power lies in its grammatical form — the particle of negation "lā" that denies the entire genus of deities, sweeping away every false object of worship, whether celestial bodies, idols, jinn, or human beings; then the exception "illā Allāh" that establishes the sole, true object of worship, the Necessary Existent, who is deserving of all devotion by virtue of His essence. Thus, the tongue articulates what the heart must affirm and the limbs must enact: that no being shares in divinity, and that all acts of worship — prayer, supplication, trust, and obedience — are due to Allah alone, without partner or associate. And this is the innermost secret of the Shahada, which the prophets proclaimed and upon which the heavens and the earth were established.

EPUB/chap_01.xhtml.title: Section 1 — Refutation of Their Doctrine of the Eternity of the World

paragraphs.text: I say: The detailed doctrine is this: The philosophers have differed concerning the eternity of the world. The opinion upon which the majority of them, both early and late, have settled is the affirmation of its eternity — that it has never ceased to exist alongside God (Exalted be He), being an effect of Him and consequent upon Him, not posterior to Him in time, but concomitant with Him as the effect is concomitant with its cause and as light is concomitant with the sun. The priority of the Creator over it is like the priority of the cause over the effect — a priority by essence and rank, not by time. It is reported of Plato that he said: The world is composed and originated. Then some of them interpreted his words [away] and refused to attribute to him the belief in the world's origination. Galen, at the end of his life, in the book he called "What Galen Believes as Opinion," adopted suspension of judgment on this question — that he does not know whether the world is eternal or originated. He perhaps indicated that it cannot be known, and that this is not due to a deficiency in him, but to the fact that this question is in itself intractable to intellects. But this is like an anomaly in their doctrine; the doctrine of all of them is that it is eternal, and that in sum it is inconceivable that an originated thing should issue from an eternal thing without any intermediary whatsoever.

Now, if I were to set out to describe what has been transmitted from them by way of arguments, and to mention the objections against them, I would blacken many pages on this question. But there is no good in prolixity. Let us omit from their arguments those that run in the manner of arbitrary assertion or weak imagination, whose solution is easy for any observer. Let us confine ourselves to presenting what has weight in the soul — that which it is not permissible for a skeptic to advance against the masters of speculation, for the skepticism of the weak is possible with the slightest confusion. This class of arguments is three:

The first: It is impossible for an originated thing to proceed from an eternal thing absolutely. They say: It is impossible for an originated thing to issue from an eternal thing absolutely, because if we suppose the eternal and the world, for example, has not issued from it, then it has not issued only because there was no preponderator for its existence; rather, the existence of the world was pure possibility. So when it occurs afterward, it is either the case that a preponderator has newly arisen, or it has not. If no preponderator has newly arisen, the world remains in pure possibility as it was before. But if a preponderator has newly arisen, then who originated that preponderator? And why did it occur now and not before? The question concerning the origination of the preponderator stands [unanswered]. In sum, if the states of the eternal are similar, then either nothing issues from it at all, or it issues perpetually. But that the state of abstention should be distinguished from the state of commencement — that is impossible.

Its verification is to say: Why did the world not occur before its occurrence? This cannot be referred to His incapacity to originate, nor to the impossibility of origination, for that would lead to the eternal being transformed from incapacity to power, and the world from impossibility to possibility — both of which are impossible. Nor can it be said: There was no purpose before, then a purpose newly arose. Nor can it be referred to the absence of an instrument, then to its presence. Rather, the closest thing that can be imagined is to say: He did not will its existence before that. Then it follows that one must say: Its existence came about because He became willing of its existence after not being willing — so the will would have originated.

But its origination in His essence is impossible, for He is not a locus for originated events; and its origination outside His essence does not make Him willing. Let us leave aside the consideration of the locus of its origination. Is not the difficulty standing concerning the very origin of the will? That from where did it originate? Why did it occur now and not before? Did it occur now not from God? For if an originated thing is permissible without an originator, then let the world be originated with no maker — otherwise, what difference is there between one originated thing and another? And if it occurred through God's causing it to occur, then why did it occur now and not before? Was it for the absence of an instrument, or power, or purpose, or nature? Then when that was replaced by existence and it occurred, the same difficulty returns. Or was it for the absence of will? Then the will would stand in need of a will, and likewise the first will, and it would regress to infinity.

So it is thereby established, by absolute statement, that the issuance of an originated thing from the eternal without any change in the eternal — in power, instrument, time, purpose, or nature — is impossible. And to suppose a change of state is impossible, for the discourse concerning that originated change is like the discourse concerning anything else — and all of it is impossible. And whenever the world is existent and its origination is impossible, its eternity is established necessarily.

This is the most confused of their arguments. In sum, their discourse in the other questions of metaphysics is flimsier than their discourse in this question, for here they are able to employ varieties of imagination of which they are incapable elsewhere. Therefore we have presented this question first, and presented their strongest arguments.
The objection is from two aspects:

One of them is to say: By what do you reject the one who says: The world originated by an eternal will that necessitated its existence at the time at which it existed, and that non-existence continued to the limit to which it continued, and that existence began from where it began; that existence before that was not willed, so it did not occur for that reason; and that at its time in which it occurred, it was willed by the eternal will, so it occurred for that reason? What prevents this belief, and what renders it impossible?

For if it is said: This is impossible, with manifest impossibility, because the originated thing is an effect and a caused thing. And just as it is impossible for an originated thing to exist without a cause and an efficient cause, so it is impossible for an efficient cause to exist whose conditions of efficiency, its pillars, and its causes have been completed such that nothing at all remains awaited, and then the caused thing is delayed. Rather, the existence of the caused thing upon the realization of the efficient cause with all its conditions complete is necessary, and its delay is impossible, just as the existence of an originated caused thing without a cause is impossible. For before the existence of the world, the willer existed, and the will existed, and its relation to the willed existed, and no willer newly arose, and no will newly arose, and no new relation of the will arose that had not been — for all of that would be change. So how did the willed newly arise? And what prevented its new arising before that? The state of new arising was not distinguished from the previous state in any of the things, or any of the matters, or any of the states, or any of the relations — rather, the matters were exactly as they had been. Then the willed did not exist, and they remained exactly as they were, then the willed existed. What is this but the extreme of impossibility?

And this applies also to conventional matters — in divorce, for example. And the impossibility of this genus is not [confined] to the necessary essential cause and effect, but even to the conventional and the stipulated. For if a man uttered the divorce of his wife and the separation did not occur immediately, it would not be conceivable that it occur afterward, because he made the utterance a cause of the ruling by stipulation and convention. So the delay of the effect is not intelligible, unless he suspends the divorce upon the coming of tomorrow or upon entering the house. Then it does not occur immediately, but occurs at the coming of tomorrow and at entering the house, for he made it a cause in relation to something awaited. So when that was not present at the time — namely, tomorrow and the entering — the occurrence of the caused thing was suspended upon the presence of what is not present. So the caused thing did not occur except with the new arising of a matter — namely, the entering and the coming of tomorrow. So much so that if he wanted to delay the caused thing from the utterance without suspending it upon the occurrence of what does not yet exist, it would not be intelligible — even though he is the stipulator and he is the chooser in the detailing of the stipulation. So if we cannot stipulate this by our own desire, and we do not find it intelligible, then how can we find it intelligible in the essential, rational, necessary causations?

As for habitual matters, what is obtained by our intention does not lag behind the intention, with the intention present, except due to an obstacle. For when the intention and the power are realized and the obstacles are removed, the delay of the intended thing is not intelligible. This is only conceivable in resolution (ʿazm), because resolution is not sufficient for the existence of the act. Rather, resolution to write does not bring about the writing unless a new intention arises — which is an impulse in the human being, newly arising at the moment of the act. So if the eternal will is in the status of our intention toward the act, then the delay of the intended thing is not conceivable except due to an obstacle, and the precedence of the intention is not conceivable — for an intention today toward a rising tomorrow is not intelligible except by way of resolution. And if the eternal will is in the status of our resolution, then that is not sufficient for the occurrence of the resolved-upon thing; rather, there must be a new arising of an intentional impulse at the moment of bringing into existence — and in that is the affirmation of change in the eternal.

### | مسألة في إبطال قولهم بقدم العالم

### | مذهب الفلاسفة

تفصيل المذهب: اختلفت الفلاسفة في قدم العالم. فالذي استقر عليه رأي
جماهيرهم المتقدمين والمتأخرين القول بقدمه وأنه لم يزل موجودا مع الله
تعالى ومعلولا له ومسوقا له غير متأخر عنه بالزمان مساوقة المعلول للعلة
ومساوقة النور للشمس، وأن تقدم الباري عليه كتقدم العلة على المعلول، وهو
تقدم بالذات والرتبة لا بالزمان. وحكي عن أفلاطن أنه قال: العالم مكون
ومحدث. ثم منهم من أول كلامه وأبى أن يكون حدث العالم معتقدا له. وذهب
جالينوس في آخر عمره في الكتاب الذي سماه "ما يعتقده جالينوس رأيا" إلى
التوقف في هذه المسألة. وأنه لا يدري العالم قديم أو محدث. وربما
دل على أنه لا يمكن أن يعرف وأن ذلك ليس لقصور فيه بل لاستعصاء هذه
المسألة في نفسها على العقول، ولكن هذا كالشاذ في مذهبهم وإنما مذهب جميعهم
أنه قديم وأنه بالجملة لا يتصور أن يصدر حادث من قديم بغير واسطة أصلا.

### | اختيار أشد أدلتهم وقعا في النفس

إيراد أدلتهم. لو ذهبت أصف ما نقل عنهم في معرض الأدلة وذكر في الاعتراض
عليه لسودت في هذه المسألة أوراقا، ولكن لا خير في التطويل. فلنحذف من
أدلتهم ما يجري مجرى التحكم أو التخيل الضعيف الذي يهون على كل ناظر حله.
ولنقتصر على إيراد ما له وقع في النفس، مما لا يجوز أن ينهض مشككا لفحول
النظار، فإن تشكيك الضعفاء بأدنى خبال ممكن.
وهذا الفن من الأدلة ثلاثة:
الأول يستحيل حدوث حادث من قديم مطلقا قولهم يستحيل صدور حادث من قديم
مطلقا، لأنا إذا فرضنا القديم ولم يصدر منه العالم مثلا فإنما لم يصدر لأنه
لم يكن للوجود مرجح بل كان وجود العالم ممكنا إمكانا صرفا، فإذا حدث بعد
ذلك لم يخل إما أن تجدد مرجح أو لم يتجدد، فإن لم يتجدد مرجح بقي العالم
على الإمكان الصرف كما قبل ذلك، وإن تجدد مرجح فمن محدث ذلك المرجح؟ ولم
حدث الآن ولم يحدث من قبل؟ والسؤال في حدوث المرجح قائم. وبالجملة فأحوال
القديم إذا كانت متشابهة فإما أن لا يوجد عنه شيء قط وإما أن يوجد على
الدوام، فأما أن يتميز حال الترك عن حال الشروع فهو محال.
## $ لم لم يحدث العالم قبل حدوثه؟ ...
وتحقيقه أن يقال: لم لم يحدث العالم قبل حدوثه؟ لا يمكن أن يحال على عجزه
عن الأحداث ولا على استحالة الحدوث، فإن ذلك يؤدي إلى أن ينقلب القديم من
العجز إلى القدرة والعالم من الاستحالة إلى الإمكان، وكلاهما محالان. ولا
أمكن أن يقال: لم يكن قبله غرض ثم تجدد غرض، ولا أمكن أن يحال على فقد آلة
ثم على وجودها، بل أقرب ما يتخيل أن يقال: لم يرد وجوده قبل ذلك. فيلزم أن
يقال: حصل وجوده لأنه صار مريدا لوجوده
بعد أن لم يكن مريدا، فيكون قد حدثت الإرادة.

### | أو قبل حدوث الإرادة؟

وحدوثه في ذاته محال لأنه ليس محل الحوادث، وحدوثه لا في ذاته لا يجعله
مريدا.
ولنترك النظر في محل حدوثه. أليس الإشكال قائما في أصل حدوثه! وأنه من
أين حدث؟ ولم حدث الآن ولم يحدث قبله؟ أحدث الآن لا من جهة الله؟ فإن جاز
حادث من غير محدث فليكن العالم حادثا لا صانع له، وإلا فأي فرق بين حادث
وحادث؟ وإن حدث بإحداث الله فلم حدث الآن ولم يحدث من قبل؟ ألعدم آلة أو
قدرة أو غرض أو طبيعة؟ فلما أن تبدل ذلك بالوجود وحدث عاد الإشكال بعينه.
أو لعدم الإرادة؟ فتفتقر الإرادة إلى إرادة وكذى الإرادة الأولى، ويتسلسل
إلى غير نهاية.
## $ يستحيل حدوث حادث من غير تغير ...
فإذن قد تحقق بالقول المطلق أن صدور الحادث من القديم من غير تغير أمر من
القديم في قدرة أو آلة أو وقت أو غرض أو طبع محال، وتقدير تغير حال محال،
لأن الكلام في ذلك التغير الحادث كالكلام في غيره
والكل محال، ومهما كان العالم موجودا واستحال حدثه ثبت قدمه لا محالة.

### | وهذا أقوى أدلتهم

فهذا أخبل أدلتهم. وبالجملة كلامهم في سائر مسائل الإلهيات أرك من كلامهم
في هذه المسألة، إذ يقدرون هاهنا على فنون من التخييل لا يتمكنون منه في
غيرها. فلذلك قدمنا هذه المسألة وقدمنا أقوى أدلتهم.

### | لماذا يستحيل حدوث حادث بإرادة قديمة؟

الاعتراض من وجهين:
أحدهما أن يقال: بم تنكرون على من يقول: إن العالم حدث بإرادة قديمة
اقتضت وجوده في الوقت الذي وجد فيه، وأن يستمر العدم إلى الغاية التي استمر
إليها، وأن يبتدئ الوجود من حيث ابتدأ، وأن الوجود قبله لم يكن مرادا فلم
يحدث لذلك، وأنه في وقته الذي حدث فيه مراد بالإرادة القديمة فحدث لذلك،
فما المانع لهذا الاعتقاد وما المحيل له؟
## $ قولهم لكل حادث سبب ...
فإن قيل: هذا محال بين الإحالة لأن الحادث موجب ومسبب. وكما يستحيل حادث
بغير سبب وموجب، يستحيل وجود موجب قد تم بشرائط إيجابه وأركانه وأسبابه حتى
لم يبق شيء منتظر البتة ثم يتأخر الموجب، بل وجود الموجب عند تحقق الموجب
بتمام شروطه ضروري وتأخره محال حسب استحالة وجود الحادث الموجب بلا موجب.
فقبل وجود العالم كان المريد موجودا والإرادة موجودة ونسبتها إلى المراد
موجودة ولم يتجدد مريد ولم يتجدد إرادة ولا تجدد للإرادة نسبة لم تكن، فإن
كل ذلك تغير فكيف تجدد المراد وما المانع من التجدد قبل ذلك؟ وحال التجدد
لم يتميز عن الحال السابق في شيء من الأشياء وأمر من الأمور وحال من
الأحوال ونسبة من النسب، بل الأمور كما كانت بعينها. ثم لم يكن يوجد
المراد، وبقيت بعينها كما كانت، فوجد المراد ما هذا إلا غاية الإحالة.
وذلك في الأمور الوضعية أيضا، في الطلاق مثلا وليس استحالة هذا الجنس في
الموجب والموجب الضروري الذاتي بل وفي العرفي والوضعي، فإن الرجل لو تلفظ
بطلاق زوجته ولم تحصل البينونة في الحال لم يتصور أن تحصل بعده لأنه جعل
اللفظ علة للحكم بالوضع
والاصطلاح، فلم يعقل تأخر المعلول إلا أن يعلق الطلاق بمجيء الغد أو
بدخول الدار، فلا يقع في الحال ولكن يقع عند مجيء الغد وعند دخول الدار،
فإنه جعله علة بالإضافة إلى شيء منتظر. فلما لم يكن حاضرا في الوقت، وهو
الغد والدخول، توقف حصول الموجب على حضور ما ليس بحاضر، فما حصل الموجب إلا
وقد تجدد أمر وهو الدخول وحضور الغد، حتى لو أراد أن يؤخر الموجب عن اللفظ
غير منوط بحصول ما ليس بحاصل، لم يعقل، مع أنه الواضع وأنه المختار في
تفصيل الوضع. فإذا لم يمكننا وضع هذا بشهوتنا ولم نعقله فكيف نعقله في
الإيجابات الذاتية العقلية الضرورية؟

### | المقصود فعله لا يتأخر إلا بمانع

وأما في العادات فما يحصل بقصدنا لا يتأخر عن القصد، مع وجود القصد إليه،
إلا بمانع، فإن تحقيق القصد والقدرة وارتفعت الموانع لم يعقل تأخر المقصود،
وإنما يتصور ذلك في العزم لأن العزم غير كاف في وجود الفعل، بل العزم على
الكتابة لا يوقع الكتابة ما لم يتجدد قصد هو انبعاث في الإنسان متجدد حال
الفعل، فإن كانت الإرادة القديمة في حكم قصدنا إلى الفعل فلا يتصور تأخر
المقصود إلا بمانع، ولا يتصور تقدم القصد، فلا يعقل قصد في اليوم
إلى قيام في الغد إلا بطريق العزم. وإن كانت الإرادة القديمة في حكم
عزمنا فليس ذلك كافيا في وقوع المعزوم عليه، بل لا بد من تجدد انبعاث قصدي
عند الإيجاد، وفيه قول بتغير القديم.

وأما في العادات فما يحصل بقصدنا لا يتأخر عن القصد، مع وجود القصد إليه،
إلا بمانع، فإن تحقيق القصد والقدرة وارتفعت الموانع لم يعقل تأخر المقصود،
وإنما يتصور ذلك في العزم لأن العزم غير كاف في وجود الفعل، بل العزم على
الكتابة لا يوقع الكتابة ما لم يتجدد قصد هو انبعاث في الإنسان متجدد حال
الفعل، فإن كانت الإرادة القديمة في حكم قصدنا إلى الفعل فلا يتصور تأخر
المقصود إلا بمانع، ولا يتصور تقدم القصد، فلا يعقل قصد في اليوم
إلى قيام في الغد إلا بطريق العزم. وإن كانت الإرادة القديمة في حكم
عزمنا فليس ذلك كافيا في وقوع المعزوم عليه، بل لا بد من تجدد انبعاث قصدي
عند الإيجاد، وفيه قول بتغير القديم.

- Root: ق-د-م (q-d-m)
 * Lisān / ʿAyn: Primordiality, precedence, that which is anterior and has no beginning; al-qadīm is that whose existence has no temporal commencement.
 * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, qidam denotes absolute non-priority by time, contrasted with ḥudūth (origination in time); it is a modal attribute of existence, not a temporal quantity.
 * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for temporal anteriority in common speech; metaphorically (majāz) transferred to ontological priority of cause over effect, as in the philosophers' usage here.
- Root: ح-د-ث (ḥ-d-th)
 * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be new, to occur after non-existence; ḥādith is that which comes into being after not having been.
 * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥudūth is the contingency of existence upon a temporal origination; the central term in the cosmological proof of the world's createdness.
 * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for temporal inception; the philosophers' denial of it for the world is a metaphorical extension of causal language.
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
 * Lisān / ʿAyn: The cause (ʿillah) is that which necessitates its effect (maʿlūl); succession of effect upon cause.
 * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In metaphysical discourse, ʿillah denotes the sufficient reason; the philosophers' claim of eternal causal concomitance (musāwaqah) is here examined.
 * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a cause-effect relation in time; the philosophers use it metaphorically for a non-temporal, essential priority.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīm wa Taʾkhīr (Fronting and Delaying) — The conditional structure "law... la..." (if... then...) governs the hypothetical arguments; the particle "innamā" (only) restricts the predicate, crucial for parsing the philosophers' claims of exclusive causality.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)

I say: The detailed doctrine is this: The philosophers have differed concerning the eternity of the world. The opinion upon which the majority of them, both early and late, have settled is the affirmation of its eternity — that it has never ceased to exist alongside God (Exalted be He), being an effect of Him and consequent upon Him, not posterior to Him in time, but concomitant with Him as the effect is concomitant with its cause and as light is concomitant with the sun. The priority of the Creator over it is like the priority of the cause over the effect — a priority by essence and rank, not by time. It is reported of Plato that he said: The world is composed and originated. Then some of them interpreted his words [away] and refused to attribute to him the belief in the world's origination. Galen, at the end of his life, in the book he called "What Galen Believes as Opinion," adopted suspension of judgment on this question — that he does not know whether the world is eternal or originated. He perhaps indicated that it cannot be known, and that this is not due to a deficiency in him, but to the fact that this question is in itself intractable to intellects. But this is like an anomaly in their doctrine; the doctrine of all of them is that it is eternal, and that in sum it is inconceivable that an originated thing should issue from an eternal thing without any intermediary whatsoever.

Now, if I were to set out to describe what has been transmitted from them by way of arguments, and to mention the objections against them, I would blacken many pages on this question. But there is no good in prolixity. Let us omit from their arguments those that run in the manner of arbitrary assertion or weak imagination, whose solution is easy for any observer. Let us confine ourselves to presenting what has weight in the soul — that which it is not permissible for a skeptic to advance against the masters of speculation, for the skepticism of the weak is possible with the slightest confusion. This class of arguments is three:

The first: It is impossible for an originated thing to proceed from an eternal thing absolutely. They say: It is impossible for an originated thing to issue from an eternal thing absolutely, because if we suppose the eternal and the world, for example, has not issued from it, then it has not issued only because there was no preponderator for its existence; rather, the existence of the world was pure possibility. So when it occurs afterward, it is either the case that a preponderator has newly arisen, or it has not. If no preponderator has newly arisen, the world remains in pure possibility as it was before. But if a preponderator has newly arisen, then who originated that preponderator? And why did it occur now and not before? The question concerning the origination of the preponderator stands [unanswered]. In sum, if the states of the eternal are similar, then either nothing issues from it at all, or it issues perpetually. But that the state of abstention should be distinguished from the state of commencement — that is impossible.

Its verification is to say: Why did the world not occur before its occurrence? This cannot be referred to His incapacity to originate, nor to the impossibility of origination, for that would lead to the eternal being transformed from incapacity to power, and the world from impossibility to possibility — both of which are impossible. Nor can it be said: There was no purpose before, then a purpose newly arose. Nor can it be referred to the absence of an instrument, then to its presence. Rather, the closest thing that can be imagined is to say: He did not will its existence before that. Then it follows that one must say: Its existence came about because He became willing of its existence after not being willing — so the will would have originated.

But its origination in His essence is impossible, for He is not a locus for originated events; and its origination outside His essence does not make Him willing. Let us leave aside the consideration of the locus of its origination. Is not the difficulty standing concerning the very origin of the will? That from where did it originate? Why did it occur now and not before? Did it occur now not from God? For if an originated thing is permissible without an originator, then let the world be originated with no maker — otherwise, what difference is there between one originated thing and another? And if it occurred through God's causing it to occur, then why did it occur now and not before? Was it for the absence of an instrument, or power, or purpose, or nature? Then when that was replaced by existence and it occurred, the same difficulty returns. Or was it for the absence of will? Then the will would stand in need of a will, and likewise the first will, and it would regress to infinity.

So it is thereby established, by absolute statement, that the issuance of an originated thing from the eternal without any change in the eternal — in power, instrument, time, purpose, or nature — is impossible. And to suppose a change of state is impossible, for the discourse concerning that originated change is like the discourse concerning anything else — and all of it is impossible. And whenever the world is existent and its origination is impossible, its eternity is established necessarily.

This is the most confused of their arguments. In sum, their discourse in the other questions of metaphysics is flimsier than their discourse in this question, for here they are able to employ varieties of imagination of which they are incapable elsewhere. Therefore we have presented this question first, and presented their strongest arguments.
The objection is from two aspects:

One of them is to say: By what do you reject the one who says: The world originated by an eternal will that necessitated its existence at the time at which it existed, and that non-existence continued to the limit to which it continued, and that existence began from where it began; that existence before that was not willed, so it did not occur for that reason; and that at its time in which it occurred, it was willed by the eternal will, so it occurred for that reason? What prevents this belief, and what renders it impossible?

For if it is said: This is impossible, with manifest impossibility, because the originated thing is an effect and a caused thing. And just as it is impossible for an originated thing to exist without a cause and an efficient cause, so it is impossible for an efficient cause to exist whose conditions of efficiency, its pillars, and its causes have been completed such that nothing at all remains awaited, and then the caused thing is delayed. Rather, the existence of the caused thing upon the realization of the efficient cause with all its conditions complete is necessary, and its delay is impossible, just as the existence of an originated caused thing without a cause is impossible. For before the existence of the world, the willer existed, and the will existed, and its relation to the willed existed, and no willer newly arose, and no will newly arose, and no new relation of the will arose that had not been — for all of that would be change. So how did the willed newly arise? And what prevented its new arising before that? The state of new arising was not distinguished from the previous state in any of the things, or any of the matters, or any of the states, or any of the relations — rather, the matters were exactly as they had been. Then the willed did not exist, and they remained exactly as they were, then the willed existed. What is this but the extreme of impossibility?

And this applies also to conventional matters — in divorce, for example. And the impossibility of this genus is not [confined] to the necessary essential cause and effect, but even to the conventional and the stipulated. For if a man uttered the divorce of his wife and the separation did not occur immediately, it would not be conceivable that it occur afterward, because he made the utterance a cause of the ruling by stipulation and convention. So the delay of the effect is not intelligible, unless he suspends the divorce upon the coming of tomorrow or upon entering the house. Then it does not occur immediately, but occurs at the coming of tomorrow and at entering the house, for he made it a cause in relation to something awaited. So when that was not present at the time — namely, tomorrow and the entering — the occurrence of the caused thing was suspended upon the presence of what is not present. So the caused thing did not occur except with the new arising of a matter — namely, the entering and the coming of tomorrow. So much so that if he wanted to delay the caused thing from the utterance without suspending it upon the occurrence of what does not yet exist, it would not be intelligible — even though he is the stipulator and he is the chooser in the detailing of the stipulation. So if we cannot stipulate this by our own desire, and we do not find it intelligible, then how can we find it intelligible in the essential, rational, necessary causations?

As for habitual matters, what is obtained by our intention does not lag behind the intention, with the intention present, except due to an obstacle. For when the intention and the power are realized and the obstacles are removed, the delay of the intended thing is not intelligible. This is only conceivable in resolution (ʿazm), because resolution is not sufficient for the existence of the act. Rather, resolution to write does not bring about the writing unless a new intention arises — which is an impulse in the human being, newly arising at the moment of the act. So if the eternal will is in the status of our intention toward the act, then the delay of the intended thing is not conceivable except due to an obstacle, and the precedence of the intention is not conceivable — for an intention today toward a rising tomorrow is not intelligible except by way of resolution. And if the eternal will is in the status of our resolution, then that is not sufficient for the occurrence of the resolved-upon thing; rather, there must be a new arising of an intentional impulse at the moment of bringing into existence — and in that is the affirmation of change in the eternal.

paragraphs.text: I say — and with God is the success:

[1] Praise be to God, the Living, the Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyūm), upon whose essential subsistence no describer's description can prevail; the Majestic, whose attribute of glory no knower's knowledge can encompass; the Mighty, before whom no mighty one exists save that he stands bowed in humility at the threshold of His might; the Glorious, before whom no king exists save that he circles about the pavilion of His majesty; the Compeller, before whom no authority exists save that it hopes for the breaths of His pardon and fears the assaults of His wrath; the Proud, before whom no friend exists save that his heart is suspended upon love of Him and his body stands in service to Him; the Merciful, before whom nothing exists save that it rides upon the back of peril in the terror of the standing-places [of Judgment], were it not for His mercy reaching it through His prior and precedent promise; the Benefactor, who if He intends good for you, there is none to repel or avert His bounty; the Avenger, who if He touches you with harm, there is none to disclose it save Him. Glorified be His majesty and sanctified be His names — no ally deceives Him, no opponent harms Him. Exalted be His sovereignty — no schemer outwits Him, no open adversary contends with Him.

He created (khalaqa) creation as factions and lineages, and ranked them in the embellishments of this world as the base and the noble. He drew them near in the realities of religion through connection and deviation, through ignorance and knowledge. He divided them in the foundations of creeds into groups and classes — they agree in harmony and separate in divergence. Thus they differed in their beliefs: in denial and acknowledgment, in waywardness and fairness, in moderation and excess, even as they differed in origin and attributes. One is rich, whose wealth multiplies daily (yawman), increasing in abundance, taking without measure and spending without measure. Another is weak, supporting weak offspring, lacking even a day's sustenance until he importunately begs of people. One is accepted in hearts, meeting in his need nothing but response and assistance. Another is hated by creation, his rights usurped through oppression and injustice. One is pious and divinely aided, increasing daily in his scrupulousness and godfearingness in abundance and radiance. Another is forsaken, increasing over the passage of days in his error and corruption in persistence and recklessness. That is the decree of your Lord, the Powerful, the Wise, from whose subjugation no authority can deviate; the Subduer, the Knowing, against whose judgment no one possesses opposition — in spite of the noses of the infidel Batinites, who denied that God makes difference among the people of truth, and did not know that difference among the community is followed by mercy, even as the lessons of their differences follow them in ranks and attributes.

And thanks be to God, who has granted us success in acknowledging His religion (dīn) openly and secretly, and has guided us to submission to His judgment in manifestation and concealment, and has not made us among the misguided Batinites — those who display with their tongues acknowledgment but conceal in their breasts persistence and obstinacy; who carry burdens of sins while proclaiming in religion piety and gravity; who accumulate loads of wrongs, because they hope not for God's majesty. Were the callers of truth to address them night and day, their calling would only increase them in flight. When the sword of the people of truth looms over them, they prefer the truth with preference; and when its shadow withdraws from them, they persist and wax proud with arrogance. So we ask God that He leave not upon the face of the earth a single habitation of them. And we pray upon His chosen Messenger, and upon his family and his rightly-guided successors after him — prayers equal to the number of raindrops, pouring forth abundantly, increasing over the passage of days in continuity, and renewing over the succession of years in pursuit and repetition.

To proceed: I have not ceased, during my residence in the City of Peace (Baghdad), longing to serve the sacred, prophetic, imamic, Mustaẓhirian stations — may God multiply their majesty and extend their shadows over the strata of creation — by composing a book in the science of religion, through which I might discharge the thanks due for the blessing and establish the mark of service, and through which I might reap, by undertaking the burden, the fruits of acceptance and nearness. But I inclined toward delay, out of deliberation in determining the science I intended to treat and specifying the art that would find the place of satisfaction with the noble prophetic opinion. This perplexity continued to cast dust in the face of the intention and to prevent the faculty from yielding and submitting — until the noble, sacred, prophetic, Mustaẓhirian commands went forth, indicating to this servant that he compose a book in refutation of the Batinites, comprising the disclosure of their innovations and errors, the varieties of their deceit and stratagem, the manner of their seduction of the common folk and their ignorant masses, the clarification of their treacheries in their obfuscation and deception, their slipping from the noose of Islam, their sloughing off and divesting themselves [of it], and the exposure of their infamies and abominations — leading to the tearing of their veils and the uncovering of their depths.

The commissioning for this task was, in appearance, a blessing that answered before the supplication and responded before the call — though in reality it was a lost object I had been seeking and a desire I had been pursuing. So I saw compliance as an obligation and haste in submission as resolve. And how should I not hasten to it? If I consider the side of the commander, I find him a commander whose rank is the shepherd of the community and the honor of religion, whose origin is the refuge of nations — the Commander of the Faithful — and the obligation of obedience to him is from the Creator of creation, the Lord of the worlds, for God the Exalted has said: {«أطيعوا الله وأطيعوا الرسول وأولي الأمر منكم»} ("Obey God and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you"). And if I turn to the commanded matter, it is the defense of the manifest truth and the struggle on behalf of the proof of religion, and the cutting off of the trailing remnant of the heretics. And if I return to myself — having been honored with this address above all the worlds — I see that haste in yielding and complying is, in my case, among the individual obligations (furūḍ al-ʿayn), for rare upon the face of the earth is one who is competent in the foundations of creeds to establish the proof and demonstration, elevating them from the lowland of conjecture and supposition to the summit of certainty and conviction. For it is the grave matter and the great affair, whose burdens the merchandise of the jurists cannot bear, and whose pillars none can uphold save one specialized in the formidable difficulty — since there have arisen in the principles of religions the passions, and there have become intermingled with the paths of the ancients — the philosophers and the sages — and from the hidden depths of their error did these [Batinites] derive their sustenance. For they vacillate between the doctrines of the Dualists and the philosophers, and hover around the limits of logic in their disputations.
Long indeed was my search for the doubts of the opponent when I was unable to suppress him — and my opponent [was equally searching]. And in such a situation it is said:
"I came to know evil — not for evil's sake, but to guard against it; and he who knows not evil among people, falls into it."

The causes of obligation and compulsion converged upon me, and I faced what was coming with embrace and commitment, and hastened to compliance and submission. I set out to compose this book, built upon ten chapters, asking God the Exalted for success in its like and correctness. And I named it *The Infamies of the Batinites and the Virtues of the Mustaẓhirians* (فضائح الباطنية وفضائل المستظهرية). And God the Exalted is the granter of success for the completion of this intention.
This is the list of the chapters:
**Chapter One:** On the exposition of the method I have followed in the course of this book.
**Chapter Two:** On the explanation of their titles and the disclosure of the cause impelling them to erect this misguiding call.
**Chapter Three:** On the explanation of the degrees of their stratagems in obfuscation and the disclosure of the cause of being deceived by their stratagems despite the manifest corruption of them.
**Chapter Four:** On the transmission of their doctrine in summary and in detail.

**Chapter Five:** On their allegorical interpretations (ta'wīlāt) of the apparent meanings of the Qur'an and their inferences from numerical matters. It contains two sections: the first section on their interpretation of apparent meanings, and the second section on their inferences from numbers and letters.

**Chapter Six:** On the presentation of their rational arguments in support of their doctrine and the disclosure of their obfuscations which they have embellished — as they claim — in the guise of demonstration, for the invalidation of rational reflection (al-naẓar al-ʿaqlī).
**Chapter Seven:** On the invalidation of their inference from the [Qur'anic] text (naṣṣ) for the installation of the infallible Imam.
**Chapter Eight:** On what the legal opinion (fatwā) of the Law requires regarding them — of declaring them unbelievers, declaring them erroneous, and the shedding of their blood.
**Chapter Nine:** On the establishment of the juristic, legal proof that the true Imam in our present age is the Imam al-Mustaẓhir bi-llāh — may God guard his shadows.
**Chapter Ten:** On the religious functions by whose constant observance the entitlement to the Imamate endures.

This is the exposition of the chapters. And the proposal to the noble prophetic opinion is to review the book as a whole, then to single out the ninth and tenth chapters for whoever desires thoroughness — so that he may know from the ninth chapter the measure of God's blessing upon him, and may discern from the tenth chapter the way of undertaking the thanks for that blessing. And he will know that God the Exalted, when He is not pleased that there be upon the face of the earth a servant of higher rank than the Commander of the Faithful, so too the Commander of the Faithful is not pleased that there be for God upon the face of the earth a servant more worshipful and more thankful than himself. We ask God the Exalted to support him with His success and to guide him to the middle path of his way.
This is the sum of the book — and God is the one whose aid is sought for treading the high road of truth and pursuing the path of sincerity.

paragraphs.text: ### | In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Praise be to Allah, who chose from the elite of His servants the band of truth and the people of the Sunnah, and singled them out from among all the sects with the distinctive favors of kindness and grace. He poured forth upon them from the light (nūr) of His guidance that by which He unveiled the realities of religion, and He made their tongues speak with His proof by which He crushed the misguidance of the atheists. He purified their innermost consciences from the whisperings of the devils, and cleansed their hearts from the incitements of the deviant. He filled their breasts with the lights of certainty (anwār al-yaqīn), until through them they were guided to the secrets of what He revealed upon the tongue of His Prophet and Chosen One, Muhammad — may Allah bless him and grant him peace — the master of the messengers. And they came to perceive the way of reconciling between the requirements of the revealed laws (sharāʾiʿ) and the dictates of the intellects (ʿuqūl); and they ascertained with certainty that there is no opposition between the transmitted Law (al-sharʿ al-manqūl) and the rational truth (al-ḥaqq al-maʿqūl).

And they knew that those among the Ḥashwiyyah who supposed the obligation of frozen adherence to blind following (taqlīd) and the pursuit of literal appearances — they only arrived at this from the weakness of intellects and the paucity of insights. And those among the philosophers and the extremist Muʿtazilah who delved deep into the exercise of reason until they collided with it against the categorical proofs of the Law — they only arrived at this from the corruption of their inner consciences. The inclination of the former is toward negligence (tafrīṭ), and the inclination of the latter is toward excess (ifrāṭ), and both are far from prudence and caution. Rather, the obligatory and binding duty in the foundations of belief is the adherence to moderation (iqtiṣād) and reliance upon the straight path; for both extremes in pursuing matters are blameworthy.

And how should right guidance be secured for one who is content with blind following of tradition and report, and denies the methodologies of inquiry and reflection — or does not know that there is no basis for the Law except the word of the master of mankind, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and that the proof of reason is that by which his truthfulness is known in what he reported? And how should one be guided to correctness who pursues pure reason alone and restricts himself to it, without being illuminated by the light of the Law nor gaining insight thereby? Would that I knew — how can one flee to reason when incapacity and perplexity afflict it? Or does he not know that reason is deficient and that its domain is narrow and confined? Far from it! He has certainly failed with absolute certainty and become entangled in the trails of misguidance — he who does not unite, through the composition of the Law and reason, this scattered disarray.

For the example of reason is sound eyesight free from defects and harm. And the example of the Qurʾān is the sun spreading its radiance. How fitting it is that the seeker of guidance be self-sufficient — but if he relies on one of them to the exclusion of the other, he is among the ranks of the foolish. For the one who turns away from reason, contenting himself with the light of the Qurʾān alone, his example is one who exposes himself to the sun's light while closing his eyelids — there is no difference between him and the blind. So reason with the Law is light upon light (nūrun ʿalā nūr), and the one who looks with a squinting eye at either one specifically is clinging to a rope of delusion.

And it will become clear to you, O aspirant yearning to examine the foundations of the creed of the people of the Sunnah, seeking to verify them by categorical proofs, that no group has been singled out for success in combining the Law and verification except this group. So thank Allah the Exalted for your following in their footsteps, your entry into the order of their system and their standard, and your mixing with their party; perhaps you will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in their company. We ask Allah the Exalted to purify our innermost secrets from the turbidities of misguidance, and to flood them with the light of truth, and to silence our tongues from speaking falsehood, and to make them speak with truth and wisdom. Indeed, He is the Generous, the Abundant in favor, the Vast in mercy.
### | Chapter

Let us open the discourse with an explanation of the name of the book, and the division of its premises, chapters, and sections. As for the name of the book, it is *Moderation in Belief* (al-Iqtiṣād fī al-Iʿtiqād). As for its arrangement, it comprises four Premises (tamhīdāt) that serve as introductions and preliminaries, and four Poles (aqṭāb) that serve as the objectives and ends.
### | The First Premise: On the Explanation That This Science Is among the Important Matters in Religion.
The Second Premise: On the Explanation That It Is Not Important for All Muslims, but Rather for a Specific Group among Them.
The Third Premise: On the Explanation That It Is among the Communal Obligations (furūḍ al-kifāyāt), Not Individual Obligations (furūḍ al-aʿyān).
The Fourth Premise: On the Detailed Exposition of the Methodologies of the Proofs That I Have Adduced in This Book.

As for the intended Poles, they are four, and their totality is confined to reflection upon Allah the Exalted. For when we look at the world, we do not look at it insofar as it is a world, a body, a heaven, or an earth, but rather insofar as it is the handiwork of Allah, glorified be He. And when we look at the Prophet, peace be upon him, we do not look at him insofar as he is a human being, noble, learned, and virtuous, but rather insofar as he is the Messenger of Allah. And when we look at his statements, we do not look at them insofar as they are statements, addresses, and communications, but rather insofar as they are definitions (taʿrīfāt) from Allah the Exalted conveyed through him. So there is no reflection except upon Allah, and no object of seeking except Allah. All the branches of this science are encompassed by reflection upon the Essence of Allah the Exalted, upon His attributes, glorified be He, upon His acts, mighty be His majesty, and upon the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and what has come to us upon his tongue of the definitions of Allah the Exalted. These are therefore four Poles:

**The First Pole:** Reflection upon the Essence of Allah the Exalted. In it we demonstrate His existence, that He is eternal (qadīm), that He is everlasting (bāqī), that He is not a substance (jawhar), nor a body (jism), nor an accident (ʿaraḍ), nor limited by a boundary, nor particularized by a direction (jihah), that He is visible (marʾī) just as He is known, and that He is one (wāḥid). These are ten claims that we demonstrate in this Pole.

**The Second Pole:** On the attributes of Allah the Exalted. In it we demonstrate that He is living (ḥayy), knowing (ʿālim), powerful (qādir), willing (murīd), hearing (samīʿ), seeing (baṣīr), and speaking (mutakallim), and that He has life (ḥayāh), knowledge (ʿilm), power (qudrah), will (irādah), hearing (samʿ), sight (baṣar), and speech (kalām). We mention the rulings of these attributes, their necessary concomitants (lawāzim), wherein they differ and wherein they agree in their rulings, and that these attributes are additional to the Essence (zāʾidah ʿalā al-dhāt), eternal (qadīmah), and subsisting in the Essence (qāʾimah bi al-dhāt), and that it is not permissible for any of the attributes to be originated (ḥādith).

**The Third Pole:** On the acts of Allah the Exalted. In it there are seven claims: that it is not obligatory upon Allah the Exalted to impose obligation (taklīf), nor to create, nor to reward for obligation, nor to observe the welfare (ṣalāḥ) of the servants; that it is not impossible for Him to obligate what is beyond one's capacity (taklīf mā lā yuṭāq); that it is not obligatory upon Him to punish for disobedience; and that it is not impossible for Him to send the prophets, peace be upon them — rather, that is permissible (jāʾiz). In the introduction to this Pole is the explanation of the meaning of the obligatory (wājib), the good (ḥasan), and the evil (qabīḥ).

**The Fourth Pole:** On the messengers of Allah, and what has come upon the tongue of our Messenger Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, concerning the gathering (ḥashr), the resurrection (nashr), paradise (jannah), the fire (nār), intercession (shafāʿah), the punishment of the grave (ʿadhāb al-qabr), the scale (mīzān), and the path (ṣirāṭ). In it there are four chapters: The First Chapter: On establishing the prophethood of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The Second Chapter: On what has been reported upon his tongue concerning the matters of the Hereafter. The Third Chapter: On the imamate (imāmah) and its conditions. The Fourth Chapter: On the explanation of the principle (qānūn) for declaring the innovating sects to be unbelievers (takfīr).
### | The First Premise: On the Explanation That This Science Is among the Important Matters in Religion.

Know, may Allah grant you success in attaining the truth and guide you to the path of right conduct, that the science of the foundations of belief (uṣūl al-ʿaqāʾid) is the most noble of the sciences and the most worthy of being pursued, for it is the science of the divine Essence and His attributes, and the science of His prophets and messengers, and the science of the Hereafter and its states.
