paragraphs.text: Praise be to Allah, the Strong, the Powerful, the Protecting Helper, the Subtle, the Subduer, the Avenger, the Forgiving, the Hidden, the Manifest, the First, the Last—He who made the intellect (al-ʿaql) the most preponderant of treasures and stores, and knowledge (al-ʿilm) the most profitable of gains and trades, the noblest of excellences and glories, the most honorable of praises and legacies, and the most praiseworthy of sources and origins. Through its affirmation, pens and inkwells were ennobled; through its hearing, prayer niches and pulpits were adorned; through its inscription, pages and registers were beautified; through its honor, the lesser were advanced over the greater; through its radiance, consciences and innermost thoughts were illuminated; through its lights, hearts and inner visions were enlightened; and in its glow, the dazzling light of the sun upon the revolving sphere was deemed insignificant, and in its inner light, the apparent gleam of pupils and eyes was reckoned small—until its radiance penetrated the deepest depths of hidden thoughts, the troops of inner reflections, even though eyesight faltered before them and veils and screens thickened upon them.

And prayers be upon Muhammad, His Messenger, of pure lineage, manifest glory, mutually supporting honor, and overflowing generosity—sent forth as a bearer of glad tidings to the believers and a warner to the disbelievers, abrogating by his Law (sharʿ) every preceding law and every passing religion; supported by the Glorious Qurʾān, which no listener wearies of and no transmitter exhausts, whose profound eloquence no prose-writer or poet can grasp, whose wonders no describer can encompass and no rememberer can recount, and every eloquent speaker falls short of tasting the understanding of the clear aspects of its secrets. And upon his Family and Companions, grant abundant peace, whose abundance exceeds the count of the most encompassing enumerator.

To proceed: The judge of the intellect—the arbiter who is neither dismissed nor replaced—and the witness of the Law—the attested, upright witness—have both declared that this world is an abode of delusion, not an abode of joy; a mount for labor, not a mount for idleness; a place of passage, not a park of delight; a station of commerce, not a dwelling of settlement; a market whose merchandise is obedience and whose profit is success on the Day the Hour arises.

And obedience is of two kinds: action and knowledge. Knowledge is the more successful and profitable of the two, for it too is an act—but it is the act of the heart, which is the noblest of organs, and the striving of the intellect, which is the most honorable of things, for it is the mount of religion and the bearer of the Trust (amānah), since it was offered to the earth, the mountains, and the heavens, and they shrank from bearing it and refused it with utmost refusal. {إِنَّا عَرَضْنَا الْأَمَانَةَ عَلَى السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَالْجِبَالِ} [We offered the Trust to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains] (Qurʾān 33:72).

Then the sciences are three: a purely rational science that the Law neither urges nor recommends, such as arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and their like—these fall between false conjectures that are blameworthy, for "some conjecture is sin" {إِنَّ بَعْضَ الظَّنِّ إِثْمٌ} (Qurʾān 49:12), and true sciences that yield no benefit; and we seek refuge in Allah from knowledge that does not profit. For benefit lies not in present appetites and splendid favors, for these are transient and passing; rather, benefit is the reward of the Hereafter.

And a purely transmitted science, such as hadiths and Qurʾānic commentaries, and sermons in their like are easy, for the young and the old are equal in mastering them, since the power of memorization suffices for transmission, and therein is no scope for the intellect.

And the noblest of sciences is that in which the intellect and revelation are wedded, and in which reasoned opinion and the Law are companions—and the science of jurisprudence (fiqh) and its principles (uṣūl) are of this kind. For it takes from the pure essence of the Law and the intellect the middle path: it is neither a mere exercise of pure reason that the Law does not accept, nor is it built on sheer emulation (taqlīd) that the intellect does not witness with support and right guidance.

And because of the nobility of the science of jurisprudence and its cause, Allah made the inclinations of creation eager for its pursuit, and its scholars are the highest of scholars in rank, the greatest in standing, and the most numerous in followers and helpers. Thus, in the prime of my youth, the distinction of this science with the benefits of religion and this world, and the reward of the Hereafter, summoned me—and it was most fitting that I devote to it the foremost portion of my life's leisure and single out for it a share of my breathing moments. So I authored many books on the branches (furūʿ) of jurisprudence and its principles. Then, after that, I turned to the science of the path of the Hereafter and the knowledge of the inner secrets of religion, and I authored in it comprehensive books like the "Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn" (The Revival of the Religious Sciences), concise ones like the "Jawāhir al-Qurʾān" (The Jewels of the Qurʾān), and intermediate ones like the "Kīmiyāʾ al-Saʿādah" (The Alchemy of Happiness).

paragraphs.text: I say — and with God is success:
### Introduction

It is necessary to mention the introduction prescribed before the five pillars (al-arkān al-khamsah), concerning the definition of qiyās (analogy), its form, the clarification of the meaning of ʿillah (effective cause) and dalālah (indication), the exposition of its divisions, and a notification of the courses of theoretical inquiry (majārī al-naẓar) within it.
As for its definition (ḥadd), the formulations and expressions have differed concerning it. We are not inclined toward prolixity in this book regarding matters to which no great benefit attaches.

The expression that defines the intended aim is to say: "Qiyās is the affirmation of the ruling of the original case (aṣl) in the derivative case (farʿ), by virtue of their sharing in the ʿillah of the ruling." This much suffices for clarification.

If you desire an expression that is guarded against objections — of the sort that definitions aim to repel in the usage of the theologians (mutakallimūn) and masters of the crafts — you would say: "It is the carrying of a known thing upon a known thing, in affirming a ruling or negating it, by virtue of sharing in an attribute, or the negation of an attribute, or a ruling, or the negation of a ruling." This is more comprehensive of all divisions of discourse and more encompassing of the totality of its parts.

In the first definition there is independence from this, for it suffices for the clarification we seek, namely, the clarification of qiyās al-maʿnā (analogy of meaning), since it is that which comprises the exposition of the ʿillah of the ruling.

If you wish to include within it qiyās al-shabah (analogy of resemblance) and qiyās al-ṭard (analogy of mere coextension), you would turn to the other expression, for all of that falls under the form of qiyās, even though it divides into sound and corrupt — for the corrupt is also qiyās.

In sum, it is necessary to establish equality between the two things, so that the form of qiyās is realized. For it is derived from the saying of the Arabs: "qāsa al-shayʾ bi-al-shayʾ" — when one makes it follow its course and equalizes it thereto. One says: "qāsa al-naʿl bi-al-naʿl" (he measured the sandal against the sandal), when he equalized it thereto.
### The Difference Between Qiyās and ʿIllah, and Between Dalālah and ʿIllah
If it is said: "Is there any difference between qiyās and ʿillah?"

We say: Yes. For the ʿillah, in its very conception, does not require an original case and a derivative case; rather, when you mention the effective cause (al-sabab al-muʾaththir) of the ruling, you have mentioned the ʿillah of the ruling.

The ʿillah, in its origin, is an expression for that by whose existence the substrate (maḥall) is affected; for this reason, illness (marad) is called ʿillah. And it is in the technical usage of the jurists (fuqahāʾ) upon this very taste.

Indeed, qiyās may be called ʿillah, because it comprises the ʿillah of the ruling, which is the greatest pillar of the aim of qiyās — just as qiyās is called naẓar (inquiry), ijtihād (effort of judgment), dalīl (proof), and iʿtilāl (causal reasoning), because it is attained through inquiry and effort, and it indicates the ruling, and it comprises the mention of the ʿillah — hence it is called iʿtilāl.

As for naming the ʿillah by itself "qiyās," there is no justification for it. Even if some jurists have been lenient in applying it, that is due to their division of the questions — in their convention — into report-based (khabariyyah) and analogy-based (qiyāsiyyah). Thus, whatever does not pertain to report is called qiyāsiyyah, because the predominant feature of questions that are not report-based is that they are called "qiyās" in the sense that they are not report-based.
If it is said: "Is there any difference between dalālah and ʿillah?"

We say: Yes. For every ʿillah may be called a dalālah, because it indicates the ruling — the efficient cause (al-muʾaththir) always indicates its effect (al-athar). But not every dalālah is called a ʿillah, because dalālah may be used to express the mere sign (al-amārah) that indicates without effecting. Thus, the cloud is a dalīl for rain, and it is also its ʿillah, because it effects it. The star is a dalīl for the qiblah, but it is not a ʿillah therein. For the dalālah has no share in necessitation (ījāb).

The ʿillah is necessitating (mūjibah): as for the rational ʿillah, it necessitates by its very essence; as for the legal ʿillah, it necessitates by the Lawgiver's making it a necessitating cause, in the sense of attributing the obligation (wujūb) to it — just as the obligation of amputation is attributed to theft, even though we know that it is only obligatory by God's command. But we must understand the necessitation as it has come in the revealed Law, and it has come that theft necessitates amputation, and adultery necessitates stoning. In this, dalālah and ʿillah differ.
We shall exhaustively pursue the aspects of the indications — which are not of the class of qiyās, nor of the class of ʿillal — in the second chapter, God Most High willing.

paragraphs.text: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace be upon Muhammad, His Prophet, and upon his family and his Companions, all of them.

It has been established and settled in the minds of those possessed of intellects (ulū al-albāb) that jurisprudence (al-fiqh) — that is, deep religious discernment — is the noblest of the sciences, the highest of them in rank, and the greatest of them in gravity and consequence. For through it the rulings are known, and the lawful is distinguished (yumayyaz) from the unlawful. Yet despite the loftiness of its rank and the magnitude of its affair, it stands in the position of a branch (farʿ) that has ramified forth from the science of the principles (uṣūl). And there is no aspiration to encompass the branch, to establish it firmly and settle its foundations, or to gain insight into its true reality, except after the root (aṣl) has been prepared and perfected — for the source of confusion and stumbling in the branches is generated and produced by confusion and stumbling in the roots.

Know that the religious sciences are three: theology (al-kalām), the principles of jurisprudence (al-uṣūl), and jurisprudence (al-fiqh). Each one of them has a material (māddah) from which it derives and draws its sustenance, and upon which it leans and rests its support; and it has a purpose (maqṣūd) to which the aspiration of the seeker and his pursuit are attached and directed. It is therefore necessary to draw attention to its material, so that the one who plunges into it may kindle and borrow from it the measure of his need, and thereby attain his quest and desire. Nor is there any dispensation from drawing attention to its purpose, lest the seeker remain in blindness and error concerning that which he seeks and pursues.

As for the science of theology (al-kalām), its material is the discrimination (al-mayz) between demonstrations (barāhīn) and fallacies (aghālīṭ), and the discrimination between genuine sciences and mere beliefs and convictions, and the discrimination between the courses of the intellects and their stopping-points and stations. As for its purpose, it is the encompassing comprehension of the origination of the world (ḥudūth al-ʿālam) and its neediness for an effective Maker (ṣāniʿ muʾaththir) — One who is qualified with what is necessary of the attributes, transcendent and exalted above what is impossible to conceive as an attribute of the Essence, powerful over the sending of the Messengers and the supporting of them with miracles.

As for the principles (al-uṣūl), its material is theology, jurisprudence, and language. The aspect of its derivation from theology is that the encompassing comprehension of the evidences erected and established upon the rulings is founded upon the acceptance of the revealed laws (al-sharāʾiʿ) and the verification of the Messengers — and there is no aspiration to that except after knowledge of the Sender (al-mursil). The aspect of its derivation from jurisprudence is that jurisprudence is the signified (al-madlūl) and the object sought, and the pursuit of the evidence while being heedless of and inattentive to the signified is a thing repudiated and rejected by the pathways of the intellects. The aspect of its derivation from language is that the legal theorist (al-uṣūlī) is driven and compelled to discourse concerning the import of the address (faḥwā al-khiṭāb), the interpretation (taʾwīl) of the reports of the Messenger — peace be upon him — and the explicit texts (nuṣūṣ) of the Book.

And its purpose is the knowledge of the definitive evidences (al-adillah al-qaṭʿiyyah) erected upon the prescriptive rulings (al-aḥkām al-taklīfiyyah), and the solitary reports (akhbār al-āḥād), and the pathways of inference (masālik al-ʿibar), and the analogies (maqāyīs), and the elicited principles (al-mustathārah). The evidences adduced by way of independent reasoning (ijtihād) are not of the principles — for they are matters of conjecture (ẓanniyyāt) that have been taken in the manner of certainties — but the legal theorist is nevertheless compelled and necessitated to mention them in order to make clear the sound from the corrupt, and the well-grounded from the deviant and perverse; and because the weighings of preponderance (al-tarjīḥāt) are among the most obscure and perplexing matters of the science of principles, and there is no way to them except by the elucidation of the ranks and degrees.

As for jurisprudence (al-fiqh), its material is the principles, and its purpose is the knowledge of the legal rulings (al-aḥkām al-sharʿiyyah) and the establishment and settling of the rulings — when the conjectural indicators (al-ʿalāmāt al-maẓnūnah) appear — as things known through definitive evidences, with no conjecture therein.
### Section

There is no science among these sciences except that it has loci of consensus (mawāqiʿ ijmāʿ) and sources of dispute (mathārāt nizāʿ). The locus of consensus in theology is the things perceived by primary necessity (al-mudrakāt bil-bidāyah), the necessary truths (al-ḍarūriyyāt), and the intelligibles (al-maʿqūlāt) in which the direction of inquiry is unified and does not multiply or diverge — like the consensus of the rational ones that the eternal (al-qadīm) does not pass away or become nonexistent. The source of disagreement therein is the conflict and opposition of evidences and ambiguities (taʿāruḍ al-adillah wal-shubuhāt).

As for the science of principles, the origin of agreement therein resembles and corresponds to the origin of agreement in theology; and the spring and fountainhead of disagreement therein is two things: one of them is the conflict of evidences and ambiguities, and the second is the intermingling and blending of the definitive (qaṭʿī) with the conjectural (ẓannī) within it.

As for jurisprudence, the locus of consensus therein is what is grounded in and supported by the text (naṣṣ) of the Book of God, or an unbrokenly transmitted report (ḥadīth mutawātir), or a consensus (ijmāʿ) that is obligatory to follow. Whatever is beyond that belongs to the loci of conjectures (maẓān al-ẓunūn); and when confusion and perplexity arise therein, the independent jurists (mujtahidūn) differ and their opinions fluctuate and waver, and they split into factions and parties.

### || CHECK في حد القياس وصورته، وقسمته، وبيان معنى العلة والدلالة

ال

### | AUTO مقدمة

المرسومة قبل الأركان الخمس
فلابد من ذكر

### | AUTO مقدمة

في حد القياس وصورته، [وبيان معنى العلة والدلالة]، وبيان قسمته،
والتنبيه على مجاري النظر فيه.
أما حده، فقد اختلفت فيه الصيغ والعبارات. ولسنا للتطويل في هذا الكتاب،
فيما لا يتعلق به كبير فائدة.
والعبارة المعرفة للمقصد المطلوب، أن يقال: «القياس: عبارة عن إثبات حكم

الأصل في الفرع، لاشتراكهما في علة الحكم».

PageV01P018
فهذا القدر كاف في البيان.
وإن أردت عبارة محترزة عن الاعتراضات -[التي تهدف الحدود لأمثالها في
عبارة المتكلمين وأرباب الصناعات] في الحدود -قلت: هو: حمل معلوم على معلوم
في إثبات حكم أو نفيه، بالاشتراك في صفة أو انتفاء صفة، أو حكم أو انتفاء
حكم. فهذا أحوى لجميع أقسام الكلام، وأحصر لجملة الأطراف.
وفي الأول غنية عنه: فإنه مفيد للبيان الذي نبغيه، وهو بيان قياس المعنى،
إذ هو المشتمل على بيان علة الحكم.
فإن أردت أن تضم إليه قياس الشبه والطرد -عدلت إلى العبارة الأخرى: فإن
جميع ذلك على شكل القياس وإن كان ينقسم إلى صحيح وفاسد، فإن الفاسد أيضا قياس.
وعلى الجملة [أيضا] لابد من التسوية بين الشيئين: لتتحقق صورة القياس،
فإن مشتق من قول العرب: قاس الشيء بالشيء، إذا حذا به حذوه وسواه عليه،
يقال: قاس النعل بالنعل، إذا سواه عليه.

PageV01P019

### || CHECK الفرق بين القياس والعلة، والدلالة والعلة

فإن قيل: فهل من فرق بين القياس والعلة؟
قلنا: نعم؛ فإن العلة في تصورها لا تستدعي أصلا وفرعا، ولكن إذا ذكرت
السبب المؤثر في الحكم، فقد ذكرت [علة الحكم].
والعلة [في الأصل]: عبارة عما يتأثر المحل بوجوده، ولذلك سمي المرض: علة.
وهي في اصطلاح الفقهاء على هذا المذاق.
نعم: قد يسمى القياس علة، لأنه يشتمل على علة الحكم، وهي الركن الأعظم من
مقصود القياس، كما يسمى القياس: نظرا واجتهادا ودليلا واعتلالا؛ لأنه
يستدرك بالنظر والاجتهاد، ويدل على الحكم، ويشتمل على ذكر العلة: فيسمى
اعتلالا.
وتسمية العلة بمجردها قياسا، لا وجه له. وإن تسامح بعض الفقهاء بإطلاقه،
فذلك لتقسيمهم المسائل -في عرفهم - إلى الخبرية والقياسية؛ فما لا يتعلق
منه بالخبر تسمى قياسية: لأن الغالب في المسائل التي ليس خبرية، فيعنون
بكونه قياسا: أنه ليس خبريا.
فإن قيل: فهي من فرق بين الدلالة والعلة؟
قلنا: نعم؛ فكل علة يجوز أن تسمى دلالة، لأنها تدل على الحكم، فالمؤثر
أبدا يدل على الأثر. ولا تسمى كل دلالة علة، لأن الدلالة [قد] يعبر بها عن
الأمارة التي توجب: فلا تؤثر، فالغيم PageV01P020 # الركم دليل على المطر وعلته أيضا، لأنه يؤثر فيه. والكوكب دليل على
القبلة، وليس علة فيها. فما للدلالة حظ في الإيجاب.
والعلة موجبة؛ أما العقلية فبذاتها، وأما الشرعية فبجعل الشرع إياها
[علة] موجبة، على معنى إضافة الوجوب إليها، كإضافة وجوب القطع إلى السرقة،
وإن كنا نعلم أنه إنما يجب بإيجاب الله تعالى؛ ولكن ينبغي أن نفهم الإيجاب
كما ورد به الشرع، وقد ورد بأن السرقة توجب القطع، والزنا يوجب الرجم. ففي
هذا تفترق الدلالة والعلة.
وسنتقصى [وجوه] الدلالات -التي ليست من قبيل الأقيسة، ولا من قبيل العلل
-في الباب الثاني [إن شاء الله تعالى].

PageV01P021
أما

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: قيس (qys)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of measuring, comparing, equalizing one thing to another; "qāsa al-naʿl bi-al-naʿl" — to equalize a sandal against another as a template.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Qiyās in juridical-theological usage denotes the transference of a ruling from an established case to a novel case via a shared attribute, requiring a disciplined method (naẓar).
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage pertains to physical measurement and equalization; metaphorical (majāz) extension applies it to juridical reasoning where the "measure" is the common ʿillah.
- Root: علل (ʿll)
 * Lisan / Ayn: The root denotes repetition and succession; a recurring condition (marad) that affects the substrate is termed ʿillah — hence "illness."
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The ʿillah is that which necessitates its effect (muʾaththir); in legal theory, it is the attribute upon which the Lawgiver (al-Shāriʿ) has made the ruling contingent.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: the affecting cause; metaphorical: the legal indicator that carries the force of necessitation (ījāb) by divine appointment, not by inherent causality.
- Root: دلل (dll)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Indication, guidance, signposting; the dalīl is that which points beyond itself.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Dalālah is broader than ʿillah — every ʿillah indicates its effect, but not every indicator effects its object; the cloud indicates rain and effects it, the star indicates the qiblah without effecting it.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: a sign (amārah) that merely points; metaphorical: when extended to legal proof, it may or may not carry causal efficacy.
- Sibawayh Rule: Bāb al-ḥaṣr wa-al-taqyīd bi-innamā (Restriction and Focused Predication) — Governing the precise delimitation of terms such as qiyās, ʿillah, and dalālah, ensuring that each definition is confined to its exact referent without equivocation or overextension.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
I say — and with God is success:
### Introduction

It is necessary to mention the introduction prescribed before the five pillars (al-arkān al-khamsah), concerning the definition of qiyās (analogy), its form, the clarification of the meaning of ʿillah (effective cause) and dalālah (indication), the exposition of its divisions, and a notification of the courses of theoretical inquiry (majārī al-naẓar) within it.
As for its definition (ḥadd), the formulations and expressions have differed concerning it. We are not inclined toward prolixity in this book regarding matters to which no great benefit attaches.

The expression that defines the intended aim is to say: "Qiyās is the affirmation of the ruling of the original case (aṣl) in the derivative case (farʿ), by virtue of their sharing in the ʿillah of the ruling." This much suffices for clarification.

If you desire an expression that is guarded against objections — of the sort that definitions aim to repel in the usage of the theologians (mutakallimūn) and masters of the crafts — you would say: "It is the carrying of a known thing upon a known thing, in affirming a ruling or negating it, by virtue of sharing in an attribute, or the negation of an attribute, or a ruling, or the negation of a ruling." This is more comprehensive of all divisions of discourse and more encompassing of the totality of its parts.

In the first definition there is independence from this, for it suffices for the clarification we seek, namely, the clarification of qiyās al-maʿnā (analogy of meaning), since it is that which comprises the exposition of the ʿillah of the ruling.

If you wish to include within it qiyās al-shabah (analogy of resemblance) and qiyās al-ṭard (analogy of mere coextension), you would turn to the other expression, for all of that falls under the form of qiyās, even though it divides into sound and corrupt — for the corrupt is also qiyās.

In sum, it is necessary to establish equality between the two things, so that the form of qiyās is realized. For it is derived from the saying of the Arabs: "qāsa al-shayʾ bi-al-shayʾ" — when one makes it follow its course and equalizes it thereto. One says: "qāsa al-naʿl bi-al-naʿl" (he measured the sandal against the sandal), when he equalized it thereto.
### The Difference Between Qiyās and ʿIllah, and Between Dalālah and ʿIllah
If it is said: "Is there any difference between qiyās and ʿillah?"

We say: Yes. For the ʿillah, in its very conception, does not require an original case and a derivative case; rather, when you mention the effective cause (al-sabab al-muʾaththir) of the ruling, you have mentioned the ʿillah of the ruling.

The ʿillah, in its origin, is an expression for that by whose existence the substrate (maḥall) is affected; for this reason, illness (marad) is called ʿillah. And it is in the technical usage of the jurists (fuqahāʾ) upon this very taste.

Indeed, qiyās may be called ʿillah, because it comprises the ʿillah of the ruling, which is the greatest pillar of the aim of qiyās — just as qiyās is called naẓar (inquiry), ijtihād (effort of judgment), dalīl (proof), and iʿtilāl (causal reasoning), because it is attained through inquiry and effort, and it indicates the ruling, and it comprises the mention of the ʿillah — hence it is called iʿtilāl.

As for naming the ʿillah by itself "qiyās," there is no justification for it. Even if some jurists have been lenient in applying it, that is due to their division of the questions — in their convention — into report-based (khabariyyah) and analogy-based (qiyāsiyyah). Thus, whatever does not pertain to report is called qiyāsiyyah, because the predominant feature of questions that are not report-based is that they are called "qiyās" in the sense that they are not report-based.
If it is said: "Is there any difference between dalālah and ʿillah?"

We say: Yes. For every ʿillah may be called a dalālah, because it indicates the ruling — the efficient cause (al-muʾaththir) always indicates its effect (al-athar). But not every dalālah is called a ʿillah, because dalālah may be used to express the mere sign (al-amārah) that indicates without effecting. Thus, the cloud is a dalīl for rain, and it is also its ʿillah, because it effects it. The star is a dalīl for the qiblah, but it is not a ʿillah therein. For the dalālah has no share in necessitation (ījāb).

The ʿillah is necessitating (mūjibah): as for the rational ʿillah, it necessitates by its very essence; as for the legal ʿillah, it necessitates by the Lawgiver's making it a necessitating cause, in the sense of attributing the obligation (wujūb) to it — just as the obligation of amputation is attributed to theft, even though we know that it is only obligatory by God's command. But we must understand the necessitation as it has come in the revealed Law, and it has come that theft necessitates amputation, and adultery necessitates stoning. In this, dalālah and ʿillah differ.
We shall exhaustively pursue the aspects of the indications — which are not of the class of qiyās, nor of the class of ʿillal — in the second chapter, God Most High willing.

paragraphs.text:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله رب العالمين والصلاة والسلام على محمد نبيه وعلى آله وصحبه
أجمعين
قد تقرر عند ذوي الألباب أن الفقه أشرف العلوم وأعلاها قدرا وأعظمها خطرا
إذ به تعرف الأحكام ويتميز الحلال عن الحرام وهو على علو قدره وتفاقم أمره
في حكم الفرع المتشعب عن علم الأصول ولا مطمع في الإحاطة بالفرع وتقريره
والاطلاع على حقيقته إلا بعد تمهيد الأصل وإتقانه إذ مثار التخبط في الفروع
ينتج عن التخبط في الأصول ولتعلم أن علوم الشرع ثلاثة الكلام والأصول
والفقه
ولكل واحد منها مادة منها استمداده وإليها استناده ومقصود به يتعلق قصد
الطالب وارتياده فلابد من التنبيه على مادته ليقتبس الخائض فيه منها مبلغ
حاجته فيتوسل إلى بغيته ولا غنى عن التنبيه على مقصوده لئلا يكون الطالب
على عماية من مطلبه فأما علم الكلام فمادته الميز بين البراهين والاغاليط
والميز بين العلوم والاعتقادات والميز بين مجاري العقول ومواقفها وأما
مقصوده فهو الإحاطة بحدوث العالم وافتقاره إلى صانع مؤثر
متصف بما يجب من الصفات منزه عما يستحيل تخيله صفة للذات قادر على بعثة
الرسل وتأييدهم بالمعجزات وأما الأصول فمادته الكلام والفقه واللغة ووجه
استمداده من الكلام أن الإحاطة بالأدلة المنصوبة على الأحكام مبناها على
تقبل الشرائع وتصديق الرسل ولا مطمع فيه إلا بعد العلم بالمرسل ووجه
استمداده من الفقه أنه المدلول وطلب الدليل مع الذهول عن المدلول مما تأباه
مسالك العقول ووجه استمداده من اللغة كون الأصولي مدفوعا إلى الكلام في
فحوى الخطاب وتأويل أخبار الرسول عليه السلام ونصوص الكتاب ومقصوده معرفة
الأدلة القطعية المنصوبة على الأحكام التكليفية وأخبار الآحاد ومسالك العبر
والمقاييس والمستثارة قال بطرق الاجتهاد ليس من
الأصول فإنها مظنونات بجانب أخذها مأخذ القطعيات ولكن افتقر
الأصولي إلى ذكرها لتبين الصحيح من الفاسد والمستند من الحائد ولأن
الترجيحات من مغمضات علم الأصول ولا سبيل إليها إلا ببيان المراتب والدرجات
وأما الفقه فمادته الأصول ومقصوده معرفة الأحكام الشرعية وتقرير الأحكام
عند ظهور العلامات المظنونة معلومة بأدلة قطعية لا ظن فيها

### | فصل

ما من علم من هذه العلوم إلا وله مواقع إجماع ومثارات نزاع فمطلع الإجماع
في الكلام المدركات بالبداية والضروريات والمعقولات التي يتحد
فيها صوب النظر ولا يتعدد كإجماع العقلاء على أن القديم لا يعدم ومثار
الخلاف فيه تعارض الأدلة والشبهات وأما علم الأصول فمنشأ الوفاق فيه يضاهي
منشأ الوفاق في الكلام ومنبع الخلاف فيه أمران أحدهما تعارض الأدلة
والشبهات والثاني امتزاج القطع فيها بالظنيات وأما الفقه فموضع الإجماع فيه
ما يستند إلى نص كتاب الله أو حديث متواتر أو إجماع واجب الإتباع وما عداها
فهو من مظان الظنون وعند الإرتباك فيها يختلف المجتهدون وتضطرب آراؤهم
فيتحزبون

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: فقه (Fiqh)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core linguistic root meaning — deep understanding and comprehension; the Ayn notes its verbal form as attaining penetrating discernment.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Theological/Kalam semantic nuance — "الفقه: هو التوصل إلى علم غائب بعلم شاهد" (attaining knowledge of the unseen through knowledge of the witnessed); it is more specific than mere knowledge (ʿilm), being the understanding of legal rulings.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal vs Metaphorical distinction — In its literal (ḥaqīqah) sense: "الفهم والفطنة" (understanding and acumen); the prophetic hadith "من أراد الله به خيرا فقهه في الدين" elevates it to religious discernment.
- Root: علم (ʿIlm)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core linguistic root meaning — a mark, sign, or trace by which something is known; the Ayn connects it to that which is imprinted and recognized.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Theological/Kalam semantic nuance — "العلم: إدراك الشيء بحقيقته" (knowledge is the apprehension of a thing in its true reality), divided into apprehension of the essence and judgment upon existence or negation.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal vs Metaphorical distinction — Literal: perception and awareness; also "معالم الطريق" (landmarks of the road) — the traces by which one is guided, here applied to the evidences of the science.
- Root: ميز (Mayz)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core linguistic root meaning — separation and distinction between things.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Theological/Kalam semantic nuance — "الميز والتمييز: الفصل بين المتشابهات" (discrimination is the separation between things that resemble one another); the faculty by which meanings are extracted.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal vs Metaphorical distinction — Literal: "مازه منه، وميزوه" (he separated it from it); Metaphorical: "تكاد تميز من الغيظ" (it almost bursts with rage) — used here for the intellect's discriminating between demonstration and fallacy.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — Governing the periodic suspension of meaning across clauses, where the full import of a construction is only realized upon its completion, as in the author's layered definitions of each science's material and purpose.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace be upon Muhammad, His Prophet, and upon his family and his Companions, all of them.

It has been established and settled in the minds of those possessed of intellects (ulū al-albāb) that jurisprudence (al-fiqh) — that is, deep religious discernment — is the noblest of the sciences, the highest of them in rank, and the greatest of them in gravity and consequence. For through it the rulings are known, and the lawful is distinguished (yumayyaz) from the unlawful. Yet despite the loftiness of its rank and the magnitude of its affair, it stands in the position of a branch (farʿ) that has ramified forth from the science of the principles (uṣūl). And there is no aspiration to encompass the branch, to establish it firmly and settle its foundations, or to gain insight into its true reality, except after the root (aṣl) has been prepared and perfected — for the source of confusion and stumbling in the branches is generated and produced by confusion and stumbling in the roots.

Know that the religious sciences are three: theology (al-kalām), the principles of jurisprudence (al-uṣūl), and jurisprudence (al-fiqh). Each one of them has a material (māddah) from which it derives and draws its sustenance, and upon which it leans and rests its support; and it has a purpose (maqṣūd) to which the aspiration of the seeker and his pursuit are attached and directed. It is therefore necessary to draw attention to its material, so that the one who plunges into it may kindle and borrow from it the measure of his need, and thereby attain his quest and desire. Nor is there any dispensation from drawing attention to its purpose, lest the seeker remain in blindness and error concerning that which he seeks and pursues.

As for the science of theology (al-kalām), its material is the discrimination (al-mayz) between demonstrations (barāhīn) and fallacies (aghālīṭ), and the discrimination between genuine sciences and mere beliefs and convictions, and the discrimination between the courses of the intellects and their stopping-points and stations. As for its purpose, it is the encompassing comprehension of the origination of the world (ḥudūth al-ʿālam) and its neediness for an effective Maker (ṣāniʿ muʾaththir) — One who is qualified with what is necessary of the attributes, transcendent and exalted above what is impossible to conceive as an attribute of the Essence, powerful over the sending of the Messengers and the supporting of them with miracles.

As for the principles (al-uṣūl), its material is theology, jurisprudence, and language. The aspect of its derivation from theology is that the encompassing comprehension of the evidences erected and established upon the rulings is founded upon the acceptance of the revealed laws (al-sharāʾiʿ) and the verification of the Messengers — and there is no aspiration to that except after knowledge of the Sender (al-mursil). The aspect of its derivation from jurisprudence is that jurisprudence is the signified (al-madlūl) and the object sought, and the pursuit of the evidence while being heedless of and inattentive to the signified is a thing repudiated and rejected by the pathways of the intellects. The aspect of its derivation from language is that the legal theorist (al-uṣūlī) is driven and compelled to discourse concerning the import of the address (faḥwā al-khiṭāb), the interpretation (taʾwīl) of the reports of the Messenger — peace be upon him — and the explicit texts (nuṣūṣ) of the Book.

And its purpose is the knowledge of the definitive evidences (al-adillah al-qaṭʿiyyah) erected upon the prescriptive rulings (al-aḥkām al-taklīfiyyah), and the solitary reports (akhbār al-āḥād), and the pathways of inference (masālik al-ʿibar), and the analogies (maqāyīs), and the elicited principles (al-mustathārah). The evidences adduced by way of independent reasoning (ijtihād) are not of the principles — for they are matters of conjecture (ẓanniyyāt) that have been taken in the manner of certainties — but the legal theorist is nevertheless compelled and necessitated to mention them in order to make clear the sound from the corrupt, and the well-grounded from the deviant and perverse; and because the weighings of preponderance (al-tarjīḥāt) are among the most obscure and perplexing matters of the science of principles, and there is no way to them except by the elucidation of the ranks and degrees.

As for jurisprudence (al-fiqh), its material is the principles, and its purpose is the knowledge of the legal rulings (al-aḥkām al-sharʿiyyah) and the establishment and settling of the rulings — when the conjectural indicators (al-ʿalāmāt al-maẓnūnah) appear — as things known through definitive evidences, with no conjecture therein.
### Section

There is no science among these sciences except that it has loci of consensus (mawāqiʿ ijmāʿ) and sources of dispute (mathārāt nizāʿ). The locus of consensus in theology is the things perceived by primary necessity (al-mudrakāt bil-bidāyah), the necessary truths (al-ḍarūriyyāt), and the intelligibles (al-maʿqūlāt) in which the direction of inquiry is unified and does not multiply or diverge — like the consensus of the rational ones that the eternal (al-qadīm) does not pass away or become nonexistent. The source of disagreement therein is the conflict and opposition of evidences and ambiguities (taʿāruḍ al-adillah wal-shubuhāt).

As for the science of principles, the origin of agreement therein resembles and corresponds to the origin of agreement in theology; and the spring and fountainhead of disagreement therein is two things: one of them is the conflict of evidences and ambiguities, and the second is the intermingling and blending of the definitive (qaṭʿī) with the conjectural (ẓannī) within it.

As for jurisprudence, the locus of consensus therein is what is grounded in and supported by the text (naṣṣ) of the Book of God, or an unbrokenly transmitted report (ḥadīth mutawātir), or a consensus (ijmāʿ) that is obligatory to follow. Whatever is beyond that belongs to the loci of conjectures (maẓān al-ẓunūn); and when confusion and perplexity arise therein, the independent jurists (mujtahidūn) differ and their opinions fluctuate and waver, and they split into factions and parties.

EPUB/chap_01.xhtml.title: Section 1 — The Opening Invocation and the Purpose of the Book

paragraphs.text: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

I praise God, firstly, with abundant and perpetual praise, even though it falls short of the due right of His majesty—the praise of all who praise Him. And I send blessings and peace, secondly, upon His messengers—a blessing that encompasses, along with the Master of mankind, all the other sent ones. And I seek His guidance, thirdly, regarding what has impelled my resolve: the composition of a book on the Revival of the Religious Sciences. And I undertake, fourthly, to silence your reproach—O you who exceed all bounds in blame among the company of the obstinate deniers, and who are immoderate in censure and rejection among the ranks of the heedless rejecters. For the knot of silence has indeed been loosed from my tongue, and the burden of speech and the necklace of utterance have been imposed upon me—[speech] against what you persist in: blindness to the clear truth, along with stubbornness in championing falsehood, beautifying ignorance, and raising clamor against one who has chosen to withdraw but slightly from the customs of the people, and to incline a little away from mere conformity to outward form, toward acting in accordance with the dictates of knowledge—hoping thereby to attain what God—exalted is He—has made His servant's duty: the purification of the soul and the reformation of the heart, and seeking to make amends for some of what has slipped away through the squandering of life, despairing of fully satisfying your need while you remain in bewilderment, and withdrawing from the throng of those of whom the Master of the Law—God's blessings and peace be upon him—said: "The most severely punished of people on the Day of Resurrection is a scholar whom God—glorified is He—did not benefit with his knowledge." {«أشد الناس عذابا يوم القيامة عالم لم ينفعه الله سبحانه بعلمه»}

By my life, there is no cause for your persistence in arrogance save the malady that has pervaded the great multitude—nay, that has encompassed the masses—namely, the failure to perceive the summit of this matter, and the ignorance that the affair is grave, the matter is serious, the Hereafter is approaching, this world is receding, the term of life is near, the journey is long, the provision is scant, the peril is immense, and the road is blocked. And nothing besides knowledge and action that are purely for the face of God is, in the sight of the discerning critic, but rejection. And traversing the path of the Hereafter, amid its many perils, without a guide and without a companion, is wearisome and toilsome. The guides of the path are the scholars, who are the heirs of the prophets. Yet the age has become empty of them, and none remain save those who merely wear the outward garb of learning. The devil has gained mastery over most of them, and tyranny has led them astray. Each one has become infatuated with his immediate share, so that he comes to see the known good as evil and the evil as good—until the science of religion has become effaced, and the beacon of guidance in the regions of the earth has been extinguished. They have made it appear to creation that there is no knowledge save a legal opinion (fatwā) for governance, by which judges aid themselves in settling disputes when the rabble clash; or a disputation (jadal) with which the seeker of vainglory arms himself to achieve victory and silencing of opponents; or embellished rhymed prose (sajʿ) by which the preacher seeks to entice the common folk. For they have seen nothing beyond these three as a trap for the forbidden and a net for the perishing. As for the knowledge of the path of the Hereafter—that upon which the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ) proceeded, which God—glorified is He—has named in His Book— which He has named in His Book as the path of guidance and the way of truth.

paragraphs.text:
### |

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
أحمد الله أولا حمدا كثيرا متواليا وإن كان يتضاءل دون حق جلاله حمد
الحامدين وأصلي واسلم على رسله ثانيا صلاة تستغرق مع سيد البشر سائر
المرسلين وأستخيره تعالى ثالثا فيما انبعث عزمي من تحرير كتاب في إحياء
علوم الدين وأنتدب لقطع تعجبك رابعا أيها العاذل المتغالي في العذل من بين
زمرة الجاحدين المسرف في التقريع (1) PageV01P001
والإنكار من بين طبقات المنكرين الغافلين فلقد حل عن لساني عقدة الصمت
وطوقني عهدة الكلام وقلادة النطق ما أنت مثابر عليه من العمى عن جلية الحق
مع اللجاج في نصرة الباطل وتحسين الجهل والتشغيب على من آثر النزوع قليلا
عن مراسم الخلق ومال ميلا يسيرا عن ملازمة الرسم إلى العمل بمقتضى العلم
طمعا في نيل ما تعبده الله تعالى به من تزكية النفس وإصلاح القلب وتداركا
لبعض ما فرط من إضاعة العمر يائسا عن تمام حاجتك في الحيرة وانحيازا عن
غمار من قال فيهم صاحب الشرع صلوات الله عليه وسلامه أشد الناس عذابا يوم
القيامة عالم لم ينفعه الله سبحانه بعلمه (1) ولعمري إنه لا سبب لإصرارك
على التكبر إلا الداء الذي عم الجم الغفير بل شمل الجماهير من القصور عن
ملاحظة ذروة هذا الأمر والجهل بأن الأمر إد والخطب جد والآخرة مقبلة
والدنيا مدبرة والأجل قريب والسفر بعيد والزاد طفيف والخطر عظيم والطريق سد
وما سوى الخالص لوجه الله من العلم والعمل عند الناقد البصير رد وسلوك طريق
الآخرة مع كثرة الغوائل من غير دليل ولا رفيق متعب ومكد فأدله الطريق هم
العلماء الذين هم ورثة الأنبياء وقد شغر منهم الزمان ولم يبق إلا المترسمون
وقد استحوذ على أكثرهم الشيطان واستغواهم الطغيان وأصبح كل واحد بعاجل حظه
مشغوفا فصار يرى المعروف منكرا والمنكر معروفا حتى ظل علم الدين مندرسا
ومنار الهدى في أقطار الأرض منطمسا ولقد خيلوا إلى الخلق أن لا علم إلا
فتوى حكومة تستعين به القضاة على فصل الخصام عند تهاوش الطغام أو جدل يتدرع
به طالب المباهاة إلى الغلبة والإفحام أو سجع مزخرف يتوسل به الواعظ إلى
استدراج العوام إذ لم يروا ما سوى هذه الثلاثة مصيدة للحرام وشبكة للحطام
فأما علم طريق الآخرة وما درج عليه السلف الصالح مما سماه الله سبحانه في

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: حمد (ḥ-m-d)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root meaning of praise, commendation, and grateful acknowledgment of beneficence.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Praise (ḥamd) is the acknowledgment of beneficence with reverence; it is due to God alone in His absolute perfection.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): "Aḥmad Allāh" — to praise God with all His praiseworthy attributes. Metaphorical (majāz): "Aḥmadtu al-arḍ" — to find the land agreeable for dwelling, extended to approving of any thing's qualities.
- Root: رسل (r-s-l)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Root meaning of sending forth with gentleness and ease; a messenger (rasūl) is one dispatched with a message.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The root denotes emission upon deliberation and composure; the messenger is one sent forth, and the term applies both to the bearer and the message conveyed.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: sending a messenger with a message. Metaphorical: "Arsala Allāh al-ʿadhāb" — God sent down punishment, extended to any divine dispensation.
- Root: علم (ʿ-l-m)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root meaning of knowledge, perception, and the mark or sign by which a thing is known.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Knowledge (ʿilm) is the apprehension of a thing as it is in itself, divided into the perception of the essence and the judgment of existence or non-existence of attributes.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "ʿalima" — to know with certainty. Metaphorical: "maʿālim al-ṭarīq" — the landmarks of the road, i.e., the traces by which the way is recognized.
- Sibawayh Rule: Rule of Prepositional Interposition (bāb al-faṣl bayna al-jār wa al-majrūr) — The permissibility of separating a preposition from its governed noun by an intervening clause, as in the author's extended invocations, where the syntactic flow is maintained despite the insertion of subordinate supplications.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

I praise God, firstly, with abundant and perpetual praise, even though it falls short of the due right of His majesty—the praise of all who praise Him. And I send blessings and peace, secondly, upon His messengers—a blessing that encompasses, along with the Master of mankind, all the other sent ones. And I seek His guidance, thirdly, regarding what has impelled my resolve: the composition of a book on the Revival of the Religious Sciences. And I undertake, fourthly, to silence your reproach—O you who exceed all bounds in blame among the company of the obstinate deniers, and who are immoderate in censure and rejection among the ranks of the heedless rejecters. For the knot of silence has indeed been loosed from my tongue, and the burden of speech and the necklace of utterance have been imposed upon me—[speech] against what you persist in: blindness to the clear truth, along with stubbornness in championing falsehood, beautifying ignorance, and raising clamor against one who has chosen to withdraw but slightly from the customs of the people, and to incline a little away from mere conformity to outward form, toward acting in accordance with the dictates of knowledge—hoping thereby to attain what God—exalted is He—has made His servant's duty: the purification of the soul and the reformation of the heart, and seeking to make amends for some of what has slipped away through the squandering of life, despairing of fully satisfying your need while you remain in bewilderment, and withdrawing from the throng of those of whom the Master of the Law—God's blessings and peace be upon him—said: "The most severely punished of people on the Day of Resurrection is a scholar whom God—glorified is He—did not benefit with his knowledge." {«أشد الناس عذابا يوم القيامة عالم لم ينفعه الله سبحانه بعلمه»}

By my life, there is no cause for your persistence in arrogance save the malady that has pervaded the great multitude—nay, that has encompassed the masses—namely, the failure to perceive the summit of this matter, and the ignorance that the affair is grave, the matter is serious, the Hereafter is approaching, this world is receding, the term of life is near, the journey is long, the provision is scant, the peril is immense, and the road is blocked. And nothing besides knowledge and action that are purely for the face of God is, in the sight of the discerning critic, but rejection. And traversing the path of the Hereafter, amid its many perils, without a guide and without a companion, is wearisome and toilsome. The guides of the path are the scholars, who are the heirs of the prophets. Yet the age has become empty of them, and none remain save those who merely wear the outward garb of learning. The devil has gained mastery over most of them, and tyranny has led them astray. Each one has become infatuated with his immediate share, so that he comes to see the known good as evil and the evil as good—until the science of religion has become effaced, and the beacon of guidance in the regions of the earth has been extinguished. They have made it appear to creation that there is no knowledge save a legal opinion (fatwā) for governance, by which judges aid themselves in settling disputes when the rabble clash; or a disputation (jadal) with which the seeker of vainglory arms himself to achieve victory and silencing of opponents; or embellished rhymed prose (sajʿ) by which the preacher seeks to entice the common folk. For they have seen nothing beyond these three as a trap for the forbidden and a net for the perishing. As for the knowledge of the path of the Hereafter—that upon which the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ) proceeded, which God—glorified is He—has named in His Book— which He has named in His Book as the path of guidance and the way of truth.

EPUB/chap_01.xhtml.title: The Ascents of Holiness in Knowledge of the Soul — Section 1: On the Soul, Heart, Spirit, and Intellect

paragraphs.text: I say: As for the soul (nafs), it is used in two senses. The first is that it is used to denote the aggregate of blameworthy attributes, namely the animal powers opposed to the rational powers. This is what is understood when the Sufis use the term, for it is said: "Among the most excellent of jihād is that you struggle against your soul." And to this refers the saying of our Prophet, peace be upon him: "Your most hostile enemy is your soul which is between your sides."

The second sense is that it is used to denote the reality of the human being and his very essence (dhāt). For the soul of every thing is its reality (ḥaqīqah). It is the substance (jawhar) that is the locus of intelligibles (maḥall al-maʿqūlāt). It belongs to the world of the divine dominion (ʿālam al-malakūt) and to the world of the command (ʿālam al-amr), as we shall explain. Indeed, its names differ according to the differing states that accrue to it. If it turns toward the right course, and the divine tranquilities (sakīnāt) descend upon it, and the breezes of the outpouring of divine generosity follow in succession upon it, then it is at peace in the remembrance of God, Mighty and Majestic, and rests in the divine cognitions, and flies to the highest horizon of the angelic realm — then it is called the "tranquil soul" (nafs muṭmaʾinnah). God, Exalted is He, said: {يا أيتها النفس المطمئنة ارجعي إلى ربك راضية مرضية} ("O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing").

But if it is with its powers and its troops in war, combat, strife, and conflict, and the battle between them is alternating — sometimes the upper hand is with it, and sometimes the upper hand is with the powers — then its state is not upright. Sometimes it inclines toward the side of the intellects, receiving the intelligibles and persisting in acts of obedience; sometimes the powers overcome it, and it descends to the lowest depth of the stations of beasts. This soul is the "blaming soul" (nafs lawwāmah). This soul is the state of most creatures. For whoever ascends to the horizon of the angels until he is adorned with the sciences, the virtues of the soul, and the good deeds — he is a corporeal angel (malak jismānī), due to his elevation above humanity and his non-participation with humans except in schematic form (al-ṣūrah al-takhṭīṭiyyah). For this reason God, Exalted is He, said: {ما هذا بشرا إن هذا إلا ملك كريم} ("This is no human; this is none other than a noble angel").

And whoever is debased until he reaches the lowest depth of beasts — if a dog or a donkey, upright in stature and speaking, were to be imagined, he would be that very thing, due to his being stripped of human virtues and his non-participation with humans except in schematic form. This is the "soul commanding to evil" (al-nafs al-ammārah bi-al-sūʾ). For most of them, if you reflect upon them, are donkeys, dogs, or wolves. And they are among the humans mentioned in the saying of God, Exalted is He: {شياطين الإنس والجن يوحي بعضهم إلى بعض زخرف القول غرورا} ("Devils among mankind and jinn inspire one another with adorned speech in delusion"). And the Commander of the Believers, ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said: "O you who resemble men, yet are not men!" Such a soul you will ever see as a slave to a stone, or clay, or a beast, or a saddle-camel. And this is the one about whom God, Glorified is He, informed us when He said: {إن النفس لأمارة بالسوء} ("Indeed the soul commands to evil").

As for the heart (qalb), it is also used in two senses. The first is the pineal-shaped flesh deposited in the interior of the human being on the left side. This is known by dissection. It is the receptacle of black blood and the source of the vapor that is the vehicle of the natural animal spirit (al-rūḥ al-ṭibbī al-ḥayawānī). This is found in all animals and is not specific to the human being. It is that which perishes at death, and all the senses are corrupted by its corruption.

The second sense — and this is the one we are concerned to explain — is the human spirit (al-rūḥ al-insānī) that bears the trust of God (amānat Allāh), is adorned with knowledge, in which the science of the primordial nature (al-fiṭrah) is implanted, and which speaks of the divine unity by its saying "Yes" (balā). It is the origin of the human being and the final end of all creatures in the world of the return (ʿālam al-maʿād). God, Exalted is He, said: {قل الروح من أمر ربي} ("Say: The spirit is from the command of my Lord"), and He said: {ألا بذكر الله تطمئن القلوب} ("Truly, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest"). And our Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The hearts of the children of Adam are all between two fingers of the fingers of the Merciful," to the end of the hadith. Wherever the heart is mentioned in the Sacred Law, what is meant is that which we are concerned to explain. And if it is used in some place for the pineal flesh, that is because it is its special attachment (mutʿallaq khāṣṣ) and its first attachment. As the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, in the interior of the son of Adam there is a morsel of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound by its soundness, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt by its corruption — and it is the heart."

As for the spirit (rūḥ), it is used to denote the subtle vapor that ascends from the source of the heart and rises to the brain, and also, by means of the veins, to the entire body. It acts in every place according to its temperament and preparedness, and it is the vehicle of life. This vapor is like the lamp, and the life that subsists through it is like the light; the manner of its influence in the body is like the manner of the lamp's illumination of the parts of the house. It is also used to denote the originated being (al-mubdaʿ) that issues from the command of God, Exalted is He, which is the locus of the sciences, revelation, and inspiration. It is of the genus of the angels, separate from the corporeal world, self-subsistent in its essence, as we shall explain. It is also used to denote the spirit that stands in opposition to all the angels, which is the First Originated Being (al-mubdaʿ al-awwal), and it is the Holy Spirit (rūḥ al-qudus). It is also used to denote the Qurʾān. In sum, it is an expression for that by which life subsists, in general.

As for the intellect (ʿaql), it is used to denote the First Intellect (al-ʿaql al-awwal), which is what is meant by "intellect" in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The first thing God created was the intellect. He said to it: 'Come forward,' and it came forward. Then He said to it: 'Go back,' and it went back" — that is, "Come forward so that you may be completed by Me, and go back so that by you the entire world may be completed, apart from you." And it is the one to whom God, Exalted is He, said: "By My might and My majesty, I have created no creature more noble to Me nor more excellent than you. By you I take, and by you I give," to the end of the hadith. And it is that which is expressed as the Pen (al-qalam), as he, peace be upon him, said: "The first thing God created was the Pen. He said to it: 'Write.' It said: 'What shall I write?' He said: 'What will be, until the Day of Resurrection — of deed, effect, provision, and term.' So it wrote what will be and what is to come until the Day of Resurrection."

The second usage is that it is used to denote the human soul (al-nafs al-insāniyyah). The third usage is that it is used to denote an attribute of the soul. It is, in relation to the soul, like sight in relation to the eye. By means of it, the soul is prepared for the apprehension of intelligibles, just as the eye, by means of sight, is prepared for the apprehension of sensibles. And it is the one about whom the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said, relating from his Lord, Mighty and Majestic: "By My might and My majesty, I shall surely conceal you in the one I love."
And wherever we use in this book the terms "soul" (nafs), "spirit" (rūḥ), "heart" (qalb), and "intellect" (ʿaql), we mean by them the human soul, which is the locus of intelligibles.
SECTION: Demonstration of the Existence of the Soul, in General

I say: The soul is too evident to need a proof for its establishment. For all the addresses of the Sacred Law are directed not to a non-existent thing, but to an existent, living being that understands the address. Nevertheless, we shall seek confirmation in its exposition, and we say:

It is a matter of certain knowledge, about which there is no doubt, that whenever things share in one thing and differ in another, the shared thing is other than the differing thing. We find all bodies sharing in that they are bodies, in which three intersecting dimensions can be supposed. Then we find them differing in movement and apprehension. If their movement were due to their corporeality, then every body ought to be moving, because realities do not differ; and what is necessary for a species is necessary for all that share in that species and that reality. But if it is due to a meaning beyond corporeality, then a principle of action (mabdaʾ al-fiʿl) is established in general, and that principle is the soul — until it becomes clear whether it is a substance or an accident.

An example of this: We see vegetable bodies nourishing, growing, generating their like, and moving with various movements of branching and veining. If these meanings were due to corporeality, then all bodies ought to be so. But if they are due to something other than corporeality — rather, to an additional meaning — then that meaning is called the "vegetative soul" (nafs nabātiyyah). Then the animal has what the plant has, and in addition senses, moves by will, is guided to its own interests, seeks what benefits it, and flees what harms it. So we know with certainty that in it there is an additional meaning beyond the vegetable bodies. Then we find the human being: in him is all that is in the plant and the animal of meanings, and he is distinguished by the apprehension of things outside sensation — such as that the whole is greater than the part. He apprehends particulars by the five senses and apprehends universals by the rational faculties (al-mashāʿir al-ʿaqliyyah). He shares with the animal in the senses and differs from it in the rational faculties. For the human being apprehends the universal from every particular, makes that universal a premise of a syllogism, and derives from it a conclusion. Neither is the apprehension of the universal denied, nor is the apprehender of it rejected. Neither the accident, nor the body receptive of accidents, nor the plant, nor the non-human animal apprehends the universal, such that the universal would subsist in it and thereby be divided by the divisions of body. For the universal, solely by virtue of being universal, is not divided at all. Thus the absolute universal "human" has no half, third, or quarter. Therefore, that which is receptive of the universal form is a substance that is neither a body nor an accident in a body, having no position (waḍʿ) and no location (ayna) by which it could be pointed to. Rather, its existence is an intellectual existence — more hidden than everything from sensation, and more manifest than everything to the intellect.
By this, the existence of the soul is established; it is established in general that it is a substance; and it is established that it is exalted above matter and corporeal forms.

paragraphs.text: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The opening of the Book: Praise be to God, the First in His Lordship, the Eternal in His Pre-Eternity, the Wise in His Sovereignty, the Generous in His Might. There is no likeness to Him in His Essence and His Handiwork, nor any equivalent to Him in His Kingdom. He is the Maker of every thing made by His Power, the Speaker through His Eternal Speech, which is not separate from His Attribute. I praise Him for His Grace, and I seek His aid in repelling His Retribution. He is God, my Lord, alone, with no partner to Him, the One in His Lordship, Who abbreviates — whomsoever He wills — by His Mercy. He sealed the Prophets with Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, and upon his Family and his Progeny.

To proceed: When I saw that the aspirations of the people of this age were confined to attaining their hidden and apparent objectives, and a group of the kings of the earth asked me to compose for them a book without equal for attaining their objectives, the seizing of dominions (mamalik), and what would aid them in that, I sought God's guidance (istikhara) and composed for them a book. I named it "The Secret of the Two Worlds and the Disclosure of What Lies in the Two Abodes," and I divided it into chapters, articles, and sections. I mentioned in it ranks with correctness, and I made it an indicator toward the pursuit of sovereignty (mamlaka), an inciter upon it, a foundation gathering its meanings, and a clarifier of the manner of its ordering and its training. For it is suitable for the ascetic scholar and for the partner in the partnership of the owner, by sweetening the hearts of the soldiers and drawing them to him through exhortations. PageV01P007 — The first who approved of it and read it upon me at the Nizamiyya school, secretly from the people, in the second session after my return from travel, was a man from the land of the Maghrib called Muhammad ibn Tumart, from the people of Salmiyya; and I discerned in him the marks of sovereignty. And this book is precious — it is not permissible to squander it, for beneath it lie secrets that require unveiling, since the natures of the world are averse to them; and beneath it lie precious sciences and many indications pointing to the obscurities of secrets known only to the master sages (fuhul al-hukama'). May God grant you success in acting upon it, for it points to all that you desire, if God Most High wills. PageV01P008
| The First Article: On Sovereignty (Al-Mulk)

Know that sovereignty is mighty and barren; upon it has fallen the clash and dispute between the righteous and the wicked, the loser and the winner. From it branches envy and every wavering passion and purpose. Thus there is no escape from a foundation, a rank, acquisition, patience, and the gathering of wealth for the attainment of aspirations. And the mother of all ventures in its acquisition is the loftiness of resolve (himmah): as Mu'awiya — may God Most High be pleased with him — said: "Resolve upon the lofty matters that you may attain them, for I was not worthy of the Caliphate, yet I resolved upon it and attained it." And the stories of the ancients have reached you, so look into their reports and their traces: no one has reached the degree of sovereignty through a door other than resolve, and how often has sovereignty been wrested from the hand of a rightful heir — such as the household of our Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace.

paragraphs.text: ### | General Preface

We are in dire need of publishing precise scholarly editions of the foundations of our ancient Arab heritage, for it is through this type of publication that texts come alive and become clear, and it becomes easy for those engaged with their subjects to read them and benefit from them. Nothing is more useful to the researcher than to have before him the primary documents, properly vocalized, critically edited, and free from the impurities of corruption (taḥrīf) and scribal error (taṣḥīf).

Our ancient books have been afflicted by the fact that many of them were published and supervised by publishers who were not specialized scholars—their only concern being the material profit from printing them. We suffer from their editions what we suffer: typographical and linguistic errors, omissions in texts here and additions there, and a complete absence of critical apparatus, commentary, explanation, and scholarly indexes of all kinds. Many times we stand before a text bewildered, with hands tied, unable to understand its meaning or to direct its interpretation—or we direct it wrongly in a way the author never intended, for no reason other than that the text contains a corruption, an omission, or an addition by a copyist, or a confusion between the text itself and a commentary written upon it. It suffices that the negative particle "lā" (لا) falls out of a sentence, or that the word "idh" (إذ) is placed instead of "idhā" (إذا) or vice versa, or that the word "al-ʿārifīn" (العارفين, the knowers) is written instead of "al-ʿIrāqiyyīn" (العراقيين, the Iraqis), or similar corruptions, for the text to become disturbed and its meaning corrupted; and often this leads the researcher to a mistaken understanding that may culminate in a false opinion or an unfounded theory.

The lot of the treatise "The Niche of Lights" (Mishkāt al-Anwār) which we publish today does not differ much from the lot of other books published in the unscientific manner we have indicated. It has been printed in Egypt in several editions: in the years 1322 AH, 1325 AH, 1929 CE, 1352 AH, and within the collection "Al-Jawāhir al-Ghawālī min Rasāʾil Ḥujjat al-Islām al-Ghazālī" in the year 1343 AH.

I have collated this edition—which is now the most widely circulated—against the manuscripts that were available for my examination, and I found it replete with serious errors and corruptions. I also found in it many additions to the original text, and an omission amounting to a full page in one place: namely, from his saying "in the station of beasts, nay lower" (بمنزلة البهائم بل أخس) to his saying "in pure darkness, namely their dark souls" (بمحض الظلمة وهى نفوسهم المظلمة).

It appears that the original from which this copy was taken was mixed with some commentaries and glosses, and the copyist transmitted all of that without distinguishing between the text and what was other than it.
It suffices that I mention some examples of the corruptions that occurred in this copy to show its gravity:
On p. 129 occurs "sirr al-kalbiyya" (سر الكلبية) with sīn (س); the correct reading is "sharr al-kalbiyya" (شر الكلبية) with shīn (ش).

On p. 130 occurs "and measure upon it the light and the day" (وقس عليه الضوء والنهار); the correct reading is "and measure upon it the mount and the fire" (وقس عليه الطور والنار), because the discourse concerns Moses who perceived from the side of the Mount a fire.
On p. 131 occurs: "and this portion of revelation" (وهذا الحظ من الوحى); the correct reading is: "and this pattern of revelation" (وهذا النمط من الوحى).

On p. 143 occurs: "and He is the one who writes what the senses have reported" (وهو الذى يكتب ما أوردته الحواس). The correct reading is: "and He is the one who verifies what the senses have reported" (وهو الذى يستثبت ما أوردته الحواس).
On p. 134 occurs: "more splendid and more luminous" (أجلى وأسنى); the correct reading is: "more majestic and more luminous" (أجل وأسنى).
And on p. 134: "let us return to the purpose of the examples" (فلنرجع إلى غرض الأمثلة); the correct reading is: "to the presentation of the examples" (إلى عرض الأمثلة) with the unpointed ʿayn (ع).
And on p. 135: "that the prophets are a luminous lamp" (كون الأنبياء سراجا منيرا); the correct reading is: "luminous lamps" (سرجا منيرة).
And on p. 137: "and the base events" (والحوادث الرديئة); the correct reading is: "and the destructive occupations" (والأشغال المردية).
And on p. 138: "and the kinds of these divisions are many" (وأصناف هذه الأقسام كثيرة); the correct reading is: "and the divisions of these kinds are many" (وأقسام هذه الأصناف كثيرة).
And on p. 139: "so nature altered it" (فأحاله الطبع); the correct reading is: "so nature altered it to the natural disposition" (فأحاله إلى الطبع).

This is a little from much, of examples of errors I have observed in this edition, in addition to the other defects I have indicated. Therefore, re-publishing this treatise and publishing other works of al-Ghazālī was a duty required by scholarly integrity (al-amāna al-ʿilmiyya), as required by fairness to the author, whose right upon us is that we understand his works in the correct manner he intended. This is what the Supreme Council for the Care of Arts, Letters, and Social Sciences resolved to undertake when it decided to publish the works of al-Ghazālī—both those already printed and those still in manuscript.
The Name of the Treatise and Its Station Among al-Ghazālī's Works:
It was given the name "Mishkāt al-Anwār" (The Niche of Lights) as it appears in "Kashf al-Ẓunūn" of Ḥājjī Khalīfa and in the printed copies.

It was also given the name "Mishkāt al-Anwār wa Miṣfāt al-Asrār" (The Niche of Lights and the Clarifier of Secrets) as it appears in the Paris manuscript and at the end of the Alexandria Municipal manuscript.
It was also named "Kitāb al-Mishkāt wa al-Miṣbāḥ" (The Book of the Niche and the Lamp) as it appears in the manuscript of Shahīd ʿAlī Pasha.

Another book is attributed to al-Ghazālī titled "Mishkāt al-Anwār fī Laṭāʾif al-Akhbār" (The Niche of Lights Concerning Subtleties of Reports) which has no connection to this treatise; rather, it is a large book of which manuscripts exist in the Egyptian Dār al-Kutub. On the title page of manuscript no. 237 (Taṣawwuf), the true author's name appears: ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, known as Ibn al-Faqīh al-Ḥāfiẓ al-Miṣrī, who died in the year 877 AH.

There is no doubt that the treatise Mishkāt al-Anwār is among al-Ghazālī's later works that represent the period of intellectual and spiritual maturity. However, we cannot assign a specific date for its composition as Professor Massignon did in his book "Recueil de textes inédits concernant l'histoire de la mystique en pays d'Islam: Paris 1929," where he says it was composed in the period between 495 and 505 AH—the period al-Ghazālī spent in Ṭūs, devoting himself to authorship and worship. Massignon lists among al-Ghazālī's works of this period the book "Miʿyār al-ʿIlm" (The Standard of Knowledge), the book "Miḥakk al-Naẓar" (The Touchstone of Contemplation), the book "Al-Maqṣad al-Asnā" (The Most Sublime Aim), and the treatise "Mishkāt al-Anwār." But we see in the "Mishkāt al-Anwār" references to all these books, which indicates that al-Ghazālī composed them before the Mishkāt; and we do not know whether he composed all of them in the same period Massignon specifies. Nor do we think that Professor Massignon has historical evidence upon which to rely in determining the years of composition of al-Ghazālī's books in the manner he has drawn.
Manuscripts of the Treatise:
There exist for this treatise no fewer than thirty-six manuscripts scattered throughout the world; we mention from them the following:

(1) Alexandria Municipal, dated 907 AH (2) Qūwīlī Ḥ 1 p. 262. (3) Mosul 176 [8] (4) Patna 2: 412 [no. 2580 (8)] (5) Berlin no. 3207 (6) Leiden no. 1988. (7) Brill manuscripts 2: 1053 (8) Ambrosiana (RSO III 573) A 64. V (9) Vatican Borghese 65. Vat. Borgh (10) Manchester i 71 (11) Princeton, Garrett Collection no. 1892, dated 937 AH (12) India Office in London no. 1237, Arberry's catalogue, dated 1096; and no. 1238, dated 1107. (13) Tehran: Majlis-i Shūrā-yi Millī no. 9015, dated 1320. (14) Āṣafiyya 1: 388 [14 (5) Arabic Taṣawwuf] (15) Tehran 2: 77. (16) Rāmpūr 1: 697. (17) Ẓāhiriyya: general no. 7621.

And in Istanbul: (18) Shahīd ʿAlī 1712, 1377. (19) Bashīr Āghā 650 (20) Sulaymāniyya 734. (21) Köprülü nos. 860, 1603: (22) Ayasofya 2075, 1711 [3], 4801. (23) Jār Allāh 1092 [1], 2075. (24) Walī al-Dīn 1829. (25) Salīm Āghā: collection no. 108. (26) Asʿad 1717/18. And in the Egyptian Dār al-Kutub: (27) 2673 Taṣawwuf, dated 1065, (28) no. 184 Taṣawwuf (within a collection), (29) Ṭalʿat collections nos. 274, 513, 326, 822, 826.
And in Paris: (30) no. 1331. (31) And in El Escorial 2, no. 631. (32) Gotha (Pertsch catalogue, part 3, vol. 2, p. 378) no. 1166, dated 1188.

paragraphs.text: The Shaykh, the Imām, the learned scholar, the Proof of Islam, and the Blessing of Mankind — Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad al-Ghazālī al-Ṭūsī — may God sanctify his soul and illuminate his grave — Amen — said:
Praise be to God, as His due praise deserves, and prayers and peace be upon the best of His creation, Muḥammad, His Messenger and servant, and upon his family and companions after him.

To proceed: Know, O you who are eager and hastening toward the acquisition of knowledge, who displays in yourself the sincerity of desire and the extremity of thirst for it — that if your purpose in seeking knowledge is rivalry, vainglory, outdoing one's peers, drawing the faces of people toward yourself, and amassing the fleeting goods of this world — then you are striving to demolish your religion, to destroy your own soul, and to sell your Hereafter for your worldly life. Your bargain is a losing one, your trade is bankrupt, and your teacher is an accomplice aiding you in your disobedience and a partner in your ruin. He is like one who sells a sword to a highway robber, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: {«Whoever aids in an act of disobedience, even by half a word, is a partner in it.»}

But if your intention and purpose — between you and God Almighty — in seeking knowledge is guidance (hidāyah) and not mere narration (riwāyah), then rejoice! For the angels spread their wings for you when you walk, and the fish of the sea seek forgiveness for you when you strive. Yet you must know, before all else, that the guidance which is the fruit of knowledge has a beginning and an end, an outward aspect and an inward aspect. There is no reaching its end except after perfecting its beginning, and no attaining its inward except after standing firm upon its outward.

And behold, I am pointing you to the beginning of guidance (bidāyat al-hidāyah), so that you may test yourself by it and examine your heart with it. If you find your heart inclining toward it, your soul submissive to it and accepting of it — then go forth to aspire to the ends and to plunge into the seas of the sciences.

But if you find your heart, when confronted with it, procrastinating, and with acting upon its requirements, delaying — then know that your soul which inclines toward seeking knowledge is the soul commanding to evil (al-nafs al-ammārah bi-l-sūʾ), and it has risen up obedient to the accursed Satan, so that he may lower you down by the rope of his delusion, and drag you by his cunning into the deep waters of destruction. His aim is to make evil appear attractive to you in the guise of good, until he joins you to {«those who are the greatest losers in deeds, those whose effort is lost in this worldly life while they think they are doing good work»} (Q. 18:103-104).

And at that point, Satan recites to you the virtue of knowledge and the rank of the scholars, and the reports and traditions that have come concerning that. And he distracts you from his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: {«Whoever increases in knowledge but does not increase in guidance, increases not in God's sight except in distance»}, and from his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: {«The most severely punished of people on the Day of Resurrection is a scholar whom God has not benefited with his knowledge»}. And he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say: {«O God, I seek refuge in You from knowledge that does not benefit, from a heart that does not humble itself, from a deed that is not raised up, and from a supplication that is not heard.»}

And from his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: {«I passed on the night of my night-journey by a people whose lips were being clipped with shears of fire. I said: Who are you? They said: We used to command good and not do it, and forbid evil and do it.»}

So beware, O poor one, of yielding to his falsification, lest he lower you down by the rope of his delusion. Woe to the ignorant one who did not learn even once, and woe to the scholar who did not act upon what he knew a thousand times.

And know that people, in seeking knowledge, are in three states: A man who seeks knowledge to make it his provision for the return to God (al-maʿād), intending thereby nothing but the Face of God and the abode of the Hereafter — this one is among the successful (al-fāʾizīn).

And a man who seeks it to aid himself in his transient life, to attain by it honor, status, and wealth — while he knows this of himself and perceives in his heart the baseness of his state and the vileness of his purpose — this one is among those who gamble with their salvation (al-mukhāṭirīn). If his appointed term overtakes him before repentance, it is feared for him an evil end, and his affair remains in the peril of the divine will. But if he is granted success in repentance before the term arrives, and he joins action to knowledge and makes up for the deficiency that preceded from him — he joins the successful, for the one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin.

And a third man — Satan has gained mastery over him, so he takes his knowledge as a means to multiplying wealth, boasting of status, and aggrandizing himself through the abundance of followers. He enters by his knowledge into every avenue, hoping to satisfy his worldly desire. And with all that, he harbors in himself the notion that he holds a station with God, because he is marked with the mark of the scholars and imitates their outward forms in dress and speech — while he clamors for the world, outwardly and inwardly. This one is among the perished (al-hālikīn), among the foolish and deluded. For hope of his repentance is cut off, because he imagines himself to be among the doers of good, heedless of the saying of God Almighty: {«O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do?»} (Q. 61:2). And he is among those of whom the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: {«I fear for you more than the Antichrist (al-Dajjāl)»} — and it was said: "And what is that, O Messenger of God?" He said: {«The evil scholars.»}
