paragraphs.text: Praise be to Allah, by whose praise every epistle and discourse is opened, and blessings upon Muhammad the Chosen, possessor of prophethood and messengership, and upon his family and his companions, the guides from error. To proceed: You have asked me, O brother in religion, that I impart to you the ultimate aims of the sciences and their secrets, and the perils of the sects and their depths; and that I relate to you what I endured in extracting the truth from amidst the turmoil of the factions, despite the divergence of paths and ways; and what I dared in ascending from the lowland of blind following (taqlīd) to the highland of clear insight (istibṣār); and what I first gained from the science of theology (kalām); and what I secondly loathed from the ways of the partisans of authoritative instruction (taʿlīmiyyah), who restrict the attainment of truth to the taqlīd of an infallible Imam; and what I thirdly disparaged from the ways of philosophy (falsafah); and what I finally embraced from the way of Sufism (taṣawwuf); and what was unveiled to me amidst my investigations into the sayings of mankind, of the pith of truth; and what turned me away from spreading knowledge in Baghdad despite the abundance of students; and what drove me back to resuming my work in Nishapur after a long interval. So I hastened to answer your request, after ascertaining the sincerity of your desire, and I said, seeking aid from Allah, relying upon Him, seeking success from Him, and taking refuge in Him:

Know — may Allah the Exalted perfect your guidance and soften for you the reins of truth — that the divergence of mankind in religions and creeds, and then the divergence of the community (ummah) in the sects, despite the multiplicity of factions and the disparity of paths, is a deep sea in which the majority have drowned, and from which none have escaped save the few. And every faction claims that it is the saved one — {«وكل حزب بما لديهم فرحون»} ("And every party rejoices in what it has") — and this is what the Master of the Messengers, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, promised us, and he is the truthful and the confirmed, when he said: "My community will split into seventy-three sects, and the saved among them is one." So what he promised came to be.

And I have not ceased, from the prime of my youth — since I reached the age of discernment, before attaining twenty, until now, as my age has surpassed fifty — to plunge into the depths of this deep sea, and to wade into its overwhelming flood with the wading of the courageous, not the wading of the timid coward; and to penetrate into every darkness, and to assault every problem, and to leap into every perilous strait, and to scrutinize the creed of every faction, and to uncover the secrets of the doctrine of every group, in order to distinguish between the truthful and the false, and between the follower of the Sunnah and the innovator. I did not leave an esotericist (bāṭinī) except that I loved to examine his esotericism, nor a literalist (ẓāhirī) except that I wished to know the outcome of his literalism, nor a philosopher except that I sought to grasp the core of his philosophy, nor a theologian (mutakallim) except that I strove to attain the limit of his discourse and disputation, nor a Sufi except that I was eager to stumble upon the secret of his purity, nor a devotee except that I watched for what the outcome of his devotion reverts to, nor a heretic (zindīq) and denier of God except that I probed behind him to become aware of the causes of his audacity in his denial and heresy.

And the thirst for grasping the realities of things had been my habit and my religion from the very beginning of my affair and the flower of my life — an instinct and a nature placed by Allah in my constitution, not by my choice or contrivance — until the bond of taqlīd was dissolved from me, and the inherited beliefs were broken upon me, given the nearness of the age of youth. For I saw that the children of Christians do not grow up except upon Christianity, and the children of Jews do not grow up except upon Judaism, and the children of Muslims do not grow up except upon Islam. And I heard the hadith related from the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, where he said: "Every newborn is born upon the fiṭrah (primordial nature), and his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian." So my inner being stirred toward seeking the reality of the primordial fiṭrah, and the reality of the beliefs that arise incidentally through the taqlīd of parents and teachers, and the distinction between these taqlīds — whose beginnings are mere inculcations — and in distinguishing the truth from falsehood among them, there are divergences.

So I said to myself: First, my aim is only knowledge of the realities of things, and therefore I must seek what the reality of knowledge itself is. Then it became clear to me that certain knowledge (al-ʿilm al-yaqīnī) is that in which the known thing is disclosed with a disclosure that leaves no room for doubt, and with which no possibility of error or illusion accompanies it, and the heart does not entertain the estimation of that — rather, security from error must be conjoined with certainty, conjoined in such a way that if someone — for example — were to challenge its falsity by turning a stone into gold and a staff into a serpent, that would not engender doubt or denial. For if I know that ten is more than three, and a speaker were to say to me: "No, rather three is more, with the proof that I turn this staff into a serpent," and he turns it, and I witness that from him, I would not doubt my knowledge because of it, and nothing would result from it for me except wonder at how he has the power to do it! As for doubt in what I know because of it — no, that does not occur. Then I knew that everything I do not know in this manner, and of which I am not certain with this type of certainty, is knowledge in which there is no confidence and with which there is no security; and every knowledge with which there is no security is not certain knowledge.

paragraphs.text: # QUAD-LEXICAL & SYNTACTIC ANCHOR CONSTELLATION

[Root: قسم]
 * Lisan / Ayn: Division, apportionment, allotment of shares
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "القسم: إفراز النصيب" — the separation and allotment of portions; used for dividing inheritance, spoils, and the apportioning of destinies
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: dividing shares of property. Metaphorical: "قلبه متقسم" — a heart divided/consumed by cares; "تقسمته الهموم" — anxieties that tear one apart

[Root: خير]
 * Lisan / Ayn: Goodness, excellence, superiority; that which is desirable
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الخير: ما يرغب فيه الكل" — that which all desire: intellect, justice, virtue, benefit. Two kinds: absolute good (good in every circumstance) and relative good (good for one, evil for another)
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: choosing the better of two things (istikhārah). The root carries the sense of preference and selection of the superior

[Root: حمد]
 * Lisan / Ayn: Praise, commendation, laudation for virtue or beneficence
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Praise rendered for voluntary beneficence; the root also relates to the intense heat of praise (ḥamīm — hot water) suggesting fervency
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "أحمد الله تعالى بجميع محامده" — praising God with all His praises. Metaphorical: "أحمدت الأرض" — found the land praiseworthy to dwell in

[Root: خلق]
 * Lisan / Ayn: Creation, origination; also: measure, proportion, estimation
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الخلق أصله: التقدير المستقيم" — its origin is right measure and proportion; used for creation from nothing (ibdāʿ) and creation from something
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: measuring/cutting leather before cutting. Metaphorical: "خلق الله الخلق: أوجده على تقدير أوجبته الحكمة" — God created creation upon a measure required by wisdom

# TRANSLATION
## THE BOOK OF UNVEILING AND CLARIFICATION CONCERNING THE DELUSION OF ALL CREATION
### In the Name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate
### The Author's Introduction

The Shaykh, the Imām, the learned and the practicing, the Proof of Islam, Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad al-Ghazālī al-Ṭūsī — may God have mercy upon him and pardon him — said: Praise be to God alone, and blessings and peace upon the best of His creation, our master Muḥammad, and upon his family and companions. This is the book of Unveiling and Clarification concerning the delusion of all creation.

Know that creation is of two kinds: animate and inanimate. And the animate is of two kinds: the obligated (mukallaf) and the neglected (muhmal). The obligated is he whom God addressed with worship and commanded him to perform it, and promised him reward upon it, and forbade him from sins and warned him of punishment.

Then the obligated is of two kinds: believer and disbeliever. And the believer is of two kinds: obedient and disobedient. And each of the obedient and the disobedient is divided into two kinds: learned and ignorant.

Then I saw that delusion (ghurūr) is inseparable from all the obligated believers and the disbelievers — except those whom God, Lord of the worlds, has protected. And I, by God's praise, shall unveil their delusion and clarify the proof concerning it, and elucidate it with the utmost elucidation, and explain it with the utmost explanation, in the most concise expression and the most exquisite allusion.

And the deluded among creation, apart from the disbelievers, are four classes: a class of the scholars (ʿulamāʾ), a class of the worshippers (ʿubbād), a class of the wealthy (arbāb al-amwāl), and a class of the Sufis (mutasawwifah).
### On the Delusion of the Disbeliever

The first thing we begin with is the delusion of the disbeliever, and it is of two kinds: among them is he whom the life of this world deluded, and among them is he whom the Deluder (al-gharūr) deluded concerning God. As for those whom the life of this world deluded — and they are those who said: "The ready cash (al-naqd) is better than the credit (al-nasīʾah); the pleasures of this world are certain (yaqīn), and the pleasures of the Hereafter are doubtful (shakk); and one does not abandon certainty for doubt." This is a corrupt analogy (qiyās fāsid), and it is the analogy of Iblīs — may God curse him — in his saying: "I am better than him" {«أنا خير منه»} — for he supposed that superiority (al-khayriyyah) lay in lineage (al-nasab).
### The Remedy for This Delusion Is Two Things
Either by affirmation (taṣdīq), which is faith (īmān), or by demonstration (burhān).

As for the affirmation, it is that one affirms the truth of God — exalted — in His saying: {«وما عند الله خير وأبقى»} ("And what is with God is better and more enduring") and {«وما الحياة الدنيا إلا متاع الغرور»} ("And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion"), and affirms the truth of the Messenger — peace be upon him — in what he brought.

As for the demonstration, it is that one recognizes the aspect of corruption in his analogy. For his saying "the world is ready cash and the Hereafter is credit" is a sound premise (muqaddimah ṣaḥīḥah). But as for his saying "the ready cash is better than the credit" — that is the locus of obfuscation (talbīs). And the matter is not so. Rather, if the ready cash equals the credit in quantity and purpose, then it is better. But if it is less than it, then the credit is better than it. And it is known that the Hereafter is eternal (abadī), and the world is not eternal. And as for his saying: "The pleasures of this world are certain and the pleasures of the Hereafter are doubtful" — this too is false. Rather, that is certain for the believers. And for this certainty there are two means of apprehension (mudrak): one of them is faith and affirmation by way of emulation (taqlīd) of the prophets and the scholars, just as one emulates the skilled physician concerning medicine. And the second means of apprehension is revelation (waḥy) for the prophets and inspiration (ilhām) for the saints (awliyāʾ). And do not suppose that the knowledge of the Prophet — peace be upon him — of the matters of the Hereafter and the matters of this world was emulation of Gabriel — peace be upon him. For emulation is not sound knowledge, and the Prophet — peace be upon him — God forbid him from that — rather, things were unveiled to him, and he witnessed them with the light of inner vision (nūr al-baṣīrah), just as you witness sensible objects with the outer eye.
### Section: On Those Among the Believers in Their Lord Who Share the Delusion of the Disbelievers

And those who believe with their tongues and their creeds — when they squander the command of God — exalted — which is the righteous deeds, and defile themselves with lusts — they are sharers with the disbelievers in this delusion. For the life of this world is a delusion for the disbelievers and the believers all together. As for the delusion of the disbelievers concerning God — exalted — its example is the saying of some of them among themselves, with their tongues: "If God is to return us, then we are more deserving of it than others" — as God — exalted — reported of them in Sūrat al-Kahf when He said: {«ما أظن أن تبيد هذه أبدا، وما أظن الساعة قائمة ولئن رددت إلى ربي لأجدن خيرا منها منقلبا»} ("I do not think that this will ever perish, and I do not think the Hour will come, and if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return").
### What Is the Cause of This Delusion

The cause of this delusion is an analogy from the analogies of Iblīs — may God curse him. For they look, at one time, at God's blessings upon them in this world, and they analogize upon them the blessings of the Hereafter. And at another time, they look at the deferment of God's punishment from them in this world, and they analogize the punishment of the Hereafter — as God — exalted — reported of them: {«ويقولون فى أنفسهم لولا يعذبنا الله بما نقول حسبهم جهنم يصلونها فبئس المصير»} ("And they say among themselves: 'Why does God not punish us for what we say?' Sufficient for them is Hell; they will burn in it, and evil is the destination"). And at another time, they look at the believers who are poor, and they despise them and say: {«أهؤلاء من الله عليهم من بيننا»} ("Are these the ones whom God has favored among us?") and they say: {«لو كان خيرا ما سبقونا إليه»} ("If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it").

The arrangement of the analogy that was organized in their hearts is that they say: "God has been good to us with the blessings of this world, and every doer of good is a lover, and every lover is a doer of good." But it is not so. Rather, one may be a doer of good without being a lover. Indeed, sometimes the good deed is the cause of one's destruction by way of gradual enticement (istidrāj). And that is pure delusion concerning God — mighty and majestic. For this reason, the Prophet — peace be upon him — said: "God — exalted — protects His servant from this world just as one of you protects his sick patient from food and drink, while He loves him." For this reason, the people of inner vision (arbāb al-baṣāʾir), when this world advanced upon them, grieved; and when poverty advanced upon them, they rejoiced and said: "Welcome to the emblem of the righteous." For God — exalted — has said: {«فأما الإنسان إذا ما ابتلاه ربه فأكرمه ونعمه»} ("As for man, when his Lord tests him and honors him and favors him...") and He — exalted — said: {«أيحسبون أنما نمدهم به من مال وبنين نسارع لهم فى الخيرات بل لا يشعرون»} ("Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children — that We hasten for them good things? Rather, they do not perceive") — the verse. And He — exalted — said: {«سنستدرجهم من حيث لا يعلمون، وأملى لهم إن كيدى متين»} ("We will gradually entice them from where they do not know, and I will respite them; indeed, My plan is firm"). And He — exalted — said: {«فلما نسوا ما ذكروا به فتحنا عليهم أبواب كل شئ حتى إذا فرحوا بما أوتوا أخذناهم بغتة فإذا هم مبلسون»} ("And when they forgot what they were reminded of, We opened upon them the doors of everything, until when they rejoiced in what they were given, We seized them suddenly, and behold, they were in despair").
So whoever believes in God — exalted — is secure from this delusion.
### From What Does This Delusion Arise

The origin of this delusion is ignorance of God — exalted — and of His attributes. For whoever knows God — exalted — is not secure from God's stratagem (makr). And they should look at Pharaoh, Hāmān, and Thamūd, and what befell them — despite the fact that God — exalted — had given them wealth. And God — exalted — has warned against His stratagem, saying: {«فلا يأمن مكر الله إلا القوم الخاسرون»} ("None is secure from God's stratagem except the people of loss"), and He — exalted — said: {«ومكروا ومكر الله والله خير الماكرين»} ("And they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters"), and He — exalted — said: {«فمهل الكافرين أمهلهم رويدا»} ("So give respite to the disbelievers; grant them respite gently"). So whoever is given a blessing should fear that it may be a punishment.
### Section: On the Delusion of the Disobedient Among the Believers
And they are those who rely upon God's pardon and neglect action.

As for the delusion of the disobedient among the believers concerning God, it is their saying: "He is Forgiving, Merciful, and His pardon is to be hoped for." So they relied upon that and neglected the deeds. This arises from hope (rajāʾ), for it is a praiseworthy station in this world, and that God's mercy is vast, His favor comprehensive, and His generosity abundant — and we are monotheists, hoping in Him through the means of faith, generosity, and beneficence.
### The Origin of That Delusion

Perhaps the origin of their state is their clinging to the righteousness of their fathers and mothers. And that is the extreme of delusion. For their fathers, despite their righteousness and piety, were fearful. And the arrangement of their analogy, which Satan embellished for them, is: "Whoever loves a person loves his children. God has loved your father, so He loves you. Therefore you have no need of acts of obedience." So they relied upon that and were deluded concerning God. And they did not know that Noah — peace be upon him — wanted to carry his son upon the ark and was prevented, and God — glorified and exalted — drowned him with the most severe drowning with which He drowned the people of Noah.

And our Prophet Muḥammad — peace be upon him — sought permission to visit his mother's grave and to seek forgiveness for her. He was granted permission for the visit but was not granted permission to seek forgiveness for her.

And they forgot His saying — glorified and exalted: {«ألا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى. وأن ليس للإنسان إلا ما سعى»} ("That no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another, and that man has nothing but what he strives for").

And whoever supposes that he will be saved by the piety of his origin is like one who supposes he will be satiated by his father's eating or quenched by his father's drinking. And piety is an individual obligation (farḍ ʿayn); no parent suffices for his child in it — {«يوم يفر المرء من أخيه وأمه وأبيه وصاحبته وبنيه»} ("On the day when a man flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his spouse, and his sons") — except by way of intercession.

And they forgot his saying — peace and blessings be upon him: "The shrewd one is he who takes account of himself and works for what is after death, and the foolish one is he who follows his soul and its desires and wishes upon God wishes (tamannī)."

And His saying — exalted: {«إن الذين آمنوا والذين هاجروا وجاهدوا فى سبيل الله أولئك يرجون رحمة الله والله غفور رحيم»} ("Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the path of God — those hope for the mercy of God, and God is Forgiving, Merciful").
And He — exalted — said: {«جزاء بما كانوا يعملون»} ("A recompense for what they used to do"). And does hope (rajāʾ) become sound except when action precedes it? Otherwise, it is delusion, inevitably.

paragraphs.text: ### | In the Name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

Praise be to God, who raised the molds (qawālib) of His chosen ones (aṣfiyāʾ) through striving (mujāhadah), and made happy the hearts of His saints (awliyāʾ) through witnessing (mushāhadah), and adorned the tongues of the believers with remembrance (dhikr), and polished the inner thoughts of the knowers (ʿārifīn) with reflection (fikr), and guarded the masses of His servants from corruption, and restrained the aspirations of the ascetics (zuhhād) upon rectitude, and purified the bodies (ashbāḥ) of the God-fearing from the darkness of lusts, and cleansed the spirits (arwāḥ) of the certain (mūqinīn) from the darkness of doubts, and accepted the deeds of the righteous through the performance of prayers, and strengthened the qualities of the free-hearted through the giving of gifts (ṣilāt).

I praise Him with the praise of one who has seen the signs of His power and His might, and who has witnessed the evidences (shawāhid) of His uniqueness (fardāniyyah) and His oneness (waḥdāniyyah), and who has been struck by the knockings of His secret and His benevolence, and who has plucked the fruits of knowledge of Him (maʿrifatihi) from the tree of His glory and His generosity. And I thank Him with the thanks of one who has crossed over and drawn from the river of His favor and His bounty. And I believe in Him with the faith of one who believes in His Book and His address (khitāb), His prophets and His chosen ones, His promise and His threat, His reward and His punishment. And I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner to Him. And I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger — He sent him as a divider against the loins of the wicked and the profligate, and as a crusher of the bonds of the deniers and the renegades, and as a conqueror over the seeker of doubt and polytheism, and as a helper to the followers of truth and excellence. May the blessings of God be upon him, and upon his family, and upon all his companions.
### | Chapter on the Knowledge of the Self (Maʿrifat al-Nafs)

Know that the key to knowledge of God, the Exalted, is knowledge of the self (nafs) — as He, Glorified and Exalted, said: {سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَاتِنَا فِي الْآفَاقِ وَفِي أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ الْحَقُّ} ("We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in their own selves until it becomes clear to them that it is the Truth"). And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "He who knows his self has known his Lord." And nothing is closer to you than your self. So if you do not know your self, how could you know your Lord? For if you say, "I do know my self!" — you only know the outward body (jism al-ẓāhir), which is the hand, the foot, the head, and the trunk — and you do not know that inner thing within you by which, when you are angry, you seek contention; and when you desire, you seek marriage; and when you are hungry, you seek food; and when you are thirsty, you seek drink. And the beasts (dawābb) share with you in these matters.

It is therefore incumbent upon you to know your self in its reality (ḥaqīqah), so that you may perceive what thing you are, and from where you came to this place, and for what purpose you were created, and in what your happiness (saʿādah) lies, and in what your misery (shaqāwah) lies. For there have been gathered within your inner being (bāṭin) attributes: among them are attributes of the beasts (bahāʾim), among them are attributes of the predators (sibāʿ), among them are attributes of the devils (shayāṭīn), and among them are attributes of the angels (malāʾikah). The spirit (rūḥ) is the reality of your substance (jawhar), and all else is a stranger (gharīb) to you, and a loan (ʿāriyyah) in your possession.

It is incumbent upon you to know this, and to know that for each one of these there is a nourishment and a happiness. For the happiness of the beasts lies in eating, drinking, sleeping, and mating. If you are of them, then strive in the works of the belly and the loins. And the happiness of the predators lies in striking and in killing. And the happiness of the devils lies in deceit, evil, and cunning. If you are of them, then occupy yourself with their occupations. And the happiness of the angels lies in witnessing the beauty of the Divine Presence (al-ḥaḍrah al-rubūbiyyah), and anger and lust have no path to them. If you are of the substance (jawhar) of the angels, then strive in knowledge of your origin — so that you may come to know the path to the Divine Presence, and attain to the witnessing of Majesty (jalāl) and Beauty (jamāl), and free your self from the bond of lust and anger. And know that these attributes were only mounted within you for a purpose; for God, the Exalted, did not create them so that you would be their captive, but rather He created them so that they would be your captives, and so that you would subjugate them for the journey that lies before you, and make one of them your mount (markab) and the other your weapon (silāḥ) — so that you may hunt your happiness with them. And when you have attained your goal, then trample them beneath your feet, and return to the place of your happiness. And that place is the abode of the elite (khawāṣṣ) of the Divine Presence, while the abode of the common folk (ʿawāmm) is the degrees of Paradise.

So you stand in need of knowledge of these meanings — so that you may know from your self something, however little. For whoever does not know these meanings, his portion is only of the husks (qushūr), because the Truth (al-ḥaqq) is veiled from him.
### | Chapter: How You Know Your Self

If you wish to know your self, then know that you are of two things: the first is this heart (qalb), and the second is called the self (nafs) and the spirit (rūḥ). And the self is the heart which you know with the inner eye (ʿayn al-bāṭin), and your reality is the inner (bāṭin); for the body (jasad) is the first and the last, and the self is the last and the first. And it is called "heart" (qalb).

And the heart is not this piece of flesh (al-qitʿah al-laḥmiyyah) which is in the chest on the left side; for that exists in the beasts and in the dead. And everything that you behold with the outer eye (ʿayn al-ẓāhir) is of this world, which is called the world of witnessing (ʿālam al-shahādah). And this [true heart] is not of this world; rather, it is of the world of the unseen (ʿālam al-ghayb). And it is, in this world, a stranger (gharīb). And that piece of flesh is a mount (markab) for it, and all the limbs of the body are its armies (ʿasākir), and it is the king (malik). Knowledge of God and witnessing of the beauty of the Presence are its attributes. Upon it is the obligation (taklīf), and to it is the address (khiṭāb). For it is the reward, and upon it is the punishment. Happiness and misery attach to it. And the animal spirit (al-rūḥ al-ḥayawānī) follows it and is with it in all its affairs. And knowledge of its reality and knowledge of its attributes is the key to knowledge of God, Glorified and Exalted. So upon you is striving (mujāhadah) until you know it; for it is a precious substance (jawhar ʿazīz) of the same kind as the substance of the angels. And the origin of its mine (maʿdin) is from the Divine Presence. From that place it came, and to that place it returns.
### | Chapter: What Is the Reality of the Heart?

As for your question — "What is the reality of the heart?" — nothing more has come in the Sacred Law (sharīʿah) than the saying of God, the Exalted: {وَيَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الرُّوحِ قُلِ الرُّوحُ مِنْ أَمْرِ رَبِّي} ("And they ask you concerning the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord"). For the spirit is of the totality of the Divine power, and it is of the world of command (ʿālam al-amr). And God, Mighty and Majestic, said: {أَلَا لَهُ الْخَلْقُ وَالْأَمْرُ} ("Verily, His is the creation and the command"). Thus man is of the world of creation (ʿālam al-khalq) from one side, and of the world of command from another side. And everything to which measurement (misāḥah), quantity (miqdār), and modality (kayfiyyah) apply is of the world of creation. And the heart has no measurement and no quantity; and for this reason it does not admit division (qismah). For were it to admit division, it would be of the world of creation, and would be ignorant from one side and knowing from another side. And everything in which knowledge and ignorance coexist is impossible (muḥāl). And in another sense, it is of the world of command; for the world of command is an expression for a thing among things to which measurement and quantification have no path.

And some have thought that the spirit is eternal (qadīm), and they have erred. And some said that it is an accident (ʿaraḍ), and they have erred; for the accident does not subsist by itself, and is dependent upon another. And the spirit is the root (aṣl) of the son of Adam, and the mold (qālab) of the son of Adam is dependent upon it. So how could it be an accident?! And some said that it is a body (jism), and they have erred; for the body admits division. And the spirit — which we have called the heart, and which is the locus of knowledge of God, the Exalted — is neither a body nor an accident; rather, it is of the kind (jins) of the angels.

And knowledge of the spirit is very difficult; for no path to its knowledge has come in religion (dīn). And this is because religion has no need of knowing it; for religion is striving (mujāhadah), and knowledge is the sign of guidance (hidāyah) — as He, Glorified and Exalted, said: {وَالَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا فِينَا لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا} ("And those who strive in Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths"). And whoever does not strive with the full measure of striving, it is not permitted that he be spoken with concerning knowledge of the reality of the spirit. And the first foundation of striving is that you know the army of the heart; for if a man does not know the army, his striving (jihād) is not sound.
### | Chapter: Why Was the Heart Created?

Know that the self (nafs) is the mount of the heart, and the heart has armies — as He, Glorified and Exalted, said: {وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ} ("And none knows the hosts of your Lord but He").

And the heart was created for the work of the Hereafter, seeking its happiness. And its happiness is knowledge of its Lord, Mighty and Majestic. And knowledge of its Lord, the Exalted, is obtained for it through the craftsmanship (ṣunʿ) of God, and it is of the totality of His world. And knowledge of the wonders of the world is not obtained except through the path of the senses (ḥawāss). And the senses are from the heart, and the mold (qālab) is its mount. Then [it needs] knowledge of its prey (ṣayd), and knowledge of its net (shabakah). And the mold does not subsist except through food, drink, heat, and moisture. And it is weak, in danger of hunger and thirst inwardly, and in danger of water and fire outwardly. And it is faced with many enemies.
### | Chapter: Knowledge of the Armies of the Heart

You need to know the two armies. That is, the outer army is lust (shahwah) and anger (ghaḍab); and their stations are in the hands, the feet, the eyes, the ears, and all the limbs. And as for the inner army, its stations are in the brain: it is the power of imagination (khayāl), reflection (tafakkur), memory (ḥifẓ), recollection (tadhakkur), and estimation (wahm). And each of these powers has a specific function. And if one of them weakens, the state of the son of Adam weakens in both abodes (al-dārayn).

And the totality of these two armies is in the heart, and it is their commander (amīr). If it commands the tongue to remember, it remembers; if it commands the hand to strike, it strikes; if it commands the foot to walk, it walks. And likewise the five senses — so that it may preserve itself, in order to store provision (zād) for the abode of the Hereafter, and obtain the prey, and complete the trade (tijārah), and gather the seed of happiness. And these are obedient to the heart, just as the angels are obedient to the Lord, Glorified and Exalted — they do not disobey Him in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded.

paragraphs.text:
أما النفس فتطلق بمعنيين أحدهما أن يطلق ويراد به المعنى الجامع للصفات
المذمومة وهي القوى الحيوانية المضادة للقوى العقلية وهو المفهوم عند اطلاق
الصوفية فيقال من أفضل الجهاد أن تجاهد نفسك واليه الإشارة بقول نبينا عليه
السلام أعدى عدوك نفسك التي بين جنبيك
والثاني أن يطلق ويراد به حقيقة الآدمي وذاته فإن نفس كل شيء حقيقته وهو
الجوهر الذي هو محل المعقولات وهو من عالم الملكوت ومن عالم الأمر على ما
نبين نعم تختلف أسماؤها باختلاف أحوالها العارضة عليها فإن اتجهت إلى صواب
الصواب ونزلت عليها السكينات الآلهية وتواترت عليها نفحات فيض الجود الإلهي
فتطمئن إلى ذكر الله عز وجل وتسكن إلى المعارف الإلهية وتطير إلى أعلى أفق
الملكية فيقال نفس مطمئنة قال الله تعالى {يا أيتها النفس المطمئنة ارجعي
إلى ربك راضية مرضية} وان كانت مع قواها
وجنودها في حراب وقتال وشجار ونزاع وكانت الحرب بينهما سجالا فتارة لها
اليد عليها وتارة للقوى عليها اليد فلا تكون حالها مستقيمة فتارة تنزع إلى
جانب العقول فتتلقى المعقولات وتثبت على الطاعات وتارة تستولي عليها القوى
فتهبط إلى حضيض منازل البهائم فهذه النفس نفس لوامة وهذه النفس هي حالة
أكثر الخلق فإن من ارتفع إلى أفق الملائكة حتى تحلى بالعلوم والفضائل
النفسية والأعمال الحسنة فهو ملك جسماني لارتفاعه عن الإنسانية وعدم
مشاركته للبشر إلا بالصورة التخطيطية ولهذا قال تعالى ماهذا بشرا إن هذا
إلا ملك كريم
ومن اتضع حتى صار في حضيض البهائم فلو تصور كلب أو حمار منتصب القامة
متكلم لكان هو اياه لانسلاخه عن الفضائل الانسانية وعدم مشاركته للانسان
إلا بالصورة التخطيطية وهذه هي النفس الأمارة بالسوء
فجلهم إذا فكرت فيهم ...

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: نفس (N-F-S)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of "self" or "soul"; Al-Farahidi notes the root's range from breath to essence, with the soul as that which desires proximity and discourse.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Distinguishes النفس as the rational soul (الروح) in Quranic usage, and as الذات (essence) in verses like {ويحذركم الله نفسه} — where the soul is the very being of God, not a separate entity.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (Haqiqah) usage denotes the blood or vital self; metaphorical (Majaz) usage extends to the essence and the blameworthy animal powers, as in the Sufi technical term.
- Root: طلق (T-L-Q)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of release from restraint; Al-Farahidi notes the verbal form's application to freeing.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): الطلاق fundamentally means "release from a tether" (التخلية من الوثاق); metaphorically applied to the soul's states — the tranquil soul is "released" from base attachments, the blaming soul is in oscillation.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal usage for freeing captives; metaphorical usage for the soul's liberation or bondage relative to the intellect.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — Governing the periodic structure where qualifying clauses (e.g., "if it turns... then it is called") interpose between subject and predicate, preserving syntactic cohesion across multi-clause theological definitions.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)

I say: As for the soul (nafs), it is used in two senses. The first is that it is used to denote the aggregate of blameworthy attributes, namely the animal powers opposed to the rational powers. This is what is understood when the Sufis use the term, for it is said: "Among the most excellent of jihād is that you struggle against your soul." And to this refers the saying of our Prophet, peace be upon him: "Your most hostile enemy is your soul which is between your sides."

The second sense is that it is used to denote the reality of the human being and his very essence (dhāt). For the soul of every thing is its reality (ḥaqīqah). It is the substance (jawhar) that is the locus of intelligibles (maḥall al-maʿqūlāt). It belongs to the world of the divine dominion (ʿālam al-malakūt) and to the world of the command (ʿālam al-amr), as we shall explain. Indeed, its names differ according to the differing states that accrue to it. If it turns toward the right course, and the divine tranquilities (sakīnāt) descend upon it, and the breezes of the outpouring of divine generosity follow in succession upon it, then it is at peace in the remembrance of God, Mighty and Majestic, and rests in the divine cognitions, and flies to the highest horizon of the angelic realm — then it is called the "tranquil soul" (nafs muṭmaʾinnah). God, Exalted is He, said: {يا أيتها النفس المطمئنة ارجعي إلى ربك راضية مرضية} ("O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and well-pleasing").

But if it is with its powers and its troops in war, combat, strife, and conflict, and the battle between them is alternating — sometimes the upper hand is with it, and sometimes the upper hand is with the powers — then its state is not upright. Sometimes it inclines toward the side of the intellects, receiving the intelligibles and persisting in acts of obedience; sometimes the powers overcome it, and it descends to the lowest depth of the stations of beasts. This soul is the "blaming soul" (nafs lawwāmah). This soul is the state of most creatures. For whoever ascends to the horizon of the angels until he is adorned with the sciences, the virtues of the soul, and the good deeds — he is a corporeal angel (malak jismānī), due to his elevation above humanity and his non-participation with humans except in schematic form (al-ṣūrah al-takhṭīṭiyyah). For this reason God, Exalted is He, said: {ما هذا بشرا إن هذا إلا ملك كريم} ("This is no human; this is none other than a noble angel").

And whoever is debased until he reaches the lowest depth of beasts — if a dog or a donkey, upright in stature and speaking, were to be imagined, he would be that very thing, due to his being stripped of human virtues and his non-participation with humans except in schematic form. This is the "soul commanding to evil" (al-nafs al-ammārah bi-al-sūʾ). For most of them, if you reflect upon them, are donkeys, dogs, or wolves. And they are among the humans mentioned in the saying of God, Exalted is He: {شياطين الإنس والجن يوحي بعضهم إلى بعض زخرف القول غرورا} ("Devils among mankind and jinn inspire one another with adorned speech in delusion"). And the Commander of the Believers, ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said: "O you who resemble men, yet are not men!" Such a soul you will ever see as a slave to a stone, or clay, or a beast, or a saddle-camel. And this is the one about whom God, Glorified is He, informed us when He said: {إن النفس لأمارة بالسوء} ("Indeed the soul commands to evil").

As for the heart (qalb), it is also used in two senses. The first is the pineal-shaped flesh deposited in the interior of the human being on the left side. This is known by dissection. It is the receptacle of black blood and the source of the vapor that is the vehicle of the natural animal spirit (al-rūḥ al-ṭibbī al-ḥayawānī). This is found in all animals and is not specific to the human being. It is that which perishes at death, and all the senses are corrupted by its corruption.

The second sense — and this is the one we are concerned to explain — is the human spirit (al-rūḥ al-insānī) that bears the trust of God (amānat Allāh), is adorned with knowledge, in which the science of the primordial nature (al-fiṭrah) is implanted, and which speaks of the divine unity by its saying "Yes" (balā). It is the origin of the human being and the final end of all creatures in the world of the return (ʿālam al-maʿād). God, Exalted is He, said: {قل الروح من أمر ربي} ("Say: The spirit is from the command of my Lord"), and He said: {ألا بذكر الله تطمئن القلوب} ("Truly, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest"). And our Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The hearts of the children of Adam are all between two fingers of the fingers of the Merciful," to the end of the hadith. Wherever the heart is mentioned in the Sacred Law, what is meant is that which we are concerned to explain. And if it is used in some place for the pineal flesh, that is because it is its special attachment (mutʿallaq khāṣṣ) and its first attachment. As the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed, in the interior of the son of Adam there is a morsel of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound by its soundness, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt by its corruption — and it is the heart."

As for the spirit (rūḥ), it is used to denote the subtle vapor that ascends from the source of the heart and rises to the brain, and also, by means of the veins, to the entire body. It acts in every place according to its temperament and preparedness, and it is the vehicle of life. This vapor is like the lamp, and the life that subsists through it is like the light; the manner of its influence in the body is like the manner of the lamp's illumination of the parts of the house. It is also used to denote the originated being (al-mubdaʿ) that issues from the command of God, Exalted is He, which is the locus of the sciences, revelation, and inspiration. It is of the genus of the angels, separate from the corporeal world, self-subsistent in its essence, as we shall explain. It is also used to denote the spirit that stands in opposition to all the angels, which is the First Originated Being (al-mubdaʿ al-awwal), and it is the Holy Spirit (rūḥ al-qudus). It is also used to denote the Qurʾān. In sum, it is an expression for that by which life subsists, in general.

As for the intellect (ʿaql), it is used to denote the First Intellect (al-ʿaql al-awwal), which is what is meant by "intellect" in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The first thing God created was the intellect. He said to it: 'Come forward,' and it came forward. Then He said to it: 'Go back,' and it went back" — that is, "Come forward so that you may be completed by Me, and go back so that by you the entire world may be completed, apart from you." And it is the one to whom God, Exalted is He, said: "By My might and My majesty, I have created no creature more noble to Me nor more excellent than you. By you I take, and by you I give," to the end of the hadith. And it is that which is expressed as the Pen (al-qalam), as he, peace be upon him, said: "The first thing God created was the Pen. He said to it: 'Write.' It said: 'What shall I write?' He said: 'What will be, until the Day of Resurrection — of deed, effect, provision, and term.' So it wrote what will be and what is to come until the Day of Resurrection."

The second usage is that it is used to denote the human soul (al-nafs al-insāniyyah). The third usage is that it is used to denote an attribute of the soul. It is, in relation to the soul, like sight in relation to the eye. By means of it, the soul is prepared for the apprehension of intelligibles, just as the eye, by means of sight, is prepared for the apprehension of sensibles. And it is the one about whom the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said, relating from his Lord, Mighty and Majestic: "By My might and My majesty, I shall surely conceal you in the one I love."
And wherever we use in this book the terms "soul" (nafs), "spirit" (rūḥ), "heart" (qalb), and "intellect" (ʿaql), we mean by them the human soul, which is the locus of intelligibles.
SECTION: Demonstration of the Existence of the Soul, in General

I say: The soul is too evident to need a proof for its establishment. For all the addresses of the Sacred Law are directed not to a non-existent thing, but to an existent, living being that understands the address. Nevertheless, we shall seek confirmation in its exposition, and we say:

It is a matter of certain knowledge, about which there is no doubt, that whenever things share in one thing and differ in another, the shared thing is other than the differing thing. We find all bodies sharing in that they are bodies, in which three intersecting dimensions can be supposed. Then we find them differing in movement and apprehension. If their movement were due to their corporeality, then every body ought to be moving, because realities do not differ; and what is necessary for a species is necessary for all that share in that species and that reality. But if it is due to a meaning beyond corporeality, then a principle of action (mabdaʾ al-fiʿl) is established in general, and that principle is the soul — until it becomes clear whether it is a substance or an accident.

An example of this: We see vegetable bodies nourishing, growing, generating their like, and moving with various movements of branching and veining. If these meanings were due to corporeality, then all bodies ought to be so. But if they are due to something other than corporeality — rather, to an additional meaning — then that meaning is called the "vegetative soul" (nafs nabātiyyah). Then the animal has what the plant has, and in addition senses, moves by will, is guided to its own interests, seeks what benefits it, and flees what harms it. So we know with certainty that in it there is an additional meaning beyond the vegetable bodies. Then we find the human being: in him is all that is in the plant and the animal of meanings, and he is distinguished by the apprehension of things outside sensation — such as that the whole is greater than the part. He apprehends particulars by the five senses and apprehends universals by the rational faculties (al-mashāʿir al-ʿaqliyyah). He shares with the animal in the senses and differs from it in the rational faculties. For the human being apprehends the universal from every particular, makes that universal a premise of a syllogism, and derives from it a conclusion. Neither is the apprehension of the universal denied, nor is the apprehender of it rejected. Neither the accident, nor the body receptive of accidents, nor the plant, nor the non-human animal apprehends the universal, such that the universal would subsist in it and thereby be divided by the divisions of body. For the universal, solely by virtue of being universal, is not divided at all. Thus the absolute universal "human" has no half, third, or quarter. Therefore, that which is receptive of the universal form is a substance that is neither a body nor an accident in a body, having no position (waḍʿ) and no location (ayna) by which it could be pointed to. Rather, its existence is an intellectual existence — more hidden than everything from sensation, and more manifest than everything to the intellect.
By this, the existence of the soul is established; it is established in general that it is a substance; and it is established that it is exalted above matter and corporeal forms.

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم فاتحة الكتاب الحمد لله الأول في ربوبيته ،
والقديم في أزليته ، والحكيم في سلطنته ، والكريم في عزته ، لا شبيه له في
ذاته وصنعته ، ولا نظير له في مملكته ، صانع كل شيء مصنوع بقدرته ، المتكلم
بكلامه الأزلي ليس بخارج من صفته ، أحمده على نعمته ، وأستعين به على دفع
نقمته ، هو الله ربي وحده لا شريك له الواحد في ربوبيته ، الذي يختصر ، من
يشاء برحمته ، ختم الأنبياء بمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم وعلى آله وعترته .
أما بعد : فلما رأيت أهل الزمان همهم قاصرة على نيل المقاصد الباطنة
والظاهرة وسألني جماعة من ملوك الأرض أن أضع لهم كتابا معدوم المثل لنيل
مقاصدهم واقتناص المماليك وما يعينهم على ذلك استخرت الله فوضعت لهم كتابا
. وسميته بكتاب ' سر العالمين وكشف ما في الدارين ' وبوبته أبوابا .
ومقالات وأحزابا . وذكرت فيه مراتب صوابا . وجعلته دالا على طلب المملكة
وحائا عليها وواضعا لتحصيلها أساسا جامعا لمعانيها . وذكرت كيفية ترتيبها
وتدريبها فهو يصلح للعالم الزاهد وشريك شرك المالك بتطييب قلوب الجند
وجذبهم إليه بالمواعظ . PageV01P007 فأول من استحسنه وقرأه على بالمدرسة
النظامية سرا من الناس . في النوبة الثانية بعد رجوعي من السفر رجل من أرض
المغرب يقال له محمد بن تومرت من أهل سلمية وتوسمت منه الملك وهو كتاب عزيز
لا يجوز بذله لان تحته أسرارا تفتقر إلى كشف إذ طباع العالم نافرة عنها
وتحته علوم عزيزة وإشارات كثيرة دالة على غوامض أسرار لا يعرفها إلا فحول
الحكماء . فالله يوفقك للعمل به فإنه دال على كل ما تريد إن شاء الله تعالى
. PageV01P008

| المقالة الأولى في الملك
أعلم أن الملك عظيم وعقيم عليه وقع الاشتباك والمناقشة بين الصالح
والطالح والخاسر والرابح فمنه يتشعب الحسد وكل عرض وغرض مزعزع فلا بد من
أصل ومرتبة وتحصيل وصبر وجمع أموال لبلوغ الآمال وأم الغرر في تحصيله هو
علو الهمة : كما قال معاوية رفي الله تعالى عنه هموا بمعالي الأمور
لتنالوها فإني لم أكن للخلافة أهلا فهممت بها فنلتها . وقد سرت بك قصص
الأولين فأنظر في أخبارهم وآثارهم فما بلغ أحد درجة الملك باب وأم غير قليل
وكم نزع الملك من يد وارث مستحق مثل بيت نبينا محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم .

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: م ل ك (Malaka)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core sense of possession, seizure, and dominion; the king (malik) is one who possesses and disposes.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Al-Mulk is the disposal of command and prohibition over a people, specific to the governance of rational beings; it is twofold: actual possession/assumption of rule, and the capacity/power for it whether or not one assumes it.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (Haqiqah): ownership and dominion over property. Metaphorical (Majaz): mastery over oneself (mamlakat al-nafs), and the seizure of a woman in marriage; sovereignty over a people is an extension of the root sense of absolute disposal.
- Root: ح م د (Hamida)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To praise, commend, or laud; the act of extolling virtues.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Praise (hamd) is the acknowledgment of beneficence with veneration; it is due to God alone in His absolute perfection, distinct from mere thanks (shukr) which is tied to a specific benefit.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "I praised God with all His praises." Metaphorical: "I found his action praiseworthy" (ahmadtu sana'i'ahu) — extending to approval of a thing's qualities.
- Root: ل ه م (Lahima)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To swallow or gulp down; the liham is the gullet.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Ilham (divine inspiration) is the casting of a thing into the heart (raw'), specifically from God or the higher assembly; its root is from swallowing (iltiham), as the soul "swallows" what is cast into it.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "God inspired him with good" — cast it into his heart. Metaphorical: a horse that "swallows the ground" (yaltahim al-ard) in swiftness; a generous man who "swallows" the burden of requests.
- Root: ب س م (Basama)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To smile; tabassama is the first degree of laughter.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Cited for the verse {فتبسم ضاحكا من قولها} (Q. 27:19) — smiling as a sign of benevolent wonder.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "He is bright-faced and smiling." Metaphorical: "The lightning smiled" and "the acacia smiled" — the bursting open of its tips; "I did not even smile upon it" meaning I did not taste it.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — The basmala and hamdala open with a suspended preposition (bi-ism) and a nominal sentence (al-hamdu lillah), establishing the periodic structure of praise before the authorial voice proceeds to narrative.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The opening of the Book: Praise be to God, the First in His Lordship, the Eternal in His Pre-Eternity, the Wise in His Sovereignty, the Generous in His Might. There is no likeness to Him in His Essence and His Handiwork, nor any equivalent to Him in His Kingdom. He is the Maker of every thing made by His Power, the Speaker through His Eternal Speech, which is not separate from His Attribute. I praise Him for His Grace, and I seek His aid in repelling His Retribution. He is God, my Lord, alone, with no partner to Him, the One in His Lordship, Who abbreviates — whomsoever He wills — by His Mercy. He sealed the Prophets with Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, and upon his Family and his Progeny.

To proceed: When I saw that the aspirations of the people of this age were confined to attaining their hidden and apparent objectives, and a group of the kings of the earth asked me to compose for them a book without equal for attaining their objectives, the seizing of dominions (mamalik), and what would aid them in that, I sought God's guidance (istikhara) and composed for them a book. I named it "The Secret of the Two Worlds and the Disclosure of What Lies in the Two Abodes," and I divided it into chapters, articles, and sections. I mentioned in it ranks with correctness, and I made it an indicator toward the pursuit of sovereignty (mamlaka), an inciter upon it, a foundation gathering its meanings, and a clarifier of the manner of its ordering and its training. For it is suitable for the ascetic scholar and for the partner in the partnership of the owner, by sweetening the hearts of the soldiers and drawing them to him through exhortations. PageV01P007 — The first who approved of it and read it upon me at the Nizamiyya school, secretly from the people, in the second session after my return from travel, was a man from the land of the Maghrib called Muhammad ibn Tumart, from the people of Salmiyya; and I discerned in him the marks of sovereignty. And this book is precious — it is not permissible to squander it, for beneath it lie secrets that require unveiling, since the natures of the world are averse to them; and beneath it lie precious sciences and many indications pointing to the obscurities of secrets known only to the master sages (fuhul al-hukama'). May God grant you success in acting upon it, for it points to all that you desire, if God Most High wills. PageV01P008
| The First Article: On Sovereignty (Al-Mulk)

Know that sovereignty is mighty and barren; upon it has fallen the clash and dispute between the righteous and the wicked, the loser and the winner. From it branches envy and every wavering passion and purpose. Thus there is no escape from a foundation, a rank, acquisition, patience, and the gathering of wealth for the attainment of aspirations. And the mother of all ventures in its acquisition is the loftiness of resolve (himmah): as Mu'awiya — may God Most High be pleased with him — said: "Resolve upon the lofty matters that you may attain them, for I was not worthy of the Caliphate, yet I resolved upon it and attained it." And the stories of the ancients have reached you, so look into their reports and their traces: no one has reached the degree of sovereignty through a door other than resolve, and how often has sovereignty been wrested from the hand of a rightful heir — such as the household of our Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace.

paragraphs.text:
### | تصدير عام

### | 1-

نحن في أمس الحاجة إلى نشر علمى دقيق لأصول تراثنا العربى القديم، فإنه
عن طريق هذا النوع من النشر تحيا النصوص وتستبين، ويسهل على المشتغلين
بموضاعاتها قراءتها والإفادة منها. وليس أجدى على الباحث من أن تكون بين
يديه الوثائق الأولى مضبوطة محققة خالية من شوائب التحريف والتصحيف.
وقد ابتليت كتبنا القديمة بأن قام على نشر الكثير منها والإشراف على
إخراجها ناشرون من غير العلماء المتخصصين، لا هم لهم سوى جنى الربح المادى
من طبعها. ونحن نعانى من نشراتهم ما نعانى من أخطاء مطبعية ولغوية، ونقص في
النصوص هنا وزيادة هناك، وخلو تام من التحقيق والتعليق والتفسير والفهارس
العلمية بشتى أنواعها. وكثيرا ما نقف من نص من النصوص حيارى مكتوفي الأيدى
لا نفهم له معنى ولا نستطيع له توجيها، أو نوجهه توجيها خاطئا لم يخطر
للمؤلف ببال، لا لسبب سوى أن في النص تحريفا أو نقصا أو إضافة من ناسخ، أو

- Root: نشر (n-sh-r)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To spread, unfold, publish, disseminate; to revive and bring forth
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Used for spreading garments, scrolls, clouds, blessings, and speech; also for the spreading forth of the dead at resurrection (nushūr)
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: spreading cloth/books; Metaphorical: God spreading the dead (resurrection), spreading mercy, reviving the earth
- Root: طبع (t-b-ʿ)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To stamp, imprint, seal; natural disposition
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): To form something into an image, as stamping a coin; more general than khatm (sealing), more specific than naqsh (engraving); God's sealing of hearts
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: stamping a sword/coin, sealing a book; Metaphorical: God sealing the heart of the disbeliever, being naturally disposed to virtue

English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
### | General Preface

We are in dire need of publishing precise scholarly editions of the foundations of our ancient Arab heritage, for it is through this type of publication that texts come alive and become clear, and it becomes easy for those engaged with their subjects to read them and benefit from them. Nothing is more useful to the researcher than to have before him the primary documents, properly vocalized, critically edited, and free from the impurities of corruption (taḥrīf) and scribal error (taṣḥīf).

Our ancient books have been afflicted by the fact that many of them were published and supervised by publishers who were not specialized scholars—their only concern being the material profit from printing them. We suffer from their editions what we suffer: typographical and linguistic errors, omissions in texts here and additions there, and a complete absence of critical apparatus, commentary, explanation, and scholarly indexes of all kinds. Many times we stand before a text bewildered, with hands tied, unable to understand its meaning or to direct its interpretation—or we direct it wrongly in a way the author never intended, for no reason other than that the text contains a corruption, an omission, or an addition by a copyist, or a confusion between the text itself and a commentary written upon it. It suffices that the negative particle "lā" (لا) falls out of a sentence, or that the word "idh" (إذ) is placed instead of "idhā" (إذا) or vice versa, or that the word "al-ʿārifīn" (العارفين, the knowers) is written instead of "al-ʿIrāqiyyīn" (العراقيين, the Iraqis), or similar corruptions, for the text to become disturbed and its meaning corrupted; and often this leads the researcher to a mistaken understanding that may culminate in a false opinion or an unfounded theory.

The lot of the treatise "The Niche of Lights" (Mishkāt al-Anwār) which we publish today does not differ much from the lot of other books published in the unscientific manner we have indicated. It has been printed in Egypt in several editions: in the years 1322 AH, 1325 AH, 1929 CE, 1352 AH, and within the collection "Al-Jawāhir al-Ghawālī min Rasāʾil Ḥujjat al-Islām al-Ghazālī" in the year 1343 AH.

I have collated this edition—which is now the most widely circulated—against the manuscripts that were available for my examination, and I found it replete with serious errors and corruptions. I also found in it many additions to the original text, and an omission amounting to a full page in one place: namely, from his saying "in the station of beasts, nay lower" (بمنزلة البهائم بل أخس) to his saying "in pure darkness, namely their dark souls" (بمحض الظلمة وهى نفوسهم المظلمة).

It appears that the original from which this copy was taken was mixed with some commentaries and glosses, and the copyist transmitted all of that without distinguishing between the text and what was other than it.
It suffices that I mention some examples of the corruptions that occurred in this copy to show its gravity:
On p. 129 occurs "sirr al-kalbiyya" (سر الكلبية) with sīn (س); the correct reading is "sharr al-kalbiyya" (شر الكلبية) with shīn (ش).

On p. 130 occurs "and measure upon it the light and the day" (وقس عليه الضوء والنهار); the correct reading is "and measure upon it the mount and the fire" (وقس عليه الطور والنار), because the discourse concerns Moses who perceived from the side of the Mount a fire.
On p. 131 occurs: "and this portion of revelation" (وهذا الحظ من الوحى); the correct reading is: "and this pattern of revelation" (وهذا النمط من الوحى).

On p. 143 occurs: "and He is the one who writes what the senses have reported" (وهو الذى يكتب ما أوردته الحواس). The correct reading is: "and He is the one who verifies what the senses have reported" (وهو الذى يستثبت ما أوردته الحواس).
On p. 134 occurs: "more splendid and more luminous" (أجلى وأسنى); the correct reading is: "more majestic and more luminous" (أجل وأسنى).
And on p. 134: "let us return to the purpose of the examples" (فلنرجع إلى غرض الأمثلة); the correct reading is: "to the presentation of the examples" (إلى عرض الأمثلة) with the unpointed ʿayn (ع).
And on p. 135: "that the prophets are a luminous lamp" (كون الأنبياء سراجا منيرا); the correct reading is: "luminous lamps" (سرجا منيرة).
And on p. 137: "and the base events" (والحوادث الرديئة); the correct reading is: "and the destructive occupations" (والأشغال المردية).
And on p. 138: "and the kinds of these divisions are many" (وأصناف هذه الأقسام كثيرة); the correct reading is: "and the divisions of these kinds are many" (وأقسام هذه الأصناف كثيرة).
And on p. 139: "so nature altered it" (فأحاله الطبع); the correct reading is: "so nature altered it to the natural disposition" (فأحاله إلى الطبع).

This is a little from much, of examples of errors I have observed in this edition, in addition to the other defects I have indicated. Therefore, re-publishing this treatise and publishing other works of al-Ghazālī was a duty required by scholarly integrity (al-amāna al-ʿilmiyya), as required by fairness to the author, whose right upon us is that we understand his works in the correct manner he intended. This is what the Supreme Council for the Care of Arts, Letters, and Social Sciences resolved to undertake when it decided to publish the works of al-Ghazālī—both those already printed and those still in manuscript.
The Name of the Treatise and Its Station Among al-Ghazālī's Works:
It was given the name "Mishkāt al-Anwār" (The Niche of Lights) as it appears in "Kashf al-Ẓunūn" of Ḥājjī Khalīfa and in the printed copies.

It was also given the name "Mishkāt al-Anwār wa Miṣfāt al-Asrār" (The Niche of Lights and the Clarifier of Secrets) as it appears in the Paris manuscript and at the end of the Alexandria Municipal manuscript.
It was also named "Kitāb al-Mishkāt wa al-Miṣbāḥ" (The Book of the Niche and the Lamp) as it appears in the manuscript of Shahīd ʿAlī Pasha.

Another book is attributed to al-Ghazālī titled "Mishkāt al-Anwār fī Laṭāʾif al-Akhbār" (The Niche of Lights Concerning Subtleties of Reports) which has no connection to this treatise; rather, it is a large book of which manuscripts exist in the Egyptian Dār al-Kutub. On the title page of manuscript no. 237 (Taṣawwuf), the true author's name appears: ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, known as Ibn al-Faqīh al-Ḥāfiẓ al-Miṣrī, who died in the year 877 AH.

There is no doubt that the treatise Mishkāt al-Anwār is among al-Ghazālī's later works that represent the period of intellectual and spiritual maturity. However, we cannot assign a specific date for its composition as Professor Massignon did in his book "Recueil de textes inédits concernant l'histoire de la mystique en pays d'Islam: Paris 1929," where he says it was composed in the period between 495 and 505 AH—the period al-Ghazālī spent in Ṭūs, devoting himself to authorship and worship. Massignon lists among al-Ghazālī's works of this period the book "Miʿyār al-ʿIlm" (The Standard of Knowledge), the book "Miḥakk al-Naẓar" (The Touchstone of Contemplation), the book "Al-Maqṣad al-Asnā" (The Most Sublime Aim), and the treatise "Mishkāt al-Anwār." But we see in the "Mishkāt al-Anwār" references to all these books, which indicates that al-Ghazālī composed them before the Mishkāt; and we do not know whether he composed all of them in the same period Massignon specifies. Nor do we think that Professor Massignon has historical evidence upon which to rely in determining the years of composition of al-Ghazālī's books in the manner he has drawn.
Manuscripts of the Treatise:
There exist for this treatise no fewer than thirty-six manuscripts scattered throughout the world; we mention from them the following:

(1) Alexandria Municipal, dated 907 AH (2) Qūwīlī Ḥ 1 p. 262. (3) Mosul 176 [8] (4) Patna 2: 412 [no. 2580 (8)] (5) Berlin no. 3207 (6) Leiden no. 1988. (7) Brill manuscripts 2: 1053 (8) Ambrosiana (RSO III 573) A 64. V (9) Vatican Borghese 65. Vat. Borgh (10) Manchester i 71 (11) Princeton, Garrett Collection no. 1892, dated 937 AH (12) India Office in London no. 1237, Arberry's catalogue, dated 1096; and no. 1238, dated 1107. (13) Tehran: Majlis-i Shūrā-yi Millī no. 9015, dated 1320. (14) Āṣafiyya 1: 388 [14 (5) Arabic Taṣawwuf] (15) Tehran 2: 77. (16) Rāmpūr 1: 697. (17) Ẓāhiriyya: general no. 7621.

And in Istanbul: (18) Shahīd ʿAlī 1712, 1377. (19) Bashīr Āghā 650 (20) Sulaymāniyya 734. (21) Köprülü nos. 860, 1603: (22) Ayasofya 2075, 1711 [3], 4801. (23) Jār Allāh 1092 [1], 2075. (24) Walī al-Dīn 1829. (25) Salīm Āghā: collection no. 108. (26) Asʿad 1717/18. And in the Egyptian Dār al-Kutub: (27) 2673 Taṣawwuf, dated 1065, (28) no. 184 Taṣawwuf (within a collection), (29) Ṭalʿat collections nos. 274, 513, 326, 822, 826.
And in Paris: (30) no. 1331. (31) And in El Escorial 2, no. 631. (32) Gotha (Pertsch catalogue, part 3, vol. 2, p. 378) no. 1166, dated 1188.

paragraphs.text:
قال الشيخ الإمام، العالم العلامة، حجة الاسلام، وبركة الأنام: أبو حامد
محمد بن محمد بن الغزالي الطوسى؛ قدس الله روحه، ونور ضريحه - آمين: الحمدلله حق حمده، والصلاة والسلام على خير خلقه، محمد رسوله وعبده، وعلى
آله وصحبه من بعده. أما بعد: فاعلم أيها الحريص المقبل على اقتباس العلم، المظهر من نفسه صدق
الرغبة، وفرط التعطش إليه.. أنك إن كنت تقصد بالعلم المنافسة، والمباهاة،
والتقدم على الأقران، واستمالة وجوه الناس إليك، وجمع حطام الدنيا؛ فأنت
ساع في هدم دينك، وإهلاك نفسك، وبيع آخرتك بدنياك؛ فصفقتك خاسرة، وتجارتك
بائرة، ومعلمك معين لك على عصيانك، وشريك لك في خسرانك، وهو كبائع سيف
لقاطع طريق، كما قال صلى الله عليه وسلم: (من أعان على معصية ولو بشطر كلمة
كان شريكا فيها) . وإن كانت نيتك وقصدك، بينك وبين الله تعالى، من طلب العلم: الهداية دون
مجرد الرواية؛ فأبشر؛ فإن الملائكة تبسط لك أجنحتها إذا مشيت، وحيتان البحر
تستغفر لك إذا سعيت. ولكن ينبغي لك أن تعلم، قبل كل شيء، أن الهداية التي
هي ثمرة العلم لها بداية
ونهاية، وظاهر وباطن، ولا وصول إلى نهايتها إلا بعد إحكام بدايتها، ولا
عثور على باطنها إلا بعد الوقوف على ظاهرها. وهأنا مشير عليك ببداية الهداية؛ لتجرب بها نفسك، وتمتحن بها قلبك، فإن
صادفت قلبك إليها مائلا، ونفسك بها مطاوعة، ولها قابلة؛ فدونك التطلع إلى
النهايات والتغلغل في بحار العلوم. وإن صادفت قلبك عند مواجهتك إياها بها مسوفا، وبالعمل بمقتضاها مماطلا؛ فاعلم أن نفسك المائلة إلى طلب العلم هي النفس الأمارة بالسوء، وقد انتهضت
مطيعة للشيطان اللعين ليدليك بحبل غروره؛ فيستدرجك بمكيدته إلى غمرة
الهلاك، وقصده أن يروج عليك الشر في معرض الخير حتى يلحقك (بالأخسرين
أعمالا، الذين ضل سعيهم في الحياة الدنيا وهم يحسبون أنهم يحسنون صنعا) . وعند ذلك يتلو عليك الشيطان فضل العلم ودرجة العلماء، وما ورد فيه من
الأخبار والآثار. ويلهيك عن قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم: (من ازداد علما ولم
يزدد هدى، لم يزدد من الله إلا بعدا) ، وعن قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم: (أشد
الناس عذابا يوم القيامة عالم لم ينفعه الله بعلمه) وكان صلى الله عليه
وسلم يقول: (اللهم إنى أعوذ بك من علم لا ينفع، وقلب لا يخشع، وعمل لا
يرفع، ودعاء لا يسمع) . وعن قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم: (مررت ليلة أسرى بي بأقوام تقرض شفاههم
بمقارض من نار، فقلت: من أنتم؟ قالوا: كنا نأمر بالخير ولا نأتيه وننهى عن
الشر ونأتيه) . فإياك يا مسكين أن تذعن لتزويره فيدليك بحبل غروره، فويل للجاهل حيث لم
يتعلم مرة واحدة، وويل للعالم حيث لم يعمل بما عمل ألف مرة. واعلم أن الناس في طلب العلم على ثلاثة أحوال: رجل طلب العلم ليتخذه زاده
إلى المعاد، ولم يقصد به إلا وجه الله والدار الآخرة؛ فهذا من الفائزين. ورجل طلبه ليستعين به على حياته العاجلة، وينال به العز والجاه والمال،
وهو عالم بذلك، مستشعر في قلب ركاكه حاله وخسة مقصده، فهذا من المخاطرين. فإن عاجله أجله قبل التوبة خيف عليه من سوء الخاتمة، وبقي أمره في خطر
المشيئة؛ وإن وفق للتوبة قبل حلول الأجل، وأضاف إلى العلم العمل، وتدارك
ما فرط منه من الخلل - التحق بالفائزين، فإن التائب من الذنب كمن لا ذنب
له. ورجل ثالث استحوذ عليه الشيطان؛ فاتخذ علمه ذريعة إلى التكاثر بالمال،
والتفاخر بالجاه، والتعزز بكثرة الأتباع، يدخل بعلمه كل مدخل رجاء أن يقضى
من الدنيا وطره، ن وهو مع ذلك يضمر في نفسه أنه عند الله بمكانة، لاتسامه
بسمة العلماء، وترسمه برسومهم في الزى والمنطق، مع تكالبه على الدنيا ظاهرا
وباطنا.. فهذا من الهالكين، ومن الحمقى المغرورين؛ إذ الرجاء منقطع عن
توبته لظنه أنه من المحسنين، وهو غافل عن قوله تعالى (يأيها الذين آمنوا لم
تقولون مالا تفعلون) . وهو ممن قال فيهم رسول الله: (أنا من غير الدجال
أخوف عليكم من الدجال) فقيل: وما هو يارسول الله؟، فقال: (علماء السوء) .

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: علم (ʿalima)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes knowing, perceiving, and the mark or trace by which something is known; al-ʿalam as a signpost or landmark.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Knowledge (al-ʿilm) is the apprehension of a thing in its true reality — either grasping the essence of a thing directly, or passing judgment upon it regarding what is or is not attributed to it.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal usage (ḥaqīqah) applies to genuine perception; metaphorical usage (majāz) extends to "knowing of a matter" as being aware of its report. The scholar (al-ʿālim) is one marked by knowledge as a distinguishing sign.
- Root: هدى (hadā)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes guidance, direction, and showing the way; also the gift of guidance bestowed.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Guidance (al-hidāyah) is the gracious bestowal of direction toward the path of truth — its beginning is outward compliance, its end is inward realization.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal usage concerns physical direction; metaphorical usage concerns spiritual and moral direction toward righteousness.
- Root: طلب (ṭalaba)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes seeking, searching out, and pursuing a thing — whether a physical object or a meaning.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Seeking (al-ṭalab) is the investigation into the existence of a thing, whether it be an entity or a concept.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal usage is the active pursuit of a goal; metaphorical usage appears in expressions like "the lamp seeks to go out" — i.e., it is on the verge of extinction.
- Root: حمد (ḥamida)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes praise, commendation, and the acknowledgment of excellence.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Praise (al-ḥamd) is the acknowledgment of beneficence with veneration and love.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal usage is verbal praise of God; metaphorical usage extends to finding a thing praiseworthy, as in "I found his character praiseworthy."
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — The rule governing the separation of a preposition from its object by an intervening clause, as in the construction "الحمدلله حق حمده" where the verbal noun phrase functions as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) qualifying the praise.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)

The Shaykh, the Imām, the learned scholar, the Proof of Islam, and the Blessing of Mankind — Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad al-Ghazālī al-Ṭūsī — may God sanctify his soul and illuminate his grave — Amen — said:
Praise be to God, as His due praise deserves, and prayers and peace be upon the best of His creation, Muḥammad, His Messenger and servant, and upon his family and companions after him.

To proceed: Know, O you who are eager and hastening toward the acquisition of knowledge, who displays in yourself the sincerity of desire and the extremity of thirst for it — that if your purpose in seeking knowledge is rivalry, vainglory, outdoing one's peers, drawing the faces of people toward yourself, and amassing the fleeting goods of this world — then you are striving to demolish your religion, to destroy your own soul, and to sell your Hereafter for your worldly life. Your bargain is a losing one, your trade is bankrupt, and your teacher is an accomplice aiding you in your disobedience and a partner in your ruin. He is like one who sells a sword to a highway robber, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: {«Whoever aids in an act of disobedience, even by half a word, is a partner in it.»}

But if your intention and purpose — between you and God Almighty — in seeking knowledge is guidance (hidāyah) and not mere narration (riwāyah), then rejoice! For the angels spread their wings for you when you walk, and the fish of the sea seek forgiveness for you when you strive. Yet you must know, before all else, that the guidance which is the fruit of knowledge has a beginning and an end, an outward aspect and an inward aspect. There is no reaching its end except after perfecting its beginning, and no attaining its inward except after standing firm upon its outward.

And behold, I am pointing you to the beginning of guidance (bidāyat al-hidāyah), so that you may test yourself by it and examine your heart with it. If you find your heart inclining toward it, your soul submissive to it and accepting of it — then go forth to aspire to the ends and to plunge into the seas of the sciences.

But if you find your heart, when confronted with it, procrastinating, and with acting upon its requirements, delaying — then know that your soul which inclines toward seeking knowledge is the soul commanding to evil (al-nafs al-ammārah bi-l-sūʾ), and it has risen up obedient to the accursed Satan, so that he may lower you down by the rope of his delusion, and drag you by his cunning into the deep waters of destruction. His aim is to make evil appear attractive to you in the guise of good, until he joins you to {«those who are the greatest losers in deeds, those whose effort is lost in this worldly life while they think they are doing good work»} (Q. 18:103-104).

And at that point, Satan recites to you the virtue of knowledge and the rank of the scholars, and the reports and traditions that have come concerning that. And he distracts you from his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: {«Whoever increases in knowledge but does not increase in guidance, increases not in God's sight except in distance»}, and from his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: {«The most severely punished of people on the Day of Resurrection is a scholar whom God has not benefited with his knowledge»}. And he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say: {«O God, I seek refuge in You from knowledge that does not benefit, from a heart that does not humble itself, from a deed that is not raised up, and from a supplication that is not heard.»}

And from his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: {«I passed on the night of my night-journey by a people whose lips were being clipped with shears of fire. I said: Who are you? They said: We used to command good and not do it, and forbid evil and do it.»}

So beware, O poor one, of yielding to his falsification, lest he lower you down by the rope of his delusion. Woe to the ignorant one who did not learn even once, and woe to the scholar who did not act upon what he knew a thousand times.

And know that people, in seeking knowledge, are in three states: A man who seeks knowledge to make it his provision for the return to God (al-maʿād), intending thereby nothing but the Face of God and the abode of the Hereafter — this one is among the successful (al-fāʾizīn).

And a man who seeks it to aid himself in his transient life, to attain by it honor, status, and wealth — while he knows this of himself and perceives in his heart the baseness of his state and the vileness of his purpose — this one is among those who gamble with their salvation (al-mukhāṭirīn). If his appointed term overtakes him before repentance, it is feared for him an evil end, and his affair remains in the peril of the divine will. But if he is granted success in repentance before the term arrives, and he joins action to knowledge and makes up for the deficiency that preceded from him — he joins the successful, for the one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin.

And a third man — Satan has gained mastery over him, so he takes his knowledge as a means to multiplying wealth, boasting of status, and aggrandizing himself through the abundance of followers. He enters by his knowledge into every avenue, hoping to satisfy his worldly desire. And with all that, he harbors in himself the notion that he holds a station with God, because he is marked with the mark of the scholars and imitates their outward forms in dress and speech — while he clamors for the world, outwardly and inwardly. This one is among the perished (al-hālikīn), among the foolish and deluded. For hope of his repentance is cut off, because he imagines himself to be among the doers of good, heedless of the saying of God Almighty: {«O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do?»} (Q. 61:2). And he is among those of whom the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: {«I fear for you more than the Antichrist (al-Dajjāl)»} — and it was said: "And what is that, O Messenger of God?" He said: {«The evil scholars.»}
