صاحب النبوة والرسالة، وعلى آله وأصحابه الهادين من الضلالة. أما بعد: فقد سألتني أيها الأخ في الدين، أن أبث إليك غاية العلوم
وأسرارها، وغائلة المذاهب وأغوارها،
وأحكي لك ما قاسيته في استخلاص الحق من بين اضطراب الفرق مع تباين
المسالك والطرق، وما استجرأت عليه من الارتفاع عن حضيض التقليد، إلى يفاع
الاستبصار، وما استفدته، أولا من علم الكلام، وما اجتويته، ثانيا من طرق
أهل التعليم، القاصرين لدرك الحق على تقليد الإمام
وما ازدريته، ثالثا من طرق التفلسف وما ارتخيته، آخرا من طريقة التصوف
وما انجلى لي في تضاعيف تفتيشي عن أقاويل الخلق، من لباب الحق، وما صرفني
عن نشر العلم ببغداد مع كثرة الطلبة وما ردني إلى معاودتي بنيسابور بعد طول
المدة، فابتدرت لإجابتك إلى مطلبك، بعد الوقوف على صدق رغبتك، وقلت مستعينا
بالله ومتوكلا عليه، ومستوفقا منه، وملتجئا إليه: اعلموا - أحسن الله تعالى
إرشادكم، وألان للحق قيادكم - أن اختلاف الخلق في الأديان والملل، ثم
اختلاف الأمة في المذاهب على كثرة بالفرق، وتباين الطرق، بحر عميق غرق فيه
الأكثرون، وما نجا منه إلا الأقلون، وكل فريق يزعم أنه الناجي، " وكل حزب
بما لديهم فرحون ". وهو الذي وعدنا به سيد المرسلين صلوات الله عليه، وهوا
لصادق المصدوق حيث قال: " ستفترق أمتي ثلاثا وسبعين فرقة، الناجية منها
واحدة " فقد كان ما وعد أن يكون
ولم أزل في عنفوان شبابي - منذ راهقت البلوغ، قبل بلوغ العشرين إلى الآن،
وقد أناف السن على الخمسين - أقتحم لجة هذا البحر العميق، وأخوض غمرته خوض
الجسور، لا خوض الجبان الحذور، وأتوغل في كل مظلمة، وأتهجم على كل مشكلة،
وأتقحم كل ورطة، وأتفحص عن عقيدة كل فرقة، وأستكشف أسرار مذهب كل طائفة،
لأميز بين محق ومبطل، ومتسنن ومبتدع، لا أغادر باطنيا إلا وأحب أن أطلع على
باطنيته، ولا ظاهريا إلا وأريد أن أعلم حاصل ظاهريته، ولا فلسفيا إلا وأقصد
الوقوف على كنه فلسفته،
ولا متكلما إلا وأجتهد في الإطلاع على غاية كلامه ومجادلته ولا صوفيا إلا
وأحرص على العثور على سر صفوته، ولا متعبدا إلا وأترصد ما يرجع إليه حاصل
عبادته، ولا زنديقا معطلا إلا وأتحسس وراءه للتنبه لأسباب جرأته في تعطيله
وزندقته. وقد كان التعطش إلى درك حقائق الأمور دأبي وديني، من أول أمري، وريعان
عمري، غريزة وفطرة من الله وضعها في جبلتي لا باختياري وحيلتي، وحتى انحلت
عني رابطة التقليد، وانكسرت علي العقائد الموروثة على قرب عهد سن الصبا، إذ
رأيت: صبيان النصارى لا يكون لهم نشوء إلا على التنصر، وصبيان اليهود لا
نشوء لهم إلا على التهود، وصبيان المسلمين لا نشوء لهم إلا على الإسلام. وسمعت الحديث المروي عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حيث قال: " كل مولود
يولد على الفطرة فأبواه يهودانه، وينصرانه، ويمجسانه " فتحرك باطني إلى طلب
حقيقة الفطرة الأصلية، وحقيقة العقائد العارضة بتقليد الوالدين والأستاذين،
والتمييز بين هذه التقليدات، وأوائلها
تلقينات، وفي تمييز الحق منها عن الباطل اختلافات فقلت في نفسي: أولا
إنما مطلوبي العلم بحقائق الأمور، فلا بد من طلب حقيقة العلم ما هي؟ فظهر
لي: أن العلم اليقيني هو الذي ينكشف فيه المعلوم انكشافا لا يبقى معه ريب،
ولا يفارقه إمكان الغلط والوهم، ولا يتسع القلب لتقدير ذلك، بل الأمان من
الخطأ ينبغي أنا يكون مقارنا لليقين، مقارنة لو تحدى بإظهار بطلانه - مثلا
- من يقلب الحجر ذهبا والعصا ثعبانا، لم يروث ذلك شكا وإنكارا، فإني إذا
علمت: أن العشرة أكثر من الثلاثة، فلو قال لي قائل: لا بل الثلاثة أكثر،
بدليل أني أقلب هذه العصا ثعبانا، وقلبها، وشاهدت ذلك منه، لم أشك بسببه في
معرفتي، ولم يحصل لي منه إلا التعجب من كيفية قدرته عليه! فأما الشك بسببه
فيما علمته فلا ثم علمت أن كل ما لا أعلمه على هذا الوجه ولا أتيقنه هذا

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: علم (ʿ-l-m)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes a mark or trace by which a thing is known; knowledge as the impression of reality upon the mind.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Al-ʿilm (knowledge) is the apprehension of a thing as it truly is; al-yaqīn (certainty) is the settled conviction leaving no room for doubt.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage pertains to direct apprehension; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to derivative forms like taʿlīm (instruction) and iʿlām (informing).
- Root: قلب (q-l-b)
 * Lisan / Ayn: The heart (qalb) is so named for its constant turning (taqallub) and fluctuation between states.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The heart is the seat of intellect and discernment (ʿaql); its "turning" signifies the oscillation between certainty and doubt that characterizes the seeker's state.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: the physical organ; metaphorical: the inner faculty of perception and moral discernment.
- Root: رشد (r-sh-d)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Right guidance (rushd) is the straight path; the opposite of error (ghayy).
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Irshād (guidance) is the divine act of directing one toward truth; the root carries the sense of maturity and sound judgment.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: following the correct road; metaphorical: adherence to true doctrine and sound practice.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الحصر والتقييد بإنما (Restriction & Focused Predication) — The particle innamā restricts the predicate to the subject alone, as in "innamā maṭlūbī al-ʿilm..." ("my aim is only knowledge..."), emphasizing the exclusive nature of the seeker's goal.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)

Praise be to Allah, by whose praise every epistle and discourse is opened, and blessings upon Muhammad the Chosen, possessor of prophethood and messengership, and upon his family and his companions, the guides from error. To proceed: You have asked me, O brother in religion, that I impart to you the ultimate aims of the sciences and their secrets, and the perils of the sects and their depths; and that I relate to you what I endured in extracting the truth from amidst the turmoil of the factions, despite the divergence of paths and ways; and what I dared in ascending from the lowland of blind following (taqlīd) to the highland of clear insight (istibṣār); and what I first gained from the science of theology (kalām); and what I secondly loathed from the ways of the partisans of authoritative instruction (taʿlīmiyyah), who restrict the attainment of truth to the taqlīd of an infallible Imam; and what I thirdly disparaged from the ways of philosophy (falsafah); and what I finally embraced from the way of Sufism (taṣawwuf); and what was unveiled to me amidst my investigations into the sayings of mankind, of the pith of truth; and what turned me away from spreading knowledge in Baghdad despite the abundance of students; and what drove me back to resuming my work in Nishapur after a long interval. So I hastened to answer your request, after ascertaining the sincerity of your desire, and I said, seeking aid from Allah, relying upon Him, seeking success from Him, and taking refuge in Him:

Know — may Allah the Exalted perfect your guidance and soften for you the reins of truth — that the divergence of mankind in religions and creeds, and then the divergence of the community (ummah) in the sects, despite the multiplicity of factions and the disparity of paths, is a deep sea in which the majority have drowned, and from which none have escaped save the few. And every faction claims that it is the saved one — {«وكل حزب بما لديهم فرحون»} ("And every party rejoices in what it has") — and this is what the Master of the Messengers, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, promised us, and he is the truthful and the confirmed, when he said: "My community will split into seventy-three sects, and the saved among them is one." So what he promised came to be.

And I have not ceased, from the prime of my youth — since I reached the age of discernment, before attaining twenty, until now, as my age has surpassed fifty — to plunge into the depths of this deep sea, and to wade into its overwhelming flood with the wading of the courageous, not the wading of the timid coward; and to penetrate into every darkness, and to assault every problem, and to leap into every perilous strait, and to scrutinize the creed of every faction, and to uncover the secrets of the doctrine of every group, in order to distinguish between the truthful and the false, and between the follower of the Sunnah and the innovator. I did not leave an esotericist (bāṭinī) except that I loved to examine his esotericism, nor a literalist (ẓāhirī) except that I wished to know the outcome of his literalism, nor a philosopher except that I sought to grasp the core of his philosophy, nor a theologian (mutakallim) except that I strove to attain the limit of his discourse and disputation, nor a Sufi except that I was eager to stumble upon the secret of his purity, nor a devotee except that I watched for what the outcome of his devotion reverts to, nor a heretic (zindīq) and denier of God except that I probed behind him to become aware of the causes of his audacity in his denial and heresy.

And the thirst for grasping the realities of things had been my habit and my religion from the very beginning of my affair and the flower of my life — an instinct and a nature placed by Allah in my constitution, not by my choice or contrivance — until the bond of taqlīd was dissolved from me, and the inherited beliefs were broken upon me, given the nearness of the age of youth. For I saw that the children of Christians do not grow up except upon Christianity, and the children of Jews do not grow up except upon Judaism, and the children of Muslims do not grow up except upon Islam. And I heard the hadith related from the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, where he said: "Every newborn is born upon the fiṭrah (primordial nature), and his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian." So my inner being stirred toward seeking the reality of the primordial fiṭrah, and the reality of the beliefs that arise incidentally through the taqlīd of parents and teachers, and the distinction between these taqlīds — whose beginnings are mere inculcations — and in distinguishing the truth from falsehood among them, there are divergences.

So I said to myself: First, my aim is only knowledge of the realities of things, and therefore I must seek what the reality of knowledge itself is. Then it became clear to me that certain knowledge (al-ʿilm al-yaqīnī) is that in which the known thing is disclosed with a disclosure that leaves no room for doubt, and with which no possibility of error or illusion accompanies it, and the heart does not entertain the estimation of that — rather, security from error must be conjoined with certainty, conjoined in such a way that if someone — for example — were to challenge its falsity by turning a stone into gold and a staff into a serpent, that would not engender doubt or denial. For if I know that ten is more than three, and a speaker were to say to me: "No, rather three is more, with the proof that I turn this staff into a serpent," and he turns it, and I witness that from him, I would not doubt my knowledge because of it, and nothing would result from it for me except wonder at how he has the power to do it! As for doubt in what I know because of it — no, that does not occur. Then I knew that everything I do not know in this manner, and of which I am not certain with this type of certainty, is knowledge in which there is no confidence and with which there is no security; and every knowledge with which there is no security is not certain knowledge.

paragraphs.text:
### | بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

### | مقدمة المؤلف

قال الشيخ الإمام العالم العامل حجة الإسلام أبو حامد محمد بن محمد
الغزالى الطوسى رحم الله وعفا عنه: الحمد لله وحده والصلاة والسلام على خير
خلقة سيدنا محمد وآله وصحبه، هذا كتاب الكشف والتبيين فى غرور الخلق
أجمعين. اعلم أن الخلق قسمان: حيوان وغير حيوان.. والحيوان قسمان: مكلف
ومهمل.. فالمكلف من خاطبه الله بالعبادة وأمره بها.. ووعده الثواب عليها
ونهاه عن المعاصى وحذره العقوبة..
ثم المكلف قسمان: مؤمن وكافر.. والمؤمن قسمان طائع وعاص.. وكل من
الطائعين والعاصين ينقسم قسمين: عالم وجاهل..
ثم رأيت الغرور لازما لجميع المؤمنين المكلفين والكافرين. إلا من عصمه
الله رب العالمين.. وأنا بحمد الله أكشف عن غرورهم وأبين الحجة فيه..
وأوضحه غاية الإيضاح. وأبينه غاية البيان بأوجز ما تكون العبارة.. وأبدع ما
يكون من الإشارة.
والمغرورون من الخلق ما عدا الكافرين أربعة أصناف: صنف من العلماء.. وصنف
من العباد.. وصنف من أرباب الأموال..وصنف من المتصوفة.

### | غرور الكافر

فأول ما نبدأ به غرور الكافر، وهو قسمان: منهم من غرته الحياة الدنيا..
ومنهم من غره بالله الغرور.. أما الذين غرتهم الحياة الدنيا وهم الذين
قالوا: النقد خير من النسيئة.. ولذات الدنيا يقين.. ولذات الآخرة شك!!..
ولا يترك اليقين بالشك.. وهذا قياس فاسد.. وهو قياس إبليس لعنه الله تعالى
فى قوله: أنا خير منه.. فظن أن الخيرية فى النسب..

### | وعلاج هذا الغرور شيئان

إما بتصديق وهو الإيمان.. وإما ببرهان.
أما التصديق فهو أن يصدق الله تعالى فى قوله (وما عند الله خير وأبقى)
(وما الحياة الدنيا إلا متاع الغرور) .. وتصديق الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم
فيما جاء به..وأما البرهان: وهو أن يعرف وجه فساد قياسه.. أن قوله: الدنيا
نقد والآخرة نسيئة مقدمة صحيحة وأما قوله: النقد خير من النسيئة. فهو محل
التلبيس.. وليس الأمر
كذلك.. بل إن كان النقد مثل النسيئة في المقدار.. والمقصود فهو خير.. وإن
كان أقل منها.. فالنسيئة خير منه.. ومعلوم أن الآخرة أبدية.. والدنيا غير
أبدية.. وأما قوله: ولذات الدنيا يقين ولذات الآخرة شك فهو أيضا باطل.. بل
ذلك يقين عند المؤمنين..
وليقينه مدر كان: أحدهما الإيمان والتصديق على وجه التقليد للأنبياء
والعلماء كما يقلد الطبيب الحاذق في الدواء.. والمدرك الثاني: الوحى
للأنبياء والإلهام للأولياء.. ولا تظن أن معرفة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
لأمور الآخرة.. ولأمور الدنيا تقليد لجبريل عليه السلام.. فإن التقليد ليس
بمعرفة صحيحة.. والنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم حاشاه الله من ذلك.. بل انكشفت
له الأشياء.. وشاهدها بنور البصيرة.. كما شاهدت أنت المحسوسات بالعين
الظاهرة..

### | فصل فيمن يشاركون الكفار غرورهم

### | من المؤمنين بربهم

والمؤمنون بألسنتهم وعقائدهم إذا ضيعوا أمر الله تعالى وهى الأعمال
الصالحة.. وتدنسوا بالشهوات.. وهم مشاركون الكفار فى هذا الغرور.. فالحياة
الدنيا للكافرين والمؤمنين جميعا غرور: فأما غرور الكافرين بالله تعالى
فمثاله:
قول بعضهم فى أنفسهم بألسنتهم: إنه إن كان الله معيدنا فنحن أحق بها من
غيرنا كما أخبر الله تعالى عنهم فى صورة الكهف حين قال: (ما أظن أن تبيد
هذه أبدا، وما أظن الساعة قائمة ولئن رددت إلى ربي لأجدن خيرا منها منقلبا)

# QUAD-LEXICAL & SYNTACTIC ANCHOR CONSTELLATION

[Root: قسم]
 * Lisan / Ayn: Division, apportionment, allotment of shares
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "القسم: إفراز النصيب" — the separation and allotment of portions; used for dividing inheritance, spoils, and the apportioning of destinies
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: dividing shares of property. Metaphorical: "قلبه متقسم" — a heart divided/consumed by cares; "تقسمته الهموم" — anxieties that tear one apart

[Root: خير]
 * Lisan / Ayn: Goodness, excellence, superiority; that which is desirable
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الخير: ما يرغب فيه الكل" — that which all desire: intellect, justice, virtue, benefit. Two kinds: absolute good (good in every circumstance) and relative good (good for one, evil for another)
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: choosing the better of two things (istikhārah). The root carries the sense of preference and selection of the superior

[Root: حمد]
 * Lisan / Ayn: Praise, commendation, laudation for virtue or beneficence
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Praise rendered for voluntary beneficence; the root also relates to the intense heat of praise (ḥamīm — hot water) suggesting fervency
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "أحمد الله تعالى بجميع محامده" — praising God with all His praises. Metaphorical: "أحمدت الأرض" — found the land praiseworthy to dwell in

[Root: خلق]
 * Lisan / Ayn: Creation, origination; also: measure, proportion, estimation
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الخلق أصله: التقدير المستقيم" — its origin is right measure and proportion; used for creation from nothing (ibdāʿ) and creation from something
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: measuring/cutting leather before cutting. Metaphorical: "خلق الله الخلق: أوجده على تقدير أوجبته الحكمة" — God created creation upon a measure required by wisdom

# TRANSLATION
## THE BOOK OF UNVEILING AND CLARIFICATION CONCERNING THE DELUSION OF ALL CREATION
### In the Name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate
### The Author's Introduction

The Shaykh, the Imām, the learned and the practicing, the Proof of Islam, Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad al-Ghazālī al-Ṭūsī — may God have mercy upon him and pardon him — said: Praise be to God alone, and blessings and peace upon the best of His creation, our master Muḥammad, and upon his family and companions. This is the book of Unveiling and Clarification concerning the delusion of all creation.

Know that creation is of two kinds: animate and inanimate. And the animate is of two kinds: the obligated (mukallaf) and the neglected (muhmal). The obligated is he whom God addressed with worship and commanded him to perform it, and promised him reward upon it, and forbade him from sins and warned him of punishment.

Then the obligated is of two kinds: believer and disbeliever. And the believer is of two kinds: obedient and disobedient. And each of the obedient and the disobedient is divided into two kinds: learned and ignorant.

Then I saw that delusion (ghurūr) is inseparable from all the obligated believers and the disbelievers — except those whom God, Lord of the worlds, has protected. And I, by God's praise, shall unveil their delusion and clarify the proof concerning it, and elucidate it with the utmost elucidation, and explain it with the utmost explanation, in the most concise expression and the most exquisite allusion.

And the deluded among creation, apart from the disbelievers, are four classes: a class of the scholars (ʿulamāʾ), a class of the worshippers (ʿubbād), a class of the wealthy (arbāb al-amwāl), and a class of the Sufis (mutasawwifah).
### On the Delusion of the Disbeliever

The first thing we begin with is the delusion of the disbeliever, and it is of two kinds: among them is he whom the life of this world deluded, and among them is he whom the Deluder (al-gharūr) deluded concerning God. As for those whom the life of this world deluded — and they are those who said: "The ready cash (al-naqd) is better than the credit (al-nasīʾah); the pleasures of this world are certain (yaqīn), and the pleasures of the Hereafter are doubtful (shakk); and one does not abandon certainty for doubt." This is a corrupt analogy (qiyās fāsid), and it is the analogy of Iblīs — may God curse him — in his saying: "I am better than him" {«أنا خير منه»} — for he supposed that superiority (al-khayriyyah) lay in lineage (al-nasab).
### The Remedy for This Delusion Is Two Things
Either by affirmation (taṣdīq), which is faith (īmān), or by demonstration (burhān).

As for the affirmation, it is that one affirms the truth of God — exalted — in His saying: {«وما عند الله خير وأبقى»} ("And what is with God is better and more enduring") and {«وما الحياة الدنيا إلا متاع الغرور»} ("And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion"), and affirms the truth of the Messenger — peace be upon him — in what he brought.

As for the demonstration, it is that one recognizes the aspect of corruption in his analogy. For his saying "the world is ready cash and the Hereafter is credit" is a sound premise (muqaddimah ṣaḥīḥah). But as for his saying "the ready cash is better than the credit" — that is the locus of obfuscation (talbīs). And the matter is not so. Rather, if the ready cash equals the credit in quantity and purpose, then it is better. But if it is less than it, then the credit is better than it. And it is known that the Hereafter is eternal (abadī), and the world is not eternal. And as for his saying: "The pleasures of this world are certain and the pleasures of the Hereafter are doubtful" — this too is false. Rather, that is certain for the believers. And for this certainty there are two means of apprehension (mudrak): one of them is faith and affirmation by way of emulation (taqlīd) of the prophets and the scholars, just as one emulates the skilled physician concerning medicine. And the second means of apprehension is revelation (waḥy) for the prophets and inspiration (ilhām) for the saints (awliyāʾ). And do not suppose that the knowledge of the Prophet — peace be upon him — of the matters of the Hereafter and the matters of this world was emulation of Gabriel — peace be upon him. For emulation is not sound knowledge, and the Prophet — peace be upon him — God forbid him from that — rather, things were unveiled to him, and he witnessed them with the light of inner vision (nūr al-baṣīrah), just as you witness sensible objects with the outer eye.
### Section: On Those Among the Believers in Their Lord Who Share the Delusion of the Disbelievers

And those who believe with their tongues and their creeds — when they squander the command of God — exalted — which is the righteous deeds, and defile themselves with lusts — they are sharers with the disbelievers in this delusion. For the life of this world is a delusion for the disbelievers and the believers all together. As for the delusion of the disbelievers concerning God — exalted — its example is the saying of some of them among themselves, with their tongues: "If God is to return us, then we are more deserving of it than others" — as God — exalted — reported of them in Sūrat al-Kahf when He said: {«ما أظن أن تبيد هذه أبدا، وما أظن الساعة قائمة ولئن رددت إلى ربي لأجدن خيرا منها منقلبا»} ("I do not think that this will ever perish, and I do not think the Hour will come, and if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return").
### What Is the Cause of This Delusion

The cause of this delusion is an analogy from the analogies of Iblīs — may God curse him. For they look, at one time, at God's blessings upon them in this world, and they analogize upon them the blessings of the Hereafter. And at another time, they look at the deferment of God's punishment from them in this world, and they analogize the punishment of the Hereafter — as God — exalted — reported of them: {«ويقولون فى أنفسهم لولا يعذبنا الله بما نقول حسبهم جهنم يصلونها فبئس المصير»} ("And they say among themselves: 'Why does God not punish us for what we say?' Sufficient for them is Hell; they will burn in it, and evil is the destination"). And at another time, they look at the believers who are poor, and they despise them and say: {«أهؤلاء من الله عليهم من بيننا»} ("Are these the ones whom God has favored among us?") and they say: {«لو كان خيرا ما سبقونا إليه»} ("If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it").

The arrangement of the analogy that was organized in their hearts is that they say: "God has been good to us with the blessings of this world, and every doer of good is a lover, and every lover is a doer of good." But it is not so. Rather, one may be a doer of good without being a lover. Indeed, sometimes the good deed is the cause of one's destruction by way of gradual enticement (istidrāj). And that is pure delusion concerning God — mighty and majestic. For this reason, the Prophet — peace be upon him — said: "God — exalted — protects His servant from this world just as one of you protects his sick patient from food and drink, while He loves him." For this reason, the people of inner vision (arbāb al-baṣāʾir), when this world advanced upon them, grieved; and when poverty advanced upon them, they rejoiced and said: "Welcome to the emblem of the righteous." For God — exalted — has said: {«فأما الإنسان إذا ما ابتلاه ربه فأكرمه ونعمه»} ("As for man, when his Lord tests him and honors him and favors him...") and He — exalted — said: {«أيحسبون أنما نمدهم به من مال وبنين نسارع لهم فى الخيرات بل لا يشعرون»} ("Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children — that We hasten for them good things? Rather, they do not perceive") — the verse. And He — exalted — said: {«سنستدرجهم من حيث لا يعلمون، وأملى لهم إن كيدى متين»} ("We will gradually entice them from where they do not know, and I will respite them; indeed, My plan is firm"). And He — exalted — said: {«فلما نسوا ما ذكروا به فتحنا عليهم أبواب كل شئ حتى إذا فرحوا بما أوتوا أخذناهم بغتة فإذا هم مبلسون»} ("And when they forgot what they were reminded of, We opened upon them the doors of everything, until when they rejoiced in what they were given, We seized them suddenly, and behold, they were in despair").
So whoever believes in God — exalted — is secure from this delusion.
### From What Does This Delusion Arise

The origin of this delusion is ignorance of God — exalted — and of His attributes. For whoever knows God — exalted — is not secure from God's stratagem (makr). And they should look at Pharaoh, Hāmān, and Thamūd, and what befell them — despite the fact that God — exalted — had given them wealth. And God — exalted — has warned against His stratagem, saying: {«فلا يأمن مكر الله إلا القوم الخاسرون»} ("None is secure from God's stratagem except the people of loss"), and He — exalted — said: {«ومكروا ومكر الله والله خير الماكرين»} ("And they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters"), and He — exalted — said: {«فمهل الكافرين أمهلهم رويدا»} ("So give respite to the disbelievers; grant them respite gently"). So whoever is given a blessing should fear that it may be a punishment.
### Section: On the Delusion of the Disobedient Among the Believers
And they are those who rely upon God's pardon and neglect action.

As for the delusion of the disobedient among the believers concerning God, it is their saying: "He is Forgiving, Merciful, and His pardon is to be hoped for." So they relied upon that and neglected the deeds. This arises from hope (rajāʾ), for it is a praiseworthy station in this world, and that God's mercy is vast, His favor comprehensive, and His generosity abundant — and we are monotheists, hoping in Him through the means of faith, generosity, and beneficence.
### The Origin of That Delusion

Perhaps the origin of their state is their clinging to the righteousness of their fathers and mothers. And that is the extreme of delusion. For their fathers, despite their righteousness and piety, were fearful. And the arrangement of their analogy, which Satan embellished for them, is: "Whoever loves a person loves his children. God has loved your father, so He loves you. Therefore you have no need of acts of obedience." So they relied upon that and were deluded concerning God. And they did not know that Noah — peace be upon him — wanted to carry his son upon the ark and was prevented, and God — glorified and exalted — drowned him with the most severe drowning with which He drowned the people of Noah.

And our Prophet Muḥammad — peace be upon him — sought permission to visit his mother's grave and to seek forgiveness for her. He was granted permission for the visit but was not granted permission to seek forgiveness for her.

And they forgot His saying — glorified and exalted: {«ألا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى. وأن ليس للإنسان إلا ما سعى»} ("That no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another, and that man has nothing but what he strives for").

And whoever supposes that he will be saved by the piety of his origin is like one who supposes he will be satiated by his father's eating or quenched by his father's drinking. And piety is an individual obligation (farḍ ʿayn); no parent suffices for his child in it — {«يوم يفر المرء من أخيه وأمه وأبيه وصاحبته وبنيه»} ("On the day when a man flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his spouse, and his sons") — except by way of intercession.

And they forgot his saying — peace and blessings be upon him: "The shrewd one is he who takes account of himself and works for what is after death, and the foolish one is he who follows his soul and its desires and wishes upon God wishes (tamannī)."

And His saying — exalted: {«إن الذين آمنوا والذين هاجروا وجاهدوا فى سبيل الله أولئك يرجون رحمة الله والله غفور رحيم»} ("Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the path of God — those hope for the mercy of God, and God is Forgiving, Merciful").
And He — exalted — said: {«جزاء بما كانوا يعملون»} ("A recompense for what they used to do"). And does hope (rajāʾ) become sound except when action precedes it? Otherwise, it is delusion, inevitably.

### | بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

الحمد لله الذي أصعد قوالب الأصفياء بالمجاهدة، وأسعد قلوب الأولياء
بالمشاهدة، وحلى ألسنة المؤمنين بالذكر، وجلى خواطر العارفين بالفكر، وحرس
سواد العباد عن الفساد، وحبس مراد الزهاد على السداد، وخلص أشباح المتقين
من ظلم الشهوات، وصفى أرواح الموقنين عن ظلم الشبهات، وقبل أعمال الأخيار
بأداء الصلوات، وأيد خصال الأحرار بإسداء الصلات.
أحمده حمد من رأى آيات قدرته وقوته، وشاهد الشواهد من فردانيته
ووحدانيته، وطرق طوارق سره وبره، وقطف ثمار معرفته من شجر مجده وجوده،
وأشكره شكر من اخترق واغترف من نهر فضله وإفضاله، وأومن به إيمان من آمن
بكتابه وخطابه، وأنبيائه وأصفيائه، ووعده ووعيده، وثوابه وعقابه.. وأشهد أن
لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له، وأشهد أن محمدا عبده ورسوله: بعثه لأصلاب
الفسقة والفجرة قاسما، ولعرى الجاحدين والمارقين فاصما، ولباغي الشك والشرك
قاهرا، ولأتباع الحق والإحسان ناصرا؛ فصلوات الله عليه، وعلى آله، وأصحابه
أجمعين.

### | فصل في معرفة النفس

اعلم أن مفتاح معرفة الله تعالى هو معرفة النفس، كما قال سبحانه وتعالى:
(سنريهم آياتنا في الآفاق وفي أنفسهم حتى يتبين لهم أنه الحق) .
وقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم:) من عرف نفسه فقد عرف ربه (. وليس شيء
أقرب إليك من نفسك، فإذا لم تعرف نفسك، فكيف تعرف ربك؟ فإن قلت: إني أعرف
نفسي! فإنما تعرف الجسم الظاهر، الذي هو اليد والرجل والرأس والجثة، ولا
تعرف ما في باطنك من الأمر الذي به إذا غضبت طلبت الخصومة، وإذا اشتهيت
طلبت النكاح، وإذا جعت طلبت الأكل، وإذا عطشت طلبت الشرب.
والدواب تشاركك في هذه الأمور.
فالواجب عليك أن تعرف نفسك بالحقيقة؛ حتى تدرك أي شيء أنت، ومن أين جئت
إلى هذا المكان، ولأي شيء خلقت، وبأي شيء سعادتك، وبأي شيء شقاؤك.
وقد جمعت في باطنك صفات: منها صفات البهائم، ومنها صفات السباع، ومنها
صفات الشياطين، ومنها صفات الملائكة، فالروح حقيقة جوهرك وغيرها غريب منك،
وعارية عندك.
فالواجب عليك أن تعرف هذا، وتعرف أن لكل واحد من هؤلاء غذاء وسعادة.
فإن سعادة البهائم في الأكل، والشرب، والنوم، والنكاح، فإن كنت منهم
فاجتهد في أعمال الجوف والفرج.
وسعادة السباع في الضرب، والفتك.
وسعادة الشياطين في المكر، والشر، والحيل. فإن كنت منهم فاشتغل
باشتغالهم.
وسعادة
الملائكة في مشاهدة جمال الحضرة الربوبية، وليس للغضب والشهوة إليهم
طريق. فإن كنت من جوهر الملائكة، فاجتهد في معرفة أصلك؛ حتى تعرف الطريق
إلى الحضرة الإلهية، وتبلغ إلى مشاهدة الجلال والجمال، وتخلص نفسك من قيد
الشهوة والغضب، وتعلم أن هذه الصفات لأي شيء ركبت فيك؛ فما خلقها الله
تعالى لتكون أسيرها، ولكن خلقها حتى تكون أسرك، وتسخرها للسفر الذي قدامك،
وتجعل إحداها مركبك، والأخرى سلاحك؛ حتى تصيد بها سعادتك. فإذا بلغت غرضك
فقاوم بها تحت قدميك، وارجع إلى مكان سعادتك. وذلك المكان قرار خواص الحضرة
الإلهية، وقرار العوام درجات الجنة.
فتحتاج إلى معرفة هذه المعاني؛ حتى تعرف من نفسك شيئا قليلا؛ فكل من لم
يعرف هذه المعاني فنصيبه من القشور؛ لأن الحق يكون عنه محجوبا.

### | فصل كيف تعرف نفسك

إذا شئت أن تعرف نفسك، فاعلم أنك من شيئين: الأول: هذا القلب، والثاني:
يسمى النفس والروح.
والنفس هو القلب الذي تعرفه بعين الباطن، وحقيقتك الباطن؛ لأن الجسد أول
وهو الآخر، والنفس آخر وهو الأول. ويسمى قلبا.
وليس القلب هذه القطعة اللحمية التي في الصدر من الجانب الأيسر؛ لأنه
يكون في الدواب والموتى. وكل شيء تبصره بعين الظاهر فهو من هذا العالم الذي
يسمى عالم الشهادة.
وأ

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: عرف (ʿarafa)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning "to know by experience, to recognize"; from عرف (ʿirf) meaning the mane of a horse — that which marks and distinguishes
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "المعرفة والعرفان: إدراك الشيء بتفكر وتدبر لأثره" — knowledge (maʿrifah) is perception of a thing through reflection and contemplation of its trace/effect; it is more specific than ʿilm (knowledge), and its opposite is inkār (denial). Used of man's knowledge of God — attained through contemplating His effects, not through grasping His essence
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage: "لأعرفن لك ما صنعت" — "I will surely make known to you what you have done" (i.e., requite you for it). The maʿrifah of the self is literal self-recognition; the maʿrifah of God is by way of His traces
- Root: نفس (nafs)
 * Lisan / Ayn: The self, soul, spirit; that which has breath (nafas); the essence of a thing
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "النفس: الروح" — the nafs is the rūḥ (spirit). In God's saying {وَيُحَذِّرُكُمُ اللَّهُ نَفْسَهُ} ("God warns you of Himself"), His nafs is His very dhāt (essence). Though the grammatical construction of mudāf/mudāf ilayh implies two things verbally, in meaning there is no duality
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas - Majaz): "دفق نفسه أي دمه" — "he poured out his nafs" means his blood (metaphorical). The nafs as the inner reality of man is distinguished from the animal spirit (al-rūḥ al-ḥayawānī)
- Root: قلب (qalb)
 * Lisan / Ayn: The heart; from qalaba (to turn over, to flip) — because it constantly turns over between states
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The heart is that which perceives and understands; it is the locus of knowledge of God
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Distinguished from the physical heart (al-mudghah) which exists in beasts and the dead
- Root: جسد (jasad) / قالب (qālab)
 * Lisan / Ayn: The body as mold/form; the qālab is the outward form that carries the inner reality
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The body is the vehicle (markab) of the soul; the soul is the rider
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الحصر والتقييد بإنما (Restriction & Focused Predication) — "إنما" restricts and focuses predication, used to distinguish the true heart from the physical heart; also applies to the structure "ليس القلب هذه القطعة اللحمية" (negative restriction)
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
### | In the Name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

Praise be to God, who raised the molds (qawālib) of His chosen ones (aṣfiyāʾ) through striving (mujāhadah), and made happy the hearts of His saints (awliyāʾ) through witnessing (mushāhadah), and adorned the tongues of the believers with remembrance (dhikr), and polished the inner thoughts of the knowers (ʿārifīn) with reflection (fikr), and guarded the masses of His servants from corruption, and restrained the aspirations of the ascetics (zuhhād) upon rectitude, and purified the bodies (ashbāḥ) of the God-fearing from the darkness of lusts, and cleansed the spirits (arwāḥ) of the certain (mūqinīn) from the darkness of doubts, and accepted the deeds of the righteous through the performance of prayers, and strengthened the qualities of the free-hearted through the giving of gifts (ṣilāt).

I praise Him with the praise of one who has seen the signs of His power and His might, and who has witnessed the evidences (shawāhid) of His uniqueness (fardāniyyah) and His oneness (waḥdāniyyah), and who has been struck by the knockings of His secret and His benevolence, and who has plucked the fruits of knowledge of Him (maʿrifatihi) from the tree of His glory and His generosity. And I thank Him with the thanks of one who has crossed over and drawn from the river of His favor and His bounty. And I believe in Him with the faith of one who believes in His Book and His address (khitāb), His prophets and His chosen ones, His promise and His threat, His reward and His punishment. And I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner to Him. And I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger — He sent him as a divider against the loins of the wicked and the profligate, and as a crusher of the bonds of the deniers and the renegades, and as a conqueror over the seeker of doubt and polytheism, and as a helper to the followers of truth and excellence. May the blessings of God be upon him, and upon his family, and upon all his companions.
### | Chapter on the Knowledge of the Self (Maʿrifat al-Nafs)

Know that the key to knowledge of God, the Exalted, is knowledge of the self (nafs) — as He, Glorified and Exalted, said: {سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَاتِنَا فِي الْآفَاقِ وَفِي أَنفُسِهِمْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُمْ أَنَّهُ الْحَقُّ} ("We will show them Our signs in the horizons and in their own selves until it becomes clear to them that it is the Truth"). And the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "He who knows his self has known his Lord." And nothing is closer to you than your self. So if you do not know your self, how could you know your Lord? For if you say, "I do know my self!" — you only know the outward body (jism al-ẓāhir), which is the hand, the foot, the head, and the trunk — and you do not know that inner thing within you by which, when you are angry, you seek contention; and when you desire, you seek marriage; and when you are hungry, you seek food; and when you are thirsty, you seek drink. And the beasts (dawābb) share with you in these matters.

It is therefore incumbent upon you to know your self in its reality (ḥaqīqah), so that you may perceive what thing you are, and from where you came to this place, and for what purpose you were created, and in what your happiness (saʿādah) lies, and in what your misery (shaqāwah) lies. For there have been gathered within your inner being (bāṭin) attributes: among them are attributes of the beasts (bahāʾim), among them are attributes of the predators (sibāʿ), among them are attributes of the devils (shayāṭīn), and among them are attributes of the angels (malāʾikah). The spirit (rūḥ) is the reality of your substance (jawhar), and all else is a stranger (gharīb) to you, and a loan (ʿāriyyah) in your possession.

It is incumbent upon you to know this, and to know that for each one of these there is a nourishment and a happiness. For the happiness of the beasts lies in eating, drinking, sleeping, and mating. If you are of them, then strive in the works of the belly and the loins. And the happiness of the predators lies in striking and in killing. And the happiness of the devils lies in deceit, evil, and cunning. If you are of them, then occupy yourself with their occupations. And the happiness of the angels lies in witnessing the beauty of the Divine Presence (al-ḥaḍrah al-rubūbiyyah), and anger and lust have no path to them. If you are of the substance (jawhar) of the angels, then strive in knowledge of your origin — so that you may come to know the path to the Divine Presence, and attain to the witnessing of Majesty (jalāl) and Beauty (jamāl), and free your self from the bond of lust and anger. And know that these attributes were only mounted within you for a purpose; for God, the Exalted, did not create them so that you would be their captive, but rather He created them so that they would be your captives, and so that you would subjugate them for the journey that lies before you, and make one of them your mount (markab) and the other your weapon (silāḥ) — so that you may hunt your happiness with them. And when you have attained your goal, then trample them beneath your feet, and return to the place of your happiness. And that place is the abode of the elite (khawāṣṣ) of the Divine Presence, while the abode of the common folk (ʿawāmm) is the degrees of Paradise.

So you stand in need of knowledge of these meanings — so that you may know from your self something, however little. For whoever does not know these meanings, his portion is only of the husks (qushūr), because the Truth (al-ḥaqq) is veiled from him.
### | Chapter: How You Know Your Self

If you wish to know your self, then know that you are of two things: the first is this heart (qalb), and the second is called the self (nafs) and the spirit (rūḥ). And the self is the heart which you know with the inner eye (ʿayn al-bāṭin), and your reality is the inner (bāṭin); for the body (jasad) is the first and the last, and the self is the last and the first. And it is called "heart" (qalb).

And the heart is not this piece of flesh (al-qitʿah al-laḥmiyyah) which is in the chest on the left side; for that exists in the beasts and in the dead. And everything that you behold with the outer eye (ʿayn al-ẓāhir) is of this world, which is called the world of witnessing (ʿālam al-shahādah). And this [true heart] is not of this world; rather, it is of the world of the unseen (ʿālam al-ghayb). And it is, in this world, a stranger (gharīb). And that piece of flesh is a mount (markab) for it, and all the limbs of the body are its armies (ʿasākir), and it is the king (malik). Knowledge of God and witnessing of the beauty of the Presence are its attributes. Upon it is the obligation (taklīf), and to it is the address (khiṭāb). For it is the reward, and upon it is the punishment. Happiness and misery attach to it. And the animal spirit (al-rūḥ al-ḥayawānī) follows it and is with it in all its affairs. And knowledge of its reality and knowledge of its attributes is the key to knowledge of God, Glorified and Exalted. So upon you is striving (mujāhadah) until you know it; for it is a precious substance (jawhar ʿazīz) of the same kind as the substance of the angels. And the origin of its mine (maʿdin) is from the Divine Presence. From that place it came, and to that place it returns.
### | Chapter: What Is the Reality of the Heart?

As for your question — "What is the reality of the heart?" — nothing more has come in the Sacred Law (sharīʿah) than the saying of God, the Exalted: {وَيَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الرُّوحِ قُلِ الرُّوحُ مِنْ أَمْرِ رَبِّي} ("And they ask you concerning the spirit. Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord"). For the spirit is of the totality of the Divine power, and it is of the world of command (ʿālam al-amr). And God, Mighty and Majestic, said: {أَلَا لَهُ الْخَلْقُ وَالْأَمْرُ} ("Verily, His is the creation and the command"). Thus man is of the world of creation (ʿālam al-khalq) from one side, and of the world of command from another side. And everything to which measurement (misāḥah), quantity (miqdār), and modality (kayfiyyah) apply is of the world of creation. And the heart has no measurement and no quantity; and for this reason it does not admit division (qismah). For were it to admit division, it would be of the world of creation, and would be ignorant from one side and knowing from another side. And everything in which knowledge and ignorance coexist is impossible (muḥāl). And in another sense, it is of the world of command; for the world of command is an expression for a thing among things to which measurement and quantification have no path.

And some have thought that the spirit is eternal (qadīm), and they have erred. And some said that it is an accident (ʿaraḍ), and they have erred; for the accident does not subsist by itself, and is dependent upon another. And the spirit is the root (aṣl) of the son of Adam, and the mold (qālab) of the son of Adam is dependent upon it. So how could it be an accident?! And some said that it is a body (jism), and they have erred; for the body admits division. And the spirit — which we have called the heart, and which is the locus of knowledge of God, the Exalted — is neither a body nor an accident; rather, it is of the kind (jins) of the angels.

And knowledge of the spirit is very difficult; for no path to its knowledge has come in religion (dīn). And this is because religion has no need of knowing it; for religion is striving (mujāhadah), and knowledge is the sign of guidance (hidāyah) — as He, Glorified and Exalted, said: {وَالَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا فِينَا لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا} ("And those who strive in Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths"). And whoever does not strive with the full measure of striving, it is not permitted that he be spoken with concerning knowledge of the reality of the spirit. And the first foundation of striving is that you know the army of the heart; for if a man does not know the army, his striving (jihād) is not sound.
### | Chapter: Why Was the Heart Created?

Know that the self (nafs) is the mount of the heart, and the heart has armies — as He, Glorified and Exalted, said: {وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ} ("And none knows the hosts of your Lord but He").

And the heart was created for the work of the Hereafter, seeking its happiness. And its happiness is knowledge of its Lord, Mighty and Majestic. And knowledge of its Lord, the Exalted, is obtained for it through the craftsmanship (ṣunʿ) of God, and it is of the totality of His world. And knowledge of the wonders of the world is not obtained except through the path of the senses (ḥawāss). And the senses are from the heart, and the mold (qālab) is its mount. Then [it needs] knowledge of its prey (ṣayd), and knowledge of its net (shabakah). And the mold does not subsist except through food, drink, heat, and moisture. And it is weak, in danger of hunger and thirst inwardly, and in danger of water and fire outwardly. And it is faced with many enemies.
### | Chapter: Knowledge of the Armies of the Heart

You need to know the two armies. That is, the outer army is lust (shahwah) and anger (ghaḍab); and their stations are in the hands, the feet, the eyes, the ears, and all the limbs. And as for the inner army, its stations are in the brain: it is the power of imagination (khayāl), reflection (tafakkur), memory (ḥifẓ), recollection (tadhakkur), and estimation (wahm). And each of these powers has a specific function. And if one of them weakens, the state of the son of Adam weakens in both abodes (al-dārayn).

And the totality of these two armies is in the heart, and it is their commander (amīr). If it commands the tongue to remember, it remembers; if it commands the hand to strike, it strikes; if it commands the foot to walk, it walks. And likewise the five senses — so that it may preserve itself, in order to store provision (zād) for the abode of the Hereafter, and obtain the prey, and complete the trade (tijārah), and gather the seed of happiness. And these are obedient to the heart, just as the angels are obedient to the Lord, Glorified and Exalted — they do not disobey Him in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded.

paragraphs.text: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Praise be to God, Who has safeguarded us from error (ḍalāl) and made known to us the slipping-place of the feet of the ignorant. And blessings and peace be upon the one singled out, from the Possessor of Majesty, for acceptance and welcome — Muḥammad the Chosen, the best of His creation — and upon his Family, the best of families.

To proceed: You have sought a healing discourse concerning the disclosure of the incoherence of the philosophers (taḥāfut al-falāsifah), the contradiction of their opinions, and the hidden places of their obfuscation and seduction. Yet there is no hope of granting your request except after acquainting you with their doctrine (madhhab) and informing you of their creed (muʿtaqad). For to ascertain the corruption of doctrines before encompassing their premises is impossible — nay, it is itself a form of blindness and error. Thus I deemed it fitting to present, before the exposition of their incoherence, a concise discourse comprising a narration of their aims (maqāṣid) across their logical, natural, and divine sciences — without distinguishing between the true among them and the false. Indeed, I intend nothing save the conveyance of understanding (tafhīm) of the ultimate purport of their speech, without prolongation by mentioning what runs in the course of filler and superfluities that fall outside the aims. And I shall present it in the manner of narration and reportage (ḥikāyah), conjoined with what they themselves held to be their proofs. And the purpose of this book is narration.

The Aims of the Philosophers — and this is its name. And I shall inform you, first, that their sciences are four divisions: the mathematical (riyāḍiyyāt), the logical (manṭiqiyyāt), the natural (ṭabīʿiyyāt), and the divine (ilāhiyyāt).

As for the mathematical sciences: they are an inquiry into arithmetic and geometry. There is nothing in the entailments of geometry and arithmetic that contradicts the intellect, nor are they of the sort that can be confronted with denial and rejection. And since this is so, we have no aim (gharaḍ) in occupying ourselves with their exposition.
As for the divine sciences: most of their beliefs therein are contrary to the truth, and correctness within them is rare.

As for the logical sciences: most of them follow the path of correctness, and error within them is rare. The only way in which they oppose the people of truth therein is in terminologies (iṣṭilāḥāt) and modes of presentation, not in meanings and aims — for their purpose is the refinement of the methods of inference (istiḍlālāt), and that is something in which all speculative thinkers share.

As for the natural sciences: therein the truth is intermixed with falsehood, and correctness is confounded with error. Thus one cannot pass judgment upon them as predominantly one or the other. And in the Book of Incoherence (al-Tahāfut), the nullity of what ought to be believed null will become clear. But let us now understand what we present in the manner of narration, set down loosely and without restriction, with no investigation into the sound and the corrupt — until, when we have finished it, we shall resume for it fresh exertion and striving in a separate book which we shall name: The Incoherence of the Philosophers (Tahāfut al-Falāsifah), God willing.
And let the beginning be made with the conveyance of logic and its presentation.

paragraphs.text: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. And may God bless our master Muhammad, his family, and grant them abundant peace.
O God, show us truth as truth and grant us success in following it, and show us falsehood as falsehood and aid us in avoiding it. Amen.

Know and ascertain — O you whose striving and will are confined to the attainment of the sciences, whose aspiration is stretched toward the secrets of rational verities, whose effort and toil are turned away from the embellishments of this world and the attainment of its base pleasures, whose earnestness and exertion are devoted to the attainment of felicity through knowledge and worship — after praising God, whose praise precedes every matter of consequence, and blessing the Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, His messenger and servant:
Indeed, the motives for composing this book, entitled *The Standard Measure of Knowledge* (Miʿyār al-ʿIlm), are two important aims:

The first is to make understood the ways of thought and reflection, and to illuminate the paths of syllogisms and proofs. For since the theoretical sciences are not bestowed and granted by nature and instinct, they are necessarily acquired and sought after. But not every seeker excels at seeking, nor is every seeker guided to the path of the sought object; nor is every traveler guided to completion, nor safe from being deceived by stopping short of the summit of perfection; nor is everyone who thinks he has reached the likeness of correctness safe from being deluded by the mirage's false glitter.

Since, in the realm of intelligibles, the slippage of feet has multiplied, and the sources of error have proliferated, and the mirror of reason has never been free of what clouds it — namely, the confusions of fancies and the obscurations of imagination — we have arranged this book as a standard measure for reflection and consideration, a scale for investigation and meditation, a polisher for the mind, and a whetstone for the power of thought and reason. It stands in relation to the proofs of intellects as prosody stands in relation to poetry, and as grammar stands in relation to inflection.

For just as the defective meter of poetry is not known from its sound one except by the measure of prosody, and the correctness of inflection is not distinguished from its error except by the touchstone of grammar, so too the corrupt from the sound, and the valid from the invalid, among arguments is not distinguished except by this book. So every reflection that is not weighed by this scale, nor measured by this standard — know that it is of corrupt measure, not safe from perils and depths.

The second motive is to provide access to what we have deposited in the book *The Incoherence of the Philosophers* (Tahāfut al-Falāsifah). For we have debated them in their own language and addressed them according to the dictates of their technical conventions upon which they have agreed in logic. And in this book, the meanings of those conventions are disclosed. So this is the more specific of the two motives, while the first is the more general and the more important of them. As for its being more important, its aspect is not hidden from you. As for its being more general, it is so in that its benefit encompasses all theoretical sciences — both the rational and the jurisprudential. For we shall make known to you that reflection in jurisprudential matters does not differ from reflection in rational matters in its arrangement, conditions, and standard measure, but only in the sources of its premises.

And since the aspirations of our age have inclined from the sciences toward jurisprudence — nay, have become confined to it — this has driven us to compose, on the methods of disputation therein: first, *The Source of Disagreement* (Maʾkhadh al-Khilāf); second, *The Core of Reflection* (Lubāb al-Naẓar); third, *The Fortification of Premises* (Taḥṣīn al-Maʾākhidh); and fourth, *The Book of Principles and Ends* (al-Mabādiʾ wa-al-Ghāyāt), which is the ultimate goal in inquiry conducted according to the method of rational reflection in its arrangement and conditions, even if it differs from it in its premises. This also moved us to include, in the method of discourse in this book, jurisprudential examples, so that its benefit might be comprehensive and its utility encompass all classes of disciplines.

Perhaps the viewer with the squinting eye — the eye of criticism and disparagement — will deny our deviation from custom in teaching certain rational truths through probable jurisprudential examples. Let him desist from his excess in criticism and disparagement, and let him testify against himself of ignorance of the art of analogy and its benefit. For analogy was not established except to make understood a hidden matter through what is more familiar to the guided interlocutor, so that he may compare his unknown to what is known to him, and thus the unknown becomes settled in his mind.

For if the discourse is with a carpenter who excels only in carpentry and the use of its tools, it is incumbent upon his guide not to strike an example for him except from the craft of carpentry, so that it may be more readily grasped by his understanding and closer to the suitability of his mind. And just as it is not proper to guide a learner except in his own language, so too it is not proper to convey the intelligible to his understanding except through examples that are most firmly established in his knowledge. We have thus made known to you, in a summary fashion, the ultimate aim of this book and its purpose. Let us now add to this an explanation and clarification, given the intense need of the reflective thinkers for this book.

EPUB/chap_01.xhtml.title: The Criterion of Moral Action — Section 1: The Exposition that Languor in Seeking Happiness is Folly

paragraphs.text: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

The Shaykh, the Imām, the Illustrious, the Proof of Islam, the Ornament of the Religion, Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad al-Ghazālī al-Ṭūsī — may Allah Most High be pleased with him and grant him His satisfaction — said:

Since happiness (saʿādah), which is the quest of the first and the last, is attained only through knowledge and action; and since each of the two requires encompassing its true reality and its measure; and since it was incumbent to know knowledge and to distinguish it from what is other than it by a criterion — and we have completed that [in our work "The Criterion of Knowledge"] — so too it became incumbent to know the action that brings happiness, and to distinguish it from the action that brings misery. This likewise required a criterion. Therefore, I desired to plunge into this matter and to explain that languor in seeking happiness is folly; then to explain knowledge and the path of acquiring it; then to explain the action that brings happiness and its path. All of this in a manner that ascends beyond the limit of the path of blind imitation (taqlīd) to the limit of clarity — and were it to be exhaustively pursued in its true reality and the discourse lengthened therein, it would ascend to the limit of demonstration (burhān) upon the conditions which we have mentioned in "The Criterion of Knowledge." Although we shall not lengthen the discourse, we shall point to its principles and its canons.
The Exposition that Languor in Seeking Happiness is Folly

The otherworldly happiness (al-saʿādāt al-ākhirāwiyyah) which we mean is: abiding without perishing, pleasure without toil, joy without sorrow, wealth without poverty, perfection without deficiency, glory without abasement — and in sum, everything that can be conceived as sought by a seeker and desired by a desirer. And this is for all eternity (abad al-ābād), in a manner that the passing of ages and epochs does not diminish it. Nay, were we to suppose the world filled with pearls, and suppose a bird that snatches away, in every thousand years, a single grain from them, the pearls would be exhausted while nothing of all eternity would be diminished. This [happiness], then, needs no urging toward seeking it, nor any disparagement of languor therein, after the belief in its existence [is established] — for no rational person would hasten to something less than it, nor would he be turned away from it by the fact that the path to it is rugged, and that it necessitates abandoning the pleasures of this world and enduring various kinds of toil here. For the duration of enduring toil is finite, and what is lost therein is little, while worldly pleasures are cut off and passing away. And the rational person finds it easy to abandon a little in ready cash in pursuit of its multiples on credit. For this reason, you see all creatures in their trades and crafts — and even in seeking knowledge — enduring humiliation, loss, toil, and fatigue, the magnitude of whose endurance is great, out of hope for obtaining a pleasure in the future that exceeds what they miss in the present by a limited increase. How, then, would they not readily abandon the present for attaining advantages that are neither measured nor limited? And there has not been created in this world a rational person who is eager in seeking wealth, devoted to spending a dinar and waiting a month in order to receive, after the month has passed, the greatest elixir (al-iksīr al-aʿẓam) that turns copper into pure gold — except that his soul would readily spend it, even though that is a loss in the present. So much so that whoever would not endure the pain of hunger, for example, for such a duration, in order to attain thereby these immense blessings, would not be counted rational — and perhaps the existence of such a person among creatures is inconceivable — even though death lies in ambush behind man, and gold avails not in the Hereafter. And perhaps he dies within the month, or a day after the month, and so derives no benefit from the gold. Yet all of that does not weaken his resolve in spending, out of hope for this compensation. How, then, would the resolve of the rational person weaken in enduring the passions, during the days of his life — the utmost of which is a hundred years — when the compensation obtained thereby is a happiness that has no end? But the languor of creatures in traversing the path of happiness is due to the weakness of their faith in the Last Day. Otherwise, even the deficient intellect would judge it incumbent to gird oneself for traversing the path of happiness — let alone the perfect one.

paragraphs.text:
المقاصد الفلاسقة
فى المنطق والحكمة الالهية والحكمة الطبيعية
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
الحمد لله الذى عصمنا من الضلال، وعرفنا مزلة أقدام الجهال
والصلاة والسلام على المخصوص من ذى الجلال بالقبول والاقبال
محمد المصطفى خير خلقه وعلى آله خير آل.
(أما بعد): فانك التمست كلاما شافيا فى الكشف عن
تهافت الفلاسفة وتناقض آرائهم ومكامن تلبيسهم وإغوائهم، ولا
مطمع فى إسعافك إلا بعد تعريفك مذهبهم، وإعلامك معتقدهم؛
فان الوقوف على فساد المذاهب قبل الاحاطة بمداركها محال بل هو
وهى فى العماية والضلال، فرأيت أن أقدم على بيان تهافتهم كلاما
وجيزا مشتملا على حكاية مقاصدهم من علومهم المنطقية والطبيعية
والالهية من غير تمييز بين الحق منها والباطل بل لا أقصد إلا تفهيم
غاية كلامهم من غير تطويل بذكر ما يجرى مجرى الحشو والزوائد
الخارجة عن المقاصد وأورده على سبيل الاقتصاص والحكاية مقرونا
بما اعتقدوه أدلة لهم ومقصود الكتاب حكاية:
(مقاصد الفلاسفة): وهو اسمه وأعرفك أولا أن علومهم
أربعة أقسام؛ الرياضيات، والمنطقيات، والطبيعيات، والالهيات
(أما الرياضيات): فهى نظر فى الحساب والهندسة، وليس فى
مقتضيات الهندسة والحساب ما يخالف العقل، ولا هى مما يمكن
أن يقابل بانكار وجحد، وإذا كان كذلك فلا غرض لنا فى
الاشتغال بايراده*
(وأما الالهيات): فأكثر عقائدهم فيها على خلاف الحق
والصواب نادر فيها.
(وأما المنطقيات): فأكثرها على منهج الصواب والخطأ نادر
فيها وإنما يخالفون أهل الحق فيها بالاصطلاحات والايرادات دون
المعانى والمقاصد إذ غرضها تهذيب طرق الاستدلالات وذلك مما
يشترك فيه النظار.
(وأما الطبيعيات): فالحق فيها مشوب بالباطل. والصواب
فيها مشتبه بالخطأ فلا يمكن الحكم عليها بغالب ومغلوب، وسيتضح
فى كتاب التهافت بطلان ما ينبغى أن يعتقد بطلانه ولنفهم الآن
ما نحن نورده على سبيل الحكاية مهملا مرسلا من غير بحث عن
الصحيح والفاسد حتى إذا فرغنا منه استأنفنا له جدا وتشميرا فى

كتاب مفرد نسميه: (تهافت الفلاسفة) إن شاء الله.
ولتقع البداية بتفهيم المنطق وإيراده.

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: حمد (Ḥ-M-D)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To praise, laud, or eulogize; the act of attributing commendation for a voluntary excellence or beneficence.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Praise (ḥamd) is the acknowledgment of beneficence (niʿmah) with reverence; it is the counterpart of shukr (gratitude), which is the acknowledgment of beneficence with the tongue, heart, and limbs.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): "Aḥmadtu Allāha bi-jamīʿi maḥāmīdih" (I praised God with all His praiseworthy attributes). Metaphorical (majāz): "Aḥmadtu al-arḍa" (I found the land praiseworthy to dwell in).
- Root: عصب (ʿ-Ṣ-B)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To protect, guard, or preserve from harm; to render immune.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): ʿIṣmah (impeccability/protection) is God's safeguarding of His servant from that which would cause ruin, whether in belief or action.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "Aʿṣamahu" (he protected him). Metaphorical: "Iʿtaṣama billāh" (he clung to God for refuge), denoting seeking inviolable protection.
- Root: زلل (Z-L-L)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To slip or slide; a lapse or misstep, whether physical (on a path) or moral (in judgment).
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Zallah (a slip) is an inadvertent fall into error, less grave than a deliberate sin (khaṭīʾah); it is the misstep of the foot from the sound path.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "Zalla ʿan al-ṭarīq" (he slipped from the road). Metaphorical: "Zallat qadamuh" (his foot slipped) — used proverbially for committing an error in speech or action.
- Root: غرض (Gh-R-Ḍ)
 * Lisan / Ayn: An aim, goal, or target; that at which one shoots, then extended to any sought objective.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Gharaḍ is the target aimed at, then made a name for every end one strives to attain. It is of two kinds: deficient (nāqiṣ) — that after which another thing is desired (like wealth or status) — and complete (tāmm) — that after which nothing else is desired (like Paradise).
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: The target of archery. Metaphorical: "Ightaraḍa fulān" (so-and-so died young), as if cut off before reaching his aim.
- Root: خطا (Kha-Ṭ-A)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To err, deviate, or miss the mark; to commit a fault.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Khaṭaʾ is deviation from the correct course. It is of types: (1) intending what one ought not to intend and doing it — this is complete error (khaṭaʾ tāmm) for which one is accountable; (2) intending what is good but the act falls short of the intention — this is akhṭāʾa (to miss), where one was right in intention but wrong in execution.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "Akhṭaʾa fī al-masʾalah" (he erred in the question). Metaphorical: "Lan yukhṭiʾaka mā kutiba lak" (what is written for you will not miss you) — i.e., destiny's decree never fails to arrive.
- Sibawayh Rule: Rule of Restriction and Focused Predication (al-ḥaṣr wa al-taqyīd bi-innamā) — The particle innamā restricts the predicate to the subject alone, negating it for all else. This governs the author's statement: "لا أقصد إلا تفهيم" (I intend nothing save the conveyance of understanding), where illā effects exclusive restriction.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Praise be to God, Who has safeguarded us from error (ḍalāl) and made known to us the slipping-place of the feet of the ignorant. And blessings and peace be upon the one singled out, from the Possessor of Majesty, for acceptance and welcome — Muḥammad the Chosen, the best of His creation — and upon his Family, the best of families.

To proceed: You have sought a healing discourse concerning the disclosure of the incoherence of the philosophers (taḥāfut al-falāsifah), the contradiction of their opinions, and the hidden places of their obfuscation and seduction. Yet there is no hope of granting your request except after acquainting you with their doctrine (madhhab) and informing you of their creed (muʿtaqad). For to ascertain the corruption of doctrines before encompassing their premises is impossible — nay, it is itself a form of blindness and error. Thus I deemed it fitting to present, before the exposition of their incoherence, a concise discourse comprising a narration of their aims (maqāṣid) across their logical, natural, and divine sciences — without distinguishing between the true among them and the false. Indeed, I intend nothing save the conveyance of understanding (tafhīm) of the ultimate purport of their speech, without prolongation by mentioning what runs in the course of filler and superfluities that fall outside the aims. And I shall present it in the manner of narration and reportage (ḥikāyah), conjoined with what they themselves held to be their proofs. And the purpose of this book is narration.

The Aims of the Philosophers — and this is its name. And I shall inform you, first, that their sciences are four divisions: the mathematical (riyāḍiyyāt), the logical (manṭiqiyyāt), the natural (ṭabīʿiyyāt), and the divine (ilāhiyyāt).

As for the mathematical sciences: they are an inquiry into arithmetic and geometry. There is nothing in the entailments of geometry and arithmetic that contradicts the intellect, nor are they of the sort that can be confronted with denial and rejection. And since this is so, we have no aim (gharaḍ) in occupying ourselves with their exposition.
As for the divine sciences: most of their beliefs therein are contrary to the truth, and correctness within them is rare.

As for the logical sciences: most of them follow the path of correctness, and error within them is rare. The only way in which they oppose the people of truth therein is in terminologies (iṣṭilāḥāt) and modes of presentation, not in meanings and aims — for their purpose is the refinement of the methods of inference (istiḍlālāt), and that is something in which all speculative thinkers share.

As for the natural sciences: therein the truth is intermixed with falsehood, and correctness is confounded with error. Thus one cannot pass judgment upon them as predominantly one or the other. And in the Book of Incoherence (al-Tahāfut), the nullity of what ought to be believed null will become clear. But let us now understand what we present in the manner of narration, set down loosely and without restriction, with no investigation into the sound and the corrupt — until, when we have finished it, we shall resume for it fresh exertion and striving in a separate book which we shall name: The Incoherence of the Philosophers (Tahāfut al-Falāsifah), God willing.
And let the beginning be made with the conveyance of logic and its presentation.

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
وصلى الله على سيدنا محمد وآله وسلم تسليما. اللهم أرنا الحق حقا ووفقنا إلى اتباعه، وأرنا الباطل باطلا وأعنا على
اجتنابه. آمين. اعلم وتحقق أيها المقصور على درك العلوم حرصه وإرادته الممدود نحو أسرار
الحقائق العقلية همته، المصروف، عن زخارف الدنيا ونيل لذاتها الحقيرة سعيه
وكده، الموقوف على درك السعادة بالعلم والعبادة جده وجهده، بعد حمد الله
الذي يقدم على كل أمر ذي بال حمده، والصلاة على النبي محمد صلى الله عليه
وسلم رسوله وعبده. إن الباعث على تحرير هذا الكتاب الملقب بمعيار العلم غرضان مهمان: أحدهما
تفهيم طرق الفكر والنظر، وتنوير مسالك الأقيسة والعبر؛ فإن العلوم النظرية
لما لم تكن بالفطرة والغريزة مبذولة وموهوبة كانت لا محالة مستحصلة مطلوبة،
وليس كل طالب يحسن الطلب، ويهتدي إلى طريق المطلب، ولا كل سالك يهتدي إلى
الإستكمال، ويأمن الإغترار بالوقوف دون ذروة الكمال ولا كل ظان الوصول إلى
شاكلة الصواب آمن من الإنخداع بلا مع السراب. فلما كثر في المعقولات مزلة الأقدام، ومثارات الضلال، ولم تنفك مرآة
العقل عما يكدرها من تخليطات الأوهام وتلبيسات الخيال، رتبنا هذا الكتاب
معيارا للنظر والإعتبار، وميزانا للبحث والإفتكار، وصيقلا للذهن، ومشحذا
لقوة الفكر والعقل، فيكون بالنسبة إلى أدلة العقول كالعروض بالنسبة إلى
الشعر،
والنحو بالإضافة إلى الإعراب. إذ كما لا يعرف منزحف الشعر عن موزونه إلا بميزان العروض ولا يميز صواب
الإعراب عن خطئه إلا بمحك النحو، كذلك لا يفرق بين فاسد الدليل وقويمه
وصحيحه وسقيمه إلا بهذا الكتاب. فكل نظر لا يتزن بهذا الميزان ولا يعيار
بهذا المعيار فاعلم أنه فاسد العيار غير مأمون الغوائل والأغوار. والباعث الثاني الإطلاع على ما أودعناه كتاب تهافت الفلاسفة، فإنا
ناظرناهم بلغتهم وخاطبناهم على حكم اصطلاحاتهم التي تواطأوا عليها في
المنطق وفي هذا الكتاب تنكشف معاني تلك الإصطلاحات؛ فهذا اخص الباعثين
والأول أعمهما وأهمهما. أما كونه أهم فلا يخفى عليك وجهه، وأما كونه أعم
فمن حيث يشمل جدواه جميع العلوم النظرية: العقلية منها والفقهية، فإنا
سنعرفك أن النظر في الفقهيات لا يباين النظر في العقليات، في ترتيبه وشروطه
وعياره، بل في مآخذ المقدمات فقط. ولما كانت الهمم في عصرنا مائلة من
العلوم إلى الفقه بل مقصورة عليه حتى حدانا ذلك إلى أن صنفنا في طرق
المناظرة فيها مأخذ الخلاف أولا، ولباب النظر ثانيا، وتحصين المآخذ ثالثا،
وكتاب المبادي والغايات رابعا، وهو الغاية القصوى في البحث الجاري على
منهاج النظر العقلي في ترتيبه وشروطه، وأن فارقه في مقدماته
رغبنا ذلك أيضا في أن نورد في منهاج الكلام في هذا الكتاب أمثلة فقهية
فتشمل فائدته وتعم سائر الأصناف جدواء وعائدته. ولعل الناظر بالعين العوراء نظر الطعن والإزراء، ينكر انحرافنا عن
العادات في تفهيم العقليات القطعية، بالأمثلة الفقهية الظنية فليكف عن
غلوائه في طعنه وإزرائه، وليشهد على نفسه بالجهل بصناعة التمثيل وفائدتها،
فإنها لم توضع إلا لتفهيم الأمر الخفي بما هو الأعرف عند المخاطب المسترشد،
ليقيس مجهوله إلى ما هو معلوم عنده فيستقر المجهول في نفسه. فإن كان الخطاب مع نجار لا يحسن إلا النجر وكيفية استعمال آلاته، وجب على
مرشده ألا يضرب له المثل إلا من صناعة النجارة، ليكون ذلك أسبق إلى فهمه
وأقرب إلى مناسبة عقله وكما لا يحسن إرشاد المتعلم إلا بلغته لا يحسن إيصال
المعقول إلى فهمه إلا بأمثلة هي أثبت في معرفته؛ فقد عرفناك غاية هذا
الكتاب وغرضه تعريفا مجملا فلنزد له شرحا وإيضاحا لشدة حاجة النظار إلى هذا
الكتاب.

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: ع-ق-ل (ʿaql)
 * Lisan / Ayn: The core root denotes binding, restraining, and holding fast — from the tying of a camel's leg to the intellect's power of restraint and comprehension.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "العقل يقال للقوة المتهيئة لقبول العلم، ويقال للعلم الذي يستفيده الإنسان بتلك القوة عقل" — ʿaql is said of the faculty prepared to receive knowledge, and of the knowledge one acquires by that faculty.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (Haqiqah): the binding/restraining faculty. Metaphorical (Majaz): "نخلة لا تعقل الإبار إذا لم تقبله" — a palm that does not accept pollination is said not to "comprehend" it, extending the root to acceptance and receptivity.
- Root: ح-س-ن (ḥusn)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Beauty, goodness, and excellence in form and character.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الحسن: عبارة عن كل مبهج مرغوب فيه" — the good is everything delightful and desirable, divided into what is good to the intellect, to desire, and to sense.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: visible beauty and excellence. Metaphorical: "فلان لا يحسن شيئا" — one who does not do anything well, extending to competence and skill.
- Root: ح-م-د (ḥamd)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Praise arising from appreciation of virtue or beneficence.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Praise (ḥamd) is the acknowledgment of beneficence with veneration; the root also yields "ḥamīm" (hot water) — a separate derivation.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "أحمد الله تعالى بجميع محامده" — to praise God with all His praises. Metaphorical: "أحمدت الأرض: رضيت سكناها" — to find a land praiseworthy as a dwelling, extending to approval and satisfaction.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — The permissibility of interposing elements between a preposition and its object when the intervening material is syntactically sound, governing the periodic sentence structure of the opening address.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. And may God bless our master Muhammad, his family, and grant them abundant peace.
O God, show us truth as truth and grant us success in following it, and show us falsehood as falsehood and aid us in avoiding it. Amen.

Know and ascertain — O you whose striving and will are confined to the attainment of the sciences, whose aspiration is stretched toward the secrets of rational verities, whose effort and toil are turned away from the embellishments of this world and the attainment of its base pleasures, whose earnestness and exertion are devoted to the attainment of felicity through knowledge and worship — after praising God, whose praise precedes every matter of consequence, and blessing the Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, His messenger and servant:
Indeed, the motives for composing this book, entitled *The Standard Measure of Knowledge* (Miʿyār al-ʿIlm), are two important aims:

The first is to make understood the ways of thought and reflection, and to illuminate the paths of syllogisms and proofs. For since the theoretical sciences are not bestowed and granted by nature and instinct, they are necessarily acquired and sought after. But not every seeker excels at seeking, nor is every seeker guided to the path of the sought object; nor is every traveler guided to completion, nor safe from being deceived by stopping short of the summit of perfection; nor is everyone who thinks he has reached the likeness of correctness safe from being deluded by the mirage's false glitter.

Since, in the realm of intelligibles, the slippage of feet has multiplied, and the sources of error have proliferated, and the mirror of reason has never been free of what clouds it — namely, the confusions of fancies and the obscurations of imagination — we have arranged this book as a standard measure for reflection and consideration, a scale for investigation and meditation, a polisher for the mind, and a whetstone for the power of thought and reason. It stands in relation to the proofs of intellects as prosody stands in relation to poetry, and as grammar stands in relation to inflection.

For just as the defective meter of poetry is not known from its sound one except by the measure of prosody, and the correctness of inflection is not distinguished from its error except by the touchstone of grammar, so too the corrupt from the sound, and the valid from the invalid, among arguments is not distinguished except by this book. So every reflection that is not weighed by this scale, nor measured by this standard — know that it is of corrupt measure, not safe from perils and depths.

The second motive is to provide access to what we have deposited in the book *The Incoherence of the Philosophers* (Tahāfut al-Falāsifah). For we have debated them in their own language and addressed them according to the dictates of their technical conventions upon which they have agreed in logic. And in this book, the meanings of those conventions are disclosed. So this is the more specific of the two motives, while the first is the more general and the more important of them. As for its being more important, its aspect is not hidden from you. As for its being more general, it is so in that its benefit encompasses all theoretical sciences — both the rational and the jurisprudential. For we shall make known to you that reflection in jurisprudential matters does not differ from reflection in rational matters in its arrangement, conditions, and standard measure, but only in the sources of its premises.

And since the aspirations of our age have inclined from the sciences toward jurisprudence — nay, have become confined to it — this has driven us to compose, on the methods of disputation therein: first, *The Source of Disagreement* (Maʾkhadh al-Khilāf); second, *The Core of Reflection* (Lubāb al-Naẓar); third, *The Fortification of Premises* (Taḥṣīn al-Maʾākhidh); and fourth, *The Book of Principles and Ends* (al-Mabādiʾ wa-al-Ghāyāt), which is the ultimate goal in inquiry conducted according to the method of rational reflection in its arrangement and conditions, even if it differs from it in its premises. This also moved us to include, in the method of discourse in this book, jurisprudential examples, so that its benefit might be comprehensive and its utility encompass all classes of disciplines.

Perhaps the viewer with the squinting eye — the eye of criticism and disparagement — will deny our deviation from custom in teaching certain rational truths through probable jurisprudential examples. Let him desist from his excess in criticism and disparagement, and let him testify against himself of ignorance of the art of analogy and its benefit. For analogy was not established except to make understood a hidden matter through what is more familiar to the guided interlocutor, so that he may compare his unknown to what is known to him, and thus the unknown becomes settled in his mind.

For if the discourse is with a carpenter who excels only in carpentry and the use of its tools, it is incumbent upon his guide not to strike an example for him except from the craft of carpentry, so that it may be more readily grasped by his understanding and closer to the suitability of his mind. And just as it is not proper to guide a learner except in his own language, so too it is not proper to convey the intelligible to his understanding except through examples that are most firmly established in his knowledge. We have thus made known to you, in a summary fashion, the ultimate aim of this book and its purpose. Let us now add to this an explanation and clarification, given the intense need of the reflective thinkers for this book.
