- Root: وجب (wajaba)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To be necessary, incumbent, obligatory; that whose non-existence cannot be conceived.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Al-Wājib al-Wujūd (the Necessary Existent) is that which has no cause for its existence but is rather the cause of every existent — a foundational metaphysical designation.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (Haqiqah) usage denotes necessary being; metaphorical (Majaz) extends to what is firmly established and unavoidable.
- Root: بدع (bada'a)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To originate, create something anew without prior model or matter.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Al-Ibdāʿ is bringing something into existence not from a pre-existing thing — distinct from khalq (creation from something), which entails composition.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: absolute origination ex nihilo; metaphorical: any novel act attributed to a doer.
- Root: خلق (khalaqa)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To measure, fashion, create; to bring forth from something prior.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Khalq in most contexts is the bringing forth of a thing from a thing preceding it (e.g., man from dust), necessitating composition (tarkīb).
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: shaping and proportioning; metaphorical: divine decree and estimation.
- Root: خلق (khalq) — second occurrence (human form)
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The human image (al-ṣūrah al-insāniyyah) is the final created thing, sealing the order of existence.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: physical formation; metaphorical: moral and spiritual constitution.
- Sibawayh Rule: Rule of Qualification (al-Naʿt) and Apposition (al-Badal) — In "الروحانيات الذين لا يستكبرون" the relative clause functions as a qualifier specifying the nature of the spiritual beings; in "الإنسان إنسانان" the predicate is a sentence-like apposition requiring careful parsing of the dual as a distributive division.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
### | Section 2
On the Classes of Existing Things and the Position of Man Among Them

Know that God Most High is the Necessary Existent (al-wājib al-wujūd), who has no cause for His existence; rather, He is the cause of every existent. And every existent — its existence is from Him and through Him Most High. The existents are of two kinds: the higher intelligibles (al-maʿqūlāt al-ʿulwiyyah) and the lower sensibles (al-maḥsūsāt al-sufliyyah). And His bringing forth of the higher intelligibles precedes His bringing forth of the lower sensibles, as has been related that the first thing God Most High created was the Pen, then the Tablet, and He said: "Write down what shall be until the Day of Resurrection." And it has been related that the first thing God created was the Intellect ('aql); He said to it: "Come forward," so it came forward. Then He said to it: "Turn back," so it turned back. Then He said: "By My Might and My Majesty, I have created no creature more honorable to Me than you; through you I take, and through you I give; to you is the reward, and upon you is the punishment." The Intellect here does not mean human intellects; rather, the reference is to a noble substance from which human intellects emanate. And some have said: "The Intellect here is an expression for the Pen mentioned in the other report." And God knows best.

Then God Most High brought into existence the spiritual beings (al-rūḥāniyyāt) who are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they grow weary. And the bringing into existence of these things is by way of ibdāʿ (origination ex nihilo). And ibdāʿ is the bringing forth of a thing not from any previously existing thing. Then He created the four elements (al-arkān al-arbaʿah), the inanimate objects (al-jamādāt), the growing things (al-nāmiyāt), and the animals; and He sealed [all that] with the human form (al-ṣūrah al-insāniyyah), as the Prophet indicated by his saying: "God Most High created on Sunday such-and-such, and on Monday such-and-such," until he said: "He created man on Friday at the end of the day." And khalq (creation) in most contexts is said of bringing a thing forth from a thing preceding it — like the creation of man from dust — and it entails composition (tarkīb). For this reason God Most High said: {«And of everything We have created pairs, that perhaps you may remember»} (Q. 51:49). And to composite things He pointed by His saying: {«Have they not seen the earth — how much We have caused to grow therein of every noble kind?»} (Q. 26:7).

Know that every thing that is an ibdāʿ-originated thing is complete, having no deficiency in it; and were there deficiency in it, that would indicate deficiency in its Originator and Maker. As for the created thing (al-makhlūq) that is composed of something, it is possible that deficiency be in it, and its deficiency would be an accident arising from that from which it is composed — not from its Composer and Agent. For this reason, the ibdāʿ-originated things among the higher things are stripped of the intrusion of corruption upon them from state to state; rather, they remain in their state until God Most High wills to raise the world.

And man is two men: one of them is Adam, who is the father of humankind, and he stands in relation to the rest of people as the seed from which others are grown. And the Creator Most High undertook by Himself his origination, his nurturing, and his teaching — as He alerted to this by His saying: {«What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?»} (Q. 38:75), and His saying: {«And He taught Adam the names, all of them»} (Q. 2:31). The second is his progeny — their originator is also the Creator Most High, but He made their origination, nurturing, and teaching to be through corporeal and spiritual intermediaries. The corporeal is like the two parents, and the spiritual is like the angels — the directors and the distributors (al-mudabbirāt wa al-muqassimāt) — who undertake his origination and nurturing, as has been related in the report: "The child remains forty days as a drop of sperm, then becomes a clot, then becomes a lump of flesh; then God sends an angel who breathes into it the spirit" — and other such reports. And because the two parents are a cause in the existence of the child, God Most High magnified their right and made incumbent, after gratitude to Him, gratitude to them, saying: {«Give thanks to Me and to your parents»} (Q. 31:14). And the child is called ibn (son), derived from banaytu al-biniyah (I built the structure), as an alert that he stands in relation to the father as a building stands in relation to its builder.

paragraphs.text:
"The Fourth Station (Al-Maqam Ar-Rabi'): Averting the lesser with the least worthy
It is that singing should only occur in weddings for women specifically with drums and in moderation, or in the remembrance of Allah (dhikr Allah), or in praise (tasbih), or in gratitude (tahmid) for what He has guided, or in light-hearted poetry, not in anything shameful or excessively long.

Ibn Rushd stated that there is no difference in this between men and women, while Ibn al-Arabi said: 'Asbagh’s statement applies only to women, and it is disliked for men of corrupt demeanor to attend, for the Prophet () attended the playing of the duff (drum), and it’s not appropriate that a man of stature be more restrictive than what was permissible by the Prophet (ya Allah).

Iyad said: 'Like weddings, the Muslim festivals and joys are [occasions for music].' Others said: 'And so for the return of someone absent, or for a birth, or for circumcision, or for memorizing the Quran by a child, or for a noble invitation.' Then, if the listener hears tunes that mention reproach or connection, or separation, or closeness, or distance, or yearning for what is lost, or longing for what is awaited, or desire, or despair, or loneliness, or finding solace, or fulfilling a promise, or breaking a promise, or fear of separation, or joy of union, or anything else that the term sama' (listening) encompasses, it must align with some aspect of the listener’s condition, making it akin to casting lots that ignite the heart’s match, thus providing ample scope to align words with his states. If the dominant longing in the listener is prohibited, this listening incites him towards the unlawful; if the dominant longing is permissible, the listening stirs the effects of yearning, fear of separation, and hope of reunion. Thus, listening to this is permissible if it reminds the listener of his conditions with his Lord, achieving two things: pleasure for himself and connection with the attributes of his Lord. However, in this state, there is a deficiency due to the self-indulgence involved. They said in this regard: 'Knowing what one seeks makes the expenditure seem trivial.'

This makes it clear that listening to music (sama') has never been a goal in itself, neither for the Sufis nor for the jurists. Is it a means? Many scholars deny it as a means to the Sufis’ seriousness, while many learned in the laws of Allah (ahkam Allah) take up the responsibility that it is a means.

Al-Qushayri said in his 'Epistle': 'Indeed, Abu Ali al-Rudhbari was the most knowledgeable of people about the path (tariqa) from among the companions of...'
(1) Abu Ali al-Rudhbari, a notable Sufi sheikh, is said to be named Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn Mansur, or Hasan ibn Harun. Residing in Egypt, he was a companion of Junaid, Abu al-Husayn al-Nuri, Abu Hamza al-Baghdadi, and Ibn al-Jalla. He narrated from Mas'ud al-Ramli and others, stating: 'My teacher in Fiqh is Ibn Siraj, in Adab (literature) is Tha’lab, and in Hadith is Ibrahim al-Harbi.'

paragraphs.text: ### | The Foundations of Faith
### | The Beginning of the Creedal Principle Which Is the Root of Faith

Know, O King, that you are a created being (makhliūq) and that you have a Creator, and He is the Creator of the world and of everything within the world. He has no partner; He is One (fard), with no likeness to Him. He was in pre-eternity (azal) and His existence has no cessation; He will be with eternity (abad) and His permanence has no annihilation. His existence is in pre-eternity and eternity, and non-existence has no path to Him. He is existent by His own essence (mawjūd bi-dhātihi), and every single one is in need of Him, while He has no need of anyone. His existence is through Himself, and the existence of everything is through Him.
### | The Second Principle: On Transcending the Creator, Exalted Is His Remembrance

Know that the Originator (al-Bāriʾ), exalted is His remembrance, has no form (ṣūrah) and no likeness. He does not descend, nor does He indwell any mold or receptacle. Exalted is He above quality (kayf) and quantity (kam), above "why" (limādhā) and "how much" (kam). He resembles nothing, and nothing resembles Him. Whatever occurs to the mind, imagination, and thought — of imagining, likening, or qualifying — He is transcendent above all of that, because those are attributes of created beings, and He is their Creator, so He is not described by them. He, exalted is His majesty, is not in a place nor upon a place, for place cannot encompass Him. Everything in the world is beneath His Throne (ʿarsh), and His Throne is beneath His power and subjugation. He was before the Throne, and He was then free of place. The Throne does not carry Him; rather, the Throne and its bearers are carried by His gentleness and power. His "establishing Himself upon the Throne" (istiwāʾ) is as He said, in the manner He said, and with the meaning He intended — an establishing (istiwāʾ) transcendent above settling, touching, resting, indwelling, and moving. He, glorified be He, is above the Throne and above everything, to the depths of the earth (tharā). Yet with all that, He is near to every existent, and He is nearer to the distant and the near than the jugular vein (ḥabl al-warīd). He is over all things Omnipotent and Witness. He does what He wills. He never ceases to possess the attributes of beauty (jamāl) and the qualities of majesty (jalāl), transcendent above passing away and moving, free from any increase of perfection. He is transcendent above any need for place, before the creation of the Throne and after the creation of the Throne. He is described with the very attribute He had in pre-eternity, and there is no path for change or alteration to reach His attributes. He, glorified be He, is sanctified above the attributes of created beings and transcendent above them. In this world He is known, and in the Hereafter He will be seen — just as we know Him in this world — without likeness and without similitude, because that vision does not resemble the vision of this world. {«لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ»} — "There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing" (Q. 42:11).
### | The Third Principle: On Divine Power (qudrah)

He, exalted be He, is Omnipotent over all things, and His dominion is at the utmost perfection. There is no path for incapacity or deficiency to reach Him. Rather, what He wills — and what He wills — He does. The seven heavens and the seven earths, the Footstool (kursī), and the Throne (ʿarsh) are all within the grasp of His power, under His domination, subjugation, and will. He is the Owner, and there is no owner except His ownership. Exalted is He above what the wrongdoers say, with a great exaltation.
### | The Fourth Principle: On Divine Knowledge (ʿilm)

He, exalted be He, is Knowing of everything knowable, and His knowledge encompasses all things. There is nothing from the heights above to the depths below (tharā) except that His knowledge has encompassed it, because all things appeared through His knowledge, He created them by His will, and they came into being by His power. He, exalted be He, knows the count of the sands of the deserts, the drops of the rains, the leaves of the trees, the hidden subtleties of thoughts, and whatever the winds and the air have carried — all is manifest in His knowledge, like the number of the stars of heaven. Everything in the world is by His will and volition. There is nothing — little or much, small or great, good or evil, benefit or harm, increase or decrease, rest or fatigue, health or sickness — except by His decree and governance, His will and determination. If all of mankind, jinn, angels, and devils were to gather to move a single atom in the world, or to still it, or to decrease it, or to increase it, without His will, His power, and His strength, they would be incapable of that and would not be able to do it. What God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. His will is not repelled. Whatever was, and is, or is coming to be, it is by His governance, His command, and His subjugation.
### | The Fifth and Sixth Principles: On His Being Hearing and Seeing

And just as He is Knowing of all knowable things, so He is Hearing of everything audible, and Seeing of everything visible. With a single hearing and a single sight, He sees the crawling of the ant in the darkest night, and the sound of the worm beneath the layers of the earth is not hidden from His hearing. His hearing is not by an ear, and His sight is not by an eye. And just as His knowledge does not arise from reflection, so His act is without instrument or tool. He says to a thing "Be!" and it comes to be (yakūn).

paragraphs.text: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful.
The Opening of the Book.

Praise be to God, the Opener (al-Fattāḥ), the Bountiful Giver (al-Mannān), Possessor of abundance, grace, and beneficence — He who bestowed upon us the blessing of faith, and favored our religion above all other religions, and through His Beloved, His Intimate Friend, His Servant, and His Messenger Muḥammad — may God bless him and grant him peace — obliterated the worship of idols, and singled him out with the miracle and with the Sunnahs that continue unbroken across the succession of ages. May God bless him, and all the other Prophets, and the families of all, as long as the two contrasting things differ, and as long as His judgments and remembrance are repeated, and the two new things (night and day) follow one another in succession.

"To proceed": Verily, the science of ḥadīth is among the most virtuous acts of drawing near to the Lord of the Worlds. And how could it not be so, for it is the elucidation of the path of the best of creation and the most noble of the first and the last? And this book — I have abridged it from the book "al-Irshād," which I in turn abridged from "ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth" of the Shaykh, the Imām, the ḥāfiẓ, the precise and verifying scholar Abū ʿAmr ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, known as Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ — may God be pleased with him. I strive in it to achieve extreme concision, God Almighty willing, without any deficiency in the intended purpose, and I am eager to clarify the expression. Upon God the Generous is my reliance, and to Him is the delegation of affairs and the seeking of support.
The Divisions of Ḥadīth.
The ḥadīth is: sound (ṣaḥīḥ) — and fair (ḥasan) — and weak (ḍaʿīf).

paragraphs.text: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate — and in Him is my trust.

To proceed: After the praise of God, and prayer upon Muhammad, the best of His creation, and upon his family — I have observed that the inquiries of the Christians concerning their doctrines are weak in foundation, feeble in force, and rugged in path. The contemplative mind that inclines toward them is driven to the utmost astonishment, and one does not attain from their complexity even the slightest of one's need. They rely in these matters upon nothing but pure taqlīd (blind acceptance), clinging with their molar teeth to the outward expressions (ẓawāhir) that the earlier ones uttered, while the later ones — due to their deficiency — did not rise to clarifying what is problematic therein. They suppose that this is the sacred law (sharʿ) that Jesus, peace be upon him, legislated for them, excusing their belief by what has come down of texts that they deem to be compelling against unbelief, not susceptible to interpretation (taʾwīl), and that diverting them from their outward senses is difficult.
In this matter, they are two sects:

- A sect — and they are the majority — who have not practiced any of the sciences by which the inquirer comes to know the impossibility of the impossible, so as to judge with certainty the impossibility of its existence; nor the necessitation of the Necessary, so as to negate the non-occurrence of what must be; nor the possibility of the possible, so that no impossibility is entailed by either side of its existence or non-existence. Rather, images have been imprinted in their minds since their youth, and obtuseness has persisted with them until this became a fixed disposition (malaka) in them. This sect — curing them of their malady is difficult.

- And a sect who possess the least degree of rationality, having touched upon a small measure of the sciences. You find them recoiling from this belief, not permitting their thoughts to approach it. They rely at times upon the taqlīd of the philosopher in the question of union (ittiḥād), due to their veneration of what it leads to in demolishing the foundations whose establishment the clear dictates of the intellects (ṣarāʾiḥ al-ʿuqūl) have mutually supported. They flee from this dilemma to pure taqlīd, believing that the philosopher has attempted the hidden sciences and rendered them clear and demonstrated. They suppose that one whose state is such is worthy of reliance upon his statements and of being followed in beliefs! Therefore, they extricate themselves from the question of union (ittiḥād) by referring it to the question of the soul's attachment (taʿalluq) to the body.

Were these wretched ones to consult their intellects and abandon caprice and partisanship, they would know that they have deviated from the highway of correctness and missed the path of truth, for several reasons:

One of them: If they make this a matter of qiyās (analogical reasoning), they err — because qiyās is: "the referring of a branch (farʿ) to a root (aṣl) by a uniting cause (ʿilla) that is the basis of the judgment (manāṭ al-ḥukm)."

And what cause has this speaker comprehended that would necessitate the reality of the attachment (taʿalluq) that the philosopher affirms, and then, after that, he extends it to the Essence of the Creator (dhāt al-Bārī) so that the qiyās might be valid for him?

And if they make it a matter of comparison and analogy (tashbīh wa-tamthīl), they also err — because the thing compared to (al-mushabbah bihī) must be known and conceived, so that knowledge of it necessitates knowledge of the similarity. And the one among them who holds this doctrine — were he to exert his utmost effort to produce the slightest doubt that would acquaint him with the reality of the soul and the reality of the attachment that the philosopher affirms — he would confess his incapacity to grasp that. So how can qiyās be valid for him when the realities are unknown to him?!

Moreover, such a qiyās is not permitted even to the practitioner of furūʿ (branches of jurisprudence) himself in its use; rather, it is among the abandoned analogies (al-aqyisa al-mahjūra), called qiyās al-taʿqīd (the analogy of complication) — namely, that one attempts to establish a hidden judgment, then establishes it by what is even more hidden than it, or by what requires, in its establishment, the exertion of thought and its extraction through obscure proofs — like the soul that the philosopher affirms, whose existence is not imagined except through complications and obscurity in its derivation. And if this is abandoned in the branches (furūʿ) built upon the slightest conjecture, how can one rely upon it in the principles (uṣūl) pertaining to the Essence of the Necessary Existent (wājib al-wujūd)?! And how can that claim be completed, when the basis of the judgment (manāṭ al-ḥukm) — even if it were stumbled upon — would require that the deity have no attachment to the essence of any human being in the manner of the soul's attachment to the body? For they say: Every soul that has attached itself to a body — the condition of its attachment is that there be between them a suitability and congruity (munāsaba wa-mulāʾama) for the sake of which the attachment occurred. And God — exalted be His name — is transcendent above anything of that sort.

Then, even if this were granted to them — that the attachment they attempted is conceivable in accordance with the philosophical opinions — they would gain no benefit from it, nor would it advance their purpose in establishing the divinity of Jesus, peace be upon him.

For the philosopher says: The soul has a governing attachment (taʿalluq tadbīrī) to the body, and that pleasure and pain occur to both by means of its attachment to it, when the sensitive faculty is affected by what is agreeable or repugnant. And it is impossible that this attachment in its entirety, along with what has been mentioned, be intended — because the occurrence of pleasures to the Essence of the Creator is impossible.

It remains that this governing relation (al-nisba al-tadbīriyya) be taken in abstraction from the occurrence of pleasures — and this too is of no avail, because the Creator is the governor (mudabbir) of every individual of the world, and to Him belongs a governing relation to every creature.

If it is said: What is meant is a relation whose effect has appeared in the breaking of customs (kharq al-ʿawāʾid) — like the reviving of the dead and other such things — then that would indicate the intended purpose.

The answer: Such a relation — by which the one characterized by it is able to perform the breaking of customs — is established for other than Jesus, peace be upon him. For they acknowledge that Moses, peace be upon him, turned the staff into a serpent.

And is the reviving of the dead anything other than the description of an inanimate thing with animality? Rather, this is more indicative of the miracle — because making what has never been characterized by life at all into a living thing is more indicative of power than restoring a thing to its former state. Then the splitting of the sea and the making of each part like a mighty mountain — these are among the wonders of miracles.
And the Torah, which they affirm as true, has testified that Moses, peace be upon him, brought forth his hand white like snow, then returned it to the color of his body.

And in the books of Kings and Judges — which are among their ancient books read in their churches — that Elijah and Elisha his disciple raised the dead. And Elijah's reviving of the widow's son is not denied among them. And the standing still of the sun for Joshua until he took the city of Jericho — these are among the marvels of miracles.

Then, how many of the prophets were prophets not sent [with a mission]? So what prevents that this relation be established for each one of them, but it did not appear due to the absence of a mission requiring the proofs issuing from it?!
A subtle point that must be noted:

The wording of the Mighty Book: {«Wa-ḍmum yadaka ilā janāḥika takhruj bayḍāʾa min ghayri sūʾ»} — "And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white without harm" (Q. 20:22). And the wording of the Torah: "Here, O you who forms, white like snow."
And the interpretation of this Hebrew expression into Arabic: "And this is your hand, leprous like snow."

The Torah explicitly stated leprosy (baraṣ), while the explicit wording of the Mighty Book states that its whiteness was "without harm" (min ghayri sūʾ). And in the heart there is a prickling of doubt about this at first glance — but the reconciliation is not difficult for the practiced and understanding one.

Its explanation: Leprosy (baraṣ) is an expression for an accident arising from a corrupted temperament (sūʾ al-mizāj), by which occurs a viscosity of phlegm that the transforming faculty (al-quwwa al-mughayyira) is too weak to convert into the color of the body. And it is known that the whiteness of Moses' hand, peace be upon him, did not arise from a corrupted temperament — because if anyone's temperament were corrupted in the manner we have described, that would occur to him; and if the transforming faculty were strengthened to convert it, then the specificity of the miracle would disappear. Rather, its whiteness was of the kind of the miraculous breaking of custom (al-muʿjiz al-khāriq). And the nature of the miraculous breaking of custom is that it be contrary to the accustomed and familiar. And to this meaning the Mighty Book alludes in His saying: "without harm" (min ghayri sūʾ) — that is, God empowered Moses to make his hand leprous without harm, and to return it to the color of his body, without a transforming faculty — so that thereby there accrues to him a specificity in the performance of the miraculous breaking of custom that is contrary to the accustomed, upon his hand.

And it is only a miracle contrary to the accustomed when one brings about the effect (al-musabbab) disjoined from its customary cause, which does not arise except from it — then expresses it by the whiteness that is among its necessary concomitants. This is a clear reconciliation.

And among what weakens their beliefs in this matter: The philosopher's principle concerning the soul and its attachment — if they are certain of its establishment, and the basis of their certainty is a good opinion of those who affirm it, while they are unable to produce its proofs — supposing that those who affirm it have invented from the hidden sciences what thought recoils from grasping, due to the obscurity of its derivation and the difficulty of its foundations. And that one whose state is such — his statements are to be deemed free from error. Then it is incumbent upon this speaker to practice taqlīd of the philosopher in that prophecies are acquired (muktasaba), that the world is eternal (qadīm) not admitting of origination and corruption (kawn wa-fasād), that the Creator does not know particulars (juzʾiyyāt), that from the One only one proceeds, that the deity of creation is a bare existence (wujūd mujarrad) with no knowledge, life, or power subsisting in His Essence — and other such things by which they have demolished the foundations of the followers of the sacred law and in which they have explicitly declared the prophets, the messengers, to be liars.

And it is a wonder that they practice taqlīd of a people who deny the conceivability of that by which the specificity of the founder of their law is established — for they explicitly state the impossibility of the formation of a child from the mere semen of his mother without the participation of a man's semen — either coagulating according to the opinion of their chief, or participating in the partiality according to the opinion of Galen.

If a speaker, driven by his partisanship and his caprice that incite him not to abandon what he has habituated, says: "What has been mentioned — the proofs have established their error in it — so they remain, in what is beyond it, upon the requirement of our opinion of them."

The answer: Whoever has appeared at times erroneous and at times correct — his statements are possible of error and correctness. And one does not resort to taqlīd of one whose state is such, in the absence of grasping the basis of his statements — while casting the statements of the followers of the sacred law behind one's back, and not deigning to rely upon the outward senses of his Book that indicate the humanity of the founder of his law — except for texts that refuse interpretation, indicating what they claim of divinity, resistant to the intellects with an evident resistance. How so, when in the Gospel there are texts explicitly stating the pure humanity of Jesus, peace be upon him, and texts witnessing that the application of divinity to him, as they claim, is impossible?
And these texts are in the most authentic of the Gospels according to them: the Gospel of John son of Zebedee.
And behold, I shall mention them text by text, clarifying the chapters inscribed therein, as a precaution against denial — because their books are not preserved in their breasts.
And before commencing their mention, it is necessary to present two principles agreed upon among the people of knowledge:

One of them: That when texts are presented — if they accord with the rational (al-maʿqūl), their outward senses are left as they are; and if they contradict the clear rational (ṣarīḥ al-maʿqūl), their interpretation (taʾwīl) is obligatory, and one must believe that their realities are not intended — in which case they must be referred to metaphor (majāz).

The second: That when evidences are mutually contradictory — some indicating the establishment of a judgment and some indicating its negation — we do not leave them in contradiction except when we have sensed from ourselves incapacity due to the impossibility of reconciliation and the prevention of making them mutually supportive upon a single meaning.
And when that is established, let us now commence the mention of the texts indicating the figurative usage (tajawwuz) in his application to himself of what suggests divinity.
And the texts indicating the figurative usage in the question of union (ittiḥād) — such as his saying:
"I and the Father are one, and whoever has seen me has seen the Father, and I am in the Father, and the Father is in me."

Then we shall follow that with the mention of the texts indicating his pure humanity, and we shall reconcile between them and the texts that stirred for them doubts — their understandings having recoiled due to their deficiency from interpreting them — so they became blind and went astray. We shall be exhaustive in clarifying them and uncovering the veil from their difficulties, to a degree with which the truth returns resplendent in appearance, manifest in luminosity.

paragraphs.text:
In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.
And through Him is my success.

The Shaykh, the Imām, the scholar, the preeminent sign, the ascetic, the ḥāfiẓ, the God-fearing, the Imām of the Shāfiʿīs in his time — Muḥyī al-Dīn Abū Zakariyyā Yaḥyā ibn Sharaf ibn Murā al-Nawawī, may Allah envelop him in His mercy and His good pleasure — said:

Praise be to Allah, Who is sanctified above any likeness to created things (al-muḥdathāt), exalted far above all deficiencies and all that is subject to change, Who is invoked by every variety of tongue and every kind of language; there is no god but He, the Creator of the earth and the heavens. I praise Him for what He has bestowed of gifts and granted of guidances. And I send blessings upon His prophets, who purified the earth from misguidances — especially upon him who was sent as the seal of the messages, supported by dazzling miracles and clear signs, the intercessor (al-mushaffaʿ) on the Appointed Time — may Allah bless him and his Family, his Companions, his wives, his progeny, and those who followed them, with an enduring blessing through the ages and the hours.

To proceed: When doubts and ambiguities appeared, and objections and obfuscations multiplied, and the doctrine of the people of caprice and partisanship spread, and tribulation from it became general throughout all regions and directions — one whose request it is obligatory to answer, and whose relief it is among the greatest of meritorious deeds to grant, asked me to compile for him the cream of the sayings of the predecessors (mutaqaddimīn) and the ultimate point upon which they relied concerning the creed regarding the letters (ḥurūf) and the sounds (aṣwāt), and what has been transmitted from them concerning that of divergent opinions, and to state explicitly what the scholars of the Sacred Law and the trustworthy transmitters of ḥadīth have adopted — following in that the methods of the later theologians (mutaʾakhkhirī al-mutakallimīn) in their investigations, proceeding according to the principles of the people of theoretical inquiry and disputation, abbreviating its expression in the clearest and most concise of phrasings — without partisanship or bias, but rather with desire to manifest the truth and to support what the Companions and the Followers — may Allah be pleased with them all — proceeded upon, and may He gather us and them in the abode of His generosity, along with all our beloved ones, our shaykhs, and our brethren. Indeed, He is the Most Generous of the generous and the Most Merciful of the merciful.

And I relate to him what has been established by transmission from the Master of the Messengers and the most noble of Allah's creation from the first to the last — Muḥammad ibn ʿAbdillāh, the Messenger of the Lord of the Worlds, may Allah bless him and all the other prophets, and the family of each, and all the righteous. So this compendium came, by the praise of Allah, as a companion for the present and a fellow-sitter for the beholder. And I have divided it — by the praise of Allah — into chapters (fuṣūl) comprising various kinds of principles and precious gems of creeds, gathered from the books of the sciences and from what I deposited from our book known as "al-Tibyān fī Ādāb Ḥamalat al-Qurʾān" and other than that. And upon Allah is my reliance, and to Him is my entrustment and my support. I have sought refuge in Allah, I have placed my trust in Allah. There is no might and no power except through Allah, the Most High, the Magnificent.
And this compendium comprises two sections:

**Section One:** Concerning what we transmit from the venerable Shaykh, the Imām, the precise scholar, the unique ḥāfiẓ — Fakhr al-Dīn Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿUthmān ibn al-Armaʾī al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — regarding what he composed in his book entitled "Ghāyat al-Marām fī Masʾalat al-Kalām."
**Section Two:** Concerning what I have set down in our book known as "al-Tibyān."

paragraphs.text: In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, and may God bless Muhammad and his family.

Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds. O God, bless Muhammad, Your servant and Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, and upon his family, his wives, and his descendants, just as You blessed Abraham and upon the family of Abraham. And bestow blessings upon Muhammad, his family, his wives, and his descendants, just as You bestowed blessings upon Abraham and the family of Abraham in the worlds. Indeed, You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.

And I bear witness that there is no god but God alone, with no partner to Him, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, whom He sent with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion, even if the polytheists detest it. To proceed:

These are principles (qawāʿid), maxims (ḍawābiṭ), important foundations (uṣūl), and sought-after objectives (maqāṣid) that the student of the [Shafiʿi] school needs—indeed, the student of knowledge in absolute terms—and none among the people of jurisprudence can dispense with their like except those who confine themselves to mere formalities.

The intended purpose of this work is to elucidate comprehensive principles, consistent maxims, to gather together analogous cases, to provide examples of branches (furūʿ) derived from a root (aṣl) or built upon it, to encompass precious scattered rulings, and to clarify the conditions of many well-known foundational matters.
I strive, God willing, in all of these to achieve clear exposition through unambiguous expressions.

And I ask God the Generous for success in completing it, preserved, beneficial, and blessed. Upon God the Generous is my reliance, to Him is my entrustment and my support. God suffices me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs. There is no might and no power except through God, the Mighty, the Wise.
**Issue 1**

The doctrine of the people of truth (ahl al-ḥaqq) is belief in divine decree (al-qadar) and affirming it, and that all occurring things—their good and their evil—are by the decree (qaḍāʾ) of God Most High and His measure (qadar).
He wills all of them entirely.
And He dislikes acts of disobedience, despite willing them, for a wisdom that He—glorified and exalted be He—knows.
Is it said that He is pleased with acts of disobedience and loves them?
On this, there are two positions among our companions, the theologians (mutakallimūn), narrated by Imām al-Ḥaramayn and others.

Imām al-Ḥaramayn said in *al-Irshād*: Among the matters on which the people of truth differed regarding the permissibility of applying [the terms]—and prohibiting their application—are love (maḥabbah) and pleasure (riḍā).

Some of our imams said: One should not absolutely state that God Most High loves acts of disobedience and is pleased with them, due to His saying: {«ولا يرضى لعباده الكفر»} (And He is not pleased with disbelief for His servants) [al-Zumar 39:7].

He said: And those of our imams who are thorough did not pay heed to the Muʿtazilites' exaggeration of this matter. Rather, they said: God Most High wills disbelief, loves it, and is pleased with it—and will (irādah), love (maḥabbah), and pleasure (riḍā) are one and the same meaning.

He said: And His saying: {«ولا يرضى لعباده الكفر»} (And He is not pleased with disbelief for His servants) means thereby the servants who are granted success (al-muwaffaqūn) to faith, and they are attributed to God Most High as an honor to them, like His saying: {«يشرب بها عباد الله»} (From which the servants of God will drink) [al-Insān 76:6]—meaning their elite, not all of them. And God knows best.
**Issue 2**
Contracts of transactions and similar matters are of four categories:

**First**: Valid (jāʾiz) from both parties—like loan (qarḍ), partnership (shirkah), agency (wakālah), deposit (wadīʿah), loan for use (ʿāriyah), profit-sharing partnership (qirāḍ), gift (hibah) before taking possession (qabḍ), reward-contract (juʿālah), and similar matters. The juʿālah is valid from both parties, even after commencement of the work; however, if the worker rescinds, he gets nothing, and if the offeror rescinds during the work, he is obligated to pay the wage for what was done.

**Second**: Binding (lāzim) from both parties—like sale (bayʿ) after the option period, salam (advance payment sale), compromise (ṣulḥ), transfer of debt (ḥawālah), sharecropping (musāqāh), lease (ijārah), gift to a non-heir after taking possession, khulʿ (divorce by redemption), and similar matters.

**Third**: Binding from one party and valid from the other—like pledge (rahn), which is binding after possession with respect to the pledgor, but valid with respect to the pledgee; and kitābah (contract of manumission) is binding with respect to the master, but not with respect to the slave. And surety (ḍamān) and guaranty (kafālah) are valid from the side of the one for whom the guarantee is made (al-maḍmūn lahu), but not from the side of the guarantor.

**Fourth**: Binding from one party with a difference of opinion regarding the other—namely marriage (nikāḥ): it is binding from the woman's side, and regarding the husband there are two views:
- One: it is valid from his side due to his power to divorce.
- The more correct (aṣaḥḥ) of the two: it is binding like sale, and his power to divorce is not a rescission (faskh); rather, it is merely disposal over what he owns, and it does not follow from that that it is non-binding—just as the buyer owns the right to sell the purchased item.
And archery competition (musābaqah), according to one view, is valid, and on the more apparent view, it is binding.
**Issue 3**

When a sale is concluded, rescission (faskh) cannot affect it except through one of seven causes:
1. Option of the session (khiyār al-majlis)
2. Option of stipulation (khiyār al-sharṭ)
3. Option of defect (khiyār al-ʿayb)
4. Option of discrepancy (khiyār al-khilaf)—such as when he stipulates that [the slave] be a scribe, and he turns out to be non-literate
5. Mutual rescission (iqālah)
6. Mutual oath-taking (taḥāluf)
7. Destruction of the sold item before possession (qabḍ)

paragraphs.text:
Ibn Abbas and Ibn Masud said: "The three categories are all in this Muhammadan nation (Ummah Muhammadia), and all of them will be in Paradise (Jannah)." This was also stated by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

Aisha (radiyallahu anha) said: "They will all enter Paradise (Jannah)." Ka'b al-Ahbar stated: "Their shoulders are leveled by the Lord of the Ka'bah, and they will differ according to their deeds."

Abu Ishaq al-Sab'i reported: "As for what I heard sixty years ago, all of them will be saved (naj)." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab recited this verse, then said: "The Messenger of Allah (sallallahu alaihi wasallam) said: 'Our foremost (saabiquna) is foremost, our moderate (muqtasiduna) is saved (naj), and our wrongdoer (zalimuna) is forgiven.'"

There is no doubt that relying on this generalization is misleading unless one adheres to the traditions of the guided leaders (imams). Maruf al-Karkhi said: "Seeking Paradise without action is a sin among sins, waiting for intercession without reason is a form of illusion, and hoping for mercy from the One who is not obeyed is foolishness and ignorance."

God willing, I will mention in this book the etiquette of these three categories mentioned by Allah, and discuss them across nine stations, some higher than others. I will start with the ninth station, then descend to the next until the first, then ascend from it to the second, then to the third, and so forth to the ninth station. I begin and end with it, completing Allah's blessing upon me with His grace. In the descent, I mention the intended concisely, and in the ascent, elaborately and extensively, following the author of "Adab al-Deen" al-Mawardi (radiyallahu anh), who said: "Hearts are comforted by diverse arts." He recounted a story about Al-Ma'mun, who said: "He would move from one place to another in his palace, and he recited the words of Abu al-Atahiya: 'The soul is not rectified when it turns away, except by moving from one state to another.'"

The reason for placing the foremost last and the wrongdoer first is to indicate the sequence of entering Paradise: the foremost enters first, being a separator between him and Paradise, as the entry is realized after them. Thus, delaying the foremost in this context is an advancement, and advancing the wrongdoer is a delay. This contemplation may yield other perspectives as reflected in the text, so contemplate it (Ruuh al-Ma'aani: 16/402).

Footnotes:
(1) Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in "Al-Ba'th wal-Nushur" (61), and al-Baghawi in "Ma'alim at-Tanzil" (981).
(2) From "Nihayat al-Arab fi Funun al-Adab" 10/199.

paragraphs.text:
### | أصول الإيمان

### | ابتداء قاعدة الاعتقاد الذي هو أصل الإيمان

اعلم أيها السلطان أنك مخلوق ولك خالق وهو خالق العالم وجميع ما في
العالم، وأنه لا شريك له، فرد لا مثل له، كان في الأزل وليس لكونه زوال،
ويكون مع الأبد وليس لبقائه فناء، وجوده في الأبد والأزل وما للعدم إليه
سبيل، وهو موجود بذاته، وكل أحد محتاج إليه وليس له إلى أحد احتياج، وجوده
به ووجود كل شيء به.

### | الأصل الثاني في تنزيه الخالق تعالى

إعلم أن البارئ، تعالى ذكره، ليس له صورة ولا مثل، وأنه لا ينزل ولا يحل
في قالب، وأنه تعالى منزه عن الكيف والكم، وعن لماذا وكم، وأنه لا يشبه
شيئا ولا يشبه شيء، وكلما يخطر في الوهم والخيال والفكر من التخيل والتمثيل
والتكيف فانه منزه عن ذلك، لأن ذلك من صفات المخلوقين وهو خالقها فلا يوصف
بها، وأنه تعالى جده ليس في مكان ولا على مكان، فإن المكان لا يحصره، وكل
ما في العالم فإنه تحت عرشه، وعرشه تحت قدرته وتسخيره، وأنه قبل العرش كان
فترها عن المكان وليس العرش بحامل له بل العرش وحملته يحملهم لطفه وقدرته،
واستواؤه على العرش كما قال، وعلى الوجه الذي قال وبالمعنى الذي أراد،
استواء منزها عن الاستقرار والمماسة والتمكن والحلول والانتقال، وهو سبحانه
فوق العرش وفوق كل شيء إلى تخوم الثرى، وهو مع ذلك قريب من كل موجود، وهو
أقرب الى البعيد
والقريب من حبل الوريد، وهوعلى كل شيء قدير وشهيد، فعال لما يريد لا يزال
في نعوت الجمال، وصفات الجلال، منزها عن الزوال والانتقال، مستعينا عن
زيادة الاستكمال، وأنه منزه عن الحاجة إلى المكان قبل خلقه العرش وبعد خلقه
العرش، وأنه متصف بالصفة التي كان عليها في الأزل، ولا سبيل إلى التغير
والانقلاب إلى صفاته، وهو سبحانه مقدس عن صفات المخلوقين ومنزه عنهم، وهو
في الدنيا معلوم وفي الآخرة مرئي كما نعلمه ي الدنيا بلا مثل ولا شبيه، لأن
تلك الرؤية لا تشابه رؤية الدنيا، ليس كمثله شيء وهو السميع البصير.

### | الأصل الثالث في القدرة

وأنه تعالى على كل شيء قدير وملكه في نهاية الكمال، ولا سبيل إلى العجز
والنقصان بل ما شاء وما يشاء يفعل، وأن السموات السبع والأرضين السبع
والكرسي والعرش في قبضة قدرته وتحت قهره وتسخيره ومشيئته، وهو مالك لا ملك
إلا ملكه، تعالى عما يقول الظالمون علوا كبيرا.

### | الأصل الرابع في العلم

وأنه تعالى عالم بكل معلوم وعلمه محيط بكل شيء، فليس شيء في العلا إلى
الثرى إلا قد أحاط به علمه لأن الأشياء جميعها بعلمه ظهرت وبإرادته خلقها
وبقدرته كونها، وأنه تعالى يعلم عدة رمال القفار، وقطرات الأمطار، وورق
الأشجار، وغوامض الأفكار، وما دارت عليه الرياح والهواء في علمه ظاهر مثل
عدد نجوم السماء. وأن جميع ما في العالم بإرادته ومشيئته وليس شيء من قليل
أو كثير، صغير أو كبير، خير أو شر، نفع أو
ضر، زيادة أو نقصان، راحة أو تعب، صحة أو صب، إلا بحكمه وتدبيره، ومشيئته
وتقديره. لو اجتمع الأنس والجن والملائكة والشياطين على أن يحركوا في
العالم ذرة أو يسكنوها أو ينقصوا منها أو يزيدوا فيها بغير إرادته وحوله
وقوته لعجزوا عن ذلك ولم يقدروا، وما شاء الله كان وما لا يشاء لا يكون،
ولا ترد مشيئته ومهما كان ويكون أو هو كائن فإنه بتدبيره وأمره وتسخيره.

### | الأصل الخامس والسادس في أنه سميع بصير

وكما أنه عالم بجميع المعلومات فإنه سميع لكل مسموع، بصير لكل مبصر، وأنه
بسمع واحد وبصر واحد يرى دبيب النملة في الليلة المظلمة، ولا يخفى عن سمعه
صوت الدود تحت أطباق الأرض، وأن سمعه ليس بأذن وبصره ليس بعين. وكما أن
علمه لا يصدر عن فكرة ففعله بغير آلة وعدة يقول للشيء كن فيكون.

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: خلق (khalaqa)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To create, to bring into existence from nothing; to measure, to proportion. The Creator (al-Khāliq) is the One who originates existence.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Creation (khalq) is bringing a thing into being according to a determined measure and wisdom, whether from nothing or from something. Applied to God, it denotes origination without precedent model.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for God's act of bringing into being; metaphorical (majāz) when attributed to creatures who merely transform.
- Root: وحد (waḥada)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To be one, unique, without second. The One (al-Wāḥid) is that which has no counterpart.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Divine unity (tawḥīd) negates all multiplicity, composition, and division from God. He is One in essence, with no partner in divinity.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal oneness of essence versus metaphorical oneness of kind or species.
- Root: قدم (qadima)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To precede, to be first, to be ancient. Pre-eternity (azal) is that which has no beginning.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Eternity (qidam) is an attribute of God alone, signifying His existence without temporal origin. His attributes are eternal as He is eternal.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal precedence in time versus metaphorical precedence in rank or honor.
- Root: عرش (ʿarsha)
 * Lisan / Ayn: The Throne; a roofed structure; the dominion of a king. The Throne of God is His supreme creation.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): The Throne (ʿarsh) is the greatest of created bodies, encompassing all of creation. God's istiwāʾ (establishing Himself) upon it is an act of His, the modality of which is unknown.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: a physical throne. Metaphorical: "استوى على عرشه إذا ملك" — establishing upon the throne means assuming dominion and sovereignty.
- Root: علم (ʿalima)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To know, to perceive, to be aware. Knowledge (ʿilm) is the perception of a thing as it truly is.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Knowledge is the apprehension of a thing's reality. God's knowledge is not acquired from things but is the cause of their existence. It encompasses all things, universal and particular, without temporal succession.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: knowledge as perception. Metaphorical: "ما علمت بخبرك" — I did not know of your news, meaning I had no awareness.
- Root: سمع (samiʿa)
 * Lisan / Ayn: To hear. Hearing (samʿ) is the perception of sound.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): God's hearing is an eternal attribute by which He perceives all audible things, without ear or organ. It is not a physical faculty.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal hearing with ears; metaphorical for God's perfect perception without instrument.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الفصل بين الجار والمجرور (Prepositional Interposition) — The rule governing the separation of a preposition from its object by an intervening clause, as in "وهو مع ذلك قريب من كل موجود" where the adverbial phrase is interposed for emphasis and rhetorical effect.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
### | The Foundations of Faith
### | The Beginning of the Creedal Principle Which Is the Root of Faith

Know, O King, that you are a created being (makhliūq) and that you have a Creator, and He is the Creator of the world and of everything within the world. He has no partner; He is One (fard), with no likeness to Him. He was in pre-eternity (azal) and His existence has no cessation; He will be with eternity (abad) and His permanence has no annihilation. His existence is in pre-eternity and eternity, and non-existence has no path to Him. He is existent by His own essence (mawjūd bi-dhātihi), and every single one is in need of Him, while He has no need of anyone. His existence is through Himself, and the existence of everything is through Him.
### | The Second Principle: On Transcending the Creator, Exalted Is His Remembrance

Know that the Originator (al-Bāriʾ), exalted is His remembrance, has no form (ṣūrah) and no likeness. He does not descend, nor does He indwell any mold or receptacle. Exalted is He above quality (kayf) and quantity (kam), above "why" (limādhā) and "how much" (kam). He resembles nothing, and nothing resembles Him. Whatever occurs to the mind, imagination, and thought — of imagining, likening, or qualifying — He is transcendent above all of that, because those are attributes of created beings, and He is their Creator, so He is not described by them. He, exalted is His majesty, is not in a place nor upon a place, for place cannot encompass Him. Everything in the world is beneath His Throne (ʿarsh), and His Throne is beneath His power and subjugation. He was before the Throne, and He was then free of place. The Throne does not carry Him; rather, the Throne and its bearers are carried by His gentleness and power. His "establishing Himself upon the Throne" (istiwāʾ) is as He said, in the manner He said, and with the meaning He intended — an establishing (istiwāʾ) transcendent above settling, touching, resting, indwelling, and moving. He, glorified be He, is above the Throne and above everything, to the depths of the earth (tharā). Yet with all that, He is near to every existent, and He is nearer to the distant and the near than the jugular vein (ḥabl al-warīd). He is over all things Omnipotent and Witness. He does what He wills. He never ceases to possess the attributes of beauty (jamāl) and the qualities of majesty (jalāl), transcendent above passing away and moving, free from any increase of perfection. He is transcendent above any need for place, before the creation of the Throne and after the creation of the Throne. He is described with the very attribute He had in pre-eternity, and there is no path for change or alteration to reach His attributes. He, glorified be He, is sanctified above the attributes of created beings and transcendent above them. In this world He is known, and in the Hereafter He will be seen — just as we know Him in this world — without likeness and without similitude, because that vision does not resemble the vision of this world. {«لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ»} — "There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing" (Q. 42:11).
### | The Third Principle: On Divine Power (qudrah)

He, exalted be He, is Omnipotent over all things, and His dominion is at the utmost perfection. There is no path for incapacity or deficiency to reach Him. Rather, what He wills — and what He wills — He does. The seven heavens and the seven earths, the Footstool (kursī), and the Throne (ʿarsh) are all within the grasp of His power, under His domination, subjugation, and will. He is the Owner, and there is no owner except His ownership. Exalted is He above what the wrongdoers say, with a great exaltation.
### | The Fourth Principle: On Divine Knowledge (ʿilm)

He, exalted be He, is Knowing of everything knowable, and His knowledge encompasses all things. There is nothing from the heights above to the depths below (tharā) except that His knowledge has encompassed it, because all things appeared through His knowledge, He created them by His will, and they came into being by His power. He, exalted be He, knows the count of the sands of the deserts, the drops of the rains, the leaves of the trees, the hidden subtleties of thoughts, and whatever the winds and the air have carried — all is manifest in His knowledge, like the number of the stars of heaven. Everything in the world is by His will and volition. There is nothing — little or much, small or great, good or evil, benefit or harm, increase or decrease, rest or fatigue, health or sickness — except by His decree and governance, His will and determination. If all of mankind, jinn, angels, and devils were to gather to move a single atom in the world, or to still it, or to decrease it, or to increase it, without His will, His power, and His strength, they would be incapable of that and would not be able to do it. What God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. His will is not repelled. Whatever was, and is, or is coming to be, it is by His governance, His command, and His subjugation.
### | The Fifth and Sixth Principles: On His Being Hearing and Seeing

And just as He is Knowing of all knowable things, so He is Hearing of everything audible, and Seeing of everything visible. With a single hearing and a single sight, He sees the crawling of the ant in the darkest night, and the sound of the worm beneath the layers of the earth is not hidden from His hearing. His hearing is not by an ear, and His sight is not by an eye. And just as His knowledge does not arise from reflection, so His act is without instrument or tool. He says to a thing "Be!" and it comes to be (yakūn).

# 
# بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
# فاتحة الكتاب
# الحمد لله الفتاح المنان، ذي الطول والفضل والإحسان، الذي من علينا

بالإيمان، وفضل ديننا على سائر الأديان، ومحا بحبيبه وخليله وعبده ورسوله

محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم عبادة الأوثان وخصه بالمعجزة والسنن المستمرة على

تعاقب الأزمان، صلى الله عليه وعلى سائر النبيين وآل كل ما اختلف الملوان

وما تكررت حكمه وذكره وتعاقب الجديدان.
# " أما بعد " فإن علم الحديث من أفضل القرب إلى رب العالمين، وكيف لا يكون

وهو بيان طريق خير الخلق وأكرم الأولين والآخرين وهذا كتاب اختصرته من كتاب

" الإرشاد " الذي اختصرته من علوم الحديث للشيخ الإمام الحافظ المتقن

المحقق أبي عمرو عثمان بن عبد الرحمن المعروف بابن الصلاح رضي الله عنه،

أبالغ فيه في الاختصار إن شاء الله تعالى من غير إخلال بالمقصود، وأحرص على

إيضاح العبارة، وعلى الله الكريم الاعتماد وإليه التفويض والاستناد.
# 
# أقسام الحديث

# الحديث: صحيح - وحسن - وضعيف.

paragraphs.text: 5-Pillar Lexicographical Apparatus (AynEngine AI v4.0 Sovereign Edition)

- Root: حمد (Ḥ-M-D)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes praise, commendation, and acknowledgment of beneficence; al-Ayn records it as foundational to expressions of gratitude.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Theological nuance: praise (ḥamd) is rendered to God alone as the ultimate bestower of grace, distinguishing it from mere thanks (shukr) which may be directed to created agents.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah): "Aḥmad Allāha bi-jamīʿi maḥāmidih" — praising God with all His praiseworthy attributes; metaphorical (majāz): "Aḥmadtu al-arḍ" — finding a land agreeable to inhabit, extended to approval of what is good.
- Root: فتح (F-T-Ḥ)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes opening, unveiling, and removing obstruction; al-Ayn links it to physical and abstract disclosure.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Twofold: (1) perceptible by sight — opening a door or lock; (2) perceptible by insight (baṣīrah) — removing distress, granting victory, or illuminating understanding; God as "al-Fattāḥ" is the Opener of all gates of mercy and judgment.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: opening a physical barrier; metaphorical: "Fataḥa Allāhu ʿalayhi" — God granted him victory or provision; "iftitāḥ" as seeking divine succor against enemies.
- Root: حدث (Ḥ-D-TH)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes origination, newness, and temporal occurrence; al-Ayn records it as signifying bringing something into being after non-existence.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "Al-ḥudūth: the coming-to-be of a thing after it was not" — whether accident or substance; "al-muḥdath" is that which is originated; God alone originates substances (jawāhir), and "ḥadīth" (speech/report) is so named for its temporal novelty.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: a recent event or novel occurrence; metaphorical: "Ṣārū aḥādīth" — they became the talk of the people; "muḥaddath" — one inspired with correct intuition, as if spoken to by truth.
- Root: سلم (S-L-M)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes safety, peace, and freedom from defect; al-Ayn records it as the opposite of faultiness.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Theological nuance: "al-salāmah" — soundness from internal and external corruption; a "ṣaḥīḥ" (sound) hadith is one whose chain and text are free from defect.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: physical safety; metaphorical: soundness of argument or report — a ḥadīth ṣaḥīḥ is one whose chain is unbroken and whose narrators are upright and precise.
- Sibawayh Rule: Bāb al-faṣl bayna al-jār wa-al-majrūr (Prepositional Interposition) — governing the permissibility of separating a prepositional phrase from its governed noun when the intervening element is semantically complete, as in the author's periodic constructions; also applied here to the balanced tripartite division (taqsīm) of ḥadīth into ṣaḥīḥ, ḥasan, and ḍaʿīf, which follows the canonical syntactic pattern of exhaustive enumeration (istiqrāʾ).
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful.
The Opening of the Book.

Praise be to God, the Opener (al-Fattāḥ), the Bountiful Giver (al-Mannān), Possessor of abundance, grace, and beneficence — He who bestowed upon us the blessing of faith, and favored our religion above all other religions, and through His Beloved, His Intimate Friend, His Servant, and His Messenger Muḥammad — may God bless him and grant him peace — obliterated the worship of idols, and singled him out with the miracle and with the Sunnahs that continue unbroken across the succession of ages. May God bless him, and all the other Prophets, and the families of all, as long as the two contrasting things differ, and as long as His judgments and remembrance are repeated, and the two new things (night and day) follow one another in succession.

"To proceed": Verily, the science of ḥadīth is among the most virtuous acts of drawing near to the Lord of the Worlds. And how could it not be so, for it is the elucidation of the path of the best of creation and the most noble of the first and the last? And this book — I have abridged it from the book "al-Irshād," which I in turn abridged from "ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth" of the Shaykh, the Imām, the ḥāfiẓ, the precise and verifying scholar Abū ʿAmr ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, known as Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ — may God be pleased with him. I strive in it to achieve extreme concision, God Almighty willing, without any deficiency in the intended purpose, and I am eager to clarify the expression. Upon God the Generous is my reliance, and to Him is the delegation of affairs and the seeking of support.
The Divisions of Ḥadīth.
The ḥadīth is: sound (ṣaḥīḥ) — and fair (ḥasan) — and weak (ḍaʿīf).

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم- وبه ثقتي:
أما بعد حمد الله، والصلاة على محمد خير خلقه وآله، فإني رأيت مباحث
النصارى «1» المتعلقة بعقائدهم؛ ضعيفة المباني، واهية القوى، وعرة المسالك،
يقضي المتأمل من عقول جنحت إليها غاية عجبه، ولا يقف من تعقيدها على اليسير
من إربه، لا يعولون فيها إلا على التقليد المحض، عاضين [بالنواجذ] على
ظواهر أطلقها الأولون، ولم ينهض بإيضاح مشكلها- لقصورهم- الآخرون، ظانين
بأن ذلك هو الشرع الذي شرعه لهم عيسى عليه السلام، معتذرين عن اعتقادها/
بما ورد من نصوص يعتقدون أنها قاهرة للكفر، غير قابلة للتأويل «2»، وأن
صرفها عن ظواهرها عسيرة «3». وهم في ذلك طائفتان:
- طائفة- وهم الأكثر- لم يمارسوا شيئا من العلوم التي يقف بها الناظر على
استحالة المستحيل، فيجزم باستحالة وجوده، وإيجاب الواجب، فينفي عدم وقوعه
وإمكان الممكن، فلا محالا لازما لطرفي وجوده وعدمه، بل PageV01P025
ارتسمت في أذهانهم صور منذ صغرهم، واستمرت بهم الغباوة «1» إلى أن صار ذلك
فيهم ملكة.
فهذه الطائفة برؤها من دائها عسير/.
وطائفة لهم أدنى معقول، وقد ألموا بيسير من العلوم، فتجدهم ناكصين عن هذا
المعتقد، لا يسامحون أفكارهم بمقاربته، يعولون تارة على تقليد الفيلسوف «2»
في مسألة الاتحاد لإعظامهم ما يؤدي إليه من هدم قواعد تظافر على ثبوتها
صرائح العقول، فارين من هذه المعضلة إلى التقليد المحض، معتقدين أن
الفيلسوف قد حاول العلوم الخفية، فأبانها جلية مبرهنة. ظانين بأن من هذا
شأنه جدير بأن يعول على أقواله، وتقلد «3» في المعتقدات! فلذلك ينفصلون عن

مسألة الاتحاد «4» بردها إلى مسألة تعلق النفس بالجسد/.
ولو راجع هؤلاء المساكين عقولهم وتركوا الهوى والتعصب، لعلموا أنهم قد
نكبوا عن محجة الصواب، وأخطئوا سبيل الحق لوجوه:
أحدها: أنهم إن جعلوا ذلك من قبيل القياس، فغلط، لأن القياس «5»:
«رد فرع إلى أصل بعلة جامعة هي مناط الحكم».
