paragraphs.text: ### | Introduction That Encompasses the Purpose of the Book, Its Arrangement, and Its Divisions

I say: Know that if you seek the condition of the valid syllogism (qiyās) and the valid definition (ḥadd), and the pointing out of the sources of error in them, you have undertaken the combination of two matters, for they are the bond of all the sciences. For the sciences consist in the apprehension of simple essences (al-dhawāt al-mufradah)—such as your knowledge of the meaning of "body," "motion," "world," "originated," and "eternal," and the rest of the simples—and in the apprehension of the relation (nisbah) of these simples to one another by negation and affirmation. For you know first the meaning of the word "world," which is a simple matter, and the meaning of the word "originated," and the meaning of the word "eternal," these also being two simple matters. Then you relate a simple to a simple by negation, as you relate eternity to the world by negation, saying: "The world is not eternal"; and you relate the originated to it by affirmation, saying: "The world is originated." It is this latter kind to which falsification and verification (takdhīb wa taṣdīq) attach. As for the former, no verification or falsification enters into it, for verification and falsification are impossible in the simples. Rather, they attach only to the statement (khabar), and no statement is composed except of two simples: a subject described (mawṣūf) and a description (waṣf). So when the description is related to the described by negation or affirmation, there is no objection to agreeing upon expressing these two kinds by two different expressions. For it is fitting that different matters have different words, since words are counterparts of meanings, and it is fitting that they correspond to meaning. Let us therefore name the first "cognition" (maʿrifah) and the second "knowledge" (ʿilm), following therein the saying of the grammarians: that cognition (maʿrifah) extends to one object, for you say "I cognized Zayd" (ʿaraftu Zaydan), while opinion (ẓann) extends to two objects, for you say "I opined Zayd to be learned" (ẓanantu Zaydan ʿāliman). Knowledge (ʿilm) also extends to two objects, for you say "I knew Zayd to be just" (ʿalimtu Zaydan ʿadlan); so it belongs to the class of opinion, not to the class of cognition. This is the linguistic usage, even though the expression of the people of theoretical inquiry (ahl al-naẓar) deviates from it in using one in place of the other. Now that this convention is established, we say: the known apprehensions are confined to cognition and knowledge. And every knowledge to which verification attaches necessarily has two cognitions preceding it; for he who does not know the simple—how should he know the composite? And he who does not understand the meaning of "world" and the meaning of "originated"—how should he know that the world is originated? Cognition is of two kinds: primary, which is not sought by inquiry, like the simples apprehended by sense; and sought (maṭlūb), whose name indicates something summary and undetailed, whose detail is then sought. Likewise, knowledge is divided into primary and sought. The sought from cognition is captured only by definition (ḥadd), and the sought from knowledge, to which verification or falsification attaches, is captured only by the proof (ḥujjah) and demonstration (burhān), which is the syllogism (qiyās). It is as though the seeker of the syllogism and the definition is the seeker of the instrument by which all the sciences and cognitions are captured. Let our book then be two parts: a part that is the locus of the syllogism, and a part that is the locus of the definition.

paragraphs.text:
### | مقدمة تحصر مقصود الكتاب وترتيبه وأقسامه

اعلم أنك إن التمست شرط القياس الصحيح والحد الصحيح والتنبيه على مثارات
الغلط فيها وقفت للجمع بين الأمرين، فإنها رباط العلوم كلها. فإن العلوم
إدراك الذوات المفردة كعلمك بمعنى الجسم والحركة والعالم والحادث والقديم
وسائر المفردات وإدراك نسبة هذه المفردات بعضها إلى البعض بالنفي والإثبات.
فإنك تعلم أولا معنى لفظ العالم وهو أمر مفرد ومعنى لفظ الحادث ومعنى لفظ
القديم وهما أيضا أمران مفردان، ثم تنسب مفردا إلى مفرد بالنفي كما تنسب
القدم إلى العالم بالنفي، فتقول ليس العالم قديما وتنسب الحادث إليه
بالإثبات فتقول العالم حادث والضرب الأخير هو الذي يتطرق إليه التكذيب
والتصديق، فأما الأول فلا يدخله تصديق وتكذيب، إذ يستحيل التصديق والتكذيب
في المفردات بل إنما يتطرق ذلك إلى الخبر ولا ينتظم خبر إلا بمفردين موصوف
ووصف، فإذا نسب الوصف إلى الموصوف بنفي أو إثبات فلا بأس أن يصطلح على
التعبير عن هذين الضربين بعبارتين مختلفتين. فإن حق الأمور المختلفة أن
تختلف ألفاظها إذ الألفاظ مثل المعاني فحقها أن يحاذي بها المعنى فلنسم
الأول معرفة ولنسم الثاني علما، متأسين فيه بقول النحاة: إن المعرفة تتعدى
إلى مفعول واحد إذ تقول عرفت زيدا، والظن يتعدى إلى مفعولين إذ تقول ظننت
زيدا عالما. والعلم أيضا يتعدى إلى مفعولين فتقول علمت زيدا عدلا، فهو من

باب الظن لا من باب المعرفة. هذا هو الوضع اللغوي وإن كانت عبارة أهل النظر
بهما تخالفه في استعمال أحدهما بدلا عن الآخر. فإذا استقر هذا الاصطلاح
فنقول الإدراكات المعلومة تنحصر في المعرفة والعلم. وكل علم يتطرق إليه
التصديق فمن ضرورته أن تتقدم عليه معرفتان، فإن من لا يعلم المفرد كيف يعلم
المركب، ومن لا يفهم معنى العالم ومعنى الحادث كيف يعلم أن العالم حادث.
والمعرفة قسمان: أولى وهو الذي لا يطلب بالبحث كالمفردات المدركة بالحس،
ومطلوب وهو الذي يدل اسمه منه على أمر جملي غير مفصل فيطلب تفصيله. وكذلك
العلم ينقسم إلى أولي وإلى مطلوب. فالمطلوب من المعرفة لا يقتنص إلا بالحد
والمطلوب من العلم الذي يتطرق إليه التصديق أو التكذيب لا يقتنص إلا بالحجة
والبرهان وهو القياس؛ وكأن طالب القياس والحد طالب الآلة التي بها تقتنص
العلوم والمعارف كلها. فليكن كتابنا قسمين قسم هو محل القياس وقسم هو محل
الحد.

- Root: علم (ʿ-l-m)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core root denotes the impression/trace by which a thing is known; also the signpost (ʿalam) by which one is guided.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "العلم: إدراك الشيء بحقيقته" — apprehension of a thing by its reality; two kinds: (1) apprehension of the essence of a thing (transitive to one object), and (2) judgment upon a thing affirming or denying something of it (transitive to two objects).
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: "ما علمت بخبرك: ما شعرت به" — to be aware/informed. Distinguishes the technical usage of the logicians from the linguistic.
- Root: عرف (ʿ-r-f)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Cognate with ʿarf (scent/patience) and the mane of a horse; maʿrifah is the apprehension of a thing's trace/sign.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Maʿrifah is the apprehension of the simple essence after reflection or by direct encounter, contrasted with ʿilm as judgment.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal usage: "عرفته:" — to know a person directly; grammarians note it takes one object.
- Root: نسب (n-s-b)
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "النسب والنسبة: اشتراك من جهة أحد الأبوين" — relation/attribution; used in logic for the copula of predication.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: kinship/lineage; Metaphorical (Majaz): "بين الشيئين مناسبة وتناسب" — the relation between two things, as in the relation of predicate to subject.
- Root: طرق (ṭ-r-q)
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): "الطريق: السبيل الذي يطرق بالأرجل" — the path beaten by feet; metaphorically, every course a man pursues in action.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal: to strike/beat (iron with a hammer); Metaphorical: "طرقني الخيال" — a phantom visited me at night; hence the "striking" of the mind toward a conclusion.
- Sibawayh Rule: باب الحصر والتقييد بإنما (Restriction & Focused Predication) — The use of "إنما" to restrict the predicate to the subject alone, as in "لا يقتنص إلا بالحد" (is captured only by definition), establishing exclusive instrumentality.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
### | Introduction That Encompasses the Purpose of the Book, Its Arrangement, and Its Divisions

I say: Know that if you seek the condition of the valid syllogism (qiyās) and the valid definition (ḥadd), and the pointing out of the sources of error in them, you have undertaken the combination of two matters, for they are the bond of all the sciences. For the sciences consist in the apprehension of simple essences (al-dhawāt al-mufradah)—such as your knowledge of the meaning of "body," "motion," "world," "originated," and "eternal," and the rest of the simples—and in the apprehension of the relation (nisbah) of these simples to one another by negation and affirmation. For you know first the meaning of the word "world," which is a simple matter, and the meaning of the word "originated," and the meaning of the word "eternal," these also being two simple matters. Then you relate a simple to a simple by negation, as you relate eternity to the world by negation, saying: "The world is not eternal"; and you relate the originated to it by affirmation, saying: "The world is originated." It is this latter kind to which falsification and verification (takdhīb wa taṣdīq) attach. As for the former, no verification or falsification enters into it, for verification and falsification are impossible in the simples. Rather, they attach only to the statement (khabar), and no statement is composed except of two simples: a subject described (mawṣūf) and a description (waṣf). So when the description is related to the described by negation or affirmation, there is no objection to agreeing upon expressing these two kinds by two different expressions. For it is fitting that different matters have different words, since words are counterparts of meanings, and it is fitting that they correspond to meaning. Let us therefore name the first "cognition" (maʿrifah) and the second "knowledge" (ʿilm), following therein the saying of the grammarians: that cognition (maʿrifah) extends to one object, for you say "I cognized Zayd" (ʿaraftu Zaydan), while opinion (ẓann) extends to two objects, for you say "I opined Zayd to be learned" (ẓanantu Zaydan ʿāliman). Knowledge (ʿilm) also extends to two objects, for you say "I knew Zayd to be just" (ʿalimtu Zaydan ʿadlan); so it belongs to the class of opinion, not to the class of cognition. This is the linguistic usage, even though the expression of the people of theoretical inquiry (ahl al-naẓar) deviates from it in using one in place of the other. Now that this convention is established, we say: the known apprehensions are confined to cognition and knowledge. And every knowledge to which verification attaches necessarily has two cognitions preceding it; for he who does not know the simple—how should he know the composite? And he who does not understand the meaning of "world" and the meaning of "originated"—how should he know that the world is originated? Cognition is of two kinds: primary, which is not sought by inquiry, like the simples apprehended by sense; and sought (maṭlūb), whose name indicates something summary and undetailed, whose detail is then sought. Likewise, knowledge is divided into primary and sought. The sought from cognition is captured only by definition (ḥadd), and the sought from knowledge, to which verification or falsification attaches, is captured only by the proof (ḥujjah) and demonstration (burhān), which is the syllogism (qiyās). It is as though the seeker of the syllogism and the definition is the seeker of the instrument by which all the sciences and cognitions are captured. Let our book then be two parts: a part that is the locus of the syllogism, and a part that is the locus of the definition.

paragraphs.text: ### Section One: On Preliminary Matters, Containing Four Chapters
**Chapter One: On Pure Waters and Their Purifying Power**

Purifying power (ṭahūriyyah) is exclusive to water among all other liquids. As for the purification of ritual impurity (ḥadath), this is by consensus (ijmāʿ). As for the purification of filth (khabath), it is [affirmed] according to al-Shāfiʿī, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah — may God be pleased with them both.

The exclusivity of purifying power to water is either a matter of devotional prescription (taʿabbud) whose meaning is not rationally comprehensible, or it may be rationally explained by water's being distinguished by a certain kind of subtlety (luṭf) and fineness, and by a uniqueness in composition in which no other liquid shares — and this latter is the more probable (al-aqrab).
### Then waters are of three categories:

**First Category:** That which remains upon the characteristics of its original creation — this is purifying (ṭahūr). Included under this are well-water, sea-water, and everything that springs from the earth or descends from the sky. This is water truly absolute (al-māʾ al-muṭlaq ḥaqqan).

Nothing is excepted from this definition save water already used (al-mustaʿmal) in [removing] ritual impurity (ḥadath). For according to al-Shāfiʿī it is pure (ṭāhir) but not purifying (ṭahūr); according to Mālik — may God be pleased with him — it is purifying, and this is also a position [narrated] of al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him; and according to Abū Ḥanīfah — may God be pleased with him — it is impure (najis).

That it is pure is evidenced by the fact that the early generations (al-awwalūn) were cautious of it [in some contexts], and that it did not come into contact with anything impure. That its purifying power is nullified is evidenced by the fact that the early generations, when water was scarce, did not collect used water to employ it a second time.

Then the nullification of purifying power is considered in terms of two meanings: one is the performance of worship through it; the other is the transfer of prohibition (al-manʿ) to it. If both meanings are absent, it is purifying — like water used in a fourth washing [of the limbs]. If one of the two meanings is present without the other, there are two positions (wajhān) — like water used in a second washing or in renewal (tajdīd), for in that case no transfer of prohibition has occurred.

As for water used by a dhimmī woman until she becomes lawful for her Muslim husband, the transfer of prohibition has occurred, but the performance of worship has not — unless we do not require her to repeat [the purification] if she embraces Islam.
### Four Subsidiary Questions (Furūʿ)

**First:** Is water used in [removing] ḥadath permissible for use in [removing] filth (khabath)? There are two positions. One: yes, because water has two powers and only one has been exhausted. The second: no, because that power is, in legal effect, a single indivisible attribute — just as water used in ḥadath is not used for major impurity (janābah), and it is not said that this power remains.

**Second:** If used water is collected until it reaches two qullas (approximately 200 liters), there are two positions. One: it reverts to being purifying, just as impure water, when collected and reaching two qullas [becomes pure], and because quantity repels the legal effect of use — so when it supervenes, it severs that effect, like impurity. The second: it does not revert to being purifying, because the legal effect of impurity is dropped when [the impurity] is submerged and consumed by the abundance of water, whereas use has nullified the power of water itself, so it becomes like rose-water and other liquids.

**Third:** If a person in major impurity (junub) immerses himself in a small quantity of water and then exits, his major impurity is removed, and the water becomes used. Al-Khaḍirī, one of our companions, said: it is not removed, because it became used upon the contact of the first part [of his body] with it. This is an error, for the legal effect of use is only established upon separation (al-infiṣāl), and is not established while [the water] is still passing over the limbs.

**Fourth:** If one with minor impurity inserts his hand into a vessel after washing his face, having intended the removal of ḥadath, the water becomes used when the hand separates from the water. The proper method is that he intend scooping (al-ightirāf) and withdrawal, so that it does not become used. If he is heedless of the intention to remove ḥadath and of the intention to scoop, the well-known position (al-mashhūr) is that it becomes used. It may be argued that the posture of scooping diverts the contact to that direction by force of custom, so it does not become used.

**Second Category:** That which has changed from its original characteristics, but by a slight change that does not strip from it the name of absolute water — this is purifying. Such as water changed by prolonged standing, or changed by a small amount of saffron that shows the slightest appearance — this is purifying according to the [correct] school (al-madhhab). Likewise, water changed by what adjoins it, such as aloes-wood, ambergris, and solid camphor. Likewise, water changed by what is difficult to guard against, such as earth, arsenic, and lime — things from which water in its place cannot be free — for the name of absolute water is not negated by these. Likewise, heated water and sun-heated water (al-mushammas).

Yes, there is disapproval (karāhah) regarding sun-heated water from the standpoint of medicine, because the heat of the sun separates from the vessel particles that rise above the water like vapor (habāʾ); when these contact the body, they cause leprosy (baraṣ).

Then they differed as to whether this disapproval is specific to hot regions, to metallic vessels, and to the intention of sun-heating. This is a difference without basis, for there is no disapproval except from the standpoint of medicine, and the harm from the medical standpoint is specific to excessive heat, is not specific to the existence of intention, and is specific to metallic substances (al-jawāhir al-munṭabiʿah). Thus it does not apply to wood, earthenware, or leather. And perhaps it does not apply to gold and silver among metals, due to the purity of their substance.

والطهورية
مختصة بالماء من بين سائر المائعات أما فى طهارة الحدث
فبالإجماع وأما فى طهارة الخبث فعند الشافعي خلافا لأبي حنيفة راضي
الله عنهما
واختصاص الطهورية به إما تعبد لا يعقل معناه وإما أن يعلل باختصاص الماء
بنوع من اللطافة والرقة وتفرد فى التركيب لا يشاركه فيها سائر المائعات وهو
الأقرب

### | ثم المياه ثلاثة أقسام

القسم الأول ما بقي على أوصاف خلقته فهو الطهور
فيدخل تحته ماء البئر وماء البحر وكل ما نبع من الأرض أو نزل من السماء
وهو الماء المطلق حقا
ولا يستثنى عن هذا الحد إلا الماء المستعمل فى الحدث فإنه عند الشافعي
طاهر غير طهور وعند مالك رضي الله عنه طهور وهو قول
للشافعي رضي الله عنه وعند أبي حنيفة رضي الله عنه نجس
ويدل على طهارته قلة احتراز الأولين منه وأنه لم يلق محلا نجسا ويدل على
سقوط طهوريته أن الأولين فى إعواز الماء لم يجمعوا الماء المستعمل
ليستعملوه ثانيا
ثم سقوط الطهورية باعتبار معنيين أحدهما تأدي العبادة به والآخر انتقال
المنع إليه فإن انتفى المعنيان فطهور كالمستعمل فى الكرة الرابعة وإن وجد
أحد
المعنيين دون الثاني فوجهان كالمستعمل فى الكرة الثانية أو فى التجديد
فإنه لم يوجد
انتقال المنع إليه
والذى استعملته الذمية حتى تحل لزوجها المسلم فإنه وجد انتقال المنع
ولم يوجد تأدي العبادة إلا إذا لم نوجب الإعادة عليها إذا أسلمت

### |

### | فروع أربعة


الأول المستعمل فى الحدث هل يستعمل فى الخبث فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لأن للماء قوتين ولم يستوف إلا إحداهما
والثاني لا لأن تلك القوة فى حكم خصلة واحدة لا تتجزأ وهذا كما أن
المستعمل فى الحدث لا يستعمل فى الجنابة ولا يقال إن هذه القوة باقية
الثاني إذا جمع الماء المستعمل حتى بلغ قلتين فوجهان
أحدهما يعود طهورا كالماء النجس إذا جمع فصار قلتين ولأن الكثرة
تدفع حكم الاستعمال فإذا طرأت تقطع حكمه كالنجاسة
والثاني لا يعود طهورا لأن حكم النجاسة يسقط إذا انغمرت واستهلكت بكثرة
الماء وأن الإستعمال أبطل قوة الماء فيلحق بماء الورد وسائر المائعات
الثالث إذا انغمس الجنب فى ماء قليل وخرج ارتفعت جنابته وصار الماء
مستعملا
وقال الخضري من أصحابنا لا ترتفع لأنه صار مستعملا بملاقاة أول جزء منه
وهو غلط إذ حكم الإستعمال إنما يثبت بالإنفصال ولا يثبت
حالة تردده على الأعضاء
الرابع المحدث إذا أدخل يده فى الإناء بعد غسل الوجه وكان قد نوى رفع
الحدث صار الماء مستعملا إذا انفصلت اليد من الماء
فطريقة أن يقصد الاغتراف والتنحية حتى لا يصير مستعملا فإن غفل عن نية
رفع الحدث وعن قصد الاغتراف فالمشهور أنه يصير مستعملا
ويتجه أن يقال هيئة الاغتراف صارفة للملاقاة إلى هذه الجهة بحكم العادة
فلا يصير مستعملا القسم الثاني فيما تغير عن وصف خلقته ولكن تغيرا يسيرا لا
يزايله اسم الماء المطلق فهو طهور كالماء المتغير بطول المكث أو المتغير
بزعفران يسير ظهر عليه أدنى ظهور فإنه طهور على المذهب
وكذلك المتغير بما يجاوره كالعود والعنبر والكافور الصلب وكذا المتغير
بما يتعذر صون الماء عنه كالتراب والزرنيخ والنورة وما لا يخلو الماء عنه
فى مقره فإن اسم الماء المطلق لا ينسلب به وكذلك المسخن والمشمس
نعم فى المشمس كراهية من جهة
الطب
لأن حمي الشمس يفصل من الإناء أجزاء تعلو الماء كالهباء فإذا لاقى البدن
أورث البرص
ثم اختلفوا فى أن هذه الكراهية هل تختص بالبلاد الحارة وبالأواني
المنطبعة وبقصد التشميس
وهذا خلاف لا وجه له لأنه لا كراهية إلا من جهة الطب والمحذور من جهة
الطب يختص بالحرارة المفرطة ولا يختص بوجود القصد ويختص بالجواهر المنطبعة
فلا يجري فى الخشب والخزف والجلد ولعله لا يجري فى الذهب والفضة من
المنطبعات لصفاء جوهريهما

- Root: ط-ه-ر (ṭ-h-r)
 * Lisan / Ayn: Core meaning of cleanliness and purity, both physical and ritual; ṭahūr denotes that which is itself pure and renders other things pure.
 * Al-Raghib (Mufradat): Ṭahārah in the legal context signifies removal of ritual impurity (ḥadath) and filth (khabath), a divine prescription distinguishing worship acts.
 * Al-Zamakhshari (Asas): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage applies to water as the primordial purifying agent; metaphorical (majāz) extension to other liquids is rejected in legal rulings.
- Sibawayh Rule: Restriction & Focused Predication (باب الحصر والتقييد بإنما) — The exclusivity of purifying power to water is expressed through restrictive syntax, emphasizing a legal singularity.
English Scholarly Translation (Verbatim Authorial Voice)
### Section One: On Preliminary Matters, Containing Four Chapters
**Chapter One: On Pure Waters and Their Purifying Power**

Purifying power (ṭahūriyyah) is exclusive to water among all other liquids. As for the purification of ritual impurity (ḥadath), this is by consensus (ijmāʿ). As for the purification of filth (khabath), it is [affirmed] according to al-Shāfiʿī, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah — may God be pleased with them both.

The exclusivity of purifying power to water is either a matter of devotional prescription (taʿabbud) whose meaning is not rationally comprehensible, or it may be rationally explained by water's being distinguished by a certain kind of subtlety (luṭf) and fineness, and by a uniqueness in composition in which no other liquid shares — and this latter is the more probable (al-aqrab).
### Then waters are of three categories:

**First Category:** That which remains upon the characteristics of its original creation — this is purifying (ṭahūr). Included under this are well-water, sea-water, and everything that springs from the earth or descends from the sky. This is water truly absolute (al-māʾ al-muṭlaq ḥaqqan).

Nothing is excepted from this definition save water already used (al-mustaʿmal) in [removing] ritual impurity (ḥadath). For according to al-Shāfiʿī it is pure (ṭāhir) but not purifying (ṭahūr); according to Mālik — may God be pleased with him — it is purifying, and this is also a position [narrated] of al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him; and according to Abū Ḥanīfah — may God be pleased with him — it is impure (najis).

That it is pure is evidenced by the fact that the early generations (al-awwalūn) were cautious of it [in some contexts], and that it did not come into contact with anything impure. That its purifying power is nullified is evidenced by the fact that the early generations, when water was scarce, did not collect used water to employ it a second time.

Then the nullification of purifying power is considered in terms of two meanings: one is the performance of worship through it; the other is the transfer of prohibition (al-manʿ) to it. If both meanings are absent, it is purifying — like water used in a fourth washing [of the limbs]. If one of the two meanings is present without the other, there are two positions (wajhān) — like water used in a second washing or in renewal (tajdīd), for in that case no transfer of prohibition has occurred.

As for water used by a dhimmī woman until she becomes lawful for her Muslim husband, the transfer of prohibition has occurred, but the performance of worship has not — unless we do not require her to repeat [the purification] if she embraces Islam.
### Four Subsidiary Questions (Furūʿ)

**First:** Is water used in [removing] ḥadath permissible for use in [removing] filth (khabath)? There are two positions. One: yes, because water has two powers and only one has been exhausted. The second: no, because that power is, in legal effect, a single indivisible attribute — just as water used in ḥadath is not used for major impurity (janābah), and it is not said that this power remains.

**Second:** If used water is collected until it reaches two qullas (approximately 200 liters), there are two positions. One: it reverts to being purifying, just as impure water, when collected and reaching two qullas [becomes pure], and because quantity repels the legal effect of use — so when it supervenes, it severs that effect, like impurity. The second: it does not revert to being purifying, because the legal effect of impurity is dropped when [the impurity] is submerged and consumed by the abundance of water, whereas use has nullified the power of water itself, so it becomes like rose-water and other liquids.

**Third:** If a person in major impurity (junub) immerses himself in a small quantity of water and then exits, his major impurity is removed, and the water becomes used. Al-Khaḍirī, one of our companions, said: it is not removed, because it became used upon the contact of the first part [of his body] with it. This is an error, for the legal effect of use is only established upon separation (al-infiṣāl), and is not established while [the water] is still passing over the limbs.

**Fourth:** If one with minor impurity inserts his hand into a vessel after washing his face, having intended the removal of ḥadath, the water becomes used when the hand separates from the water. The proper method is that he intend scooping (al-ightirāf) and withdrawal, so that it does not become used. If he is heedless of the intention to remove ḥadath and of the intention to scoop, the well-known position (al-mashhūr) is that it becomes used. It may be argued that the posture of scooping diverts the contact to that direction by force of custom, so it does not become used.

**Second Category:** That which has changed from its original characteristics, but by a slight change that does not strip from it the name of absolute water — this is purifying. Such as water changed by prolonged standing, or changed by a small amount of saffron that shows the slightest appearance — this is purifying according to the [correct] school (al-madhhab). Likewise, water changed by what adjoins it, such as aloes-wood, ambergris, and solid camphor. Likewise, water changed by what is difficult to guard against, such as earth, arsenic, and lime — things from which water in its place cannot be free — for the name of absolute water is not negated by these. Likewise, heated water and sun-heated water (al-mushammas).

Yes, there is disapproval (karāhah) regarding sun-heated water from the standpoint of medicine, because the heat of the sun separates from the vessel particles that rise above the water like vapor (habāʾ); when these contact the body, they cause leprosy (baraṣ).

Then they differed as to whether this disapproval is specific to hot regions, to metallic vessels, and to the intention of sun-heating. This is a difference without basis, for there is no disapproval except from the standpoint of medicine, and the harm from the medical standpoint is specific to excessive heat, is not specific to the existence of intention, and is specific to metallic substances (al-jawāhir al-munṭabiʿah). Thus it does not apply to wood, earthenware, or leather. And perhaps it does not apply to gold and silver among metals, due to the purity of their substance.
